Meaning, "yellow head." The original bearer was a "two spirit" and thus the name may be considered gender neutral.

Fictional name meant to be derived from Chinese 火 (huǒ) meaning "fire, flame" or 敖 (áo) meaning "proud, arrogant" combined with 災 (zāi) meaning "disaster, catastrophe" or 載 (zài) meaning "to carry". This is the name of the main antagonist of the show 'Avatar: The Last Airbender'.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عزير (see Uzayr).
Transferred use of the surname Ozanam. This name is given after blessed Antoine-Frédéric Ozanam, the founder of the Catholic order Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.
Medieval Polish diminutive of Ożanna and Zuzanna.
Variant of Osanne. Ozanne-Anne Achon was the wife of Pierre Tremblay, one of the first settlers of Nouvelle-France ("New France" in English), the area colonized by France in North America.
From Serbian озарити (ozariti) or озарен (ozaren) meaning "to make radiant" and "radiant" respectively.
Derived from öz meaning "self" and ay meaning "moon".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عزير (see Uzayr).

A combination of the Turkish root öz meaning "true, genuine, self" and çay meaning "stream, river, valley". It carries the serene meaning of "a true stream" or "one's own valley". Crucially, the element çay (çaj) is a native Turkic word for a natural brook and should not be confused with the Persian/Mandarin homophone for tea. It symbolizes an unstoppable, crystal-clear current of authenticity carving its own path.

Derived from the Turkish root öz meaning "essence, self, soul, core", combined with the diminutive/equative suffix -ce. The name metaphorically symbolizes "a pure, genuine soul" or "one who is true to their own nature," a gentle reflection of absolute sincerity.
Derived from öz meaning "self" and dal meaning "catch, capture".
Derived from öz meaning "self" and delik meaning "wish, desire".
Probably means "pure iron" and is related to Demir. It's also a surname and a village in Turkey.
Czech and Slovak form of Hosea.
Transferred use of the surname Ozell.
Means "strong" in Hebrew. This name appears on two characters in the Bible.
From Turkish öz meaning "essence, kernel, self" and er meaning "man, hero, brave".
From the Hebrew word for "helper" or "strength".
Possibly a combination of the given name Özge and the word can, meaning "soul, life".
Means "characteristic" or "appropriate, incidental, particular" in Turkish.
From Turkish öz meaning "essence, self" and gül meaning "rose".

Means "original, unique" in Turkish, from öz "self" and -gün, a form of the adjective-forming suffix -gin (whose vowel shifts to correspond to the last vowel of the preceding root word).Both males and females use this name. Compare and see also Öz, Özge.
From the Turkish özgün meaning "original, unique" and ay meaning "moon".
From the name of the Mao celebration ozho koso meaning "feast of merit", ultimately from ozhe meaning "rice beer".
Means "woman of the green glade", or "green prairie woman", deriving in part from the Ojibwe element ikwe ("woman").
The name originates from Eastern part of Nigeria from the Igbo speaking states. Predominatly from Imo state.Name means "message from God" or "Gods message" 'Ozi - message Chi - God'
Directly taken from Hungarian őzike "doe; fawn".
Derived from the Uzbek o'z meaning "oneself" and boy meaning "rich, wealthy".
Creole variant of Ozille and possibly related to Ozella.
Certainly related to Ozile and possibly to Ozella.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Osiris.
Most likely a Creole form of Osithe.
Derived from the Uzbek o'z meaning "oneself" and jon meaning "soul, spirit".
Princess Ozma of Oz is a fictional character created by L. Frank Baum.
Possibly means "my hearing" from Hebrew אֹ֫זֶן ('ozen) "ear". In the Old Testament this name belonged to a son of Gad.
Means "free" in Uzbek and Tajik, of Persian origin.
Derived from Uzbek ozoda meaning "neat, tidy" and gul meaning "rose, flower".
From the given name Ozod and the work bek, a military title.
Means " let what has happened before not happen again" in Igbo.
Means "monkey" in Nahuatl, the eleventh day-sign of the tonalpohualli.
Ozon is the German word for ozone, the gas occurring in the high atmosphere and protecting against too much of UV radiation from the sun.The name was officially admitted in Berlin in 2013.
Amharic name, said to come from a biblical name meaning "strength of the Lord" (in which case it is partly from Hebrew ’az "force, strength" and a relative of Oz 2).
Possibly derived from a Hebrew word for "helper".

Derived from the passive voice of an older Slavic verb ozreti se meaning "to look, glance".This is the name of three mountains, two in Serbia and one in Bosnia and Herzegovina.-------------------------------------From Serbian озарити/ozariti meaning "to make radiant".

Form of Azriel used in the Douay-Rheims Bible (1582-1610) and the Clementine Vulgate (1592). The latter was the official Bible of the Roman Catholic Church for nearly four centuries: from the year it was published until 1979.Please note that in both Bibles, the form Ozriel only appears in verse 27:19 of 1 Chronicles. In other verses, either Esriel or Ezriel is used.Lastly, in the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament) Ozriel occurs only in verse 12:7 of 1 Chronicles, where it is a form of Azarel.

A compound name formed from the Turkish elements öz meaning "essence, core" and su meaning "water". It translates literally to "sap", "fruit juice", or "essential fluid". The name metaphorically symbolizes the persona as "the liquid of life", the ultimate vital energy, and the pure, unblemished nourishment of the soul.
Possibly from the Turkish öz meaning "gist, core", "self", or a dated word meaning "creek, small river" and tün meaning "night".

Derived from the Turkish root öz meaning "essence, soul, core", combined with the first-person possessive suffix -m. It carries the poetic and deep meaning of "my own self", "my very essence", or "my solution". It symbolizes an intimate, irreplaceable inner warmth and personal truth.

Derived from the Turkish root öz ("essence, core, soul") paired with the second-person possessive or nominalizing suffix -ün. It translates beautifully to "your true essence", "your origin", or "your unique soul". It serves as a poetic, symbolic mirror reflecting one's deepest inner light and ancestral heritage.
A name who came from the town of the same name.

This particular spelling of the name was popularised through the poem 'Ozymandias' by Percy Bysshe Shelley.It is a variant of the Ancient Greek name for Pharaoh Ramesses II, Osymandyas (Greek: Ὀσυμανδύας).The recent revival of the name is probably triggered by a villain named Ozymandias in 'Watchmen' (TV series).
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Pái.
Means "takes the wrong weapon or coup" in Siksika.
Skolt Sami cognate of Pelagia or Paula.

Paaliaq is a satellite of Saturn. It was named after a giant from the Inuit Mythology. This name was used by writer Michael Kusugak for the fictional shaman in the book 'The Curse of the Shaman' (2006).
Son of Pahoran¹, Nephite rebel (c. 52 BC).
Means "life belongs to him" in Egyptian.
Variant transcription of Naarai, using the p to transcribe the נ (n). This form is used in the New Living Translation of the Bible.
Estonian adaption and contraction of Bernhard.
From Greenlandic paarnaq ‎meaning “berry" and -nnguaq, endearing diminutive suffix.
Directly from paarnaq "berry, fruit", specially crowberry.
Name meaning friend to all origins unknown
Originally a diminutive of Päären, now used as a given name in its own right.

Short form of masculine names that are derived from Greek and Latin pascha meaning "Easter" as well as "Passover", such as Paschalis, Pascharius and Paschasius and their Dutch forms.This name was once quite common, especially in the Middle Ages (during which time it was spelled as Paes). These days it is extinct, but it still survives in several patronymic surnames, such as Paas and Paes.

Derived from the Georgian adjective პატარა (patara) meaning "little, small" as well as "young" (sometimes in reference to a child). Also compare the Georgian adjective პაწაწინა (patsatsina) meaning "wee, tiny".Notable Georgian bearers of this name include prince Paata of Kartli (1720-1765), the poet Paata Shamugia (b. 1983) and the opera singer Paata Burchuladze (b. 1955).
Means "all things will pass in this world" in Ijaw.
Bengali and Assamese form of Pavana.
Fabricius It is believed that the name arrived to the Philippine Islands through Malaysians of the same name.

Feminine diminutive of Pablo, sometimes used as a diminutive of the related name Paula. Known bearers of this name were Pablita Velarde (1918-2006), a Pueblo (Native American) artist and painter from New Mexico, United States, and Pablita Abeyta (1953-2017), a Navajo (Native American) activist and sculptor who was also from New Mexico.

From the Roman cognomen Pacatianus of unknown origin. This was the name of the 3rd-Century Roman usurper during the time of Philip the Arab whose full name was Tiberius Claudius Marinus Pacatianus. The 4th-century Roman governor of Britain is also known by this name in the English language.
Derived from Italian pace "peace", ultimately from Latin Pax.
Possibly a variant of Paciencia.A bearer of this name is Pacencia Laurel, the 3rd First Lady of the Philippines.
Pachacamac is the creator god in Inca Mythology. His name derives From Pacha Kamaq, meaning “Earth Shaker”.
From the Aymara pacha meaning "epoch, time and space, cosmos" and possibly lliju lliju meaning "flash of lightning, vivid light".
Directly taken from the Caló word pachandra meaning "Easter". This name is used as the Caló form of Pascua and Pascuala.
From the Aymara pacha meaning "epoch, time and space, cosmos" and qhana meaning "clear, evident".
From the Aymara pacha meaning "epoch, time and space, cosmos" and qura meaning "herb, medicinal plant".
Alternate transcription of Thai พชร (see Phachara).

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai พัชรี (see Phatchari) or ปาจรีย์ (see Pachari).
Derived from Sanskrit प्राचार्य (pracharya) meaning "teacher of teachers".
From the Aymara pacha meaning "epoch, time and space, cosmos" and wara wara meaning "star".

This ancient surname dates back to Roman times cerca 92 BC, from a Roman general named Vivio Pacieco (a descendant of Pro-consul Lucio Viminio Pacieco who served Julius Caesar during the conquest of of what is now Portugal and Spain). It is generally accepted that the Pro-consul settled in this area and that one of the general's descendants, a Don Diego López Pacheco, known as "el grande" was the first bearer of the Pacheco name in Spain.
Derived from the Polish word for "scent" or "aroma"; compare Polish pachnąć "to smell of". This was used as a feminine given name in medieval Poland.
The name of a sweet smelling flower.
King of Nephite dissenters in land of Zarahemla (c. 61 BC)
Recorded in Lithuania in the 16th-century on a Muslim Tatar woman, most likely a diminutive form of Fatima.
English and Provençal form of Pacianus.

Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of Pacianus. This name was borne by the Filipino general and revolutionary Paciano Rizal (1851-1930), the brother of physician and writer Dr. José Rizal (who is himself considered the greatest national hero of the Philippines).

Late Latin name, a derivative of Latin pax "peace" (genitive pacis). This name was borne by a 4th-century Spanish saint, a bishop of Barcelona who is mentioned in Jerome's De Viris Illustribus (which is dedicated to Saint Pacianus's son, Nummius Aemilianus Dexter).
Derived from Jèrriais pâcienche "patience" (ultimately from Latin patientia via Old French pacience). This is a newly coined name, intended as a Jèrriais equivalent of Patience.
Feminine form of Pacificus. Originally it was used in Renaissance Italy, but nowadays it's more popular in Kenya.
Masculine version of Pacífica meaning "peaceful", from the Latin name Pacificus.
Mostly a diminutive of Pacita. This could also be used as a diminutive of Pacencia, Paciana, and other names containing pac.
Masculine diminutive of Pace, which is derived from Latin pax meaning "peace".
Likely derived from the Latin word "pax", meaning "peace". Pacius was used as a Roman family name (cognomen), often among lower or middle-class citizens.
Possibly means "medicine snake", from Nahuatl patli "medicine, herb; poison" and coatl "snake, serpent; twin".
French and Vietnamese form of Pachomius.
Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Pachomius.
Italian, Galician and Spanish form of Pachomius.
Latinized form of Pakor via its Greek form Pakoros. This name was borne by two kings of Parthia.
Means "order, perfect" in Caló. This name is used as the Caló form of Perfecto.

Son of Pahoran fifth Nephite chief judge (c. 52 BC), brother of Pahoran, the son of Pahoran, and a contender for the judgement-seat over the people of Nephi. After the death of his brother Pahoran, Pacumeni acquired the judgement-seat, but he didn't keep it long; for the land was being invaded by Lamanites, and Coriantumr, a large and mighty man and descendant of Zarahemla and dissenter from the Nephites, caught Pacumeni in his attempt to run away, and killed him at the city walls. Helaman, son of Helaman, succeeded him as chief judge.
Possibly coming from the Old English word pad, meaning "toad".
Dialectal form of Pàdraig used on the Isle of Arran.

Alternate transcription of Thai เผด็จ (see Phadet).
Derived from Egyptian pꜣ-dj-pꜣ-rꜥ meaning "he who is given by Ra" or "the gift of the sun god (Ra)". Older form of Potiphar.
Meaning "One Who Lives in a Lotus".
Meaning "One Who Was Born from Lotus".
Means "lotus bud" from Sanskrit पद्म (padma) "lotus" and कलिका (kalikā) "bud" (source of Hindi कली (kalī)). It is allegedly one of the names of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
Means "one with lotus-like eyes" from Sanskrit पद्म (padma) meaning "lotus" and अक्षि (akshi) meaning "eye".
Meaning "One Who Was Born in a Lotus House".

Name of Sanskrit origin, predominantly common in India. It is derived from the words "Padma", meaning "lotus flower", and "Man", which refers to the mind or self. A notable bearer is Padman Surasena, the Sri Lankan Chief of Justice.

Means "shining lotus" from Sanskrit पद्म (padma) meaning "lotus" and प्रभा (prabhā) meaning "to shine, light, radiance". In Jain tradition this is the name of the sixth of the 24 tirthankaras (enlightened spiritual teachers).

Means "lotus-born" from Sanskrit पद्म (padma) meaning "lotus" and सम्भव (sambhava) meaning "being, coming together, birth, origin". This was the name of a legendary 8th-century Buddhist teacher and mystic credited with introducing tantric Buddhism (Vajrayana) to Tibet.
Possibly derived from Padma, meaning "lotus" in Sanskrit. Padmé Amidala is a fictional character in the 'Star Wars' saga, created by George Lucas.
Means "lotus" in Javanese, ultimately from Sanskrit पद्म (padma).

Means "the highest lotus" from Sanskrit पद्म (padma) meaning "lotus" combined with उत्तर (uttara) meaning "upper, higher, better, superior". In Buddhist tradition this is the name of the 13th of the 27 buddhas preceding Siddhartha Gautama, known in Pali as Padumuttara.
Anglicised form of Pádraig or Pàdraig.
Alternate spelling and pronunciation of Pádraigín.
Variant of Padrut, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Romansh form of Peter, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Catalan form of Padua. This name is always given as the compound name Antoni de Pàdua, never alone.

From name of the Italian city of Padua, after saint Anthony of Padua. This name is always given as the compound names Antonio de Padua and Francisco de Padua (after Francis of Paola), but never Padua alone.
Alternate transcription of Thai ผดุง (see Phadung).
Alternate transcription of Thai ผดุงเดช (see Phadungdet).
Alternate transcription of Thai ผดุงเดช (see Phadungdet).
Alternate transcription of Thai ผดุงเดช (see Phadungdet).

Means "destitute, hardness" interpreted as "humble" in Tongan.
Latinized form of Paieon, which is the Epic Greek form of Paian. Paian or Paean was the physician of the gods in Greek mythology.
The name of several characters in Greek mythology, including a son of Poseidon, a son of Endymion and eponymous founder of Paeonia, and a son of Ares.
Means "one hundred ridges" in Maori, it also means "meeting place of the dead". Paerau is a river in New Zealand's South Island.
Coptic form of the Egyptian name Paiset.
Hellenized form of Paesi, ultimately derived from Egyptian Paiset.

Means "silk and golden water", in part from the Thai ผ้าแพ (pâa pae "silk fabric, silk cloth") and สีทอง (sĕe tong "(to be) gold"). This is the name of the current Prime Minister of Thailand, who is also known by her nickname Ung Ing.
Modern Greek form of Paphnoutios (see Paphnutius).
Variant transcription of Pafnutiy. A known bearer of this name was Pafnuty Chebyshev (1821-1894), a Russian mathematician.
Modern Greek form of Pausanias. A known bearer of this name was the Greek army officer and politician Pafsanias Katsotas (1896-1991).
Son of the brother of Jared.

From Latin paganus meaning "rustic, rural" and later "heathen", which was often given to children whose baptism had been postponed or adults whose religious zeal was lacking. An Anglo-Norman bearer was Sir Pain or Pagan fitzJohn (died 1137), one of the English king Henry I's "new men". In Thomas Hardy's novel 'Tess of the d'Urbervilles' (1891) Sir Pagan d'Urberville is the founder of the d'Urberville and Durbeyfield families, of which the eponymous Tess Durbeyfield is a member.

Diminutive of Pagano. A known bearer of this name was the Italian politician Paganello "Nello" de' Pannocchieschi (ca. 1248-after 1322), a leader of the Guelphs who allegedly ordered a servant to murder his first wife, Pia de' Tolomei. (Dante alluded to the story in his 13th-century poem the Divine Comedy, in which the narrator briefly meets Pia.)
Ligurian and Milanese Lombard form of Paganino.
Milanese Lombard feminine form of Paganin.
Diminutive of Pagano, as it contains the Italian masculine diminutive suffix -ino.
Derived from Italian pagano meaning "pagan, heathen", which ultimately comes from Latin paganus (see Pagan).
The name Pageral comes from the Filipino word ‘Pag-iral’ which literally means ‘Existence’
Transferred use of the surname Pagés.

Means "encounter with God" or "event of God" in Hebrew, derived from Hebrew paga "to encounter, to meet, to approach" combined with el "God". In the bible, this is the name of a man from the tribe of Asher.
Alternate transcription of Khmer បញ្ញា (see Panha).

Possibly means "Yahweh acts", derived from Hebrew פָּעַל (paʿal) meaning "to do, to act" combined with יָהּ (yah) referring to the Hebrew God. This is the name of an angel belonging to the order of the Thrones. He is one of the 72 angels bearing the explicit name of God (the Shem HaMephorash), as interpreted by some Christian Kabbalists.

Means "governer of Moab, prefect of Moab" from Hebrew פַּחַת (pāḥaṯ) which comes from Akkadian 𒉺𒄩𒌅 (pāḫātu), which means "district" or "governorate" and the biblical place name and personal name Moab which is a derivative of אָב (ʾav) meaning "father". Pahath-moab was the ancestor of a Judahite clan that returned from the Babylonian Exile and assisted in rebuilding Jerusalem. (Book of Ezra 2:6; 8:4; 10:30; Book of Nehemiah 3:11, 7:11, 10:14).
Ancient Egyptian masculine name meaning "servant of the god".
Older Azerbaijani form of the medieval Persian name Pahlavan (see Pahlavon). The modern form is Pəhlivan.

Tajik and Uzbek form of the medieval Persian name Pahlavan, which was derived from the Persian noun پهلوان (pahlavan) meaning "hero, paladin, champion".A notable bearer of this name was the Persian Sufi philosopher, poet and renowned wrestler Pahlavan Mahmud (1247-1326), who is known as Pahlavon Mahmud in Tajik and Uzbek. He spent most of his life in what is now Uzbekistan, eventually passing away in the city of Khiva, where he was also buried. He posthumously became the patron saint of the city and a grand mausoleum has since been built around his tomb, which still exists to this day and is an important piece of architecture.
Combination of Pahlavon with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".

Modern Azerbaijani form of the medieval Persian name Pahlavan (see Pahlavon). The older form is Pəhləvan.A notable bearer of this name is Pəhlivan Fərzəliyev (1958-1992), an Azerbaijani soldier who lost his life during the Nagorno-Karabakh War (1988-1994). He was posthumously awarded the title of National Hero of Azerbaijan, in recognition of his bravery and achievements.
Of uncertain meaning. This was the original Paiute name of the war leader known to the English-speaking world as Chief Paulina (died 1867).
Alternate transcription of Russian Пахо́м (Pakhom), which is a variant form of Pakhomiy. This was the name of the main character in Leo Tolstoy's short story "How Much Land Does A Man Need?" (1886).
Croatian and Serbian form of Pachomius.
From Egyptian pꜣ-ḥr meaning "the one of Horus", derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with the name of the god Horus.
Various characters in the Book of Mormon.
Old Norse byname, Old Norse pái meaning "peafowl".

Derived from Ancient Greek παιάν (paian) meaning "paean, solemn chant, war song, hymn" and/or the related παιών (paeon) meaning "doctor, physician". This was the name of the physician of the gods in Greek mythology, later becoming an epithet of Apollo, Asclepius, and sometimes Helios.

Diminutive of Pádraig, utilising the diminutive suffix -ín.
Combination of the given name Paige and suffix lyn.
Derived from the obsolete Latvian word paija "toy". This is the name of a character in the play Maija un Paija by Anna Brigadere.

In Maori legend, Paikea is the name assumed by Kahutia-te-rangi because he was assisted by humpback whales (paikea) to survive an attempt on his life by his half-brother Ruatapu. New Zealand writer Witi Ihimaera based his novel Whale Rider on this myth which was turned into a movie in 2002.Note: While the Paikea of the legend is a boy, the protagonist (of the same name) of Ihimaera's novel and the movie is a girl.
Malayalam form of Paul or Biblical Paulos
Alternate transcription of Thai ไพลิน (see Phailin).
From Javanese Paing referring to the second day of the Javanese five-day week combined with the masculine suffix -min.

Of uncertain origin and meaning. One theory connects this name to Finnish and Estonian paimen "shepherd". However, since there are no other Livonian names with this root recorded, some modern-day academics doubt this derivation. They rather see a link to Estonian paimendama "to guard; to protect".

Likely from Hebrew פַּעֲמֹן (paʿamon) meaning "bell", specifically referring to the tinkling sound of a bell. This is the name of a demon who appears in many works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown), the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer and the Dictionnaire Infernal (1818) by French occultist Jacques Collin de Plancy. It is also borne by the (female) deuteragonist of the 2020 video game Genshin Impact, who was named after the spirit.
Means "agile runner" in Nahuatl, from paina "to run fast".
From Javanese Paing referring to the second day of the Javanese five-day week combined with the feminine suffix -nem.
Transferred use of the surname Painter.
Alternate transcription of Thai ไพรัช (see Phairat).

From Egyptian pꜣ-js.t meaning "the one of Isis", derived from pꜣ "the aforementioned; the; he of" combined with the name of the goddess Isis.

Georgian form of Païsios as well as an alternate transcription of Russian Паисий (see Paisiy).A known bearer of this name was Paisi Kaysarov (1783-1844), a Russian general who served during the Napoleonic Wars.
Latinized form of Pishoy via its hellenized form Païsios. This is the name of several saints, including Saint Paisius Velichkovsky (1722-1794).
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Paisius.
Combination of Paisley and the popular name suffix lyn. Also compare Aislynn.

Means "link, union, relationship, oath" in Persian.
The Finnish goddess of the sun, who is associated with silver, silver yarn and beauty. Her name is derived from päivä meaning "day" and an old poetic term for the sun, and the feminine ending -tar.
Finnish form of Peivas as well as a direct derivation from Finnish päivä "day". While this name is exclusively masculine today, up until the 1940s it was also occasionally used as a feminine name.

Diminutive of Pavel, Pavla, and Pavlina.

Derived from Hmong paj meaning "flower" and hnub meaning "sun".
Derived from Hmong paj meaning "flower" and ntaub meaning "cloth", ultimately referring to a kind of flowery embroidery.
Croatian and Serbian form of Paisius.
Derived from Albanian pajtim "accord, accordance; placation, conciliation".
Derived from Hmong paj meaning "flower" and tshiab meaning "new".
Greenlandic name meaning "oarsman", "rowing one" (in a kayak).
From the Aymara paka meaning "eagle" and wara wara meaning "star".
The Hong Kong Romanization form of Bozhi.
Alternate transcription of Thai ภักดี (see Phakdi).
From the Kurdish pak meaning "immaculate" and dil meaning "heart".
Pakhangba is the supreme God of the Meitei tradition as well as Manipuri mythology that is used as a heraldic emblem in Manipur.
Means "descended from god Pakhangba" in Meitei.
Means "she who scratches" in Ancient Egyptian. This was the name of a lion-headed war goddess.

From Egyptian pꜣ-ꜥẖm meaning "he of the (holy) falcon," derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with ꜥẖm "falcon" or "cultic image of a falcon or god". The falcon was the symbol of the Egyptian god Horus, so one could say that this name essentially means "he who belongs to Horus."
Alternate transcription of Russian Пахомий and Ukrainian Пахомій (see Pakhomiy).
Russian and Ukrainian form of Pachomios.
Variant transcription of Pakhomiy. A known bearer of this name was the Russian revolutionary Pakhomy Andreyushkin (1865-1887).

Means "fine weather" in Maori. This name is a personal name and a surname. This was the name of a Waikato Chief, and of Paki Whara, a Ngati Tama Elder who in the 1800s gathered information on the Chatham Islands which contributed to the invasion of Chatham Islands.
Derived from Persian پاکیزه (pākize) meaning "clean, pure, chaste".
Derived from Persian پاکیزه (pâkize) meaning "tidy, neat, clean".
Pakku means the word, "パック" (pack). Also the name is used in the show, "Avatar: The Last Airbender".

Rapa Nui form of Pachomius, a Catholic saint. This was the name of Pakomio Maori Ure Kino, the husband of prophetess Angata Veri Tahi Hare Koho (1853-1915), Roman Catholic religious leaders in Rapa Nui. This is not only a first name but last name as well.
Means "scripture, book, composition" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रकरण (prakaraṇa).
From Thai ปกรณ์ (pakon) meaning "story, book, scripture, composition" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Alternate transcription of Thai ปกรณ์ (see Pakon).
The name is composed of the Old Polish elements 'Pako' meaning "more; again" and 'sław' meaning "glory."
Means "big man" in Yavapai. Name borne by a 19th century Yavapai leader that attended a peace conference with Ulysses S. Grant in 1872.
Alternate transcription of Thai ภาคภูมิ (see Phakphum).

Means "bird" in Javanese, ultimately from Sanskrit पक्षिन् (pakṣin).
Allegedly a variant of Pukuna, a Miwok name meaning "deer jumping when running downhill".

Of Middle Iranian origin, most likely Parthian. The meaning of this name is uncertain, but sources regularly associate it with Parthian bgpwhr or bag-puhr meaning "son of a god".Pakur was the name of several rulers of Parthian origin, who are usually known under the latinized form of their name. The territories over which they ruled include Armenia, Caucasian Iberia (modern-day Georgia), Colchis (now Georgia), Media Atropatene (modern-day Iran), Parthia (now Iran) and Persis (now Iran).
Means "wild plant, wild fruit" in Guarani.
Means "powerful man" or "strong man" in Mende.
Taken from the English word palace, meaning “royal residence”.
The name of two Tolkien characters.
Paladine is the female knight who tried to rescue the squire captured by Argante.
A lover of Morgan le Fay slain by Arthur, causing a rift between Arthur and Morgan.
Alternate transcription of Thai ภราดร (see Pharadon).

Means "ancient inhabitant, indigenous; that which has been long in a country" in Ancient Greek, derived from πάλαι (palai) meaning "long ago" and χθών (chthon) meaning "earth, ground, soil". In one account, this was the name of an autochthonous man (born of the earth orGaia) who became the father of Pelasgus, though in most other accounts Pelasgus himself is an autochthon and does not have a father.

Latinized form of Palaimon. This name was borne by several characters in Greek mythology.In real life, a known bearer of this name was the Roman grammarian Remmius Palaemon, who lived in the 1st century AD.

From Greek παλαιστής (palaistes) meaning "wrestler" or the verb παλαιστέω (palaisteo) "to thrust away with the hand" (from παλαιστή (palaiste) "palm of the hand", a later form of παλαστή (palaste)). This is the name of two characters in Greek mythology, both associated with the god Hermes: a mortal lover of Hermes; and his daughter, the goddess of wrestling. In literature, this name belongs to a slave girl in the Onos (or the Ass) attributed to Lucian.

Derived from the Greek verb παλαιμονέω (palaimoneo) meaning "to wrestle, to fight", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb παλαίω (palaio) meaning "to wrestle". Also compare the similar-looking Greek words πάλαι (palai) meaning "long ago" and παλαιός (palaios) meaning "old (in years), aged, ancient".
Hawaiian form of Blaine and Brian.
From pālama meaning "sacred wood enclosure" in Hawaiian. Also Hawaiian translation of English words "palm" and "plum".
French and Norman form of Palamedes.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek παλάμη (palame) meaning "palm of the hand" or "device, cunning". Alternatively, it could derive from παλαίω (palaio) meaning "to wrestle, fight, overcome, endeavour", or perhaps πάλαι (palai) "long ago, in the past, before", combined with μήδομαι (medomai) "to plan, plot, devise, contrive". In Greek mythology Palamedes was a son of King Nauplius, and credited with the invention of dice, numbers, and letters, among other things. This was also the name of a Saracen Knight of the Round Table in Arthurian legend.
From Tamil பழனி (Paḻaṉi), the name of a town in Tamil Nadu, India, and வேல் (vēl) referring to a divine spear in Hindu mythology.
Khanty and Mansi form of Pelagia and rare Ukrainian variant of Palazhka.
Name of an early Roman Christian Saint and Martyr.

Derived from Palatium, which is the Latin name for the Palatine Hill in Rome. The word is of uncertain origin; theories include a derivation from Etruscan 𐌚𐌀𐌋𐌀𐌃 (falad), meaning "sky", Latin palatum, meaning "vault, dome" or Latin palus, meaning "enclosure". Additionally, according to the Roman historian Livy, the Palatine Hill got its name from the Arcadian settlers from Pallantium, named from its founder Pallas, son of Lycaon.Palatua was a Roman goddess and the guardian deity of the southern peak of the Palatine Hill.
The name of the sister of Melusine in the English translation of the story.
From the Hawaiian word which can mean "to tell tall tales, talk", "war club", or "taro".
Samoan adaptation of Brown. This was the name Samoans called to British missionary George Brown, who became an important figure in Samoa. Thereafter it was popularised as a given name.

Georgian form of the medieval Persian name Pahlavan (see Pahlavon).This name is archaic and now only survives in the patronymic surname of ფალავანდიშვილი (Palavandishvili) meaning "child of Palavand".
Probably derived from diminutive of Palahiya, but used standalone. Mostly used in Vinnytsya Oblast.
From Tibetan དཔལ་ཆེན (dpal-chen) meaning "great glory", derived from དཔལ (dpal) meaning "glory, splendour" and ཆེན (chen) meaning "great, big, large".
Perhaps from pal meaning "hill" and dar meaning "tree, wood" in Kurdish.
From Tibetan དཔལ་ལྡན (dpal-ldan) meaning "glorious, illustrious, splendous".
French form of Palaimon via its latinized form Palaemon.
Spanish form of Palaimon via its latinized form Palaemon.
Lithuanian form of Palaimon via its latinized form Palaemon.
Italian form of Palaimon via its latinized form Palaemon.
Hawaiian form of Brenda and Brent.

Meaning unknown, possibly of Etruscan origin. This was the name of a deity of shepherds, flocks and livestock in Roman mythology, regarded as male by some sources and female by others. The mythological figure appears in pastoral plays of the 16th and 17th centuries.
From the place name Palestina. Also compare Falasteen.

Modern name, probably based on the sounds found in other names such as Paisley and Hayley; in other words, a combination of the popular phonetic elements pay and lee. It also coincides with the surname Paley.
From Nivkh paln meaning "mountain", indicating a child born in the mountains.
East Prussian German short form of Apollonia.
Diminutive of Pavle, as it contains the Georgian diminutive suffix -იკო (-iko).

Polynesian name for the Hawaiian honeycreeper, an endangered bird native to Hawai'i. In Hawaiian mythology, Palila, a grandchild of goddess Hina, is a warrior hero of Kauai. He killed warriors of Hamakua and became the ruling chief of Hilo. Palila means "with a spirit as free as a bird" in Tahitian.
Feminine form of Páll. In other words, you could also say that Pálína is the Icelandic form of Paulina.Currently, this name is more popular than Pála.
In the Aeneid, Palinurus is a navigator on Aeneas's ship, who dies as a sacrifice to Neptune.

Means "pursuit back, retreat, rally" in Ancient Greek, derived from πάλιν (palin) meaning "back, backwards; again, once more" and ἰωκή (ioke) meaning "rout, pursuit, attack". In Greek mythology, Palioxis was the personification of backrush or retreat in battle, probably one of the Machai, daemons of the battlefield.
From Tibetan དཔལ་འབྱོར (dpal-'byor) meaning "wealth, glory, riches, prosperity".
In Korean mythology, he is the sun god and founder of the realm of light.
Possibly derived from Hindi पालकी (palki) "palanquin", ultimately from Sanskrit, or from Punjabi ਪਲਕ (palak) "eyelid; eyeblink, instant", borrowed from Persian.
Meaning unknown, possibly of Frisian origin.
Meaning unknown. Was the name of one of the two mysterious Blue Wizards from the legendarium of J. R. R. Tolkien.
Likely related to Pallas 1. In Greek Mythology, it was the the name of one of the Alkyonides, as well as the name of a daughter of King Sithon.
Either a variant of Polly or a diminutive of Opal, Pauline, or other names containing Pal- or Paul-.

In Dutch literature, Pallieter is the name of the eponymous character of the novel Pallieter (1916) written by the Flemish author and poet Felix Timmermans (1886-1947). A film based on the novel was released in 1975 under the same title.The name has no meaning, as the author invented the name and even went so far as to have his character state explicitly in the novel that his name has no meaning at all. However, scholars think it likely that Timmermans was inspired by the Flemish dialectal word palloeter or paloeter meaning "fraudster, impostor" as well as "lazy person".Due to the success, popularity and the resulting influence of the novel, the protagonist's name has since become a regular word in Dutch. It means "bon vivant", in reference to the character's approach to life.
Alternate transcription of Thai พัลลภ (see Phanlop).

Short form of Palmarius and Palmatius.Today, this name is obsolete, but it still survives in several patronymic surnames, of which Palm and Palmen are the most notable. They are chiefly prevalent in the historical Rhineland region in western Germany, and in the Limburgish language area (primarily located in the southern Netherlands and eastern Flanders in Belgium).
Faroese and Hungarian form of Palma.
Possibly a masculine form of Palma, or perhaps from the Norwegian given name Paulmar.

Derived from the Latin adjective palmarius meaning "of the palm" as well as "superior, excellent". It is ultimately derived from the Latin noun palma meaning "palm tree" as well as "flat hand, palm of the hand".In the medieval period, the word palmarius (also palmerius by then) was often used to refer to a Christian pilgrim to the Holy Land, as they would bring back a customary palm branch from their pilgrimage (see Palmer). As a result, the word eventually took on the additional meaning of "pilgrim".The use of the word as a given name is generally thought to have started in reference to Palm Sunday, i.e. it was bestowed upon a male child that was born on that day. However, it could also have started in honour of the Italian pilgrim saint Raymond the Palmer (12th century), who was frequently called Raimundus Palmarius in Latin.Lastly, as a given name, Palmarius was confused with Palmatius to the point that the names were often used interchangeably. This was partly because Palmatius is etymologically related and very similar in appearance, and partly because it was also associated with Palm Sunday.

Derived from the Latin adjective palmatus meaning "bearing palms, decorated with palm branches", itself ultimately derived from the Latin noun palma meaning "palm tree" as well as "flat hand, palm of the hand".Also compare the Latin noun palmatias meaning "a slight earthquake", which ultimately comes from the Greek noun παλματίας (palmatias) meaning "an earthquake with violent shocks". In turn, it is ultimately derived from the Greek noun παλμός (palmos) meaning "quivering motion, pulsation, vibration".This name was notably borne by saint Palmatius of Trier (3rd century).

Variant of Pálmi. This is also a Swedish surname. The name was adopted by a notable Swedish family in honor of their ancestor Palme Lyder (born 1570s, died 1630), a merchant who immigrated to Sweden from the Netherlands or Germany in the early 1600s.
Transferred use of the surname Palmerston, or from the place name Palmerston.

Icelandic name of uncertain derivation, possibly a feminine form of Pálmi using the Old Norse suffix ey meaning "island" or ey meaning "good fortune". Alternatively, this could be formed from Pála and the Old Norse element mey meaning "maid, girl" (poetic for "daughter", an alternative form of mær).
Combination of Pálmi and the Old Norse element fríðr meaning "beautiful", originally "beloved".
Masculine form of Palmina. This name is usually given to an infant male born on Palm Sunday.
French variant and Walloon form of Palmyre.
Diminutive of Palma, as it contains the Spanish feminine diminutive suffix -ita.
From Tibetan དཔལ་མོ (dpal-mo) meaning "glorious woman", derived from དཔལ (dpal) meaning "glory, splendour" and the feminine particle མོ (mo). This is the Tibetan name for the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
Czech, Slovak and Greek form of Palmyra.
French form of Palmira. This also coincides with the French name of the ancient oasis city of Syria, known in English as Palmyra.
Possibly means "Tóki son of Pálni", from the names Pálni and Tóki. Pálnatóki was a legendary Danish hero and chieftain of the island of Fyn.
The origin and meaning is uncertain. Some theories include, from Old Danish pólina meaning "pole" or from Old Danish páll meaning "pole".
Derived from Vulgar Latin palumba meaning "dove; pigeon".
Emperor Palpatine the main villain of the star wars saga
Formed from Pála and the Old Norse name suffix rún meaning "secret lore, rune".
This name was apparently found inscripted on a few ancient seals. a variant of Palta

Hellenized form of an Indian name, of which both the original form and the meaning are unknown.In Greek mythology, this is the name of a chieftain of the Indian tribe of the Zabioi (known in Latin as the Zabii). They armed themselves against the Greek god Dionysos in the Indian War, even though Palthanor was privately in agreement with Dionysos. After the war, he followed Dionysos to Thebes and settled there.
Means "my escape, my deliverance" in Hebrew.
The name of one of Lot's daughters according to the lost Book of Jasher.
Allegedly a sea god of the Caroline Islands.
Romansh form of Apollonia, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.

Meaning unknown, possibly derived from Pallas 1-Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, or the word parthena, meaning "virgin" in Greek (see Parthenia). Palutena is the name of the benevolent goddess of light in the Kid Icarus video game series by Nintendo.
Transferred use of the surname Paluzzi, itself ultimately from Paoluccio. This was the name of an Italian Catholic Cardinal, Paluzzo Paluzzi Altieri degli Albertoni (1623-1698).
From Finnish word pälvi, meaning a snow free patch on the ground, melted by the sun.
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਪਲਵਿੰਦਰ (see Palwinder).
Turkmen form of Palvan, which is a medieval Persian contraction of the Persian name Pahlavan (see Pahlavon).
Alternate transcription of Pashto پلوشه (see Palwasha).
From Sanskrit पाल (pāla) meaning "guard, protector" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra.
Possibly a variant of Amadou, itself a form of Ahmad.
Name of the "pond sachem" of Assawamsett.

Means "the one of Ombos", derived from the possessive masculine prefix ⲡⲁ- (pa-) combined with Ombos, the name of several cities in ancient Egypt. Saint Pambo of Nitria was a 4th-century hermit, disciple of St. Anthony. He is venerated by both Catholic and Orthodox Churches on 18 July.
Possibly from the Azerbaijani pambıq meaning "cotton".
An elaboration of the name Pamela used in the Romany culture.
Elaboration of Pamela using the popular name suffix lyn.
Form of Pamphilos in various languages.
Polish form of Pamphilos, which is primarily used to polonize Russian Памфил and Ukrainian Памфіл (see Pamfil for both). The actual Polish form of the name is the aforementioned Pamfil.
Gascon and Provençal form of Pamphilus.
Greenlandic name meaning 'terminal peg of harpoon'.
Means "cause me to cry tears of joy" in Yoruba.

From Egyptian pꜣ-mn meaning "he of Min", derived from the masculine possessive prefix pꜣ "the aforementioned, the, he of" combined with the name of the god Min. Alternatively, it can also derive from the demotic writing of a word meaning "so-and-so", used to replace personal names in model documents.
Pamina is a character in Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's opera The Magic Flute (Die Zauberflöte in German, 1791).

From Egyptian pꜣ-mjw or pꜣ-my meaning "the cat, the tomcat" or "he who belongs to the cat Bastet". It is sometimes incorrectly translated as pꜣ-mꜣj "the lion". This was the birth name of a pharaoh of the 22nd Dynasty.

Latinized form of a Greek name deriving from Ancient Greek παμμάχος (pammachos) meaning "ready for every battle, fighting with all means", composed of πᾶν (pan) "all" and μάχη (mache) "battle". This name was borne by a saint from the 5th century AD.

column12: Derived from Greek πᾶν (pan) meaning "all, every" and μένω (meno) meaning "to stay, wait, remain". Alternatively, the second element could be μένος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage".

Perhaps derived from Ancient Greek παν (pan) meaning "all, every", combined with μέροψ (merops) meaning "dividing the voice, articulate" or "bee-eater" (species Merops apiaster; compare Merops, Merope), an epithet used for mortal men. In Greek legend this was borne by an Eleusinian princess, one of the daughters of King Celeus and Metanira.
Means "of Amon" or "he who belongs to Amon" in Coptic. The name ultimately derives from the Egyptian masculine prefix (or article/pronoun) pa combined with Amoun, the Coptic form of Amon.
Probably derived from the Spanish word pampa "steppe, prairie".
Dutch form of Pamphilus via its French form Pamphile.

Variant of Pamphile 2 used for a character in the medieval French romance Palamedes (ca. 1240), in which Pamphille was the wife of Brun (a descendant of Brutus, the first Briton) and the mother of Yrlande and Gialle.

Possibly means "all-illuminating", from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" and φῶς (phos) meaning "light". Pamphos was a legendary Athenian tragic poet, supposedly a contemporary of Linus of Thrace.

Derived from Latin pampineus meaning "garlanded with vine-leaves, flourishing". The Italian novelist Boccaccio used this name in his work The Decameron (1350), where it belongs to one of the seven young women at the heart of the story (alongside Fiammetta, Filomena, Emilia, Lauretta, Neifile, and Elissa).K. M. Sheard writes: 'The pampinea corona referred specifically to the crown of vine leaves worn by the god Dionysus, who, as god of drama as well as of wine, was an appropriate allusion for Boccaccio to make in the name of the character who initiates the book's story-telling, and is thus the driving force behind the whole work.'
Means "final, ultimate, end" in Indonesian and Javanese.

Romanian, Ukrainian and Russian form of Pambo. Pamvo (non-canonical name Pavlo) Berynda was a Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra monk who created one of the oldest bilingual Church Slavic-Old Ukrainian dictionaries.
In Inuit mythology, Pana was the god who cared for souls in the underworld (Adlivun) before they were reincarnated.Pana also means 'snow knife' in Inuktitut.

Latinized form of Greek Πανάκεια (Panakeia), from Greek πανακής (panakês) "all-healing". This word, πανάκεια (panakeia), was used of various herbs reputed to have universal healing powers, and was personified as a goddess of remedies, cures and universal healing, daughter to Asclepius and Epione. A known bearer of this name was the Blessed Panacea De' Muzzi (1368-1383), a virtuous Italian girl whose stepmother killed her while she was at prayer.
Alternate transcription of Thai ปนัดดา (see Panatda).
Alternate transcription of Thai ปนัดดา (see Panatda).

Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from Ancient Greek pan (pan) meaning "all" and αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise, fame" (compare Pantaenus). Panaenus was an Athenian painter who lived in the 5th century BC.
Latinized form of Panaitios. Bearers of this name include the Stoic philosopher Panaetius of Rhodes (2nd century BC) and a Greek tyrant of Leontini in Sicily (7th century BC).
Italian form and Greek variant of Panagiotis.
Derived from Persian پناه (panâh) meaning "shelter, refuge, protection".
Alternate transcription of Greek Παναγιωτα (see Panagiota).
Romanian form of Panagiotis via Panaghiot.

Derived from the Greek adjective παναίτιος (panaitios) meaning "cause of all, to whom all the guilt belongs". It is a compound word, of which the first element consists of πᾶν (pan), the neuter singular of Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, every, each". The second element is derived from the Greek adjective αἴτιος (aitios) meaning "culpable, responsible". Also compare the Greek noun αἰτία (aitia) meaning "responsibility, guilt, blame, cause".
Russian diminutive of Afanasiy. It can be also a short form of Panagiotis.
Alternate transcription of Thai พนัส (see Phanat).
Means "great-grandchild" in Thai, ultimately from Pali panattā.

Possibly means "one of the donkey, donkey driver", derived from Egyptian pȝ "the aforementioned; the; he of" combined with nj "of, belonging to" and ꜥꜣ "donkey, ass". It could also mean "he of Set", with "donkey" representing the Egyptian god Set.
Alternate transcription of Greek Παναγιώτα (see Panagiota).
Bulgarian diminutive or variant of Panagiota
Means "five" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit पञ्चन् (pañcan).
From Indonesian panca meaning "five" (of Sanskrit origin) combined with the feminine suffix -wati.
Meaning uncertain. It is possibly a Macedonian derivative of a Greek name, such as Pan and Panteleimon.A notable bearer of this name is the Macedonian politician Panče Toškovski (b. 1982).

Means "from the kingdom of Panchala" in Sanskrit. This is an epithet of Draupadi, the wife of the Pandavas in the Indian epic the Mahabharata.It is proposed that the kingdom of Panchala was formed from five tribes or clans, its name being derived from पञ्च (pancha), the Sanskrit word for the number five.

Means "five faces" from Sanskrit from पञ्च (pañca) meaning "five" and आनन (ānana) meaning "face". This is an epithet of the Hindu god Shiva, who is sometimes depicted with five faces (representing his five divine activities) in Hindu iconography.

column3: ปัญจพล, ปัญจพร(Thai)
column12: From Thai ปัญจ (pancha) meaning "five" and พล (phon) meaning "strength, power" or พร (phon) meaning "blessing". The spelling ปัญจพล is masculine while ปัญจพร is feminine.

Derived from Greek πᾶν (pan) meaning "all, every" combined with either the Greek noun χαρά (chara) meaning "joy, delight, happiness" or the Greek noun χάρις (charis) meaning "grace, kindness" (see Chares) which in means either "all happiness" or "all kindness".
Probably means "yellow banner" in Nahuatl, derived from panitl "flag, banner" and coztic "yellow".
French and Walloon form of Pancratius.
Spanish and Galician feminine form of Pancratius.
Italian feminine form of Pancratius and Corsican feminine form of Pancraziu.
Form the name of the animal. The animal's name comes from the Nepalese words nigalya ponya, which means "eater of bamboo".
Etymology unknown. Pandaie was a daughter of Heracles in Greek mythology, and supposedly the eponymous first queen of the Pandya dynasty in southern India.

Meaning "pandan", a type of fragrant plant leaves used in Southeast Asian cuisines. Usually not used as a standalone name, this name is used in combination such as Pandan Arum ("fragrant pandan"), Pandan Wangi (also "fragrant pandan"), Pandan Sari ("pandan essence"), etc.

Possibly a variant of Greek Πάνδαρος (Pandaros) (see Pandarus). This was the name of either one or two minor characters in Greek mythology, the son of Merops and a nymph, father of Aëdon and other daughters, and a friend of Tantalus.

Latinized form of Greek Πάνδαρος (Pandaros), which was possibly derived from παν (pan) "all" and δέρω (dero) meaning "to skin, flay; to beat, cudgel". This is the name of a mythical archer who appears in stories of the Trojan War, and ‘who by an arrow-shot violates the truce between the Trojans and Greeks, and is afterwards slain by Diomedes.’ In Homer's Iliad he is portrayed as an energetic and impetuous warrior, but in medieval literature he becomes a witty and licentious figure who facilitates the affair between Troilus and Cressida. In Shakespeare's play 'Troilus and Cressida' (1602) he is portrayed as an aged degenerate and coward, who ends the play by telling the audience he will bequeath them "my diseases".
From a title given to a member of a clan of blacksmiths, probably derived from Balinese memande meaning "metalsmith, ironsmith".

From Greek πάνδημος (pandemos) meaning "of all people, belonging to all people; public, common", composed of πᾶν (pan) "all" and δῆμος (demos) "the people". This was an epithet of the goddess Aphrodite. It was also an epithet of Zeus at Athens.
A longer form of Pandulf. Pandenulf was the name of a 9th-century count of Capua (Italy).

In some cases this is a latinized form of Greek Πανδείη (Pandeie) or Πανδεία (Pandeia) - though the spelling Πανδία (Pandia) has also been used - which may be related to the word πανδῖος (pandios) meaning "all-divine". This was either an epithet of the Greek moon goddess Selene or the name of her daughter, an obscure figure who was perhaps a goddess of the full moon.
The name of a dynasty which ruled southern india for many centuries...

Derived from Ancient Greek πανδῖος (pandios) meaning "all-divine", composed of πᾶν (pan) "all" and δῖος (dios) "heavenly, divine, noble". This was the name of several kings and heroes in Greek mythology.

The name Pandiya is a family of the royal Pandiyan family of the Pandiya empire in south India. Which lasted from 4th BC to 1618 AD around 2018 years of existence safe to assure it is a name of royalty, High class, old, bravery, courage and strength.
Older spelling of Panji influenced by Dutch orthography.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Pandolfo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
A character in Moliere's "L'Étourdi ou les Contretemps".
A genus of climbing vines native to Australasia. Named after Pandora from Greek mythology, because the plant's tightly packed seed pod recalls the myth of "Pandora's box".
Ancient Greek name with the elements πᾶν (pan) "all" and δῶρον (doron) "gift" meaning "all gifted". It is the masculine form of Pandora

A Greek king who had enslaved a group of Trojan exiles. He was fought, and defeated, by Brutus, who then claimed the hand of Pandras’ s reluctant daughter, Ignoge. Brutus also compelled Pandras to release his Trojan slaves, and to equip and provision them to enable them to leave Greece. So equipped, Brutus left Greece, taking the Trojans with him.

A Greek king who had enslaved a group of Trojan exiles. He was fought, and defeated, by Brutus, who then claimed the hand of Pandrasus’ reluctant daughter, Ignoge. Brutus also compelled Pandrasus to release his Trojan slaves, and to equip and provision them to enable them to leave Greece. So equipped, Brutus left Greece, taking the Trojans with him.
Spanish and Italian form of Pandrosus.

Derived from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" and δρόσος (drosos) meaning "dew". In Greek mythology, Pandrosos was one of the three daughters of Kekrops, the first king of Athens, along with her sisters Aglauros and Herse. They are sometimes referred to as the dew sisters.
Means "guard, scout, guide, pathfinder" in Indonesian.

The first element of this name comes from banda, which is derived from Langobardic bando "flag, banner" or from Old High German banz "province, countryside." The first element might also come from Greek pan "all", but this is unlikely. The second element of this Germanic name is derived from Gothic vulfs "wolf." Pandulf I was a 10th-century prince of Benevento (Italy) and Capua (Italy).

Means "pale-coloured, one with a pale complexion" from Sanskrit पाण्डु (pāṇḍu) meaning "pale, whitish, yellow" and रङ्ग (raṅga) meaning "colour, hue". This is an epithet of the regional Hindu god Vithoba.
This was the name of an obscure saint, who may have been a virgin martyr; Pandwyna (died ca. 904) was a nun at Eltisley in Cambridgeshire, England.
Greenlandic pet form of names beginning with Pane-/Pani-.
Possibly means "sound, language, words" in Thai.
From Egyptian pꜣ-nḥsj meaning "the Nubian" (see Phinehas). This was the name of two ancient Egyptian priests and one vizier.
Means "dried meat, dried fish" in Greenlandic.
From the name of the former super continent Pangaea.
Means "to consult or advise each other" in Shona.
Indonesian and Malay form of Prince
From Javanese pangèstu meaning "prayers, blessings, good wishes".
North Greenlandic name for broad-leaved willow herb.

An Old Irish cat name possibly meaning ”a fuller” (a step in woollen clothmaking), loaned from Welsh pannwr.Pangur Bán (meaning White Pangur) was a cat belonging to a 9th century Irish monk residing in Germany, whose skill for mouse hunting was immortalized in an eponymous poem.In modern times, Pangur Bán has been used as a cat name in historical fiction and fantasy, such as Fay Sampson’s titular book series and the 2009 animated film The Secret of Kells.
Means "knowledge, wisdom, intellect" in Khmer, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रज्ञा (prajñā).

From a combination of the characters 盘 (pan, meaning "plate") and 瓠 (hu, meaning "gourd"). This is the name of a hound in Chinese mythology who possessed a five-colored pelt. He is considered the ancestor of several ethnic minorities in southern China, such as the Yao and She peoples.
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 欢 (huān) meaning "joyous, merry, happy".

Means "water, ointment" in Māori. Pania, often styled 'Pania of the Reef', was the Māori goddess of the reef, and is a symbol of the New Zealand city of Napier. A known bearer is Pania Rose (1984-), an Australian model of partial Māori descent.
Alternate transcription of Thai พนิดา (see Phanida).
Means "step daughter, foster daughter" in Greenlandic.

Possibly derived from the possessive masculine prefix ⲡⲁ- (pa-) and genetive marker ⲛ (n) combined with either ⲉⲓⲛⲉ (eine) "chain, fetter" or ⲉⲓⲛⲉ "thumb", the former giving the meaning "he of the chain; guardian", the latter "he of the thumbs", referring to the story of the Coptic saint Symphronios, who was called Panine after his broken thumbs were miraculously healed.
Greenlandic name meaning 'sweet little daughter' with the combination of Panik and -nnguaq 'sweet, dear'.

Means "descendant of Panin" in Sanskrit, from the given name पणिन् (Pāṇin). This was the name of an ancient Indian scholar and grammarian who lived sometime between the 6th-4th centuries BCE. He most famously authored the Aṣṭādhyāyī, a grammatical text on the Sanskrit language.

Means "the one of the names" or "the one of many honours", derived from the masculine possessive suffix ⲡⲁ- (pa-) and the plural definite article ⲛⲓ- (ni-) combined with‎ ⲣⲁⲛ (ran) "name, honour, reputation, fame".
Possibly from Thai ปาณิ (pani) meaning "hand, palm".
Alternate transcription of Thai พนิตา (see Phanita).
Means "banner, flag" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit पञ्जी (pañjī).
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 捷 (jié) meaning "win, victory, triumph".
Czech and Slovak form of Pancratius (see Pancras).
Slovene variant of Pankracij and Kashubian form of Pankratios.
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 灵 (líng) meaning "spirit, soul".
Alternate transcription of Thai พัลลภ (see Phanlop).
From Hindi पन्ना (panna) meaning "emerald, leaf, page".
Alternate transcription of Thai พรรณี (see Phanni).

In the case of Baroness Pannonica "Nica" de Koenigswarter (1913-1988), a patron of several New York City jazz musicians and a member of the Rothschild family of Jewish bankers (born Kathleen Annie Pannonica Rothschild), it was derived from the place name Pannonia and given in reference to Eastern Europe's Pannonian plain. Pannonica de Koenigswarter's mother was a Hungarian baroness, of Austrian-Jewish descent.
Means "troublesome" in Dhona.A famous bearer is the Zimbabwean Central Bank governor John Panonetsa Mangudya.
Latinized form of Greek Πανοπαία (Panopaia), which is a variant form of Panope. In Greek mythology, Panopaea was the name of one of the Nereids.

Means "all-seeing", derived from Ancient Greek παν (pan) meaning "all" and ωψ (ops) meaning "eye, face". In Greek mythology, Panope is the name of one of the fifty daughters of Thespius and Megamede, and had a son, Threpsippas, by Heracles.
Italian and Spanish form of Panopeus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Panopeus.
Masculine form of Panope. In Greek mythology, Panopeus and his twin brother Crisus were sons of Phocus.
Means "of Anubis" or "he who belongs to Anubis" in Coptic. The name ultimately derives from the Egyptian masculine prefix (or article/pronoun) pa combined with Anoub, the Coptic form of Anubis.
Means "the God" or simply "God" in the Coptic language. The name ultimately derives from the Egyptian masculine prefix (or article/pronoun) pa combined with Egyptian nuti "God".
From the Aymara panqara meaning "flower" and wara wara meaning "star".
Alternate transcription of Thai พรรษา (see Phansa).
Derived from Romanian panseluță, the diminutive of pansea "pansy".

Latinized form of Pantakles. A known bearer of this name was the Olympic victor Pantacles of Athens, who won the stadion race at respectively the 21st Olympiad (696 BC) and the 22nd Olympiad (692 BC).
Latinized form of Pantainos. A notable bearer of this name was the Greek theologian and saint Pantaenus the Philosopher (died around 200 AD).
Means "wholly good, beneficial for everything" in Ancient Greek, derived from πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" (genitive παντός) and ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good".
Latinized form of Pantagathos. A known bearer of this name was Saint Pantagathus of Vienne (France), who lived in the 6th century AD.
Italian and Spanish form of Pantagathos via Latinized form Pantagathus.
Derived from Greek πάντα (panta), a form of πᾶν (pan) "all, every", and γνωτός (gnotos) meaning "known, perceived, understood" (compare gnostos).

The first element of this name is derived from Greek πάντες (pantes) meaning "all", which is ultimately derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, for all, of all". The second element is derived from Hagarene gruel meaning "thirsty". This was the name of one of the main characters in "The Life of Gargantua and of Pantagruel", a series of novels written by the French author François Rabelais (16th century). The author had invented the name, because he wanted to make a reference to the fact that his character was born during a time of great drought.

The first element of this name is derived from Greek παντός (pantos), which is the genitive singular of Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, every, each". The second element is derived from the Greek adjective αἰνετός (ainetos) meaning "praiseworthy". The latter word is ultimately derived from the Greek noun αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise, fame" (see Aeneas).

The first element of this name is derived from Greek παντός (pantos), which is the genitive singular of Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, every, each". The second element is derived from the Greek noun αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise, fame" (see Aeneas).

The first element of this name is derived from Greek παντός (pantos), which is the genitive singular of Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, every, each". The second element is derived from the Greek noun κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".

Form of Panteleimon used by Philip Pullman in his series of children's fantasy novels 'His Dark Materials' (1995-2000). Lyra's dæmon, Pantalaimon appears in the 2007 film adaption of the first book, 'The Golden Compass'.
French and Franco-Provençal form of Pantaleon.

Derived from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" (genitive παντός) and ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".Also compare the Greek name Pantenor, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

Derived from Ancient Greek παντάριστος (pantaristos) meaning "best of all", composed of πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" (genitive παντός) and ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best". In Greek mythology, Pantariste was an Amazon who fought on Hippolyte's side against Heracles and his troops.
Means "like the sun" from Thai ปาน (pan) meaning "as, like" and ตะวัน (tawan) meaning "sun".

Persian form of Panthea. Pantea Arteshbod was a 6th-century BC Persian commander during the reign of Cyrus the Great. She was said to be the most beautiful woman in Asia, so she wore a mask during battle to stop men from falling in love with her.
Used by Panteha Abareshi, a nonbinary Canadian artist of Jamaican and Iranian descent.
Modern Greek diminutive of Pantelis, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek adverb πάντῃ (pantei) meaning "(in) every way, on every side" or the Greek adverb πάντως (pantos) meaning "in all ways". Both are ultimately derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, every". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".Also compare the Greek name Pantandros, which is closely related and essentially means the same.
It is spanish for the word, "Panther King". It is also the name of Grimmjows Sword in the anime/manga BLEACH.
From Javanese pantês meaning "fitting, proper, worthy".

Derived from Ancient Greek πανθαλής (panthales) meaning "giver of all bloom, flowering", composed of πᾶν (pan) "all" and θάλλω (thallo) meaning "to blossom". This was the name of one of Helen of Troy’s maidservants in Greek mythology.

From the Greek Πάνθεια (Pantheia) meaning "all goddess", derived from πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" combined with θεά (thea) meaning "goddess" (compare Pasithea and the Greek adjective πάνθειος (pantheios) meaning "of all gods" or "common to all gods"). According to the 4th-century BC Greek historian Xenophon, Pantheia was the wife of the possibly legendary king Abradatas of Susa, in Iran. After her husband died heroically in battle, she committed suicide by his grave.In ancient Rome, Diva Drusilla Panthea was the name under which the emperor Caligula deified his favourite sister, Julia Drusilla (16-38), after her death at age 21. This name was also borne by a mistress of Roman co-emperor Lucius Verus (130-169).In theatre, it was used by Beaumont and Fletcher for a princess in their play A King and No King (1619) and by Percy Bysshe Shelley for an Oceanid in his play Prometheus Unbound (1820). Oscar Wilde also wrote a poem entitled Panthea (1881). Panthea Vyne was the titular lady in the television film The Lady and the Highwayman (1989), based on Barbara Cartland's historical novel Cupid Rides Pillion (1952).

Latinized form of Greek Πάνθοος (Panthoos), derived from πᾶν (pan) meaning "all" and θοός (thoos) meaning "swift" (from the verb θέω (theô) "to run"). In Greek mythology Panthous was originally a priest of Apollo at Delphi. When Priam, after Troy had been destroyed by Heracles, sent a son of Antenor to Delphi to inquire whether it was appropriate to build a new citadel on the foundations of the destroyed city, said son of Antenor was charmed by Panthous' beauty and carried him off. Panthous, in accord with Priam's will, continued to perform his duties as a priest of Apollo at Troy.
Probably a diminutive of Panteleimon and its short form Pante, as it contains the Georgian diminutive suffix -იკო (-iko).
Older spelling of Panca influenced by Dutch orthography.
Basque and Occitan form of Françoise or Francesca.

From Thai ปาน (pan) meaning "as if, like, resembling" and วาด (wat) meaning "draw, sketch".
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 希 (xī) meaning "hope" or "rare".
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 潇 (xiāo) meaning "sound of beating wind and rain".

Uncertain etymology, possibly related to a river known to the Ancient Greeks as Πανύασος (Panyasos) in Macedonia. Panyassis of Halicarnassus was a Greek epic poet from Halicarnassus in the Persian Empire (modern-day Bodrum, Turkey).
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 怡 (yí) meaning "happy, joyful".
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 月 (yuè) meaning "moon".
From the Chinese 盼 (pàn) meaning "look, gaze, expect, hope for" and 珍 (zhēn) meaning "precious, valuable, rare".
Means "to hit, strike" and "to sing" in Māori and Tahitian, as well as "strong odour" and "unlucky" in Hawaiian. Variant spelling of Pawa meaning "smoke".
Italian combination of Paolo and Antonio.
Feminine diminutive of Paol and cognate of Paulette.
A known bearer of this name is the Indian actress Paoli Dam (1980-).
Diminutive of Paol, as it contains the Breton diminutive suffix -ig.

Medieval Italian diminutive of Paolo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.Known bearers of this name include the 14th-century Italian painter Paolo "Paoluccio" di Lazzarino and the 18th-century Italian painter Paoluccio Cattamara of Naples.
Means "we will see good things" in Chewa.

Of Australian Aboriginal origin (Pintupi, to be precise), the meaning of this name is not yet known to me at the moment. A known bearer of this name was Papalya Nangala, the mother of Australian Aboriginal painter Takariya Napaltjarri (b. circa 1960).
From the fruit papaya, which is a large, yellow, melonlike fruit of a tropical American shrub or small tree, Carica papaya, eaten raw or cooked.
Feminine form of Paphnutius.Paphnutia the Virgin was an Egyptian alchemist living around the time of 300 C.E.

Probably derived from the name of a town in Cyprus known as the birthplace of Aphrodite and a centre of worship for the goddess. This was the name of the daughter or son of Pygmalion and the statue that Aphrodite brought to life. It was also the name of a Jewish martyr, who was martyred alongside his brother Lulianos in the second century CE.
The surname "Papi" stems from medieval Italy. It is often a diminutive or patronymic form of the name Papa, or a variation of Giacopo (Jacob) (from ancestry.com)
Belarusian form of Cinderella, from Belarusian попел (popiel) "ash".
Ancient Greek name, possibly connected to Greek πάππος (pappos) "grandfather" or πάππας (pappas) "papa". This was the name of multiple saints.

Contraction of Russian партийная пирамида (partiynaya piramida) meaning "pyramid of the (ruling / communist) Party", perchance eluding to child becoming high member of the party. Coincides with some Soviet languages word for "paper" such as Ukrainian.
An infidel king who served Feirefiz, Perceval’s half-brother.
Derived from Egyptian pa-ph-nuti meaning "the (man) of God" or "he who belongs to God".
Derived from papoula, the Brazilian Portuguese word for "poppy".Papoula Pomfrey is the name of Madame Pomfrey in Brazilian translations of Harry Potter.
Romansh form of Caspar, traditionally found in the Lower Engadine valley.

One of the three goddesses of fate in relation to birthing. See also Nona and Decima. Parca or Partula oversees partus, birth as the initial separation from the mother's body (as in English '"postpartum"). At the very moment of birth, or immediately after, Parca establishes that the new life will have a limit, and therefore she is also a goddess of death called Morta (English "mortal"). The profatio Parcae, "prophecy of Parca," marked the child as a mortal being, and was not a pronouncement of individual destiny. The first week of the child's life was regarded as an extremely perilous and tentative time, and the child was not recognized as an individual until the dies lustricus.

In Irish mythology Partholan led the second legendary group of invaders to settle in Ireland following the Biblical Flood. His story, primarily recorded in the medieval Lebor Gabála Érenn (Book of Invasions), details how he and his followers introduced civilization to the island before a tragic end.According to legend, Partholón was the son of a Greek king who fled his homeland after murdering his parents. Hoping to outrun a curse that doomed all his endeavors, he sailed to Ireland with his wife (Dalgnet), his three sons, and a small group of retainers. They landed at Inber Scéne (modern-day Kenmare Bay, County Kerry). When they arrived, Ireland was a largely desolate wilderness featuring only one fertile plain, three lakes, and nine rivers. The Partholónians are then credited with introducing the first major infrastructure to Ireland.

The earliest known bearer of this name is the 7th-century saint Pascharius of Nantes. He was a native of the city, which is located in the cultural and historical region of Brittany in western France. This means that he was likely of Celtic origin, but a Germanic origin is also possible, as at the time Nantes was located in Neustria, the western part of the Kingdom of the Franks.His name is either fully or partially Latin (i.e. a hybrid). In both cases, the first element is ultimately derived from the Latin noun pascha meaning "Easter" as well as "Passover". The second element can consist of the Latin adjectival suffix -arius, in which case the meaning of the name is virtually the same as that of Paschalis.In the case of a hybrid, the second element is either of Celtic or Germanic origin. For the former, it might possibly come from Old Breton air meaning "battle, carnage", in which case the overall meaning of the name is the same as that of the Breton name Pascweten (ultimately also a hybrid). As for a Germanic origin, the most likely candidate appears to be Frankish *hari meaning "army".Lastly, it is important to note that this name is often conflated with the older but related name Paschasius. This has been happening since the medieval period, and is at least partly due to the similarity in appearance and meaning between the two names.
