The first element of this name is uncertain; it might possibly be derived from Old Breton Pasc meaning "Easter". The second element consists of Old Breton uueten or uuethen (also guethen), which is a derivation of Old Breton uueith (also gueith) meaning "battle, fight" as well as "warrior".This name was borne by a 9th-century count of Vannes, who was a claimant to the rule of Brittany. He is known as Pasquitan (also Pasquite and Pasquiten) in French and as Paskwezhen in modern Breton.

From Egyptian pꜣ-sbꜣ-ḫꜥ-n-nwt meaning "the star appearing in the city", derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with sbꜣ "star; meteor", ḫꜥ "appearing", m "in", and nwt "town, city", usually referring to Thebes.
Short form of Pacisepa, a variant of Vaciseva, Fijian form of Bathsheba. English translation from the Fijian bible reads, "Daughter of abundance". This passage refers to Bathsheba.

column3: 葉芹, 葉世里(Japanese Kanji)|ぱせり(Japanese Hiragana)|パセリ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: Japanese transliteration of the English word parsley, referring to the type of flowering plant that has been widely used in European, Middle Eastern and American cooking.This name can also be written into kanji with 葉 (you, ha) meaning "blade, leaf, needle" being combined with either 芹 (kin, seri), which refers to the Java waterdropwort, or 世 (se, sei, sou, sanjuu, yo) meaning "generation" and 里 (ri, sato), referring to a unit of distance known as ri or else, a village.This name is very rarely given to girls, if given at all.

Name of the ancient King of Powys, Pasgen ap Cadeyrn (Pasgen, son of Cadeyrn), father of Mawgan ap Pasgen. He appears in the Harleian genealogies and his name appears inscribed on the Pillar of Eliseg. In the Historia Brittonum, he's listed as a son of Vortigern.Scholars place the beginning of his reign around 417 AD or 480—510 AD.
An old baptismal name given for children born on Easter in reference to the latin pascal. See also Paschal.
From the Armenian word փաշայ (pʿašay) meaning "pasha", the title of a high-ranking Ottoman military officer.
Derived from the name Pasha and -ئاي‎ (-'ay) meaning "moon".

From Egyptian pꜣ-šr-n-ptḥ meaning "son of Ptah", derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with šr "boy, child, young man; son" and the name of the god Ptah. This was the name of a high priest of Ptah during the Ptolemaic dynasty.
Derived from Egyptian name possibly meaning "portion of the god horus". Used in Hebrew as "passover" indicating sparing and deliverance. Used multiple times in the old testament.
Derived from Albanian pashka, a variant of pashkët "Easter".

Pashmina is a fine wool from the undercoat of Himalayan goats, which is also known as cashmere. The term "pashmina" can refer to either the wool itself or to the luxurious shawls and scarves made from it. These products are known for their extraordinary softness, lightness, and warmth. As a given name symbolizes warmth and comfort.
Means "one of the acacia tree", derived from the masculine possessive prefix ⲡⲁ- (pa-) combined with ϣⲟⲛϯ (šonti) "acacia, thorn tree".
From Sanskrit पशु (paśu) meaning "cattle" and पति (pati) meaning "lord", thus "lord of animals". Pashupati is a Hindu deity and an incarnation of Shiva 1.
Variation of Passion, as used by Pashyn Santos, a Hawaiian actress and activist.
Latinized form of Pasikles. A bearer of this name was Pasicles of Thebes, a Greek philosopher from the 4th century BC.
French and Italian form of Pasikrates.
Latinized form of Pasikrates. This was the name of a Christian martyr from the 3rd century AD.
Croatian and Serbian form of Pasiphaë.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Pasiphaë.
Derived from Ancient Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all" and γενής (genes) meaning "born".
Means "glorious in everything", derived from Ancient Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all" and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Bulgarian, Russian, Serbian and Ukrainian form of Pasikrates.
Derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, for all, of all" and κρατος (kratos) meaning "power".
Derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, for all, of all" combined with μενος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage, spirit."
Likely a diminutive of Pascuala or Pascual.
Means "all-victorious, winner in all", derived from Ancient Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all" and νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".

Means "passion" in Spanish, referring to the Passion of Jesus Christ.Masculine usage of this name is restricted to areas outside of Spain, particularly Mexico and Peru where males with this name outnumber the females.
Means "their ground, earth" in Tumbuka, often given after repeated deaths in the family. Refers to the fact that the child will eventually also die and be buried in the earth.
Means "visible to all" in Ancient Greek, derived from πᾶς (pas) "all" and φανής (phanes) "appearing", itself from φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to show, appear, manifest" or "to give light, shine".
Means "friend of all, loved by all", derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, for all, of all" and φιλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" or "beloved, dear".
Latinized form of Pasiphilos. A bearer of this name was Fabius Felix Pasiphilus Paulinus, a praefectus urbi from the 4th century AD.
Derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, for all, of all" combined with either φωνη (phone) meaning "voice" or a relative of φάος (phaos) meaning "light".
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Pasithea.

Means "goddess of all", derived from Greek πᾶς (pas) meaning "all, for all, of all" combined with Greek θεα (thea) meaning "goddess". In Greek mythology she was one of the Charites, married to Hypnos, the god of sleep and dreams; she may have been regarded as a goddess of rest and relaxation or of hallucinations and hallucinogenic drugs.
Derived from the Middle English word Pask meaning "Easter".In modern Breton, Pask also means "Easter", but as a given name it is usually a short form of Paskal.
Basque form of Pascuala and Pascale.
Diminutive of Paskal, as it contains the Breton diminutive suffix -ig.
Indonesian form of Pascasius, which is a variant of Paschasius.
Croatian form of Pascasius, which is a variant of Paschasius.
Norwegian form of Paschalis. This is also the Norwegian word for Easter.
Feminine form of Paskal and variant of Paskella.
Breton form of Pascharius, probably via its French form Pasquier.
Basque form of Pascuala and Pascale.
Diminutive of Paskal, which was probably taken directly from French Pascou.
Of uncertain etymology. Name borne by a magician from Arzawa, known from a text that details a ritual dedicated to the goddess Uliliyašši to cure impotence.
Croatian feminine form of Pascal.Famous bearer: football (soccer) player Paškvalina Gabrić
Means "the plain", referring to the prairies, in Cree.
French form of Pascharius. It appears to have been rare, or at least it was never as common as the form Pasquier.
Catalan and Ladin form of Pascal.
Corsican variant and Sicilian form of Pasquale.
Cremish Lombard feminine form of Pasquàl.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Pasquale, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Italian compound name created from Pasqua and Rosa 1.

French form of Pascharius. It originated in the medieval period, during which time it was fairly common. The name has since nearly fallen out of use; nowadays it is much more common as a patronymic surname.
Derived from Italian Pasqua "Easter". This is also the Corsican feminine form of Pasquinu.
Alternate transcription of Thai ภาสกร (see Phatsakon).
Alternate transcription of Thai ภาสกร (see Phatsakon).

Meaning and origin uncertain. It might possibly be derived from the Greek noun πασσάριος (passarios) meaning "cross" or even from Πασσαρών (Passaron), a city in the region of Epirus in ancient Greece.Alternatively, the name might be a variant of Bessarion, since Passarion has certainly been confused or otherwise associated with it (and vice versa).The best known bearer of this name is saint Passarion of Palestine († 428 AD).

Dutch, Flemish and Frisian form of Pascharius, probably via its French form Pasquier.This name was fairly common during the medieval period, but is nearly extinct in this day and age; it now primarily survives as a patronymic surname.

First recorded as a given name in the 16th century, and originally used by Christian parents in reference to the Passion of Christ, a term denoting the sufferings of Jesus from the night of the Last Supper to the Crucifixion. The word itself is derived from Latin passio meaning "suffering", ultimately from Latin patior "to suffer; to endure" and was originally used to describe any suffering or pain concerning the body. Its meaning of sexual desire dates to the 17th century. The name had gone extinct and was revived in the 20th century, no doubt for its current English meaning.
Derived from the English word Passionate meaning "Full of passion". It is mostly masculine in Nigeria but mostly feminine in other countries.
Italian form of Pasithea. A known bearer was the Blessed Passitea Crogi (1564-1615), a Cistercian nun of Siena who beat herself with thorns and washed the wounds with vinegar, salt and pepper.
From mid 17th century: via French from Italian pastello, diminutive of pasta ‘paste’.
Short form, or variant form, of Apostolis.

From Italian pastorella meaning "little shepherdess" or "young shepherdess". Alternatively it could be a feminine diminutive of Pastor. Edmund Spenser used this name for a minor character in his epic poem 'The Faerie Queene' (1590-1596); Pastorella is raised by shepherds, but in the last Canto of Book 6 she is revealed to be the daughter of Sir Bellamoure and Lady Claribell.
Probably a variant of Pastora. It was used by American author L. Frank Baum for a male character (King Pastoria of Oz, father of Princess Ozma) in his Oz series of fantasy books.
Alternate transcription of Thai ผาสุก (see Phasuk).

This is an Indian and Telugu feminine name. Pasupuleti Kannamba (1911-1964) was an Indian versatile actress, playback singer and film producer of Telugu cinema, Andhra Pradesh, India. She acted in more than 170 films and produced about 25 films in Telugu and Tamil languages during the 1930s to the 1960s.
Alternate transcription of Greek Πασχάλης (see Paschalis).
Alternate transcription of Thai ปัทมา (see Patthama).
Combination of Patricia and Ana. Patana, also known as her alter-ego La Sombra (The Shadow), a character in the Chilean puppet show 31 Minutos, bears this name.

From Egyptian pꜣ-dj-ḥp meaning "given by Apis" or "given by Hapi", derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with‎ dj "given" and the name of either Apis, the sacred bull, or Hapi, god of the Nile river's annual flooding.
Hellenized form of Patape. Saint Patapios of Egypt was an early Christian desert hermit and thaumaturge. He is venerated by Orthodox Church on December 8th.
Latinized form of Patape via it's Hellenized form Patapios.
Means "clear, bright, open, transparent" in Toba Batak.
Alternate transcription of Thai ภัทรพล (see Phattharaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai ภัทรพล (see Phattharaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai ภัทรพร (see Phattharaphon).
Means "the land rejoices in her" in Egyptian.
Chechen and Ingush form of Batradz.

Short form of Patrick, coming from how the sequence ⟨tr⟩ is pronounced like ⟨ch⟩ in many dialects of American English.A notable bearer is content creator Patrick "Patch" Lacey, better known as TierZoo.
Alternate transcription of Thai พัดชา (see Phatcha).
Alternate transcription of Thai พัชรี (see Phatchari).
Alternate transcription of Thai พัชรี (see Phatchari).
From Thai พัชร (phatchara) meaning "diamond" and อินทร์ (in) referring to the Hindu god Indra.
From the English word patches, which is a plural noun of patch.
Patchouli comes from the bushy herb of the mint family and bears tiny pink-white flowers. A bearer of this name is Patchouli Knowledge, a character from the Touhou Project.
Greenlandic name meaning "(dwarf) willow" or "alder" (Lat. Alnus crispa).
Greenlandic name meaning "little birch tree" or a combination of Patdleĸ and -paluk "dear little".

Possibly derived from Nahuatl pahtli "medicine, potion, poison" and -tecatl, a suffix indicating affiliation. This was the name of an Aztec god of healing and fertility, lord of pulque (an alcoholic beverage made from maguey sap).
From the Gujarati word પટેલ (paṭēl) meaning "chief, village headsman". This is the most common surname among Indian-Americans.
Derived from Egyptian Pa-tȝ-rnn.t meaning "the one of Thermouthis" (see Thermuthis).
Hellenized form of Patermoute. This name was borne by two Egyptian saints from the 4th century AD; one was martyred in Egypt and the other in Palestine.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Patermouthios.

Latinized form of Patermouthios, which is one of the many hellenizations of the Coptic name Patermoute.This name was borne by two Egyptian saints from the 4th century AD; one was martyred in Egypt and the other in Palestine.
Polish form of Paternus and French variant of Paterne.
Italian and Spanish form of Paternianus.
Roman cognomen and diminutive of Paternus.
Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese form of Paternus.
Transferred use of the surname Paterson.
Alternate transcription of Thai ปัทมา (see Patthama).
Form of Peter used by Malayalam-speaking Saint Thomas Christians.
Transferred use of the surname Pathé.
Means "first, primary" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रथम (prathama).
From Thai ปฐม (pathom) meaning "first, primary" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Alternate transcription of Malayalam പത്രോസ് (see Pathrose).
Form of Petros (see Peter) used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.
Short form of Patman, which is now primarily used as an independent name rather than as an unofficial nickname.
Means "evil spirit of the unborn babies". It was given to protect child from evil spirits.
From the element Patiens "patience" used by two saints.
From the Late Latin name Patiens. It was also used by the Puritans as a vocabulary name, from the English word patient.

Taken directly from Latin patientia "patience, endurance, forbearance" (also "suffering" or "submission, subjection") – the ancestral cognate of Patience. This name was borne by St. Patientia of Loret (alias Santa Paciencia de Huesca), wife of Saint Orentius of Loret, both of whom were martyred in 240; their mutual feast day is May 1, with their joint patronage being against vermin. Pious Spanish tradition makes the couple the parents of St. Lawrence of Rome (d. 258).
Marathi and Kannada form of Patel.
Indonesian and Lak form of Fatimah.
Indonesian and Malay form of Fatimah.
Form of Fatimah used in Dagestan.
Patina is a thin layer that variously forms on the surface of stone, on copper, bronze and similar metals, on wooden furniture or any such acquired change of a surface through age and exposure.
Means "declaration, oath, pledge" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रतिज्ञा (pratijñā).
Alternate transcription of Thai ปฏิภาณ (see Patiphan).
Alternate transcription of Thai ปฏิภาณ (see Patiphan).
Means "quick-witted, clever, sharp" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रतिभान (pratibhāna).
Means "reform, change, improve" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रतिरूप (pratirūpa).
Means "overthrow, revolution" or "rolling back, turning back" in Thai, ultimately from Pali paṭivatti.
Diminutive form of Fatimat or Patimat.
Means "man of honour", from Pashto pat "honour" and man "self".
Alternate transcription of Thai ปฐม (see Pathom).
Meaning as of yet unknown. A known bearer of this name is Dr. Patoni Isaaqzai Teichmann, an Afghan feminist and social activist.
Possibly a variant of Petra or a short form of Cleopatra.
Variant of Patrekur, the usual Icelandic form of Patrick (via Old Norse Patrekr). This name is known from the village Patreksfjörður (Patrick's Fjord) in Iceland.
A blend of Patricia and Katriana.
Extended form of Patrice 2 or variant of Patricia.
Romanian form of Patricius, used to refer to Saint Patrick of Ireland.
Catalan and Occitan form of Patrick.
Short form of Patricia, which is comparable to Patrice 2.This name is extremely rare as an official name on birth certificates; it is almost always used informally.
A rare Estonian variant of Patrick, mimicking the English pronunciation.
Feminine form of Patrick. This name is borne by American actress Patrika Darbo.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque form of Patricia.
Feminine diminutive of Patrick influenced by Katrina
Probably derived from the French name Patrice 1.Patrisse Cullors is an artist, activist, and co-founder of 'Black Lives Matter'.
Variant of Patricius. A bearer of this name was Patritius Sporer, a German Franciscan moral theologian from the 17th century AD.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Patricius.

Contracted form of Patrobios. Also compare similar contractions, such as Annas, Cleopas and Silas.In the New Testament, Patrobas is the name of a Roman Christian mentioned in Paul's letter to the Romans.

Meaning not quite certain. The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πάτρα (patra) meaning "fatherland, native land" or from Greek πατρός (patros) meaning "of a father".The second element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun βία (bia) meaning "bodily strength, force" or the Greek noun βίος (bios) meaning "life".
Latinized form of Patrobios. This was the name of a prominent and influential freedman, who was one of the favourites of the Roman emperor Nero (1st century AD).

Latinized form of the rare Greek name Πατρόβουλος (Patroboulos), which was derived from Greek πατρόβουλος (patroboulos), the name for a hereditary senator.This was the name of a bishop of Puteoli, who was one of the Seventy Disciples (also known as the Seventy Apostles).
Means "protector, patron" in Ancient Greek, derived from Latin patronus. This was the name of an Epicurean philosopher, more commonly called Patro in English.
Variant of Petronella meaning "rock" or alternatively derived from Latin patrones meaning "protector, father".
Alternate transcription of Thai ภาสกร (see Phatsakon).
Alternate transcription of Thai ภาสกร (see Phatsakon).
Kazakh spelling variant of the Ottoman Turkish and Persian title padishah, meaning "emperor". In the Kazakh language, this is the most frequent word used for "king".
Alternate transcription of Thai ปัทมา (see Patthama).

Transferred use of the surname Patterson.
Means "lotus" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit पद्म (padma).

From Thai ปัทมา (patthama) meaning "lotus" and วรรณ (wan) meaning "colour, tint".

column12: Variant and feminine form of Patton.
Means "part from one another" in Tumbuka.

Patu means "weapon, kill" and Kawenga means "burden". This was the name of the Senior Ngati Mutunga Chief Patukawenga (d. 1836-1837?) who was one of the chiefs who invaded what is now Chatham Islands in 1835 before enslaving and committing genocide against the Moriori population.
From patu meaning "to strike, weapon, kill" and tai meaning "tide, coast" or "friend" in Māori.
Of uncertain etymology. Name borne by an indigenous Australian woman (fl. 1780) of the Cammeraygal clan of the Eora nation.
Spanish short form of Paula and Paulina.
Hawaiian unisex name either meaning "consumed by fire" or "putting out fire".

column3: パウチ カムイ(Ainu Katakana, Japanese Katakana)
column12: Ainu god (Kamuy) of insanity, said to plague humanity with stomach aches, seizures, and uncontrollable dancing.

From the name of a type of flowering tree that produces vivid orange-red blooms (scientific name Butea monosperma). This word can also mean "prospect, opportunity" and "manner, style (of speaking)", among many other definitions.
Finnish dialectal pet form of Paulus.
Variant of the name Paulina, influenced by the spelling of the name Laina.
Lithuanian form of Paulus (see Paul). Also compare Paulius and Povilas.
Contemporary Basque form of Paula, as proposed by Sabino Arana in his 'Santoral vasco'. In the Middle Ages, however, Paule was a masculine name, thus a form of Paul.
Lithuanian form of Paula, which is the feminine form of Paulus (see Paul). Also compare Povilė.
Silesian diminutive of Paweł via German Paul.
Gascon and Provençal form of Paulette.
Transferred use of the surname Pauley.
Combination of Paul and the Norse name element fríðr "beautiful" or friðr "peace, protection".
German variant of Pauline, intended to reflect a bona fide French pronunciation.
A Belarusian form of Paulina and variant of Palina.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Paulinus. This name was borne by a Roman senator and consul from the 3rd century AD, as well by the younger brother of Saint Jerome (4th century AD).
Corsican and Sicilian form of Paulinus.
Possibly a feminine form of Paul.
Diminutive of Paviel. This name has been borne by a number of Belarusian poets, such as Paŭliuk Šukajla (1904-1939) and Paŭliuk Trus (1904-1929).
Variant of Paul recorded in the 16th century.
Form of Paulus (see Paul) used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.
From the name of the genus of flowering plants which were named after the Russian-Dutch queen Anna Pavlovna/Anna Paulowna.
Transferred use of the surname Paulson.
Variant of Pauline or feminization of Paul with the popular suffix -lyn.

Medieval Limburgish variant of Palm, which was likely influenced by Old French paume meaning "palm" and paumier meaning "palmer" (as in, a medieval Christian pilgrim).Today, the name is no longer in use, but it still survives in the patronymic surname Paumen, which is still primarily prevalent in the Limburgish language area.
Derived from Romanian păun "peacock". The name was borne by Păuna Greceanu-Cantacuzino, a Princess consort of Wallachia.
Derived from Bulgarian, Macedonian and Serbo-Croatian паун (paun) "peacock".
Derived from Sanskrit पौण्ड्र (pauṇḍra) referring to the conch shell of the Hindu god Bhima.
Latinized form of Pausikakos. A notable bearer of this name was saint Pausicacus of Synnada (died around 606 AD).

Derived from the Greek adjective παυσίκακος (pausikakos) meaning "ending evils", which consists of the Greek noun παῦσις (pausis) meaning "stopping, ceasing" and the Greek noun κάκη (kake) meaning "wickedness, vice". Also compare the Greek adjective κακός (kakos) meaning "bad".

Derived from the Greek adjective παυσίλυπος (pausilypos) meaning "ending pain", which consists of the Greek noun παῦσις (pausis) meaning "stopping, ceasing" and the Greek noun λύπη (lype) meaning "pain, suffering" as well as "grief, sadness".
Latinized form of Pausilypos. This was the name of a 2nd-century Christian martyr who miraculously escaped imprisonment after being sentenced to death, but died of his injuries soon after.
Malay and Indonesian form of Fawzi.
Malay and Indonesian form of Fawzia.
Possibly a feminine form of Pavel.
From Sanskrit प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".
The name of a minor Roman goddess, who protects against childhood fears (pavor), protects against sudden fright and comforts those who have been frightened.

Medieval English name of uncertain origin and meaning. Current theories include a derivation from Old French pavie "peach" and a derivation from Old French Pavie "woman from Pavia", a historic city in Italy. Modern-day scholars theorize that the name of said city might be derived from Italian papia "of a pope".In modern times, this name has been occasionally found again since the 19th century.
From Pavi Elle, the name of a 1983 Avon perfume.
Means "pure", potentially a masculine form of Pavitra. Notably used by Pavitr Prabhakar.
From Sanskrit पवित्र (pavitra) meaning "pure, holy, sacred, purifying, averting evil".
Modern Greek diminutive of Pavlos, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.
Diminutive of Pavel or Pavao.It was borne as a surname by Croatian writer Mihovil Pavlek Miškina (1887-1942).
Diminutive of Pavla, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Modern Greek spelling of Paulinos, which is the ancient Greek form of Paulinus.
Diminutive of Pavla and Pavlina. Also compare Pavluška.
Diminutive of Pavla and Pavlina. Also compare Pavluša.
Derived from Jèrriais pavot "poppy" (ultimately from Latin papāver). This is a newly coined name, intended as a Jèrriais equivalent of Poppy.
Russian variant of Pavsikakiy and Ukrainian form of Παυσικακίος (Pausikakios), which is an extremely rare variant of Pausikakos.
Serbian form of Παυσικακίος (Pausikakios), which is an extremely rare variant of Pausikakos.
Russian form of Παυσικακίος (Pausikakios), which is an extremely rare variant of Pausikakos.

Armenian form of Faustus via its hellenized (ancient Greek) form Phaustos. Also compare Favstos, which is the modern Greek spelling of the latter name.This name was borne by an Armenian historian from the 5th century AD.

Paw refers to the soft foot of a mammal or other animal, generally a quadruped, that has claws or nails; comparable to a human hand or foot. It is a modern name in the US and first appeared in the name records in 2008.
Means "smoke, dust" in Māori and Moriori. Pawa is a figure from Māori mythology. This was also the name of a Moriori elder Pawa Ngamunanga Kahuki.
From the given name Pawan and Sanskrit प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".

column12: Variant transcription of Thai ภาวัฒน์ or ภวัต (see Phawat).
Alternate transcription of Thai ปวีณ (see Pawin).
Alternate transcription of Thai ปวีณา (see Pawina).
Form of Paweł used outside of Poland.
Means "white hair" from Osage paha "hair" and skah "white".
Means "wise, clever, skilled" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रवीण (pravīṇa).
From Javanese pawira meaning "hero, warrior, brave".
Welsh and Cornish form of Paulus (see Paul).
From the name of the Pawnee, an Indigenous people of the Great Plains in the United States.
Upper Sorbian and Silesian form of Paul and medieval Polish variant of Paweł. Jan Pawoł Nagel (German: Jan Paul Nagel), born 1934, was a Sorbian conductor.
Transferred use of the surname Paxson.
Derived from Uzbek paxta meaning "cotton, cotton plant" and gul meaning "rose, flower".
Variant or feminine form of Paxton.
From Kurdish payedar meaning "existing, lasting", or, possibly, paye meaning "admiration" and dar meaning "tree, wood".
Combination of Pa, Yeeb, and Xa.
Means "one who knows the secrets of the Sioux" in Cree.
Manx palatalized form of Paul, probably introduced from Scotland.
From the Armenian word փայլակ (pʿaylak) meaning "the light emitted by a lightning strike; brilliance, radiance".
From the Armenian փայլ (payl) meaning "shine, splendour, lustre" and անուշ (anush) meaning "sweet".
Alternate transcription of Persian پیمان (see Peyman).
Transferred use of the surname Payne.
Alternate transcription of Thai พยอม (see Phayom).

Payoshni is an ancient river mentioned in the epic Mahabharata. Pandavas had visited this place as part of their pilgrimage. It lies in the territory of Vidarbha. Payoshni is mentioned as lying in the northern entrance of the great Dandaka Forest an ancient forest that is spread throughout south-central India.
Derived from the Tatar байрам (bayram) meaning "holiday" and гол (gol) meaning "flower".
Derived from the Tatar байрам (bayram) meaning "holiday" and сул (sul) meaning "beautiful".
Transferred use of the surname Payson.
Means "fire" in Lakota. From the Lakota pȟéta (pay'-tah) 'fire'.

Of Australian Aboriginal origin (Pintupi, to be precise), the meaning of this name is not yet known to me at the moment. A known bearer of this name is Payu Napaltjarri (b. circa 1952), an Australian Aboriginal artist who also happens to be the sister of fellow artists Yakari Napaltjarri (b. circa 1925) and Parara Napaltjarri (c. 1944-2003).
Rusyn diminutive of Pelagiya (Пелаґія) or Paraskeva (Параскева).
Short form of Pascuala, Pacencia, and other names starting with a similar sound. Usage of this name is inspired by the Spanish word and name "Paz 1" meaning "peace".
Variant of Pezaine, a French corruption of Perseveranda. The 8th-century saint Perseveranda is known as Pazanne in the region of Nantes (France).
Diminutive of names containing the name element badu "battle", e.g., Baduhilt.
Means "my gold" in Hebrew, a diminutive of Paz 2.
Combination of Paz 2 and El means "gold of God" in Hebrew, also used as a surname.
Possibly the Uygur form of Fadl.
Combination of the names Paz 2 and Or means "golden light" in Hebrew.
Pazt is a latinised version of the Polish Piast, used in the chronicles of Gallus Anonimus.
This is the name of one of the main characters in the Studio Ghibli movie, "Castle in the Sky".

Etymology unknown. Pazuzu is a Mesopotamian demonic deity linked to destructive winds. He is typically depicted with a dog-like face and protruding eyes, a scaled body, a snake-headed phallus, birdlike talons, and often a pair of wings.
A short form of Petra.The German singer Pe Werner bears this name.
Variant of Pero. The name coincides with Piedmontese pé "foot".
Truncated form of names that end in -pea such as Ampea or Poppea. This name has been in use since the 19th century.
From Anglo-Norman pesible, peisible, Middle French paisible, from pais (“peace”) + -ible; Meaning, "free from argument or conflict; peaceful."

Derived from the name of the fruit, which itself derived its name from Late Latin persica, which came from older Latin malum persicum meaning "Persian fruit." In popular culture, this is the name of the Nintendo video game character Princess Peach, whom Mario often rescues from the evil Bowser.

Literally derived from the English word peaches, which is the plural form of peach, the fruit. It is derived from Late Middle English from Old French pesche, from medieval Latin persica, from Latin persicum, meaning "Persian apple".
Combination of the word peach and the popular suffix -lyn.
Blend of the phrase "peach tree" and Anna.
Likely from the American English slang meaning "fine; excellent".
Old English name of unknown meaning, likely of Brittonic Celtic origin. A notable bearer was Peada of Mercia, son of Penda.
Romansh form of Peter, traditionally found in central Grisons.
From Chinese 平 (píng) meaning "peace".Special thanks to Rose Yuen.

Back-formation from pease, originally an uncountable noun meaning "peas" that was construed as a plural, combined with Middle English nute, note, from Old English hnutu, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts (“nut”) (compare West Frisian nút, Dutch noot, German Nuss, Danish nød, Swedish nöt, Norwegian nøtt), from Proto-Indo-European *knew- (compare Irish cnó, Latin nux (“walnut”), Albanian nyç (“a gnarl”)).
Latinate form of Pearl; in some cases it may also be a borrowing of Perla.
a spelling variant of Pearline used chiefly by African Americans
Combination of Pearl and the popular suffix -etta.
Anglicized form of Perlette. A known bearer of this name is Pearlette Louisy (b. 1946), the Governor-General of the Caribbean island of Saint Lucia.
Transferred use of the surname Pearley.
Anglicized form of Perline. Also compare Perlina.
Anglicized variant of Perlita, or a combination of Pearl and the Spanish diminutive suffix -ita (to mean "little pearl").
Combination of Pearl and Lynn, primarily used as a Western name in Singapore.

From English pea's blossom, referring to the small flower of a pea plant. This name was used by Shakespeare in his comedy 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' (1595), where it belongs to one of the servants to the fairy queen Titania.

Pebbles Flintstone is a character in the classic American cartoon series The Flintstones (1960-1966). The series and the character are largely responsible for the occasional use of this name from the latter 20th century onwards.
From the smooth brown tree nut.

Old Prussian god of Hell and darkness, often compared to Greek Pluto.His name is derived from either Old Prussian pickūls "devil" or Old Prussian pyculs "hell".His servants were the so-called Pockols, flying evil spirits, often compared to the Furies of Roman Mythology.

Meaning unknown, perhaps an invented name. The American author Toni Morrison used it in her novel The Bluest Eye (1970) for the protagonist, a young African-American girl named Pecola Breedlove who descends into madness as a result of abuse.

Means "pecan" in Comanche. A noted bearer was Pecos, son of Peta and Nadua (Cynthia Ann Parker), and younger brother of Quanah.A modern bearer is American musician Pecos Hurley (1995-), the lead singer of Pecos & The Rooftops.
Pedahel Prince of the tribe of Naphtali; one of those appointed by Moses to superintend the division of Canaan amongst the tribe (Num. 34:28).
Pedahzur was a member of the house of Manasseh according to Numbers 1:10. He was the father of Gamaliel.

Means "redemption of Yahweh" or "he upgrades to the standard of Yahweh." The name of several men in the Bible, including a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. 1 Chronicles 3:18-19 lists Pedaiah as a son of King Jehoiachin and the father of Zerubbabel, although most other Biblical mentions claim that Shealtiel was Zerubbabel's father.
Georgian form of the Russian name Fedosiya.
Contraction of Pedro and the surname Arias. A famous bearer was the conquistador Pedro Arias de Ávila "Pedrarias", who founded Panama, framed Vasco Nuñez de Balboa, and had him beheaded.

Diminutive of Pedro with an added diminutive Italian suffix -lino. Pedrolino is a primo Zanni of the commedia dell'arte. Contemporary illustrations suggest that his white blouse and trousers constituted "a variant of the typical Zanni suit", and his Bergamasque dialect marked him as a member of the "low" rustic class.
Variant of Petros, influenced by the spelling of Pedro.This name is used in America among people of Armenian or Greek descent.
Konkani form of Peter, borrowed from Portuguese Pedro. Used by Konkani Catholics.
From Egyptian pꜢ-dj-bꜣstt meaning "the given of Bastet", derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with‎ dj "given" and the name of the cat goddess Bastet. This was the name of several pharaohs.
From Egyptian pꜣ-dj-ḥr (or pꜣ-dj-ḥr-mḥn) meaning "given by Horus", derived from pꜣ "the; he of" combined with dj "given" and the name of the god Horus.
Used by the Katu people of Laos and Vietnam.
Originally a short form of Peeter, used as a given name in its own right.
Phonetic spelling of the initials PJ.
Originally a diminutive of Peeter, now used as a given name in its own right.
Alternate transcription of Thai พีระ (see Phira).

column12: Form of Peter used by Malayalam-speaking Saint Thomas Christians.
Diminutive of Peer, as it contains the Dutch and Limburgian diminutive suffix -ke.A notable bearer of this name is the beatified Dutch priest Petrus "Peerke" Donders (1809-1887).
Transferred use of the surname Peerless. It coincides with an English word meaning "having no equal, matchless". A known bearer is American football player Peerless Price (1976-).

Short form of Peeter (Estonian) as well as Peter and Petrus (Afrikaans, Dutch and Limburgish).This name is extremely rare as an official name on birth certificates; it is primarily used informally for men who are officially named one of the names mentioned above.

This is the name of the male protagonist in Suzanne Collins' young adult novel "The Hunger Games" and its sequels. Collins has never stated how she came up with the name but it has been speculated that it is related to pita bread, given that the character was born into a family of bakers, or that it could be a form of Peter.

When borne by a female person, this name is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Peet) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix -je to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix. Also compare Pietje.In the past, which is as recently as the first half of the 20th century, Peetje was also a familial nickname based on one's status as a peetouder ("godparent"). In Dutch, a male godparent can be called peetvader ("godfather") as well as peetoom ("god-uncle"), whereas a female godparent can be called peetmoeder ("godmother") as well as peettante ("god-aunt").

Peeush means amrita, the nectar(drink) which makes someone immortal. This word is derived from Sanskrit word(पीयूष) originally. It is used in India in Hindi speaking regions. And its variation Piyush can be found more commonly all over India.
Nickname denoting someone of small stature.
Means "his breath (comes from) the arms of Bastet" in Egyptian.
Possibly a combination of the diminutive of Margaret, Peg, with Margaret?
Extended form of Pegasos (see Pegasus). Also compare Pegasios.
Variant of Pegasos (see Pegasus). Also compare Pegasias.
Latinized form of Pegasios. St. Pegasius was a Persian Christian and ordained priest who was arrested and slain for the faith during the reign of King Shapur II. His feastday is on November 2nd.
Italian and Spanish form of Pegasus.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Pegasus.
Elaboration of Peggy, used as a diminutive of Margaret.
Diminutive of Pagona and Pelagia influenced by the unrelated English name Peggy.
Ancient Egyptian masculine name meaning "At (his) end there's good".
Means "sings good, sings nice" in Cheyenne.

column12: From Chinese 培 (péi) meaning "foster, cultivate, nourish", 配 (pèi) meaning "match, join, deserve", 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full, copious" or 佩 (pèi) meaning "wear, admire", as well as other characters that are pronounced similarly.
From the Chinese 珮 (pèi) meaning "jade ornament" and 冰 (bīng) meaning "ice".
Gaelic form of Pic, or derived from Old English peac "thickset man".
Wade-Giles romanisation of Peizhen, used in Taiwan.
From Chinese 佩 (pèi) meaning "to wear, to respect" combined with 凡 (fán) meaning "ordinary". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 佩芬, 沛芬, 培汾, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 佩 (pèi) meaning "pendant, ornament, to wear, to hang from the waist", 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full, copious" or 培 (péi) meaning "foster, cultivate" combined with 芬 (fēn) meaning "fragrance, aroma, perfume" or 汾 (fén) referring to the Fen River in Shanxi province. Other character combinations can form this name as well.
Diminutive of Mairéad or Maighread. This was borne by Irish memoirist Máiréad "Peig" Sayers (1873-1958).
Irish pet form of Mairead or Maighread.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 虹 (hóng) meaning "rainbow".
From 佩 (pèi) meaning "belt ornament, pendant" and 瑚 (hú) meaning "coral".
From 霈 (pèi) meaning "heavy rain" and 冀 (jì) meaning "to wish, to hope" .
From 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full copious" and 珈 (jiā), referring to a type of ornament worn on a woman's hairpin.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 瑾 (jǐn) meaning "brilliance of gems, fine jade".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 晶 (jīng) meaning "crystal".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 娟 (juān) meaning "beautiful, graceful".

Meaning uncertain. It could be derived from Finnish peikko "troll" or poika "boy" (the Swedish word for boy, pojke, is derived from the Finnish word). The name appears in folk tales in the Swedish-speaking parts of Finland.In Denmark, Peik is a Frisian diminutive of Pay, a form of Paulus. Norwegian author Barbra Ring used it in her novel "Peik" where it was a short form of Pavel.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 蓝 (lán) meaning "blue, blueness".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 丽 (lì) meaning "beautiful".
From Chinese 佩 (pèi) meaning "to wear, to respect" or 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full, swift" combined with 玲 (líng) meaning "tinkling of jade, exquisite". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
Alternate transcription of Persian پیمان (see Peyman).
Alternate transcription of Persian پیمانه (see Peymaneh).
From Chinese 培 (péi) meaning "to cultivate, to educate" and 萌 (méng) meaning "bud, sprout".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 妙 (miào) meaning "mysterious, subtle, exquisite".
From the Shipibo pei meaning "wing, feather, leaf" and the genitive suffix -n.
From 培 (péi) meaning "to cultivate, to educate, to foster" or 佩 (pèi) meaning "belt ornament, pendant" combined with themselves. Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 娆 (ráo) meaning "graceful, charming".
Transferred use of the surname Pierce.

The name of a naiad of a freshwater spring of the same name, located in Corinth, in Greek mythology. She had twin sons, Cenchrias and Leches, by the god Poseidon, and dissolved into a fountain of tears to form the eponymous spring upon hearing of her son’s accidental death. Possibly derived from Ancient Greek πειραίνω (peiraino) meaning "fastened by the ends, tied fast" or "to bring to an end, accomplish", perhaps referring to a road linking the twin ports of Corinth, or to a myth in which Bellerophon yoked Pegasus beside her spring. Alternatively, could derive from πεῖρα (peira) meaning "trial, attempt, experience", or from πείρω (peiro) meaning "to pierce, run through".
Saint Peirio was a 6th-century pre-congregational saint of Wales and a child of King Caw of Strathclyde.
Derived from either πεῖρα (peira) meaning "trial, attempt" and θοός  (thoos) meaning "quick, swift" or περί (peri) meaning "around; exceedingly" and θέω (theo) meaning "to run, to fly".
Medieval Spanish, medieval Occitan and Aragonese form of Peter.
Gascon and Provençal form of Petronilla.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)".The second element of this name is derived from either the Greek verb ἀγορεύω (agoreuo) meaning "to orate, to speak publicly" or the Greek noun ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly" as well as "market, marketplace".Also compare the Greek name Peithagoras, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

Variant form of Pisander, which is the main latinized form of Peisandros (as Greek names starting with Peis- are usually latinized to Pis-, another example of this is Peisistratos, which becomes Pisistratus in Latin).A known bearer of this name was the epic poet Peisander of Camirus, who lived in the 7th century BC.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from Greek ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".Also compare the Greek name Peithandros, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".Also compare the Greek name Peithanor, which is closely related and essentially means the same.This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of which is one of the many suitors of Penelope.

column12: Wade-Giles romanization of Peishan used in Taiwan.

From Chinese 培 (péi) meaning "foster, cultivate, nourish", 配 (pèi) meaning "match, join, deserve", 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full, copious" or 佩 (pèi) meaning "wear, admire", and 时 (shí) meaning "time, era, season", 实 (shí) meaning "real, honest", 史 (shǐ) meaning "history" or 石 (shí) meaning "stone".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 姝 (shū) meaning "beautiful girl".
Feminine form of Peisianax. In Greek mythology, Peisianassa is a Tyrian maid who attends to Semele.

Derived from either Greek πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion" (both ultimately derived from πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)") and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord, king".

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people".Also compare the Greek name Peithidemos, which is closely related and essentially means the same.
Latinized form of Peisidike. This name is borne by several characters in Greek mythology, most of whom are princesses.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, judgement" as well as "custom, usage".This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, most of whom are princesses.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun λαός (laos) meaning "(the) people".Also compare the Greek name Peitholaos, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek noun πεῖσα (peisa) meaning "obedience" or the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion". Both words are ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun νόος (noos) meaning "mind".In Greek mythology, this is the name of a siren, who is also known as Peisithoe.

Derived from the Greek noun πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion" as well as "affection, susceptibility". It is ultimately derived from Greek πείσομαι (peisomai), which is the first-person singular future middle indicative of the Greek verbs πάσχω (pascho) meaning "to undergo, to experience, to feel (an emotion)" and πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)".A known bearer of this name is Peisis of Thespiae, the leader of the 292 BC revolt against Macedonian rule.In Greek mythology, Peisis is the name of a Trojan captive woman, who might possibly have been a daughter of king Priam of Troy.

Derived from Ancient Greek πεῖσις (peisis) meaning "persuasion", ultimately from πείθω (peitho) "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)", and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army". Also compare the name Peithostratos, which is closely related and essentially has the same meaning.This name was borne by an ancient Greek tyrant of Athens from the 6th century BC, as well as by two characters in Greek mythology.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 桃 (táo) meaning "peach".

Derived from Ancient Greek πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)" combined with either ἀγορεύω (agoreuo) meaning "to orate, to speak publicly" or ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly, marketplace" as well as "speech".Also compare the Greek name Peisagoras, which is closely related and essentially means the same.This name was borne by a Macedonian seer and general from the 4th century BC.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek adjective πειθός (peithos) meaning "persuasive" as well as "obedient", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from Greek ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".Also compare the Greek name Peisandros, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

Derived from the Greek noun πειθάνωρ (peithanor) meaning "obeying men", which consists of the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".Also compare the Greek name Peisenor, which is closely related and essentially means the same.
Peitharchia is the personification of obedience in Greek mythology. She is sometimes depicted as the wife of Soter (who is otherwise the husband of Praxidike), where their daughter is Eupraxia.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek adjective πειθός (peithos) meaning "persuasive" as well as "obedient", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people".Also compare the Greek name Peisidemos, which is closely related and essentially means the same.
Latinized form of Peithidemos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 3rd century BC.

Derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)".In Greek mythology, this was the name of the daimon (spirit) of persuasion, seduction and charming speech. In a more forceful incarnation, she could also symbolize forced inducement, rape and bridal abduction. She was a companion of Aphrodite and her symbols were a white dove and a ball of binding twine.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek adjective πειθός (peithos) meaning "persuasive" as well as "obedient", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun λαός (laos) meaning "(the) people".Also compare the Greek name Peisilaos, which is closely related and essentially means the same.
Latinized form of Peitholaos. This was the name of an ancient Greek tyrant of Pherae, who lived in the 4th century BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". Not to be confused with Python. This name was borne by two satraps from the 4th century BC: one was a satrap of India and the other was a satrap of Media.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek adjective πειθός (peithos) meaning "persuasive" as well as "obedient", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".Also compare the Greek name Peisistratos, which is closely related and essentially means the same.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, copious, sudden" and 婷 (tíng) meaning "pretty, graceful".
Meaning unknown. Possibly from Finnish peitsi meaning "lance" and “pace (gait of a horse)”.
Derived from Sami peivas "son of the day".
From the Chinese 霈 (pèi) meaning "torrential rains" and 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns".

column3: 培信, 培新, 沛欣, 培鑫, 佩鑫, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 培 (péi) meaning "to cultivate, to educate" combined with 信 (xìn) meaning "trust, believe" or 新 (xīn) "fresh, new". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 珮 (pèi) meaning "jade ornament" and 幸 (xìng) meaning "luck, favour, fortunately".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" or 佩 (pèi) meaning "belt ornament, pendant" and 璇 (xuán) meaning "beautiful jade, star" or 炫 (xuàn) meaning "shine, glitter".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full, copious, sudden" and 雪 (xuě) meaning "snow".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 燕 (yàn) meaning "swallow (bird)".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 瑶 (yáo) meaning "precious jade".
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 怡 (yí) meaning "happy, joyful".

column3: 佩愉, 培愉, 佩玉, 培玉, 佩雨, 培雨, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 佩 (pèi) meaning "belt ornament, pendant" or 培 (péi) meaning "foster, cultivate, nourish" combined with 愉 (yú) meaning "pleasant, delightful" or 玉 (yù) meaning "jade, precious stone, gem" or 雨 (yǔ) meaning "rain". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full" and 媛 (yuàn) meaning "beauty, beautiful woman". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 沛 (pèi) meaning "abundant, full, copious, sudden" and 悦 (yuè) meaning "pleased, contented".
Feminine form of Pejo. It was also occasionally used as a diminutive of Pelagija.
Etymology uncertain, perhaps an alternate transcription of Kurdish pêçan meaning "bandage".
Means "open-eyed, eye-opener" in Hebrew, from the root פקח (peqah) “to open one's eyes, to give sight to”. This was the name of the eighteenth and penultimate king of Israel.

From the Hebrew name פְּקַחְיָה (Pəqaḥya) meaning "Yahweh has opened the eyes", from the roots פֶּקַח (peqah) "to open (one's eyes)" and יָה (yah) referring to the Hebrew God. This was the name of the seventeenth king of Israel, the son of Menahem.
Derived from Turkish pek meaning "many, much" and can meaning "life, soul".
Hawaiian form of Becky and Betsy / Betty.
French form of Pelagios via Pelagius.
Estonian and German transcription of Russian Пелагея (see Pelageya).
Hungarian and Portuguese form of Pelagia.
Gascon form and Provençal variant of Pelagia.
Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian form of Pelagios via Pelagius.
Italian and Spanish form of Pelagios via Pelagius.
Polish and Kashubian form of Pelagius.
Bulgarian and Russian form of Pelagios (see Pelagius).
Means "of the sea", derived from Ancient Greek πέλαγος (pelagos) meaning "sea".
Possibly a derivative of Peleg, with a suffix of unknown origin.
Catalan and Aragonese form of Pelagius.

Means "Pelasgian, of Pelasgia" in Ancient Greek, of uncertain etymology, probably pre-Greek in origin. This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including the eponymous ancestor of the Pelasgian people.
Pelatiah, meaning "Refugee of God" Ezekiel 11:1, son of Benaiah, a prince of the people, among the 25 Ezekiel saw at the East Gate; he fell dead upon hearing the prophecy regrarding Jerusalem.

The meaning of 'Pelda' is beginning of spring. In Kurdish 'Pel' means tree leaf and 'da' means giving. After the winter ends, the leaves start to grow from the branches of the trees, you understand that spring has come, and this is what the name Pelda means.

Famous bearer of this name is Pelé (Born as Edson Arantes do Nascimento) and is widely regarded as the greatest player of all time.He received the nickname "Pelé" during his school days, when it is claimed he was given it because of his pronunciation of the name of his favorite player, local Vasco da Gama goalkeeper Bilé, which he misspoke but the more he complained the more it stuck. In his autobiography, Pelé stated he had no idea what the name means, nor did his old friends.
Means "dove, pigeon" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a Cypriot woman who killed herself after her husband, Melos, hung himself, and was changed into a dove by Aphrodite.
Croatian and Serbian form of Peleus.
Hawaiian form of Frederick and Fred.
Hawaiian, Samoan, and Tongan form of Blake.
Italian and Spanish form of Peleus.
French form of Peregrinus and variant of Pérégrin.
Peleth, of the Tribe of Reuben, was the father of On, a participant in Korah’s rebellion against Moses according to Numbers 16:1.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Peleus.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Peleus.
Derived from Kurdish pelên meaning "petals" and gula meaning "rose".

Of uncertain etymology. Probably from Pelgo, Pelkko, which means "God-fearing" in Finnish. The name was born by the elder of the small Finno-Ugric tribe of Izhora circa 1240. An associate of Alexander Nevsky.
Transferred usage of the surname Pelham.
Derived from Hebrew פלא (péle) meaning "miracle, wonder".

Means "hazards, perils, dangers" in Spanish, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de los Peligros, meaning "The Virgin of the Hazards."She is venerated at the neoclassical niche just near the Puente de los Peligros in Murcia.

Possibly means "fighter" or "the brightest" in Guanche. This name was borne by a mencey (leader) of the menceycato (kingdom) of Adeje, in the island of Tenerife, at the time of the conquest of the island in the 15th century. However, modern historians claim that this name was invented by Spanish poet Antonio de Viana for his poem La Conquista de Tenerife.
French form of Pelleas used by Belgian playwright Maurice Maeterlinck for a character in his play Pelléas and Mélisande (1893), which was later adapted by Claude Debussy into an opera (1902).

"Pellegan" might be a variant of "pelican," referencing the bird. In symbolic terms, pelicans are often associated with self-sacrifice and nurturing due to ancient legends about their behavior. A family with this name might have once been known for their generosity or protective nature.
Derived from Finnish word pelto "field". In Finnish mytholofy Pellervo (also known as Sampsa Pellervoinen) was a god of fertility, fields and crops.
In Roman mythology, Pellonia was a goddess who was believed to protect people from their enemies by driving the latter off. Her name likely derives from Latin pello "to hit, push, thrust off"
Derived from Albanian pëllumbeshë "dove, pigeon; (endearing) child, daughter".
Perhaps a feminine form of Pelops. In Greek mythology this was the name of several women, including the mother of Aegisthus, whose grandfather was Pelops.

Means "son of Pelops" in Greek, derived from the name Pelops combined with ίδας (idas), which is the Aeolic and Doric Greek form of the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This name was notably borne by an important Greek statesman and general (4th century BC) from the city of Thebes in the Greek region of Boeotia.
Derived from Kurdish pelçima meaning "leaf" and şîn meaning "blue".
Borne by the titular character of the cartoon Pelswick (2000-2002).
Diminutive of Pelagiya or Pelahiya and variants.
From Tibetan པདྨ (pdma) meaning "lotus", ultimately from Sanskrit पद्म (padma).

From Tibetan པདྨ (pdma) meaning "lotus" and འབྱུང་གནས ('byung gnas) meaning "origin, source", a calque of Sanskrit पद्मसम्भव (padmasambhāva). This is the Tibetan name for the Buddhist mystic Padmasambhava.

Allegedly an Australian Aboriginal name of Bundjalung origin. This is borne by Pemau Stone Bancroft (2018-), daughter of Australian actress Yael Stone and Jack Manning Bancroft; his mother, artist Bronwyn Bancroft, "has said that her great-great-great-grandmother Pemau was one of only two or three survivors from her clan (the Djanbun clan of the Bundjalung nation), the rest murdered when their land was settled by a white farmer."
Transferred use of the surname Pemberley. This also coincides with the fictional estate owned by one of the characters in Jane Austen's 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice.
Transferred use of the surname Pemberton.
Transferred use of the surname Pembroke.
Variant of Pamela, reflecting the English pronunciation.

Meaning unknown. A possible variant of Emma or a diminutive of Pamela, or possibly derived from the surname Pemma, of unknown meaning or origin.Television actor David Krumholtz and his wife gave this name to his daughter in 2014.
Alternate transcription of Tibetan སྤེན་པ (see Pemba).
From Egyptian pȝ-msḥ meaning "the crocodile", derived from the masculine prefix pȝ "the aforementioned; the; he of" combined with mzḥ "crocodile".

The name of a prominent Bidjigal Aboriginal warrior of the Eora nation who lead a resistance against Sydney colonists in the 1790s - 1800s. He was also considered a carradhy or ‘clever man’. He convinced many surrounding Aboriginal nations to join his resistance against the British and was considered to be exceptional in most everything he did.

Means "rock" in Spanish, taken from the Spanish titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de la Peña and Nuestra Señora de la Peña, meaning "The Virgin of the Rock" and "Our Lady of the Rock" respectively.
Originally a variant of Benjamin. Rare as a given name, but is often used as a pet name for Pentti.

Taken from the Spanish titles of the Virgin Mary, Nuestra Señora de Peñafrancia/Nuestra Señora de la Peña de Francia and La Virgen de la Peña de Francia, meaning "The Virgin of the Rock of France" and "Our Lady of the Rock of France" respectively, venerated in Naga City though originating from the image enshrined in Salamanca, Spain.
Means "chief beauty" or "most fair", derived from the Welsh elements pen "head, chief, foremost" and arddun "fair, beautiful". In Welsh mythology she was a wife of the sea-god Llyr.
Taken from the title of the Virgin Mary, Nuestra Señora de Peñarroya, meaning "Our Lady of Peñarroya."She is the patroness of Argamasilla de Alba in the central Spanish province of Ciudad Real.
Alternate transcription of Tibetan སྤེན་པ (see Pemba).
Old English name of unknown meaning, possibly of Brythonic (Celtic) origin. This was the name of a famous king of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia (7th century).
Means "thought, visualisation" in Persian. Usage may be influenced by the Persian phrase پندار نیک (pendâr-i nik) "good thoughts", which describes one of the three pillars of Zoroastrianism.
Transferred use of the surname Pendleton.

Old English name deriving from Old English personal name Penda of unknown origin, and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom". A notable bearer was Pendred the Moneyer, a minter who lived during the reign of King Offa of Mercia.

Transferred use of the surname Pendragon.The surname of Kings Arthur and Uther, meaning “head dragon” or “dragon’s head.” As first told by Geoffrey of Monmouth, Uther adopted the symbol of the dragon because of the comet with the dragon’s head that Merlin had seen in Wales, heralding the death of King Ambrosius Aurelius, Uther’s brother. In Welsh legend, it is also the surname of one “Gwen Pendragon,” who once kept Arthur prisoner. In the Prose and Vulgate Merlins, the name Pendragon is given to the character elsewhere called Ambrosius Aurelianus: the son of Constantine and Ivoire, the uncle of Arthur, and the king of Britain between Vortigern and Uther, Pendragon’s brother. Pendragon allied with Merlin, defeated Vortigern and Hengist, died fighting the Saxons, and was buried at Stonehenge. Uther is said to have adopted his brother’s name as a surname in memory of the slain king.Source: Christopher Bruce's Arthurian Name Dictionary
Hawaiian, Māori and Samoan form of Benjamin.
The name of an early Egyptian queen, meaning "Seat of the Two Lords".

Derived from Ancient Greek λεώς (leos), the Attic form of λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk", and an uncertain first element; possibilities include Πηνειός (Peneus), the name of a Thessalian river and its deity, πήνη (pene) meaning "thread, bobbin, spool", or the related πένομαι (penomai) meaning "to toil, labour, work". This was the name of a suitor of Helen of Troy and soldier in the Trojan War in Greek mythology. An asteroid was named after him.
The name of a character from Final Fantasy who is a friend of Vaan's.
Epic form of Penelope. Homer's epic the 'Odyssey' was written in Epic Greek (or Homeric Greek).
Italian and Spanish form of Peneus.
Feminine form of Per using the popular suffix netta, found in such names as Annette and Jeanette.

Latinized form of Greek Πηνειός (Peneios), most likely derived from Proto-Indo-European *pen- meaning "wet, mire, swamp, mud, water". The Indo-European root *(s)pen- "to spin" has also been suggested as a possible root, via either Ancient Greek πῆνος (pēnos) "web" or πήνη (pēnē) "thread, weft". In Greek mythology, Peneus was a Thessalian river god, the son of Oceanus and Tethys.
Diminutive of any name containing the sounds /f/ or /p/.
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 晨 (chén) meaning "early morning, daybreak".
From Chinese 鹏 (péng) referring to a large, legendary bird in Chinese mythology combined with 飞 (fēi) meaning "to fly". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 朋锋, 朋奉, etc.(Chinese)|朋鋒, 朋奉, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" combined with 锋 (fēng) meaning "pointed edge" or 奉 (fèng) meaning "offer, receive, serve, respect". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 花 (huā) meaning "flower".
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 慧 (huì) meaning "bright, intelligent".
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 娟 (juān) meaning "beautiful, graceful".

column3: 朋坤, 鹏坤, 朋昆, 鹏昆, etc.(Chinese)|朋坤, 鵬坤, 朋昆, 鵬昆, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" or 鹏 (péng), referring to a giant bird in Chinese mythology combined with 坤 (kūn) meaning "earth, female" or 昆 (kūn) meaning "elder brother". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From Chinese 鹏 combined with 理. Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 路 (lù) meaning "road, path, journey".
Means "teaching sage". In Tolkien's Legendarium this is the name of the in-universe author of The Silmarillion.

column3: 朋朋, 鹏鹏, 蓬蓬, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" or 鹏 (péng), referring toa large bird in Chinese mythology or 蓬 (péng) meaning "flourishing, prospering, vigorous" combined with themselves. Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 轻 (qīng) meaning "easy, light, gentle".

column3: 朋瑞, 鹏瑞, etc.(Chinese)|朋瑞, 鵬瑞, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" or 鹏 péng), refering to a large bird in Chinese mythology, combined with 瑞 (ruì) meaning "felicitous omen, auspicious". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 杉 (shān) meaning "pine, fir".
From the Chinese 芃 (péng) meaning "luxuriant growth" and 劭 (shào) meaning "encourage, excel".
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful, tranquil".

column3: 鹏翔, etc.(Chinese)|鵬翔, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 鹏 (péng) referring to a giant bird in Chinese mythology combined with 翔 (xiáng) meaning "soar, glide". Other hanzi combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 暄 (xuān) meaning "warm, genial".
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 雨 (yǔ) meaning "rain".
From the Chinese 朋 (péng) meaning "friend" and 园 (yuán) meaning "garden, park, orchard".
From the Chinese 捧 (pěng) meaning "hold in both hands" and 月 (yuè) meaning "moon".
Derived from Portuguese penha "cliff, rock", usually used in reference to the title of the Virgin Mary Nossa Senhora da Penha.

Means "poverty, deficiency, need" in Ancient Greek. Penia was the personification of poverty and need in Greek mythology, called the mother of Eros ("love") by Poros ("provision") in Plato’s Symposium.
Hawaiian, Māori, and Samoan form of Benjamin.
From a biblical place name (Gen 32:30) meaning "face of God".It was also the name of a protestant missionary organisation active in Alaska.
Transferred use of the surname Peniston.Bearers of this name include Peniston Lamb, 1st Viscount Melbourne, and his son, the Hon. Peniston Lamb.
Means "head, top" in Welsh. This was the name of two characters in Welsh legend. It can also come from the English surname which was from a place name meaning "hill" in Old English.
The Latin word for "feather, wing". American actor Ian Ziering has a daughter named Penna, born 2013.
Place name from Cwm Pennant and transferred use of the surname Pennant.
Alternate transcription of Thai เพ็ญนภา (see Phennapha).
Alternate transcription of Thai เพ็ญนภา (see Phennapha).
Transferred use of the surname Pennington.
Means "our God" in Coptic. The name ultimately derives from Egyptian pen "our" combined with Egyptian nuti "God".
From the name of the American state of Pennsylvania, which is composed from the surname Penn 1 after William Penn, with English sylvan "woods, forest" (after Latin silva).
Variant of Peny influenced by the unrelated English name Penny.
Likely given in reference to the Beatles' song Penny Lane.
Pennywise is the main character of Stephen King's novel 'It'. It is also known as 'Pennywise the Dancing Clown'.
Alternate transcription of Tibetan སྤེན་པ (see Pemba).

column3: เพ็ญพักตร์(Thai)

column12: Transferred use of the surname Penrose.
Derived from Welsh ap Henry meaning "son of Henry".
Used as the name of he main character in the 'Penryn and the End of Days' series by Susan Ee.
Derived from French pensée "pansy (the flower); thought, idea".
Alternate transcription of Thai เพ็ญศิริ (see Phensiri).

Possibly derived from the Greek prefix penta meaning "five". This is the name of the protagonist of the Italian fairy tale Penta of the Chopped-Off Hands (1634) by Giambattista Basile. In the story, Penta is a princess who has her hands cut off so she can escape the advances of her brother, who wants to marry her.
Meaning unknown. Pentaquod is the name of the 16th century first character in the novel 'Chesapeake' (1978) written by J.A. Michener.

From the name of the Christian festival which commemorates the descent of the Holy Ghost upon the apostles, celebrated on the fiftieth day after Easter, ultimately deriving from Greek pentekoste (hemera) "fiftieth (day)". This name was traditionally given to children born at Whitsuntide. It can also be from a nickname given to a person with some connection to that time of year, such as owing a feudal obligation then.

Greek Πεντηκοστή "the fiftieth Day", the Greek name of the Feast of Weeks, which in Christian traditions was celebrated as the feast commemorating the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.This name was usually given to children who were born or baptised on or near this feast.
Italian and Spanish form of Pentheus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Pentheus.
Feminine form of Pentheus. This was used (perhaps invented) by John Ford for a character in his tragic play 'The Broken Heart' (1633).

Derived from Ancient Greek πένθος (penthos) meaning "grief, sadness, mourning", possibly combined with λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk". In Greek mythology, Penthesilea was an Amazonian queen, daughter of Ares and Otrera, and sister of Hippolyta, Antiope and Melanippe. She led her troops to the Trojan War in support of King Priamos.

Derived from Ancient Greek πένθος (penthos) meaning "grief, sorrow, sadness, mourning". In Greek mythology, Pentheus was the name of a king of Thebes who banned the worship of Dionysos, bringing down the god’s wrath.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek πένθος (penthos) meaning "grief, sorrow, sadness, mourning" or "misery, misfortune". This was the name of two figures in Greek mythology, one a king of Messenia, the other a son of Orestes.
The Hurrian form of Belet-ekallim, which was itself the Akkadian name for the goddess Ninegal. In Hurro-Hittite texts Pentikalli is depicted as a concubine of the god Teshub.
Penumbra means the partial shadow surrounding a perfect shadow (as in an eclipse)
Diminutive of Panagiota, Panorea, Despina and Pinelopi.
Derived from Old English Peohtas "Pict" and weald "powerful, mighty" or "authority, leader". The first element refers to the Picts, an ancient Celtic people from northern and eastern Scotland.

Derived from Old English Peohtas "Pict" and wine "friend". The first element refers to the Picts, a group of peoples who lived in Britain north of the Forth–Clyde isthmus in the Pre-Viking, Early Middle Ages. This name was borne by an 8th-century Anglo-Saxon Bishop of Whithorn, in Scotland.

Unknown origin, possibly devised as a variant of Paola. It was used in Fannie Hurst's novel Imitation of Life (1933) and its 1934 film adaptation, where it belongs to a young light-skinned African American woman who decides to pass as white.
Catalan diminutive of Josep and Romansh diminutive of Gisep and Giusep traditionally found in the Lower Engadine region.
Cremish Lombard short form of Üsèpa.
Spanish and Catalan diminutive of Josefa (or María José) and Josepa respectively (feminine), as well as a Czech diminutive of Josef (masculine).
Finnish pet form of Pertti or a Finnish pet form of Pellervo.
Swedish children's book heroine Pippi Longstocking is known as Pepė Ilgakojinė in Lithuanian.
Means "Disorderly Woman", often used in the sense of a humorous nickname.
Derived from the Georgian noun პეპელა (pepela) meaning "butterfly", which is ultimately derived from the Old Georgian noun პეპელი (pepeli) meaning "butterfly".
The name of a female kitten in the 1989 novel Felidae, which was made into a 1994 German animated, film noir, mystery, featuring cats as the central characters.
Serbo-Croat form of Cinderella, from Serbo-Croat pepel "ash". Not used as given name.
Sundanese diminutive of masculine names containing the sound pen (or other similar sounds), such as Ependi.
Combination of Pepe and Ramón, used as a diminutive of the compound name José Ramón.
Diminutive of Josefa and Maria Jose.
In Latvian Pippi Longstocking is called Pepija Garzeķe.
From Egyptian ppjj-nḫt meaning "Pepi is strong", derived from the name of king Pepi II and nḫt "to be strong, victorious".
Spanish double diminutive of Joseph. Nickname of Argentinian actor José Maronne (1915-1990).

Diminutive of José (Spanish) or Josep (Catalan). Known bearers include the retired Spanish tennis player José 'Pepo' Clavet (1965-) and Spanish soccer player Josep 'Pepo' Campanera (2000-; born in Catalonia).Note, Pepe (Spanish) and Pep (Catalan) are more common than Pepo.
Diminutive of Jose, Felipe and Rafael.
Diminutive of Giuseppa, Giosepa and Giusepa.
Diminutive of Giusepa, Giuseppa and Giuseppina.
The name of Peppy Hare, a rabbit who is a member of Team Star Fox. He is later the general of the Cornerian Army.
Probably derived from Greek πεπρωμένος (pepromenos) meaning "fated". This was the name of a goddess of destiny and fate in Greek mythology.
After the carbonated cola brand. This is the name of American educational professional Marijuana Pepsi Vandyck.
Combination of the names Perach and Bar which together creates the meaning of "wildflower", this is the full name of the Israeli actress Bar Miniely (born 2001)
It means "silver". It was the fifth and most famous bendahara of the Sultanate of Malacca, Tun Perak, who served under four sultans from 1456 to 1498.
Meaning "child playing with a spatula". The name of Peramonkoro Sunazawa, Ainu activist and one of the most respected Japanese textile artists of the twentieth century.
Derived from Petrus combined with the diminutive suffix -an.

A duke of Manaheim who was saved by Erec from a pack of robbers. His brothers, Joachim, Perant, and Malcheus, were also abducted and liberated. Erec sent them to Arthur’s court to relate the adventure.

Sir Percard was the first of four brothers who had for a "long time ... holden war against the knights of the Round Table" and whom was the third knight Gareth encountered on his way to fight Sir Ironside at Castle Dangerous. After a two-hour joust and duel, Gareth killed Sir Percard and continued his adventure.The other brothers, Pertolepe, Perimones, and Persant, all became knights of the Round Table, as no doubt Percard also would have, had he survived, for on learning of his death Arthur and many knights of the court called it “great pity”.
From the English surname, Percell, and occupational surname for a swineherd.

A variant of Perceval, the knight most closely associated with the Quest for the Holy Grail. Early legends have him raised in the wilds of Wales, but others state he was the only surviving son of Evrawc, Earl of the North. There was a real Peredur, who was king of York between 560-580 AD.

A variant of Perceval, the knight most closely associated with the Quest for the Holy Grail. Early legends have him raised in the wilds of Wales, but others state he was the only surviving son of Evrawc, Earl of the North. There was a real Peredur, who was king of York between 560-580 AD.

From the Armenian word պերճ (perch) meaning "magnificent, elegant, splendid, famous".
Medieval Dutch short form of Perchevael.
Medieval Dutch variant form of Perchevael.
