From Sanskrit समर (samara) meaning "war, battle, conflict" or "coming together, meeting" combined with तुङ्ग (tuṅga) meaning "lofty, tall, high". This was the name of a 9th-century ruler of Java who oversaw the construction of the Borobudur temple.
Combination of Samar with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Invented name based on the sounds in names like Jamari, Kamari and Amari.

From the New Testament place name Samaria, which ultimately comes from the Hebrew verb שָׁמַר (shamar) meaning "to guard, to keep". (The place also appears in the Old Testament under the name שמרון (Shomron).) The 'Good Samaritan' in the story told by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke was a man from Samaria.

The use of this extremely rare name was inspired by a character from the 1992 book "Ik ook van jou" (English: "I love you too" - the literal translation is "I also of you"), who is featured much more prominently in the 2000 sequel "Ik omhels je met duizend armen" (English: "I embrace you with a thousand arms"). Both books were written by Dutch author Ronald Giphart (b. 1965) and both have been made into films. The author has stated that he derived the name from Samarinda, a major city on the Indonesian island Borneo. The city derives its name from Indonesian samarenda meaning "equal in height", which was a term originally used in reference to the way in which the Bugis people constructed their houses.

From the word Samaritan, referring to the people of Samaria. In the Bible, Luke 10:25-37 tells the parable of the Good Samaritan, where a Samaritan man helped another man who had been robbed. Because of the parable, the term “Good Samaritan” has been used to describe a charitable person who helps or assists someone else, especially a stranger.
From Latin Samaritana meaning "Samaritan, woman from Samaria".
From the Karachay-Balker шам (şam) meaning "holy, sacred", "native, dear" or "beautiful" and ариу (ariw) meaning "beautiful, good".
Variation of Samara used in reference to the novel 'Appointment in Samarra' in which Samarra refers to Samarra, Iraq.
Alternate transcription of Thai สามารถ (see Samat).
From Sanskrit समर्थ (samartha) meaning "strong, powerful, capable, suitable".
Means "Shamash created the offspring", deriving from the Akkadian element zēru ("seed; offspring; sown, arable land").
Means "capable, able to, suitable for" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit समर्थ (samartha).
From Sanskrit समता (samatā) meaning "equality, sameness, equanimity".
This Somali name means "doing good" or just "good."
Derived from Sanskrit समाधान (samādhāna) "calm, tranquility; concentration" or "unity, joining; equality, justice". This is also a form of Buddhist meditation.
Means "loftiness, highness, exaltedness" or "sky, firmament" in Arabic.
Means "tranquil, peaceful" in Sanskrit. From the Sanskrit सामय (sAmaya), from सामयति (sAmayati).
Senegalese Fula name used to denote a second-born son.
Means "skill, readiness, quick wit" in Mongolian.
Means "fortune, wealth, prosperity" in Khmer, ultimately from Sanskrit सम्पत्ति (sampatti).
Means "to enrich" or "to become rich" in Tumbuka.
Sambhaji ruled from 1681 to 1689 as the second king (Chhatrapati) of the Maratha Empire, a prominent state in early modern India. He was the eldest son of Shivaji, the founder of the Maratha Empire.

Means "lord of being" from Sanskrit सम्भव (sambhava) meaning "being, coming together, birth, origin" and नाथ (nātha) meaning "master, lord". In Jain tradition this is the name of the third of the 24 tirthankaras (enlightened spiritual teachers).
Anglicized form of Marathi-origin name referential to the Goddess Durga
Sambice was a late 5th-century Iranian noblewoman from the Sasanian dynasty, who was the sister-wife of king (shah) Kavad I.

a form of the word 'Vidya' which means wisdom/knowledge. Sum is a prefix which makes it a positive wisdom, wise, knowledgable person defined as sambid. For further reference, look into a Nepali,Hindi,Sanskrit dictionary.
Uzbek girls' name derived from the name of a type of willow.

'In its origin the name has no connection with Samuel. The meaning is uncertain, though similar words occur in several African languages, and the name itself was planted in American by African-born slaves.'In the long run it became the most common of the African names, and even came to stand as a generic name for a black. The influence of Samuel (often, Sam) was undoubtedly a factor in this popularity. Like Samuel, Sambo declined in popularity toward the end of the 19th century.'(Source: George Rippey Stewart, 1979)
From Javanese sambada meaning "suitable, fitting, appropriate", ultimately from Sanskrit संबन्ध (saṃbandha).
Derived from the Slavic name elements sam "alone; oneself" and boji "battle; to fight".
Means "to fight alone" or "alone in battle", derived from Slavic sam "alone, lone, lonely" combined with Slavic bor "battle" or borit "to fight".
From the Karachay-Balker шам (şam) meaning "holy, sacred", "native, dear" or "beautiful" and дарий (dariy) meaning "silk".
Alternate transcription of Tibetan བསམ་གྲུབ (see Samdup).
From Tibetan བསམ་གྲུབ (bsam-grub) meaning "fulfillment (of one's desires or wishes)".

As an Urdu masculine name, means "one who hears." It is a convention to use either a prefix Abdus or a suffix Ullah along the name, which gives meanings of the servant of All Hearing or hearer of God respectively.It is also used in English as a diminutive of Samuel or Samantha.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سميحة (see Samiha).

Arabic variant form (or simplified transcription) of Thameen and Persian and Urdu form of Thameen. Also compare the Arabic feminine name Samina.With that said, it should be noted that it appears that the name Sameen is strictly masculine in Arabic, whereas it is a unisex name in Persian and Urdu.
Anglicized form of Nepali-origin name meaning “beside,” “near,” or “warm”
Alternate transcription of Arabic سامحة or سميحة (see Samiha), chiefly used in Egypt.
From the Portuguese title of the Virgin Mary, Nossa Senhora do Sameiro, meaning "Our Lady of Sameiro," venerated at the sanctuary in Espinho in the municipality of Braga in northern Portugal.
Likely coined by the English poet Robert Greene in the late sixteenth century for his poem 'Samela'. Samela is most likely a reworking of Semele.
Norwegian dialectal variant of Samuline recorded in Austlandet.
Feminized elaboration of Sam 1 or Samuel using the popular name suffix -ella (Compare Samuella/Samuela 1, Samatha and Samellen).
Variant transcription of Shimri, as used in 1 Chronicles 11:45.This transcription is used in English translations of the Septuagint Bible.
Meaning "equal to a lord", from Sanskrit साम्य (samya) meaning "equality" and ईश (isha) meaning "lord, ruler"
Transferred use of the surname Sameth.
From the Karachay-Balker шам (şam) meaning "holy, sacred", "native, dear" or "beautiful".

From Irish and Scottish Gaelic Samhain, referring to the Gaelic festival, marking the end of the harvest season and beginning of winter, which is celebrated on the evening of 31st October and 1st November.
Derived from Irish samhradh "summer" combined with a diminutive suffix.

Form of Gamigin used in the 1904 version of The Lesser Key of Solomon by Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley.
Tatar version of Arabic Samiullah (سمیع اللہ), which means ”Listening to Allah”.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سامحة/سميحة (see Samiha), as well as a Malay variant.

Samiris – Significado e OrigemSamiris é um nome único e de origem incerta, escolhido originalmente por pais que gostaram de sua sonoridade. Embora não haja registros históricos da sua etimologia, o nome passou a ser associado ao significado "pequena estrela amante da lua".Esse significado reflete uma conexão especial com o céu, simbolizando brilho, delicadeza e fascinação pelo universo. "Pequena estrela" representa luz e singularidade, enquanto "amante da lua" remete à admiração pela beleza e mistério do cosmos.Por ser um nome raro, Samiris carrega um ar de exclusividade, sendo perfeito para pessoas que se identificam com o encanto das estrelas e o magnetismo da lua.

Hellenized form of Shamuna, which is a name that is likely to be of Semitic origin (e.g. Arabic, Aramaic or Hebrew). Its meaning is as of yet uncertain.The first notable bearer of this name was the Syrian saint Samonas of Edessa (died in 305 AD), who was also known under the name Shamuna. Several centuries later, Samonas was also the name of an influential Byzantine official and eunuch, who was of Arab origin and born around 875 in Melitene (now Malatya in eastern Turkey).
Possibly a variant of Samara. It was given to 16 girls born in the United States in 2011.
Derived from Gaulish samo- "calm; summer" and rīx "king".

Means "He who walks over much" in Algonquin. This was the name of an Abenaki chief. He was the first Native American to make contact with the Pilgrims at Plymouth, Massachusetts and introduced them to Tisquantum (Squanto).

Subject of a unique and darkly comical episode in the Serbo-Russian Povest’ o Tryshchane.Samsiz was a king who arrived at Arthur’s camp and challenged all of his knights. He defeated thirteen of them, including Palamedes, Lancelot, and Arthur, and took them as prisoners back to his island. Guinevere sought out Tristan’s assistance.After several adventures, Tristan, Guinevere, and Isolde arrived at the Black Island disguised as Venetians. Tristan was forced to protect the ladies from Samsiz’s lecherous subjects while devising a plan to free the king. Samsiz himself desired Isolde and offered to either fight Tristan or to play a game of chess for her.Tristan had put on a great show of being a simple merchant, and Samsiz felt he had little to fear. Tristan chose combat, and by the time Samsiz realized his mistake, Tristan had sliced off both of his hands. Tristan freed Samsiz’s prisoners.

From Latin Samuelis, which is the genitive of the third declension of Samuel, the biblical Latin form of the Hebrew name Shemu'el.In the Netherlands, this has been used as a Latin form of Samuel (thus basically making it a latinization of a latinization) since at least late medieval times.With that said, the name Samuelis is also in use in Lithuania, where it is simply the Lithuanian form of Samuel. As far as I know, the circumstances of the name are different in Lithuania than in the Netherlands, meaning that it does not derive from the Latin genitive like it does in the Netherlands.
Feminine form of Samuel and Sámuel.

In the mythology of Fiji, Samulayo is a god or spirit of war and those dead souls who died in battle. He lives in underworld.
Judeo-Anglo-Norman feminine form of Samuel and Faroese form of Samuline.

Means "simoom" in Turkish, a hot, dry, dust-laden wind blowing in the desert.
Breton form of Samson. Sant Samzun (known as Saint Samson of Dol in English, born c. late 5th century) is counted among the seven founder saints of Brittany.

From Sino-Vietnamese 產 (sản) meaning "to produce" or 㦃 (sản) meaning "perfect character, many, plenty".

A classic Turkish name traditionally connected to the root sanç- meaning "to pierce, to rout an enemy". However, alternative onomastic lineages connect it to an ancient root meaning "predatory; a type of raptor", placing it alongside traditional Turkic avian names like Doğan, Kartal, Sungur, Toygar, Turna, and Atmaca. It symbolizes sharp vision, soaring freedom, and swift justice.The name is highly celebrated through two major figures: Sultan Ahmet Sancar, the illustrious ruler of the Great Seljuk Empire known for his cultural enlightenment and military might, and the fictional Göktürk hero Sencer in the historical-epic novels of Nihal Atsız, embodying ultimate loyalty and martial honor.

Etymology unknown.Known completely as Sanddef Pryd Angel (Sanddef Angel's Form) is a figure in Welsh mythology. He is a warrior of King Arthur's court, and is distinguished by his phenomenal beauty which gives him the epithet Pryd or Bryd Angel (Angel's Form).Sanddef's beauty contrasts with the hideousness of Morfran, with whom Sanddef is associated. Both are mentioned in the medieval prose tale Culhwch ac Olwen, where it is said that they survived the Battle of Camlann due to their looks. In Sanddef's case, no one dared strike him because they thought he was "an angel helping" due to his beauty. He is further mentioned in an early poem lamenting the death of Duran fab Arthur, in which Arthur asks him to shoo a crow from his son's corpse.

A rare Lithuanian masculine name possibly derived from the Lithuanian word sąžinė, meaning "conscience", or related to sąžiningas, meaning "honest", "conscientious", or "just". The element sąžin may relate to moral awareness, while the suffix -as is a typical masculine nominative ending in Lithuanian. Though not widely attested, Sanginas may have been created in the 20th century as part of the Lithuanian national revival and name restoration movements, which encouraged native-language names reflecting virtues and ideals.

Feminine form of Sanginas, possibly derived from the Lithuanian word sąžinė, meaning "conscience", or related to sąžininga, the feminine form of sąžiningas, meaning "honest", "conscientious", or "just". The root element sąžin relates to moral awareness, and the suffix -ė is a standard feminine ending in Lithuanian names. Sanginė may have been coined during modern Lithuanian name revival efforts that emphasized virtue-based or meaning-rich names formed from native roots.

The name 'Sang-ki' has its origins in Korea, a country rich in history and culture. The earliest known use of this name dates back to ancient times, when it was commonly given to boys as a symbol of strength and resilience. The name was often bestowed upon children with the hope that they would grow up to be courageous and determined individuals. Over the years, the popularity of the name 'Sang-ki' has experienced various trends and fluctuations. While it may not be as widely used as some other names, it has maintained a steady presence throughout history. There have been notable spikes in usage during times of national pride and unity, such as during periods of Korean independence movements or significant cultural milestones. The name means benevolence and vigour.

This first name is predominantly found in South America, although it is not very common there: one is much more likely to encounter the name as a surname there instead. Because of that, it is possible that the bearers' parents were inspired to give their sons the surname as a first name, just like it is done in English-speaking countries these days. The surname is a variant form of the surname Zarco, which is ultimately derived from the Spanish word zarco meaning "light blue" (for more information, see Zarco), which is in reference to the eye colour of the surname's original bearer. However, given the fact that the word zarco is still in use in modern Spanish, it is also possible that in the case of some bearers, their parents deliberately named them after the colour, but chose to alter the spelling somewhat. It ultimately doesn't matter either way, as the etymology is the same in both scenarios. So, to make a long story short, one could say that Sarco is a variant spelling of Zarco. It is also slightly more common (as a first name) in South America than Zarco.

Probably an ancient Greek corruption of the name of the historical Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. According to the Greek writer Ctesias of Cnidus, Sardanapalus is the last king of Assyria, although in actuality Ashur-uballit II (612-605 BC) holds that distinction. Ctesias' 'Persica' is lost, but we know of its contents by later compilations and from the work of Diodorus (II.27). In this account Sardanapalus, supposed to have lived in the 7th century BC, is portrayed as a decadent figure who spends his life in self-indulgence and dies in an orgy of destruction. His legendary decadence later became a theme in literature and art, especially in the Romantic era. Though the name and dates correspond to Ashurbanipal, the story of Sardanapalus bears no similarity to the true king. The story of this ficticious king is likely an amalgamation of what was known of the end of the Assyrian empire, mixed with literary embellishments.

Derived from Greek σάρδιον (sardion), which is the name that the ancient Greeks had for carnelian, a precious stone. It is not completely certain what the ancient Greeks had derived the name from. Some sources (including Pliny the Elder) claim that the precious stone was named after the city of Sardis in Lydia, as allegedly the stone was first found there. Other sources claim that the stone's name was ultimately derived from the Persian word سرد (sered) meaning "yellowish-red". Either way, the ancient Greeks did not use Sardion as a first name - as far as I know, the use of Sardion as a first name is limited to Georgia only.

This is the name of a king in the 12th-century epic poem The Knight in the Panther's Skin written by the Georgian poet Shota Rustaveli (1172-1216). He was the father of the titular knight of the poem, namely prince Tariel of India.Sources state that the name is of Persian origin, which is hardly surprising, given that virtually all characters in Rustaveli's poem bear names of Persian origin. It is, however, unclear from which Persian root Rustaveli derived the name from. He may have derived it from Middle Persian srūdan meaning "to sing" as well as "to recite" - the modern Persian equivalent is سرودن (sorudan). An other possible derivation might be Middle Persian srāyīdan meaning "to protect". Either way, whatever the meaning is, it seems that the name Saridan never really caught on with the Georgian people; throughout the centuries, few parents were inspired to name their son Saridan. That is in sharp contrast to other names that originated from Rustaveli's poem, such as Avtandil, Darejan and Nestan, which have long been popular and remain so today.

Sarutahiko Ōkami is the name of the leader of the earthly kami, deity of the Japanese religion of Shinto. Norito also mentions him with the title Daimyōjin (great bright god, or greatly virtuous god) instead of Ōkami (great god).Sarutahiko Ōkami is seen as a symbol of Misogi, strength and guidance, which is why he is the patron of martial arts such as aikido. He enshrined at Tsubaki Grand Shrine in Mie Prefecture, first among the 2000 shrines of Sarutahiko Ōkami, Sarutahiko Jinja in Ise, Mie and Ōasahiko Shrine in Tokushima Prefecture. In the Nihon Shoki, he is the one who meets Ninigi-no-Mikoto, the grandson of Amaterasu, the Sun goddess, when he descends from Takama-ga-hara. He is depicted as a towering man with a large beard, jeweled spear, ruddy face, and long nose. At first he is unwilling to let Ninigi pass until persuaded by Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, the kami of dance and the arts, whom he later marries.His Paredros and children created the Sarume no Kimi clan along with an order of female court and religious dancers. It was the origin of Kagura and Noh. Other descendants includes the Ujitoko clan from Ise province. According to Kojiki, he went in Ise where a giant clam trapped his hand on Isuzu river at Azaka, thus he drowned. But strangely, Sarutahiko was considered by Ueshiba Morihei as a kind of god of the cosmic life : the god of Aiki. According to O-Senseï, the practice of Aikidō was practice of Misogi purification itself (and thus, like Sarutahiko standing of Ame-no-Ukibashi, standing between Heaven and Earth, being one with the Universe, and so achieving peace with the world, the next step being World Peace itself)... which doesn't fit very well this Kojiki story of Sarutahiko's death (although it is unknown if he really died from it).

From Sino-Vietnamese 察 (sát) meaning "to investigate, to notice".
Means "iron" in Vietnamese or variant of Sắc.

column3: 咲多恵, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|サタヱ(Japanese Katakana)|さたえ(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 咲 (sa) meaning "blossom", 多 (ta) meaning "many, much" combined with 恵 (e) meaning "favour". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Satan.
Greek and Latin form of Satan.

Means "mother of one-hundred (sons)" from Persian صد (sad) (through the Iranian root */sata-/) meaning "(one) hundred" combined with the Northwest Caucasian root /na/ meaning "mother" (descended into Kabardian анэ (ānă) and Adyghe ны (nə)) and the Indo-Iranian suffix /-ya/ meaning "the one who is". This refers to Satanaya’s one-hundred giant sons (Narts) in Caucasian mythology.Satanaya Guasha (or Satana) was the matriarch of the Narts (a race of giants) and an important figure in the 'Nart' sagas and Caucasian mythology. To the Ossetians, she was the daughter of the Uastyrdzhi and mother of Soslan. She was also viewed as a deity of fertility similar to the Greek Demeter but was portrayed as a goddess of crafts and women's work in Vainakh (Chechen and Ingush) belief.

Meaning unknown, although the second element of the name (hepa) likely derives from the Hurrian sun goddess Ḫepat. Name borne by a Hittite queen (1390 BC-1365 BC). Satanduhepa was the first wife of Tudhaliya III. She was replaced as queen by Daduhepa for unknown reasons.
Feminisation or Latinisation of Satan. Often associated with death metal music.
Combination of the phonetic element sa and the name Tanya, probably modelled on Latanya.

Means "one hundred years old" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit शतायुस् (śatāyus).
Meaning uncertain, perhaps a variant of Sasha. A known bearer is Honduran-American television journalist and news anchor Satcha Pretto (1980-).
Alternate transcription of Hindi सतीश (see Satish).

Possibly derived from Latin satelles "attendant, guard". A known bearer of this name was Satella Sharps (1856-1875), daughter of American gunsmith Christian Sharps (1810-1874). Another known bearer is her daughter (who was named after her mother, because she had died while giving birth to her), American author Satella Sharps Waterstone (1875-1938).

Derived from the Egyptian word sṯ, meaning "eject", "shoot", "pour" or "throw". It is the name of an Egyptian goddess and her name can be translated as "she who shoots" or "she who pours". As a warrior goddess, she protected Egypt's southern frontier by killing the pharoah's enemies with arrows; as a fertility goddess, she granted the wishes of those who sought love.
Brother of King Netor of Bulgaria.
Means "long-lasting, enduring, stable, steadfast" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit स्थावर (sthāvara).
Alternate transcription of Thai สถาพร (see Sathaphon).

Means "stability, constancy, security". From Thai เสถียร (sathianra) meaning "stable, certain" and ภาพ (phap) meaning "state, existence".
Alternate transcription of Thai สาธิต (see Sathit).
Alternate transcription of Thai เสถียร (see Sathian).
Means "to demonstrate, to show" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit साधित (sādhita).

SATHIYA = TRUTH,JOHN:18:37,NESAN = LOVE, SATHIYANESAN = LOVES THE WORD OF GOD Rev.Sathiyanesan,Pastor of a Baptist church in India,Chennai.He stated that there is a negative state for GRAVITATIONAL FORCE.
Name of God. God grants all wish if pooja done sincerely.
The name of a Celtic goddess worshipped in Roman Britain. Etymology is uncertain, but may be related to the Proto-Celtic *sāti- meaning ‘saturation’ or *satjā- meaning ‘swarm’.
Ancient Egyptian feminine name meaning "Daughter of the Moon".
Alternate transcription of Thai เสถียร (see Sathian).
Alternate transcription of Thai สาธิต (see Sathit).
Alternate transcription of Thai เสถียร (see Sathian).
Maybe a variant of Oryza sativa belongs to the genus Oryza. Or a variant of Latifah
From the French word satin, referring to the fabric satin. This was used by the French author Émile Zola as a name for a prostitute in his novel "Nana" (1880). It is not used as a name in France.
From the Fijian word for "satin", meaning "soft and gentle".
Variant of Satyendra used by Sikhs.

Derived from satin, the French word for the fabric satin, combined with -e, a French feminine suffix. It was popularized in France after it was used as the name of a character, a courtesan, in the 2001 film Moulin Rouge!.
Alternate transcription of Armenian Սաթինե (see Satine 2).
Spanish and Portuguese form of Satyros.
Alternate transcription of Thai สาธิต (see Sathit).
From Javanese sêtiti meaning "careful, accurate, scrupulous, meticulous".
Derived from the Latin sativa, meaning "sown, cultivated". This name can be given in reference to Cannabis sativa, a plant which produces the drug cannabis.
Probably means "daughter of Khnum" in Ancient Egyptian. The reading is uncertain, so the name can also be read as Satba.
From Sanskrit सत्य (satya) meaning "true, real" combined with नाम (nama) meaning "name".

column3: さと(Japanese Hiragana)|郷, 慧, 賢, 悟, 識, 聡, 智, 都, 里, 惺, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|Սաթո(Armenian)
column12: From Japanese 郷 (sato) meaning "hometown", 慧 (sato) meaning "bright; intelligent", 賢 (sato) meaning "intelligence", 悟 (sato) meaning "enlightenment", 識 (sato) meaning "acquaintanceship", 聡 (sato) meaning "intelligent, clever, bright", 智 (sato) meaning "knowledge, wisdom", 都 (sato) meaning "capital (city)", 里 (sato) meaning "village" or 惺 (sato) meaning "intelligent, clever, astute". Other kanji or kanji combinations can form this name as well.
From Japanese 郷 (sato) meaning "village" combined with 恵 (e) meaning "favour, benefit". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 郷 (sato) meaning "village" combined with 弘 (hiro) meaning "spread, enlarge, expand". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 慧衣, 聡衣, 里依, 怜衣, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 慧 (sato) meaning "intelligence", 聡 (sato) meaning "intelligent, clever, bright", 里 (sato) meaning "village" or 怜 (sato) meaning "pity, sympathize" combined with 衣 (i) meaning "clothing". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: さとか(Japanese Hiragana)|サトカ(Japanese Katakana)|里佳, 里香, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Japanese feminine name derived from 里 (sato) meaning "village" and 佳 (ka) meaning "excellent, beautiful". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 達輝, 知樹, 里樹, 達樹, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 達 (sato, satoru, satoshi) meaning "official notice" combined with 輝 (ki) meaning "brightness" or 樹 (ki) meaning "tree". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: サトコ(Japanese Katakana)|さとこ(Japanese Hiragana)|郷子, 聖火, 哲子, 敏火, 邑子, 怜火, 惺子, 聰火, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 郷 (sato) meaning "hometown, township, village, countryside", 聖 (sato) meaning "virtuous, holy, sacred", 哲 (sato) meaning "philosophy, clear", 敏 (sato) meaning "alert, quick, agile, sharp", 邑 (sato) meaning "capital city, village", 怜 (sato) meaning "wise", or 聰 (sato) meaning "wise, intelligent" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child" or 火 (ko) meaning "fire". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 里真, 里万, 里茉, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 里 (sato) meaning "village" combined with 真 (ma) meaning "true, reality". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 智美子, 聡美子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 聡 (sato) meaning "intelligent, clever, bright" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful", and 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 慧音, 郷音, 紗音流, 紗戸音, 里音, 玲音, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 慧 (sato) meaning "bright; intelligent" combined with 音 (ne) meaning "sound". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 覚 (sato) meaning "to wake up from sleep, conscious" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.
Derived from Latin sator "sower, planter; founder; progenitor; originator".

column3: 沙都里, 悟理, 咲藤李, 聡, 智凜, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand", 都 (to) meaning "capital (city)" combined with 里 (ri) meaning "village". Other combinations of kanji characters are also possible.

Variation of Sartorius, which is a transferred use of the surname Sartorius.Sartorius, known as Takuma Saiou in the original Japanese language version, is a fictional character in the Yu-Gi-Oh! GX anime series.
Late Greek variant of Satourninos, which is the ancient Greek form of Saturninus.
From Japanese 啓 (satoshi) meaning "disclose, say, open, begin" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Short form of Isatou.Satou Sabally is a professional women basketball player in the WNBA. She's of German nationality and has a Gambian father.
From Japanese 里 (sato) meaning "village" combined with 和 (wa) meaning "peace, harmony". Other kanji combinations are also possible.

column12: From Japanese 鋭 (sato) meaning "sharp", 郷 (sato) meaning "village", 恵 (sato) meaning "favour, benefit", 賢 (sato) meaning "intelligence, clever", 仁 (sato) meaning "humaneness, benevolence, kindness", 聖 (sato) meaning "holy, sacred" or 聡 (sato) meaning "intelligent, clever, bright" combined with 代 (yo) meaning "generation". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Sanskrit सत्य (satya) meaning "true, real" combined with पाल (pāla) meaning "guard, protector".
From Sanskrit सत्य (satya) meaning "true, real" combined with प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".

Means "let (it) stop" in Chechen, a compulsive form of саца (satsa) meaning "to stop". It was traditionally given by parents who desired a son (in order to "stop" more daughters from being born).
Diminutive or folk form of an unknown name or several names which contained sa, such as Isaak, Sava, Saveliy, Savvatiy, Savyn (see Sabinus), Samson, Isay, Samiylo etc.
Ancient Egyptian feminine name meaning "Daughter of Sobek".

column12: From the Japanese kanji 薩 (satsu), a transcription of Sattva (सत्त्व), a Buddhist concept that means "a living being, creature, person or sentient being".Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 皐, 皐月, 五月, 小月(Japanese Kanji)|さつき(Japanese Hiragana)|サツキ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese kanji 皐 (satsuki) meaning "shore" or 皐月/五月 (satsuki), the fifth month of the lunar calendar. It can be also the combination of 小 (sa) meaning "little; small" and 月 (tsuki) meaning "moon".Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 颯 (satsu) meaning "the sound of the wind", 希 (ki) meaning "hope, rare" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 札子, 颪子, 颯子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column3: 薩夫, 察男, 左都夫, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 薩 (satsu, sachi, suku.u) meaning "Buddha, salvation" or 察 (satsu, sacchi, sasseru) meaning "to understand, observe, infer or perceive" combined with 生 (o, shi, iku) meaning "life, birth, genuine". Other kanji combinations can be used.
From Japanese 颯 (satsu) meaning "the sound of the wind" combined with 斗 (to), which refers to a Chinese constellation. Other kanji combinations are also possible.

column3: 幸矢, 札矢, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 幸 (satsu) meaning "good fortune, happiness" and 矢 (ya) meaning "arrow". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 薩陽, 察世, 左都昌, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 薩 (satsu) meaning "Buddha, salvation" or 察 (satsu) meaning "guess" combined with 陽 (yō) meaning "light, sun, male". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column12: Means "virtuous son" in Thai and Lanna.
Means "veiler, concealer, coverer" in Arabic, from the root ستر (sattara) meaning "to cover up, to hide, to enveil". In Islamic tradition الستار (as-Sattār) is an attribute of Allah.
Tajik and Uzbek form of Sattar.
Means "science, knowledge, principles" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit शास्त्र (śāstra).
Roman cognomen derived from the name of the Roman god Saturnus (see Saturn).
French, Gascon, Provençal and Polish form of Saturninus.
Form of Saturn in several Romance languages.
Saturus in Latin means: "about to sow", "about to plant", "satisfied".
Comes from the Indian word meaning "existence."

Means "pure, virtuous" or "truthful, true" in Sanskrit. This is a transcription of both the masculine form सत्य and the feminine form सत्या.

Means "truly victorious, conquering by truth" from Sanskrit सत्य (satya) meaning "truth, reality" combined with जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering". A notable bearer was Indian film director and composer Satyajit Ray (1921-1992).
From Sanskrit satya meaning "truth" (compare Sati). American actress Alyson Hannigan gave the name to her daughter in 2009.
From Sanskrit सत्य (satya) meaning "truth, reality" combined with the name of the Hindu god Narayana. This is an epithet of Vishnu, also regarded as one of his alternate forms.
One of the 108 names of Satyanarayana
Means "sweet life", derived from Kazakh тәтті (tätti) or Kyrgyz таттуу (tattuu) both meaning "sweet, delicious" combined with Kazakh and Kyrgyz бал (bal) "honey".
Means "lord of truth" or "truth" in Dogri and Kashmiri.
From Sanskrit सत्य (satya) meaning "truth" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra.
Derived from Greek satyros meaning "satyr" (see also Satyros). In Greek mythology, this was the name of a nymph who had a son with Poseidon.

Means "satyr" in Ancient Greek, as in the name of the mythological half-goat creature from Greek mythology. This was the name of several historical figures, including an architect from ancient Greece, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Ossetian form of the Scythian name Sawarmag (see Saurmag).
From the Karachay-Balkar сау (sau) meaning "alive, healthy" and бар (bar) meaning "to go", idiomatically "go (through life) in good health".
Means "black rider" in Ossetian. This is the name of the Ossetian God of darkness and thieves, comparable to the Biblical figure Satan.
Gascon form of Salvator. Folk etymology, however, likes to derive this name from Gascon saubadé, saubadìs, saubadìu "(he who can be) saved".

It means “wistfulness, melancholy, nostalgia, longing” or “the feeling of missing something or someone”, an important concept in Portuguese culture and literature.As a given name, it is sometimes given as a Marian name — Maria da Saudade —, referrencing Our Lady of Saudade (Nossa Senbora da Saudade; feast day: March 30).Although they have the same etymological origin, it’s should not be confused with the name Soledade, which means “loneliness” and which was given in honour of his Our Lady of Solitude (feast day September 15).
Alternate transcription of Arabic سودة (see Sawda), as well as the Indonesian and Malay form.

Feminine form of Saufeius. While Saufeia Alexandria was a Vestal Virgin, another bearer of this name was apparently a priestess of the Bona Dea, whose immodest sexual desires and drunkenness in connection with the rites of that goddess are twice mentioned by Juvenal.
Catalan and French form of Saul.
Derived from Latvian saule "sun" and cerēt "to hope".
Derived from Lativan saule "sun" and nest "to bring; to carry".

Spanish, Portuguese and Italian form of Saul. Known bearers of this name include the Spanish poet Saulo Torón Navarro (1885-1974), the Brazilian pop singer Saulo Roston (b. 1989) and the Brazilian kickboxer Saulo Cavalari (b. 1989).
Alternate transcription of Bengali সৌমেন (see Soumen).
From Sanskrit सौम्या (saumya) meaning "gentle, soft, pleasing, agreeable", derived from the name of the ritual drink सोम (soma). This is an epithet of the Hindu goddess Durga.
The Hong Kong Romanization form of Xiuna.
Of uncertain meaning. Name recorded as belonging to an Iroquois man in 1637.
Transferred use of the surname Saunders.
From sāuni meaning "ready, to be prepared" in Samoan.
Means "to arrive, to reach, to become" in Toba Batak.
Alternate transcription of Bengali সৌরভ (see Saurabh).
MEANING - "son of sun", a name of Saturn, Indian- Laurel, clammyweeds plant
MEANING - Celestial, heavenly, paradise, relating to spirituous liquor
From Old Occitan saur "blond" and mond "world". This is the name of an evil entity who manifested herself as a girl with fair hair and blue eyes.

Georgian form of the Scythian personal name Sawarmag, which literally means "black hand". It is derived from Scythian syāva meaning "black" combined with Scythian arma meaning "hand" and the suffix -aka. Also compare modern Ossetian сау (sau) or (saw) meaning "black" and modern Ossetian арм (arm) meaning "hand". Those are significant, because the Ossetian language is a descendant of the Scythian language.This name was borne by two kings of Iberia, who are each better known under the name Sauromaces. One lived in the 2nd century BC whilst the other lived in the 4th century AD.
Derived from the Italian surname Sauro, in honour of the Italian irredentist Nazario Sauro (1880-1916).There might possibly also be cases where this name is a short form of Isauro.
Latinized form of the Scythian personal name Sawarmag (see Saurmag) via its hellenized form Σαυρομακης (Sauromakes). Also compare Sauromates.

Derived from the Roman cognomen Sauromates, itself derived from Greek Σαυρομάτης (Sauromates) meaning "a Sarmatian". The Sarmatians were an Iranian people that spoke Sarmatian, a Scythian language. It is not certain what the Sarmatians called themselves in their native language, but since foreign adaptions of their native etnonym seem very close to what it must have been in Sarmatian, the original Sarmatian form must have been Sauromata (or something along those lines). The etnonym most likely meant "black cloaks" or "black mantles", derived from Scytho-Sarmatian saw (or sau) "black" combined with roma "fur" (which means "mantle, cloak" in a figurative sense) and the plural suffix -ta. Also compare Sauromaces. Finally, this name was borne by two Roman client kings of the Bosporan Kingdom, namely Sauromates I (d. 123 AD) and Sauromates II (d. 211 AD).
Means "to happen, to be fulfilled" in Toba Batak.
Gascon and Provençal form of Salvator.
Alternate transcription of Bengali সৌভিক (see Souvik).
Most likely a transferred use of the surname Savag, which is a "Manxified" form of the English surname Savage.
Means "heaven, paradise" in Lao, ultimately from Sanskrit स्वर्ग (svarga).
From Germanic sav or saba, both of unknown meaning and rik, meaning powerful.
Croatian and Serbian form of Sabbatios via Sabbatius.
Variant of Savon, the spelling influenced by that of Vaughn.
Sanskrit word with deep and complex shades that could mean "being of the same age (adjective)", "coeval, friend (masculine noun)" or "a woman's female confidante (feminine noun)".

column3: Савета(Romanian Cyrillic, Serbian, Croatian Cyrillic, Macedonian, Ukrainian)
column12: Romanian and Macedonian truncated form of Elisaveta and Serbian and Croatian truncated form of Jelisaveta. Ukrainian folk form of Yelyzaveta.
From the Turkish sevgili meaning "dear, beloved".

Dutch form of Saviel. It is predominantly a masculine name in the Netherlands, but occasionally the name is also bestowed upon females. Saviël as a feminine name is slightly less common than its proper feminine counterpart Saviëlle.
Meaning unknown. It might possibly be a variant form of Xaviel.
Alternate transcription of Thai สาวิณี (see Sawini).
French form of Sabinianus. Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac, a French author and the inspiration for Edmond Rostand’s most famous drama Cyrano de Bergerac, is a bearer of this name.
Diminutive form of Savin or Savina.
Modern Greek spelling of Sabinos, which is the ancient Greek form of Sabinus.
Sicilian form of Sabinus and Savinus.
Vietnamese form of Savio. This name is usually used in combination with Đaminh to honor Saint Dominic Savio.
Meaning unknown. Possibly a variant of Xavier or Savyon. Savyon is a Hebrew name for “Senecio,” a genus of the daisy family.

From the English word savior meaning "one who saves", ultimately from Late Latin salvare meaning "to save", making it a cognate of Salvador. In Christianity this is a title of Jesus Christ. Also compare Messiah.
Variant of Savior using the international spelling.
The name of a minor character in Romanian author Liviu Rebreanu's novel "Ion".
Alternate transcription of Thai สาวิตรี (see Sawitri) or Hindi सावित्री (see Savitri).

column3: Савка(Croatian Cyrillic, Serbian, Bosnian Cyrillic, Macedonian, Montenegrin, Bulgarian)
column12: Feminine form of Sava. In Serbian and Montenegrin it was also occasionally used as a short form of Jelisavka.
Derived from savlat meaning "pride and joy" or "splendor, magnificance" and bibi meaning "learned woman".

Of uncertain origin, perhaps a combination of phonetic elements sa and von. It also coincides with the French word for "soap". This was the name of a character played by Ice Cube in the 1992 movie Trespass.
Savona Bailey-McClain is an American community organizer and art producer, and the director of the West Harlem Art Fund.
Meaning unknown. This is the name of a Kalmyk folk hero.
Means "before turning the sun" in Chuvash.
Uzbek feminine name refering to a kind of Iris flower.
Derived from the name of a kind of Iris flower and oy meaning "moon".
The name of a Hurrian goddess mentioned by the Assyrian king Sargon II.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Sabbatios.
Greek feminine name, a cognate of the given name Sabine.
Means "shrewd, well-informed", from Tok Pisin (an English-based Creole) save or Nigerian Pidgin sabi, both meaning "to know". In some cases, it is a diminutive of Savannah.
From Sanskrit सव्यसाची (savyasācī) meaning "ambidextrous, skillful in shooting an arrow with both hands". This is an epithet of the hero Arjuna.

column12: Probably from the Japanese kanji 沢 (Kun reading sawa) "mountain stream" or "marsh, swamp; wetlands". This kanji can also be pronounced Taku (Kan'on reading) or Jaku (Goon reading).This name is notable as being borne by the fictional Sawa, the orphaned heroine of the influential 1998 anime "A カイト" ("Kite").
Means "to search, to seek, to pursue, to strive for" in Thai, of Khmer origin.

column3: 咲環花, 沙和香, 佐和香, 佐和花, 沙羽花, 紗若, 爽加, 爽和香, 早和香, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|さわか(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 咲 (sa) meaning "blossom", 環 (wa) meaning "circle, ring, wheel" combined with 花 (ka) meaning "flower". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 爽子, 沢子, 佐和子, 三和子, 咲和子, 咲羽子, 小和子, 小羽子, 早和子, 沙和子, 沙羽子(Japanese Kanji)|さわ子(Kanji/Hiragana)|サワ子(Kanji/Katakana)|さわこ(Japanese Hiragana)|サワコ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name combines 爽 (sou, aki.raka, sawa.yaka, tagau) meaning "refreshing, bracing, resonant, sweet, clear" or 沢 (taku, sawa, uruo.i, uruo.su, tsuya) meaning "swamp, marsh, brilliance, grace" with 子 (shi, su, tsu, ko, -ko, -ne) meaning "child, sign of the rat (1st sign of the Chinese zodiac)."Examples of Sawako with 3 kanji inclide 佐和子, 三和子, 咲和子, 咲羽子, 小和子, 小羽子, 早和子, 沙和子 and 沙羽子 with 佐 (sa) meaning "assistant, help", 三 (san, zou, mi, mi'.tsu, mi.tsu, sa) meaning "three", 咲 (shou, sa.ku, -zaki) meaning "bloom, blossom", 小 (shou, chii.sai, o-, ko-, sa-) meaning "little, small", 早 (sou, sa', haya.i, haya, haya-, haya.maru, haya.meru, sa-) meaning "early, fast", 沙 (sa, sha, suna, yonageru) meaning "sand", 和 (o, ka, wa, nago.mu, nago.yaka, yawa.ragu, yawa.rageru) meaning "harmony, Japan, Japanese style, peace, soften" and 羽 (u, ha, hane, wa) meaning "feathers."You can also combine さわ or サワ, which are the hiragana & katakana characters for Sawa, with 子.
Means "be in power, hold sway" in Arabic.
From the Arabic صَوَالِح‎ (ṣawāliḥ) meaning "advantages, benefits".

column3: สว่างจิตต์(Thai)
column12: From Thai สว่าง (sawang) meaning "bright, brilliant, shining" and จิตต์ (chit) meaning "mind, heart, thought".

column3: サワオ(Japanese Katakana)|さわお(Japanese Hiragana)|皐夫, 澤夫, 沢男, 佐和雄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沢 (sawa) meaning "a mountain stream, swamp; marsh; wetlands" combined with 男 (o) meaning "male". Other kanji combinations are possible.Famous bearers are Sawao Yamanaka, a member of the Japanese alternative rock band "The Pillows" and Sawao Kato, a retired Japanese gymnast and one of the most successful Olympic athletes of all time.
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਸਵਰਨ (see Swaran).
Means "happiness, wellbeing, welfare" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit स्वस्ति (svasti).

column3: မိစဴဗု(Mon)|စောပု(Burmese)
column12: Of uncertain meaning. A famous bearer of that name was a Queen of the Hanthawaddy empire.
Means "(female) disciple, follower, listener" in Thai.
Alternate transcription of Thai สาวิณี (see Sawini).
Arabized form of Severus. This was the name of a 10th-century Coptic Orthodox bishop.
Alternate transcription of Thai สาวิตรี (see Sawitri).
Thai and Indonesian form of Savitri.
Derived from the Arabic word شُهْرَة ‎(šuhra) meaning "famous" or "renowned".
Alternate transcription of Arabic سوسن (see Sawsan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سوسن (see Sawsan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سوسن (see Sawsan).
Means "generosity" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic سخاوة (sakhāwa).
Old Norse name derived from either saxar "Saxon", referring to a member of the Germanic tribe the Saxons, or its origin, sax "dagger, short sword".
Derived from Old English seax "dagger" and leofu "love".
Latinized form of Saxi. Saxo Grammaticus was a medieval Danish chronicler.
Presumably a feminine form of Saxon.
Allegoric personification of the state of Saxony (Germany). Very rarely used as a given name.
Transferred use of the surname Saxton.

column3: サヤ(Japanese Katakana)|沙耶, 小椰, 紗弥, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|शय(Sanskrit)|茶悦(Chinese)
column12: From 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" or 小 (sa) meaning "small, little" and 耶 (ya) meaning "question mark" or 椰 (ya) meaning "palm tree". Other kanji combinations can be used.
From Mongolian сая (saya) meaning "million" and болд (bold) meaning "steel".
Derived from Persian سایه (sâye) meaning "shadow" and Kazakh гүл (gül) meaning "flower" (of Persian origin).

column3: サヤハ(Japanese Katakana)|さやは(Japanese Hiragana)|紗弥華, 沙耶花, 彩葉, 爽羽, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 咲 (sa) meaning "blossom", 也 (ya) meaning "also" combined with 葉 (ha) meaning "leaf". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: さやこ(Japanese Hiragana)|サヤコ(Japanese Katakana)|清子, 彩家子, 佐冶子, 小哉子, 道椰子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" or 紗 (sa) meaning "thread, silk" with 也 (ya) meaning "also" or 耶 (ya), an interjection, combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are usable.
Sanskrit. Name of beautiful white flower: Jasminum multiflorum

column3: さやみ(Japanese Hiragana)|沙也美, 沙弥美, 彩美, 紗也美, 紗耶子, 爽見, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand", 也 (ya) meaning "also" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "fitting, suitable, worthy" in Ottoman Turkish.

column3: 清菜(Japanese Kanji)|Саяна(Tuvan, Buryat Cyrillic)|Саяна(Mongolian Cyrillic, Buryat Cyrillic)
column12: From the Japanese 清 (saya) "clear," "bright," "clean" and 菜 (na) "vegetable," "greens."

column3: 彩也音, 沙耶音, 咲耶音, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|さやね(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 彩 (sa) meaning "colour", 也 (ya) meaning "also" combined with 音 (ne) meaning "sound". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "love, affection, darling, dear, kind, beloved" in Malay.
From Bashkir шаян (šayan) meaning "playful" and гөл (göl) meaning "flower".

column3: さやの(Japanese Hiragana)|沙夜乃, 沙耶乃, 咲也乃, 紗哉乃, 紗也乃, 紗耶乃, 紗弥乃, 紗矢乃, 聖乃, 早也乃, 早弥乃, 涼乃, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand", 咲 (sa) meaning "blossom", 紗 (sa) meaning "gauze", 聖 (saya) meaning "holy, saint, sage, master, priest", 早 (sa) meaning "early, fast" or 涼 (saya) meaning "cool, refreshing", 夜 (ya) meaning "night", 耶 (ya), an interjection, 也 (ya) meaning "also", 哉 (ya), an exclamation, 弥 (ya) meaning "all the more, increasingly" or 矢 (ya) meaning "dart, arrow" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.
Means "relating to the evening, vespertine", ultimately from Sanskrit सायन्तन (sāyantana).
Means "millions of flowers" in Mongolian, from сая (saya) meaning "million" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
Means "she counts, respects, regards, values, takes into account, or considers" in Turkish.

column3: 沙矢斗, 清人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand", 矢 (ya) meaning "arrow" combined with 斗 (to), which refers to a Chinese constellation. Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Mongolian сая (saya) meaning "million" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
girl's name is a variant of Saida  -------------------------------------Shadow of mother
Possibly a variant of Zayden.According to the USA Social Security Administration, 7 baby boys were recorded with the name Sayden in 2017.
From the given name Saydi and g'ani meaning "wealthy, rich".
From the given name Saydi and rasul meaning "prophet, messenger".
From the given name Saydi and yor meaning "friend".
Alternate transcription of Persian سایه (see Sayeh).
Alternate transcription of Urdu سعیدہ or Bengali সাঈদা (see Saida).

Bashkir and Tatar form of Sayyid.
Medieval English form of Old English Sægiefu.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سيف (see Saif).
Means "sword of Islam" from Arabic سيف (sayf) meaning "sword" and إسلام (Islam).
Alternate transcription of Arabic سيف الرحمن (see Sayf ar-Rahman).
Means "sword of the merciful" from Arabic سيف (sayf) meaning "sword" combined with رحْمن (raḥman) meaning "merciful".
Alternate transcription of Arabic سيف الدين (see Sayf ad-Din), chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Tajik and Uzbek form of Saifullah.
The given name Sayid followed by the Uzbek afzal meaning "better".
Derived from the given names Sayid and Ali 1.
Derived from the given names Sayid and Amin.
Derived from the given names Sayid and Amir 1.
Derived from the Arabic name Sa'id and gul meaning "rose, flower",
Derived from the Arabic name Sa'id and oy meaning "moon".
Means "polish, lustre, shine" in Kyrgyz, ultimately from Persian صیقل (sayqal).
Alternate transcription of Lao ໄຊຄຳ (see Xaykham).
Invented name, possibly combining Saylor and the phonetic element lee.
Potentially derived from sayli, a type of melon, and gul meaning "rose, flower".
Means "wagtail (a type of bird)" in Tuvan.
Sayna means light and dark in jungle.this word used in north of iran and it is a regional word.
The mother of Agunda in the Ossetian 'Nart' sagas.
From the Persian sâye-nûr meaning “the shadow of the light”.

column3: 早世, 咲代, 沙四, 紗夜, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 小 (sa) meaning "less, little, small" or 咲 (sa) meaning "bloom" combined with 世 (yo) meaning "world" or 代 (yo) meaning "generation". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 小夜子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|さよこ(Japanese Hiragana)|サヨコ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 小 (sa) meaning "small", 夜 (yo) meaning "night" and 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other combinations of kanji characters are possible.
Alternate transcription of Thai สยมภู (see Sayomphu).

column3: さよみ(Japanese Hiragana)|小世美, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 小 (sa) meaning "small", 世 (yo) meaning "world", and 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful, beauty". Other kanji combinations can be used.
Alternate transcription of Thai สยมภู (see Sayomphu).
Means "self-existing, self-created" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit स्वयम्भू (svayambhū).
Alternate transcription of Thai สยมภู (see Sayomphu).
Alternate transcription of Thai สยมภู (see Sayomphu).
From Japanese さようなら (sayonara) meaning "farewell, so long, goodbye".
Sayonsom means "A name like no other" or "the perfect name" for any particular thing

column3: さより(Japanese Hiragana)|サヨリ(Japanese Katakana)|沙よ理(Kanji/Hiragana)|小夜里, 小由, 紗依, 桜依, 咲依, 早和, 颯依, 沙頼, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 小 (sa) meaning "little, less, small", 夜 (yo) meaning "night" combined with 里 (ri) meaning "village". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 粧裕, 沙優, 早柚(Japanese Kanji)|さゆ(Japanese Hiragana)|サユ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 粧 (sa) meaning "adornment, makeup", 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" or 早 (sa) meaning "early" combined with 裕 (yu) meaning "abundant, rich, plentiful", 優 (sa) meaning "excellence" or 柚 (yu) meaning "citron". Other kanji combinations are possible.This name is borne by a character in the manga series Death Note, bearing the combinations 粧裕. A character in Higehiro, a light novel series, also has this name with the combinations 沙優, as does a character, 早柚, in miHoYo's video game Genshin Impact.

column3: さゆか(Japanese Hiragana)|サユカ(Japanese Katakana)|沙有華, 沙友佳, 沙友香, 紗由香, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" or 冴 (sa) meaning "cold, severe", 有 (yu) meaning "exist" or 友 (yu) meaning "friend", combined with 佳 (ka) meaning "beautiful, good" or 香 (ka) meaning "fragrance". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 沙幸, 沙雪, 紗友希, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" combined with 幸 (yuki) meaning "happiness" or 雪 (yuki) meaning "snow". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: さゆこ(Japanese Hiragana)|サユコ(Japanese Katakana)|早裕子, 佐夕子, 紗友子, 紗由子, 小夜子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From meaning 小 (sa) meaning "small", 裕 (yu) meaning "abundant" and 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: さゆみ(Japanese Hiragana)|沙弓, 佐弓, 小弓, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 早 (sa) meaning "fast", and 弓 (yumi) meaning "bow and arrow". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 彩結菜, 咲夢菜, 咲夢奈, 紗優奈, 早唯奈, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 彩 (sa) meaning "colour", 結 (yu) meaning "tie, fasten, join, organize" combined with 菜 (na) meaning "vegetables, greens". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From the name of 15th-century Islamic scholar, jurist and mystic Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, whose name was derived from the city of Asyut in Egypt.

column3: 幸優, 佐友, 佐祐, 沙愈, 沙優, 沙有, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 幸 (sa) meaning "fortunate; lucky" combined with 優 (yuu) meaning "easily, skillfully". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From the name of 13th-century Moroccan Sufi and scholar Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili.

column3: さざみ(Japanese Hiragana)|三三三, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 三 (sa) meaning "three", 三 (za) meaning "three" combined with 三 (mi) meaning "three". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 授(Japanese Kanji)|さずく(Japanese Hiragana)|サズク(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From classical verb 授く (sazuku), modern sazukeru, meaning "to grant, give, award; to teach, instruct."This name is very rarely used.

A warrior in the service of King Arthur who was the son of King Fflergant of Armorica.He is thought by many scholars to be equal to Duke Alan Fyrgan (1084-1112). Alan married William the Conqueror’s daughter.
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Zbigniew.
Derived from the Germanic name elements sær "sea" and bjǫrn "bear".
The name for a Dryad of chess in the poem 'Scacchia Ludus' published in 1527 by Marco Girolamo Vida. Compare to Caïssa, a more modern English name for the personifaction of Chess.

Derived from the feminine form of Ancient Greek σκαιός (skaios) meaning "left, on or with the left hand; west, western" as well as "unlucky, mischievous" and "awkward, clumsy". Scaea was one of the fifty daughters of King Danaus in Greek mythology, killing her husband, Daiphron, on their wedding night. In some accounts, she later remarried to Archander.

Latinized form of Skamandros. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a river god, who is the personification of the Scamander River (nowadays called Karamenderes River), the largest river of the plain of Troy.
French form of Skamandros via Scamander.
Latinized form of Ancient Greek Σκαμάνδριος (Skamandrios) meaning "of the Scamander" or "son of Skamandros". This was the name of a Trojan soldier in Homer's Illiad.
Italian form of Skamandros via Scamander.
Latinized form of Skamandronymos. This was the earliest and most commonly attested name of Sappho's father, who died when she was six.
Feminine form of Scantius. Scantia was one of the Vestal Virigns.
Name of the antagonist in The Lion King, likely named for the scar on left eye. His real name is Taka.
Form of Zechariah used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.
Alternate transcription of Malayalam സ്കറിയ (see Scaria).

Possibly derived from medieval Latin scarlatum meaning "scarlet cloth", itself ultimately derived from an Arabic or Persian word. It was primarily in use in the 1700s and 1800sThis name was borne by two princes of Moldavia and Wallachia, namely Scarlat Ghica (1715-1766) and his grandson Scarlat Callimachi (1773-1821).
Combination of Scarlett and Rose (See aslo Scarletrose - a less popular variant).
Possibly a quasi-feminization of the surname Scarlott influenced by Charlotte or a contraction of Scarlett and Charlotte.

Scarmiglione is one of the twelve named Malebranche in the 8th Circle of Hell's 5th Gulf, where corrupt politicians are immersed in burning pitch, the Malebolge, from the Inferno of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Derived from Italian scarpetta meaning "small shoe", which is a diminutive of Italian scarpa meaning "shoe". As such, this name is comparable to Latin Caligula.A known bearer of this name was the Italian nobleman Scarpetta Ordelaffi (died around 1315).
Meaning unknown. It may be related to the Cherokee wa ya "wolf, wolves".

the lady "of the Shadowy Isle". She is a warrior, also associated with smithcraft and oracular wisdom. She dwells in Albannach (Scotland), on (most tales agree) the Isle of Skye (Scaith) A great warrior Goddess whose name means "she who strikes fear", Scatha was also called "the shadowy one". She taught many of the legendary Celtic heroes all their skills, including battlefield magic. They traveled great distances to study with her; to learn strategy and martial arts. During their stay of a year and a day, she taught them fierce battle cries and terrifying leaps and bounds, making them undefeatable in combat. Upon completion of their studies, the students would return to their people to do great deeds. Scatha is best known as the tutor of Cuchulainn in the arts of both love and war in the Táin Bó Cualgne.
Feminine form of Scaurus. A bearer of this name was Aemilia Scaura, the second wife of Pompey the Great (1st century BC).
Roman cognomen which was derived from Scaurus. A bearer of this name was Decimus Terentius Scaurianus, a Roman governor of Dacia from the 2nd century AD.

Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin adjective scaurus meaning "with swollen ankles, club-footed." The word is ultimately derived from Greek σκαῦρος (skauros) meaning "lame", which is etymologically related to Sanskrit khora "lame". A bearer of this name was Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, a Roman consul from the 2nd century BC.
Sceafa was a legendary Lombardic king from English legend.

Latinized form of Greek Σκέλμις (Skelmis). In Greek mythology this was the name of one of the Telchines, sea spirits (daemons) native to the island of Rhodes, who were killed by the gods when they turned to evil magic. According to Hesiod, Scelmis was one of the Dactyls or Daktyloi, more commonly known as Celmis.
Means "sceptre" in Latin. This is the traditional name of the star 53 Eridani in the constellation Eridanus.

Origin and meaning uncertain; theories include a derivation from Albanian herdhe "nest; herd", ultimately from Proto-Albanian *skarda- "herd" and Proto-Albanian *laida "to leave, to die, to lead", thus meaning something like "herd or flock leader". This name was borne by Scerdilaidas (ruled 218-206 BC), a ruler of the Illyrian kingdom under the Labeatan dynasty. He was the grandfather of Gentius.
Short form of Paschaas and Paschasius (masculine) as well as Paschasia (feminine).
Variation of Shaphan used in the german bible translations.
Germanised spelling of Jacqueline, officially admitted in Eschweiler (near Aachen) in 2013.
German transcription of Georgian შალვა (see Shalva).
German transcription of the Biblical name Shamir.Older Bibles give the name as Samir.
Derived from the name of the leader of the Caucasian resistance to Imperial Russia in the 1800s, Imam Shamil. A notable bearer was Swedish film director Schamyl Bauman (1893-1966).

Austrian German vernacular form of Jean 1 and in some cases an Austrian German borrowing of Sanyi. The name coincides with the Austrian German vernacular term Schani "servant, henchman", the informal term Schani "good friend" and the obsolescent East Austrian German term Schani "waiter".
German transcription of Zhanna, a Russian form of Jeanne.
A known bearer of this name is Schapelle Corby, an Australian woman convicted of drug smuggling in Indonesia in 2005. The 2014 TV movie 'Schapelle' told her story.
Vernacular form of Charles reflecting the French pronunciation.
East Prussian German spelling variant of Charlotte, not uncommon in the late 1700s and early 1800s.
Derived from the archaic Romanian word şcheau which used to mean "Bulgarian", in certain cases "Serb" and later on "Slav" in general.

Derives from the Arabic word şadr, meaning "breast" (referring to the star's placement near the "heart" of the constellation). This is the traditional name of the star Alpha Cassiopeiae in the constellation Cassiopeia.Alternative names for it include Al Dhāt al Kursiyy ("the lady in the chair") and Dath Elkarti.
Derived from Ancient Greek σχεδόν (schedon) meaning "near, nearby" or "nearly, almost". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a suitor of Penelope.
German transcription of Shayna.It can also be associated with the German verb scheinen "to shine".
Transferred use of the surname Schenley.
Vernacular diminutive of Eugenie via French Eugénie.
Variant of Scheherazade.Mademoiselle Scherazade was a nineteenth century elephant trainer, known as the only female elephant trainer in Europe (sometimes "the world").

The burgrave of the city of Bearosche under Duke Lyppaut.He enlisted the assistance of Gawain in a battle against King Meliant of Lis, who was attacking Lyppaut because Lyppaut’s daughter Obie had rejected him.
Shetlandic variant of Sigurðr found in 17th century Shetland Islands. This appears to be the most common variant of this name.
When combined with the last name Wegey, it means the gorgeous man who defiles the gods in a fictional ancient language. This name is born by Puyo Puyo character Schezo Wegey.
Short form of Beschier and Passchier and their many variants.This name is not to be confused with the Dutch word schier meaning "almost, nearly".
Romansh form of Simon 1, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
A name used in homage to Oskar Schindler. It is an occupational name for a person who made or laid wooden roof tiles.
German transcription of the originally Persian name Shirin.
Name of a giant who (according to the legend) founded the Alsatian city Sélestat (German name Schlettstadt).
The name is derived from the surname Schley.It was given to at least 10 baby boys in the USA in 1898, probably in honor of the rear admiral Winfield Scott Schley.
One of the Yiddish forms of Shemaiah.

German name meaning "sorrowful, painful".According to the legend of Genoveva von Brabant (8th century), Schmerzenreich is the name of duchess Genoveva and palsgrave Siegfried's son. It is not used as given name in Germany, though.

Originally Spanish name Senior (meaning "Master")Many American Jews who bore this name chose the English name Seymour.Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liady, founder of Chabad movement held this name after his maternal grandfather Schneur Zalman Loewe.The President of Israel Zalman Shazar who was a Hassid of Chabad held a last name which was an acronym to his original full name: Schneur Zalman Rubishov.Schneur Zalman Heshin was an Israeli chief judge and Zalman Schneur was the pen name of a famous Israeli Hebrew and Yiddish author.Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson the last Chabad Rebbe, held a family name pointing to the founding of the Chabad movement, and until his own death it was common for Chabad Hassids to call their firstborn boys Schneor
Short form and pet name for Jeannine.
From Romani schuker nak "beautiful nose".The name is borne by the musician Schnuckenack Reinhardt, a cousin of Django Reinhardt.
Maybe related to the German word Sternschnuppe "shooting star, falling star".

Paternal grandmother of Perceval, wife of King Gandin of Anjou, and mother of Galoes, Gahmuret, Limmire and Flurdamurs.After Gahmuret left home in search of adventure, and Gandin and Galoes died, Schoette perished from loneliness.

From Ancient Greek σχοινεύς (schoineus), the name of an unknown type of bird, derived from σχοῖνος (schoinos) meaning "rush, reed, bed of rushes". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a son of Hippodamia and Autonous who was turned into a bird along with the rest of his family when his brother was devoured by their starving horses.
Latin word used in reference to singing and learning. May be used as a diminutive of Scholastica.
Masculine form of Scholastica. This name was borne by an 8th-century exarch of Ravenna.
Czech and German form of Scholastica.
Transferred use of an anglicized version of the surname Schön.

Derived from German schön meaning "beautiful". This name was borne by Schönche Jeannette Rothschild (1771-1859), the oldest child of Mayer Rothschild, founder of the Rothschild banking family. See also Shayna.
Derived from Yiddish shein "beautiful". The name coincides with German Schöne "beautiful woman" (compare Beila and Shayna).
derived from Schön "beautiful" and man "man". unlike its female counterpart, Schönfrau Schönman was rarely given to boys.

20th century coinage from the usual German word schön "beautiful" and the name element traud (related to the Old High German name element drud "strength").Schöntraud is extremely rare as a given name, despite its constant presence in reliable German name books.

Recorded in 13th-century Germany, it is possibly composed of the elements schön meaning "beautiful" and Wipfel meaning "peak, top, head, treetop", the meaning might imply the peak of beauty, or a beautiful face or head.
Germanized form of the French name Georges as well as the Hunsrik form of Jorge.
Vernacular diminutive of Georg via French Georges.
Vernacular form of Joseph, influenced by the French pronunciation of this name.
She married Kyot of Katelangen and died giving birth to her daughter Sigune. Prior to this, she raised Condwiramurs (Kondviramur), the hereditary Queen of Brabant, who became Perceval’s wife.
A pietistic name translating to "much fright" not allowed as a given name anymore in Germany.

Transferred use of the surname Schroeder. Used as a first name in 1951 by Charles Schulz for a character in his comic strip "Peanuts". Derived from the German surname Schröder 1 or Schröder 2 with the usual replacement spelling oe for ö.Despite the use in the popular comic strip it is not admitted as a given name in Germany because of its surname nature.
German transcription of the modern Hebrew name Shulamith.

Variant of Skuld used by John Thelwall in his play The Fairy of the Lake (written 1801; based on Arthurian legend), where it belongs to one of the three Fatal Sisters - the others being Urd and Verandi - who preside over the past, present and future. In Thelwall's play, Rowenna, wife of Vortigern, seeks their foresight during her quest to seduce Arthur.
Feminization of Schuyler in the trend of Skyla.
The name is formed from the German name elements SCHWAN "swan" and ger "javelin, spear".It was used in the nobility in south-west Germany until the early modern time.

Transferred use of the surname Schwarz as a given name. In Minahasa, this name is used in honor of Johann Gottlieb Schwarz, a German missionary who brought Christianity to the local people, alongside with Johann Friedrich Riedel.
Derived from Old Saxon swîth "strong" and either heri "army" or hard (cognate of Old Frisian herd) "hardy; brave".
Contracted form of Schweder, first recorded in the 1400s.Even though this name phonetically coincides with the modern German word for "heavy; difficult", it is still occasionally used today.
Either a variant of Swidger oder derived from Old High German swigen "to be silent, to keep silence" and hard "hard".
A new coinage from the German word Schwert "sword" and the name element helm "helmet, protection".The name occurs as a suggested German name for boys in 'Deutsches Famlienstambuch' 1937.
Transferred from the name of an early form of accolade. Schwertleite is the name of one of the valkyries in Richard Wagner's opera 'Die Walküre'.
Derived from Sicilian sciarra meaning "fight, brawl" as well as "quarrel, dispute", which is ultimately of Arabic origin.
From the English word science, derived from Latin scientia, from scire "to know".
Transferred use of the surname Scifres.
Sassarese and Gallurese form of Simon 1.
Means "mistral, northwest Mediterranean wind" in Ancient Greek, literally "wind blowing from the direction of the Scironian rocks". This was the name of a Corinthian bandit in Greek mythology.
Possibly derived from Old English scir "bright, pure" (compare Old Norse Skírnir) and weald "power, ruler".
Diminutive of Roscoe in the case of American actor and television personality Roscoe 'Scoey' Mitchell (1930-2022).
English vernacular form of Scholastica. In England it was used as a Christian name from the late 12th century until the Protestant Reformation.
Italian, Romansh and Romanian form of Scholastica.
From Old High German scôni "beautiful"; was in use in 9th century.
This is the name used for Shaggy's dog in the 'Scooby Doo' Franchise
English nickname coming from the word "scooter". Sometimes it might be used as a diminutive of Scott.

Uncertain etymology, possibly related to Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopos) meaning "watcher, lookout, guardian, scout; target, mark" or σκοπέω (skopeo) meaning "to look at, behold, consider". Scopas was a well-known Ancient Greek sculptor.

Derived from Late Latin Scotia, ultimately derived from Scoti or Scotti, a Latin name for the Gaels, first attested in the late 3rd century. At first it referred to all Gaels, whether in Ireland or Great Britain, as did the term Scotia for the lands they inhabited. From the 9th century, its meaning gradually shifted, so that it came to mean only the part of Britain lying north of the Firth of Forth: the Kingdom of Scotland. By the later Middle Ages it had become the fixed Latin term for what in English is called Scotland. The Romans referred to Ireland as "Scotia" around 500 A.D.In Irish mythology, Scottish mythology and pseudohistory, Scotia is the name given to the mythological daughter of an Egyptian pharaoh. Manuscripts of the Lebor Gabála Érenn contain a legend of a Scotia who was the wife of Goidel's descendant Míl Espáine of ancient Iberia. Scotia is said to have come to Ireland in 1700 BC to avenge the death of her husband, the King, who had been wounded in a previous ambush in south Kerry. She was killed in battle with the legendary Tuatha Dé Danann on the nearby Slieve Mish Mountains. This Scotia's Grave is a famous landmark in Munster, Ireland.According to Geoffrey Keating's 1634 narrative history of Ireland Foras Feasa ar Éirinn ("Foundation of Knowledge on Ireland" but most often known in English as "The History of Ireland"), the feminine name Scotia is derived from Irish scoṫ or scoth, meaning "blossom".
From the name of the country of Scotland, which means "land of the Scots", from Latin Scoti meaning "Gaelic speaker".
Feminine variant of Scotland using the popular name suffix lyn.
Either a variant of Scotia or a feminine form of Scott.
Variant form of Scottina. A known bearer of this name is the American actress Brett Rossi (b. 1989), who was born as Scottine Ross.
Feminine elaboration of Scott using the popular name suffix lyn, perhaps influenced by the place name Scotland.
Variant of Scotlyn, an alteration of Scotland formed using the feminine name suffix lyn. It can also be taken as a combination of Scott and Lynn.
Meaning unknown. This was the Roman name for the Greek figure Erebus.
Transferred use of the surname Scovel.
Scrat is a sabre-toothed squirrel who is obsessed with collecting acorns, constantly putting his life in danger to obtain and defend them in the Ice Age films.
Feminine form of Scribonius. Scribonia was the name of the second wife of Augustus, the first Roman emperor, and the mother of his daughter Julia.
This Roman cognomen is an extended form of Scribonius. A known bearer of this name was Lucius Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus, a Roman usurper from the 1st century AD.
Roman nomen gentile, which is derived from Scribonus.

Possibly derived from Latin scribere "to write", perhaps even in combination with Latin bonus "good, well", thus meaning "to write well." This was the name of Scribonus Largus, a Roman physician from the 1st century AD.
IDK it's just my last name
A character in "The Faerie Queene" by Edmund Spenser.
Name of a medieval Irish saint with strong Welsh connections.
Transferred use of the surname Scully.

Latinized form of Greek Σκυλακεύς (Skylakeus), which is a more elaborate form of Scylax. In Greek mythology, Scylaceus was a Lycian comrade-in-arms of Sarpedon and Glaucus. Him being Lycian means that he was of non-Greek origin, as Lycians were an Anatolian people. This might be important information for the origin of the name Scylax (the root of the name Scylaceus), since that name might possibly be Carian in origin - and Carian is an extinct Anatolian language.
Latinized form of Greek Σκύλαξ (Skylax), which means "young dog, whelp, puppy" in Ancient Greek. It’s theorised to be a calque (translation) of an unattested Carian name.
Variant of Skjǫldr used in the Old English poem Beowulf.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek σκύλλω (skyllo) meaning "to pluck, tear, flay, plunder" or "to trouble, annoy, torment". In Greek mythology, Scylla was a man-eating sea monster that lived on one side of a narrow channel of water, opposite its counterpart Charybdis. In later myths, the monster was said to have originally been a nymph. Scylla was also the name of a princess of Megara, who betrayed her father Nisus by cutting his magical lock of hair that made him and their city invincible.
Uncertain etymology. Possibly related to Scylla.

Means "Scythian, of Scythia" in Ancient Greek. Scythes was a son of Hercules and Echidna in Greek mythology, and the eponymous king of Scythia. This was also the name of a tyrant of Zancle appointed circa 494 BC.
Latinized form of Skythianos. This was the name of an Alexandrian religious teacher who was allegedly the first Alexandrian to visit India.

Form of Səadət used in langauges that don't have letter ə.

Séadna, also Séanna, is an Irish Gaelic personal name known mostly due to the popularity of the book Séadna, by Father Peadar Ua Laoghaire (occasionally known in English as Peter O'Leary), which was published in 1904. The story of Séadna, which concerns a cobbler who makes a deal with the devil, is thought to be an Irish folk tale related to the story of Faust.

Transferred use of the surname Seafield.A known bearer of this name is the English actor and singer Murray Head (b. 1946). It is one of his middle names, and honours his father Seafield Head (1919-2009).

Transferred use of the surname Seaforth. Kenneth Ivo Brownley Langwell Mackenzie (1913-1955) was an Australian poet and novelist. His first and best-known novel, 'The Young Desire It' (1937), was published under the pen name Seaforth Mackenzie.
Derived from the Old English elements sæ "sea" and fugol "bird".
Transferred use of the surname Seager.
Variant of Séaghdha as well as an older form of Sean.

Form of the name Shealtiel, an archangel in Eastern Orthodox and some Catholic traditions, meaning "Prayer of God."
Possibly given to a child who was spared during a sea journey.
Diminutive of Séamus.The name notably features in the song 'An bhFaca Tú Mo Shéamuisín?' by Na Casaidigh.
Latinazed feminine form of Seán. Seána came into use in the 20th century.
Anglicized form of Seána and variant of Seanna.
From Chinese 上海 (shànghǎi) meaning Shanghai.
A diminutive form of Seán, given to 22 boys in Ireland in 2025.
Feminine form and diminutive of Sean.
Possibly a blend of Shawnte and Shanique, the spelling influenced by that of Sean.
