column12: From Sino-Korean 素 (so) meaning "plain, simple", 昭 (so) meaning "bright, luminous" or 少 (so) meaning "few, little" combined with 潤 (yun) meaning "soft, sleek" or 允 (yun) meaning "allow, consent" or 昀 (yun) meaning "sunlight" or 尹 (yun) meaning "govern, oversee". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Old Norse combination of sær "sea" and vár "spring".
Meaning unknown. It might possibly be related to the Ossetian name Sozyr, which is ultimately of Iranian origin.
Russian and Romanian form of Sozon.
The god of Fertility and family.

The name of a Filipino woman from Santa Maria, Bulacan, whose father named her after the popular pasta dish spaghetti. She has siblings named Macaroni ‘85 and Sincerely Yours ’98, with the numbers indicating their years of birth; their late father chose the names believing that they sounded both 'unique' and 'modern'.The woman herself, whose full name is Spaghetti '88, has children named Cheese Pimiento, Parmesan Cheese and Mozzarella Cheese.
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Spakr.
From Old Norse spakr meaning "wise, sensible, peaceable".
Transferred use of the surname Spalding.A notable bearer of this name is the American actor and playwright Spalding Gray (1941-2004).
From Tibetan དཔལ་མཛེས (dpal-mdzes) meaning "glorious beauty", derived from དཔལ (dpal) meaning "glorious, magnificent" and མཛེས (mdzes) meaning "beautiful, fine".
From Sanskrit स्पन्दन (spandana) meaning "throbbing, pulsating, quickening (as in a child growing in the womb)".
Short form of Spandarat, which has now become the modern form of the name.

Armenian form of Esfandiar via its Middle Persian form Spandadat. A known bearer of this name was the Armenian doctor and scientist Spandarat Kamsarakan (1876-1942), who played a crucial role in establishing the Armenian Red Cross National Society.
Middle Persian form of Spenta Armaiti.
Derived from Latin Hispania "Iberian peninsula, Spain", itself possibly derived from Punic אישפן "coast of hyraxes".
Old Norse byname, from Old Norse spár meaning "prophetic".
Originally a transferred use of the surname Spark. It is now used as an adoption of the English word (which is derived from Old English spearca via Middle English sparke meaning "spark").
Middle English frequentative (verb) or diminutive (noun) of spark.
Old Norse byname or personal name meaning, ‘sprightly’, ‘vivacious’
Transferred use of the surname Sparks. Also sometimes used as a nickname for Mark coinciding with the English word sparks.
act of touching; touch; contact; the quality of touch or tangibility; whit, jot; effect of touch or contact; any of the consonants.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek σπάρτον (sparton) meaning "rope, cable", in reference to cords laid at the city of Sparta’s foundations to mark its boundaries, but this could be folk etymology. In Greek mythology, this was the name of the eponymous first queen of Sparta.
Form of Spartak with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Cognate of Spas as well as a derivation from Macedonian спас (spas) "rescue, salvation".
Derived from Bulgarian спасена (spasena), the indefinite feminine singular past passive participle of спася (spasja) "to save, to rescue" referring to Jesus Christ.
Diminutive of Spasena, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Either a short form of Spasena or derived from Bulgarian спася (spasja) "to save, to rescue" referring to Jesus Christ.
Cognate of Spasia as well as a short form of Aspasija.

The first element of this name is derived from Bulgarian spasjá or spasjávam "to save, to rescue". Also compare Serbo-Croatian spasiti and Russian spasát', both of which mean "to save, to rescue". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, the meaning of this name is roughly "to save peace".
Feminine form of Spas and Spase as well as a Macedonian diminutive of Spasa.
Diminutive of Spase, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Derived from Serbian spasiti meaning "to save".
Means "sparrowhawk" in Old English, ultimately derived from the elements spearwa "sparrow" and hafoc "hawk". This name was borne by an 11th-century Anglo-Saxon artist and Benedictine monk.
From the English word special meaning "Unique".
Derived from the Latin adjective speciosus meaning "good-looking, handsome, beautiful".This name was borne by a 6th-century saint from Italy.
Given to Speck Wildhorse Mellencamp, son of John Mellencamp and Elaine Irwin.
From the Kurdish spêde meaning "early morning, sunrise".
Transferred use of the surname Speed.

Derived from σπεῖος (speios), the Epic Greek form of σπέος (speos) meaning "cave, cavern, grotto". This was the name of a Nereid in Greek myth; with the exception of Pausanias, all of the Greek poets (Hesiod, Homer, Apollodorus and Hyginus) and even the Roman poet Virgil list Speio among the ranks of the Haliad Nymphs known as the Nereides.
Diminutive of Špela, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Short form of Spencer or transferred use of the surname Spence.
Possibly a feminine form of Spencer.

A Zoroastrian divinity, one of the six creative or divine manifestations of Wisdom and Ahura Mazda. Her name means "creative harmony", although she was later associated with religious devotion. She is associated with the Mother Earth figure and her holy day is associated with love.
This is the name of the 13th-century patron saint of Cingoli, Italy.
Derived from the Italian phrase spera in Dio meaning "hope in God".
A character in "Mother Bombie" an Elizabethan era stage play, by John Lyly.

From the Italian word speranza meaning "hope" (compare Speranza); perhaps in some cases a Greek form of the Romanian name Speranța. It was adopted by the Greek actress Sperantza Vrana (1928-2009), whose birth name was Elpida (also meaning "hope").
Derived from the Latin word for "home". This was the name of 2nd century Sicilian saint.
Transferred use of the surname Spero.
Transferred from the English surname Sperry.

Derived from Ancient Greek σπεύδω (speudo) meaning "to urge on, hasten; to seek eagerly, strive after" (compare σπουδή (spoude) "haste, speed; earnestness, diligence, zeal") and ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".
German form of Speusippos via its latinized form Speusippus.
French form of Speusippos via its latinized form Speusippus.
Italian form of Speusippos via its latinized form Speusippus.

Derived from Greek σπεύδω (speudo) meaning "to hasten; to urge on, to set going" (compare the closely related σπουδή (spoude) meaning "haste, speed" as well as "earnestness, diligence, zeal") and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Latinized form of Speusippos. This name was borne by an ancient Greek philosopher from the 4th century BC.
Polish form of Speusippos via its latinized form Speusippus.

A character in 'Mostellaria', a play by the Roman author Plautus. Its name translates from Latin as "The Ghost (play)" (with the word fabula understood in the title). The play is believed to be an adaptation of a lost comedy of the Athenian poet Philemon called Phasma (the Ghost).
Derived from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaira) meaning "ball, globe, sphere".

Probably from the English word sphere, ultimately from Greek σφαῖρα (sphaira) meaning "globe, ball". Two famous bearers of this name are American jazz pianist Thelonious Sphere Monk (1917-1982) and his son Thelonious Sphere "T. S." Monk III (1949-), a jazz drummer.
Old Swedish form of Spialli and Old Swedish short form of Spiælbodhi.
From Old Norse spjalli meaning "companion, friend".
Possibly taken from the English word "spicy".
The name of a witch and antagonist in the Latvian epic poem 'Lāčplēsis' but she turns good towards the end of the story.
Meaning unknown. In the Latvian national epic Lāčplēsis this is the name of a witch enslaved by the devil, but eventually rescued by the hero Koknesis (whom she then marries).

Meaning uncertain. It might possibly be a diminutive or short form of Spiridon.In Georgian literature, Spidona is the name of a character from the novel Mikela (1904) written by Davit Kldiashvili (1862-1931). A film based on the novel was released in 1965 under the same name.

Probably a Dutchification of Spike. Alternatively, this name might be derived from the Dutch word spijker meaning "nail" (as in, the metal object), which is also etymologically related to the aforementioned given name.
Variant of Spyridon via its short form Spyros.
Derived from Italian spinetta meaning "thornlet, small thorn".
Likely transferred from the surname Spinner.
Means "silver" in Pashto, derived from سپين (spin) meaning "white" and زر (zar) "metal".
Derived from Ancient Greek σπέος (speos) meaning "cave, cavern, grotto". Spio is a sea nymph and one of the fifty nereids in Greek mythology.

Hellenized form of Old Persian *Spiθradātah, possibly meaning "given by heaven", from Old Persian *spiθrah “heaven” and 𐎭𐎠𐎫 (d-a-t) "given, created". This was the name of a Persian satrap of Lydia and Ionia under the high king Darius III Codomannus.
From Old French spirer, and its source, Latin spīrō (“to breathe”). Possible relation to Spiro.
Probably derived from Italian Sirito Santo "Holy Spirit".The name was borne by the architect-priest Spirito Maria Chiappetta.
Croatian and Serbian form of Spyros.
Possibly a Romani form of Esperanza.
Armenian form of Snow White, from Armenian սպիտակ (spitak) "white" and ձյուն (dzyun) "snow". Not used as given name in Armenia.
Derived from Old Persian spita "white" combined with Old Persian manah "mind, intelligence, mentality", thus meaning something like "clear-minded".
Hellenized form of Spitamaneh. This was the name of a Sogdian warlord from the 4th century BC.
From unknown name element and Polish gniew "anger".
Modern transcription of Spiuti, originally a byname derived from Old Norse spjót "spear". It appears on several runestones in Sweden as sbiuti and sbiut.
Means "brighter" in Cornish. This is a modern Cornish name.

Medieval English name (found in a Curia Regis Roll item dated 1213), derived from Latin splendor meaning "brilliance, brightness, lustre, distinction". (It was listed in 'A Dictionary of English Surnames' by Dr Reaney, who noted: 'In the Middle Ages there was a fashion for fanciful feminine names, few of which have survived, or given rise to surnames.') This is also the name a small town in the U.S. state of Texas.

Derived from the English word splinter, which usually refers to a long and sharp fragment of material (often wood).This is the name of several characters in popular culture, the most famous being Splinter from the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles series.
Derived from Latvian spodrs "shiny; bright; clean".
Alternate transcription of Pashto سپوږمۍ (see Spogmai).

Means "libation, drink-offering (to the gods)" as well as "treaty, truce" in Ancient Greek. Sponde was the seventh of the twelve Horae presiding over hours of the day in Greek mythology, overseeing the hour after lunch during which libations were poured. A moon of Jupiter is named after her.
Alternate transcription of Bengali স্পন্দন (see Spandan).

The name of the main character in a popular kid's cartoon series, Spongebob SquarePants. Originally his name was SpongeBoy, however it was changed upon discovering that the name was taken for a mop product.
Variant of Spontaneous. This is borne by Spontaniouse Grant, who was a contestant on the ninth season of the reality television series America's Next Top Model.
Alternate transcription of Pashto سپوږمۍ (see Spogmai).

Derived from the Greek noun σπόρος (sporos) meaning "a sowing" as well as "seed, semen" and "harvest, crop".A notable bearer of this name was Sporos of Nicaea, a Greek mathematician and astronomer from the 3rd century AD.

Sportacus is a fictional character from the children's television show LazyTown. His name is a portmanteau of the ancient figure Spartacus and the word sport, which represents his athleticism. Sportacus humbly describes himself as a "slightly above-average hero", though his friends have a higher opinion of him, calling him a "superhero".
Probably derived from Icelandic sporður meaning "tail of a fish or whale".

Latinized form of Sporos. This was the name of a young slave boy from the 1st century AD. The Roman emperor Nero had taken a liking to him, because he bore a striking resemblance to his late wife Poppaea Sabina. Nero subsequently had the boy castrated, after which he married him. He treated him as his wife, though in reality Sporus was actually his sex slave. After the death of Nero in 68 AD, Sporus continued to be used as a sex slave (most notably by the subsequent Roman emperors Otho and Vitellius) until his own death by suicide in 69 AD.
Transferred use of the surname Spotswood.
Transferred use of the surname Spottswood.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek noun σπουδή (spoude) meaning "haste, speed" as well as "earnestness, diligence, zeal". It is ultimately derived from the Greek verb σπεύδω (speudo) meaning "to hasten" as well as "to urge on" and "to set going". Also compare the closely related Greek adjective σπουδαῖος (spoudaios) meaning "in haste, hasty, quick" as well as "earnest, diligent, zealous". The second element of this name is derived from Greek ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man". In other words, this name is basically a variant form of Speusandros.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek noun σπουδή (spoude) meaning "haste, speed" as well as "earnestness, diligence, zeal". It is ultimately derived from the Greek verb σπεύδω (speudo) meaning "to hasten" as well as "to urge on" and "to set going". Also compare the closely related Greek adjective σπουδαῖος (spoudaios) meaning "in haste, hasty, quick" as well as "earnest, diligent, zealous". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun ‘ιππος (hippos) meaning "horse". In other words, this name is basically a variant form of Speusippos.
Variant of Spogmai reflecting the Southern Pashto pronunciation of the name.
Alternate transcription of Pashto سپوږمۍ (see Spozhmai).
Transferred use of the surname Sprague, itself a variant of the English word sprack meaning "lively".
Of uncertain etymology, possibly a transferred use of the surname Sprainger. Spranger Barry (23 November 1719 – 10 January 1777) was an Irish actor.
From the word sprig, meaning both "a small shoot: twig; branch" and "youth, heir". Usage might relate to the existence of Sprigg as a surname.
Dutch-Yiddish form of Shprintze (see also Sprinz and Sprinze).

Sprota (born c. 910) was a woman who William I, Duke of Normandy took as a wife in the Viking fashion (more danico) and was the mother of his successor, Richard I, Duke of Normandy. After the death of her husband William, she married Esperleng and had Rodulf of Ivry.
Based on Old Norse word sproti meaning 'sprout'.
From the Latvian spulgs meaning "bright; radiant."
Transferred use of the surname Spurgeon. In many cases, especially among devout Christians, the name is given in honour of the English preacher Charles Spurgeon (1834-1892).

Means "satellite, traveling companion, fellow traveler" in Russian. It was adopted as a stage name by American professional wrestler and civil rights activist Sputnik Monroe (1928-2006), real name Roscoe Monroe Brumbaugh. It was also used for a bull terrier (dog) in the movie Space Buddies (2009).
Derived from Slavic spyci "pointless, futile, unnecessary" combined with Polish gniew "anger" (which is derived from Slavic gnev "anger").
Derived from Slavic spyci "pointless, futile, unnecessary" combined with Slavic mirŭ "peace".
Derived from Slavic spyci "pointless, futile, unnecessary" combined with Slavic slav "glory".
Modern Greek diminutive of Spyros, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.
From the English word "squall". This is the main protagonist in 'Final Fantasy VIII'.
Squanto is a native name especially known for the Native American tribe who helped in the Mayflower.

A combination of the animal squid and the name Edward. This is the name of a major character in the SpongeBob Squarepants cartoon franchise. Despite it being in the name, Squidward is not a squid and is actually an octopus.

Either from the English occupational surname (see Squire), or else directly from the English word. It is derived from Old French esquier, escuier "squire", literally "shield-bearer" (from Latin scutarius, a derivative of scutum "shield").
Alternate transcription of Bengali শ্রাবন্তী (see Srabanti).
Alternate transcription of Telugu స్రవంతి (see Sravanti).
Means "peace of the Serbs", derived from Serbian Srbi meaning "Serbs" combined with the Slavic element mir meaning "peace".
Means "fame of the Serbs" from Serbian Srbi "Serbs" combined with the Slavic element slav "glory".
Derived from the Serbian noun Србин (Srbin) meaning "Serb".
Derived from Srbin, meaning "a Serb", and ljubiti, meaning "to kiss, to love".
Derived from Macedonian сребро (srebro) “silver”. Srebra Apostolova Ushlinova (1886–1942) was a Macedonian Bulgarian revolutionary.
Srecha (English: happiness, luck) is the Serbian goddess of fate. She spins the thread of life as an assistant to the great goddess Mokosh.The name is related to the Ukrainian goddess Stricha.
Malayalam and Tamil form of Shridhara.
Sreeja is a sanskrit word meaning the one who is born in prosperity.Sreeja,The Jatika of Goddess Lakshmi indicates born out of beauty and grace or out of goddess Lakshmi

Means "conqueror of Lakshmi" from Sanskrit श्री (śrī) referring to the Hindu goddess Lakshmi and जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering". This is another name of the god Vishnu, the husband of Lakshmi.
it means goddess Lakshmi's victorySree- means Goddess Lakshmi (Goddess of wealth and prosperity)Jitha- means victory
Derived from South Slavic sreča meaning "luck".
Alternate transcription of Thai เศรษฐา (see Settha).
Means "woman, lady, girl" in Khmer, ultimately from Sanskrit स्त्री (strī).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শ্রেয়সী (see Shreyasi).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শ্রেয়সী (see Shreyasi).
From Khmer ស្រី (srey) meaning "woman, lady, beautiful, excellent" and possibly ម៉ុម (mom) meaning "dear, beloved, darling".
Derived from Khmer ស្រី (srey) meaning "woman, lady".
From Khmer ស្រី (srey) meaning "woman, lady, girl" and នាង (neang) meaning "miss, young woman, girl".
From Khmer ស្រី (srey) meaning "woman, lady, girl" and នាថ (neath) meaning "chief, head" or "help, support, assistance".
Alternate transcription of Bengali শ্রেয়সী (see Shreyasi).
Tamil and Malayalam variant of Shridhara.
From Sanskrit श्री (śrī) meaning "radiance, splendour, beauty" combined with हरि (hari) meaning "yellow, tawny".
From Shri, another name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi, and Sanskrit ज (ja) meaning "born" (therefore meaning "born from Shri").
From Nepali srijan or Sanskrit sṛjanā, meaning "creation".
Alternate transcription of Telugu శ్రీకాంత్, Kannada ಶ್ರೀಕಾಂತ್, Tamil ஸ்ரீகாந்த்/சிறீகாந்த் or Malayalam ശ്രീകാന്ത് (see Srikanth).
Bengali and Odia form of Shrikanta.
Indian origin. It means the creative power of the almighty godess of wealth and good luck.
Variant of Srimaya. It means “good luck” and is associated with the Goddess Lakshmi.
Means "receptacle of beauty" in Sanskrit, Hindi and Tamil.
Alternate transcription of Telugu శ్రీనివాస, Kannada ಶ್ರೀನಿವಾಸ್ or Tamil ஸ்ரீனிவாஸ் (see Srinivas). A notable bearer was Indian mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887-1920).
Means "creation, letting loose, emission" in Sanskrit.
Alternate transcription of Thai ศรีสุดา (see Sisuda).
Name: Srit ( सृत)MEANING - going, gone, running ,escape, moving, flight Usage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Alternate transcription of Bengali স্মৃতি (see Smriti).
Telugu feminine name derived from శ్రీ (sri) meaning "wealth, riches, beauty, glory" and విద్య (vidya) meaning "knowledge, science, learning".
From the Indonesian title of respect sri, ultimately from Sanskrit श्री (shri), combined with the feminine suffix -wati.
From the name Sri combined with the Indonesian feminine suffix -yati.
Derived from Macedonian срна (srna) and Serbo-Croatian srna "doe, female deer".
The name of a star that shines in the month of Srabon (between July and August).
A Gujurati Indian name, meaning universe.
Name: Srut स्रुतMEANING : -emitting, flowing with, distilled》 It shouldn't be confused with ShrutUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Alternate transcription of Malayalam ശ്രുതി, Tamil சுருதி, Telugu శ్రుతి or Kannada ಶ್ರುತಿ (see Shruthi).
Alternate transcription of Malayalam ശ്രുതി or Tamil சுருதி (see Shruthi).
Alternate transcription of Tamil சுருதி (see Shruthi).
Variant spelling of Stacia, which is the English equivalent of the Greek and Russian name Stasia.
Not available.It was the byname of Heinrich Trollmann, brother of the German boxing champion Johann Rukeli Trollmann.
Variant of Stacyann using Stacey. 7 girls were named STACEYANN in 1991.

From Ancient Greek στάχυς (stachys) meaning "head of grain, ear of corn" as well as "scion, progeny". It was also the name of the brightest star in the constellation Virgo.This name was borne by Stachys the Apostle, the second bishop of Byzantium (1st century AD).

Elaboration of Stacia in the style of Eliana 1 or a combination of Staci/Stacy with Ana/Anna (Compare Stacyann/Stacyanna).Staciana Stitts is an American former competition swimmer and breaststroke specialist. She is a 2000 Summer Olympics and 1999 Pan American Games gold medalist, and 1998 Goodwill Games silver medalist.
Variant of Stacy (See also Staci). Film actress Stacii Jae Johnson bears this name.
Means "last child (according the parents desire)" in Vlach.
Old Norse combination of stein "stone" and bjǫrg 'help, save, rescue'.
Ancient Scandinavian with the combination of steinn "stone" and fríðr "beautiful, good, alive, peaceful, safe".
Derived from the Germanic name elements steinn "stone" and hildr "battle, fight".
Old Norse short form of Stæinkætill.
Derived from Old Norse steinn "stone" and ketill "cauldron hat", "helmet".
Old Norse combination of steinn "stone" and laug possibly meaning "betrothed woman".
Dutch short form of Gustaaf, influenced by the variant form Gustaf. A known bearer of this name is the Flemish actor and television presenter Staf Coppens (b. 1981).
Diminutive of Stafford. It can also be from the surname Staff.
Early New High German form of Stephen.
Derived from the Germanic name elements stafn "stem (of a ship, prow or stern)" and grímr "person wearing a face mask".
Belarusian form of the Slavic name Stanisław meaning "standing strong in glory"
Russian and Ukrainian form of Stachys.

Means "morning star" in Totonac. From staku "star", pun "to be born" and tsisaj "at dawn", literally "star born at dawn". It was the name of a mythical Totonac princess, from whom the vanilla flower was born when she died.

Combination of Stalin and Beria, which were the surnames of the Soviet politicians Joseph Stalin (1878-1953) and Lavrentiy Beria (1899-1953). This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.This name is also encountered as a short form of the related name Lenstalberi.
Old Swedish and Swedish younger form of Stáli.
Transferred use of the surname Staley. While it was used as a rare masculine name during the 20th century, in modern times, it's more often used as a feminine name.

From the surname of Joseph Stalin (1878-1953), the Russian revolutionist and secretary general of the Communist party of the Soviet Union. Despite the controversial character of the politician, the name is used as a given name in India and Latin America (particularly Ecuador).

Feminine form of surname Stalin, which was adopted by Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. The surname itself is derived from Russian сталь (stal) meaning "steel". This name was coined after the Russian Revolution, and it was occasionally given to Soviet girls born from the 1920s to the 1950s. At that point, the Soviet government condemned Stalin, and the name Stalina dropped out of use.
Perhaps a combination of the name Stalin and Sanskrit जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Transferred use of the surname Stall.
Stamford means "stone ford" and comes from Old English.

Combination of the surnames of Сталин (Stalin) and Энгельс (Engels), which refer to Joseph Stalin (1878-1953) and Friedrich Engels (1820-1895). This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.
Unrecorded Old English name, composed of stan meaning "stone" and burg meaning "fortress". Could also be related to the Old Norse name Stæinborg.
Transferred use of the surname Stanbury, meaning "stone fortification" in Old English.
Originally a diminutive of Stana, used as a given name in its own right.

Diminutive form of Stanisław. Stańczyk was the most famous Polish court jester. He was employed by three Polish kings: Alexander, Sigismund the Old, and Sigismund Augustus. He is also the main content in Jan Matejko's painting, which is the same name.

Transferred use of the English surname Standfast, or simply means "to stand firm, to stand one's ground"; compare the English word steadfast meaning "firm or unwavering in purpose, resolution or faith" and the name Stand-fast-on-high.
Referencing putting your full trust in God.
Transferred use of the surname Standiford.
Transferred use of the surname Standish.
Transferred use of the surname Staney.
Derived from Old English stan "stone, rock, gem" and flæd, possibly meaning "beauty".
Old English cognate of Germanic Steinhard, derived from the elements stan "stone" and heard "hard, firm, brave, hardy".
Transferred use of the surname Stanhope.
Diminutive of Stana, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
This name comes from the Old English name Stanhild, "stone battle". It derives from the Anglo-Saxon elements stan meaning "Stone", and hild meaning "Battle".
Short form of Stanislas, used as a given name in its own right.
Recorded in Montenegro in the early 1600s.
Variant of Stanley. Sometimes it can also be feminine from

In Flanders (Belgium), this given name is strictly masculine, as it is a variant form of Stan 3, which is a short form of Constans and related names (such as Constant and Constantijn).In the Netherlands, this given name is unisex, but it is more often encountered on women than on men. For women, the name is a short form of Constance and related names, such as Constantia and Constantina. It could even be a short form of Christianne in some cases. For men, the etymology is the same as it is for men in Flanders.With that said, you might also want to take a look at the related name Stanneke.

Transferred use of the surname Starbuck.Other sources say that a starbuck was someone who gathered willow-twigs and reed along the riverside for the weaving of baskets. Mostly, these people lived along those riversides as well. As such, it could very well be that these people were referred to as people from the (great) river, which would have been stor bokki during the time where the Vikings came to England. Over the years, language sound shifts probably resulted in them being called starbecks and finally starbucks.In literature, Starbuck was the name of the chief mate in Herman Melville's novel Moby-Dick (1851). Also, in popular culture, Starbuck was the callsign of a character in the TV series Battlestar Galactica. The character was male in the original series from 1978, but female in the re-imagined series from 2004.A notable bearer of this name in real life is Gabriel Starbuck Brown (b. 1989), one of the people featured in the American reality television series Alaskan Bush People (2014).

Possibly a combination of the English word star and the first name Daryl.The name was notably born by Staryl C. Austin, an Oregon native who served as a brigadier general in the United States Air Force during World War II.
Latinized form of Stasandros. This name was borne by Stasander of Cyprus (4th century BC), who was an officer in the service of Alexander the Great.

Derived from Ancient Greek στάσις (stasis) meaning "standing, placing, setting; stature, posture", ultimately derived from ἵστημι (histemi) meaning "to stand, set up", and ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man". One could then say that the meaning of this name is roughly "the standing of a man" or perhaps "the man who stands still".

Derived from Ancient Greek στάσις (stasis) meaning "standing, placing, setting; stature, posture", ultimately derived from ἵστημι (histemi) meaning "to stand, set up", and ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man". One could then say that the meaning of this name is roughly "the standing of a man" or perhaps "the man who stands still". A known bearer of this name was Stasanor of Cyprus (4th century BC), an officer in the service of Alexander the Great, who was later made a satrap of Aria and then of Drangiana.
Romansh short form of Anastasia, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Rare variant of Stacy, and a short form of Anastasia.
English and Romansh short form of Anastasia as well as a Russian variant transliteration of Стася (see Stasya).

Derived from Ancient Greek στάσις (stasis) meaning "standing, placing, setting; stature, posture", ultimately from ἵστημι (histemi) meaning "to stand, set up, stand still", and κράτος (kratos) meaning "power, strength".
Derived from Greek στάσις (stasis) meaning "standing, posture, position" and νίκη (nike) meaning "victory". Compare Nikostasis.

Stass SHOSTAK took part in the FIRST "international" series of the T.V. programme "Gladiators". He is RUSSIAN.

Allegedly means "creation of the stars", in which case it would be related to Persian sitareh "star". This was probably the usual name of Alexander the Great's second wife, a daughter of the Persian king Darius III, formally named Barsine. After Alexander's death Stateira was murdered by his first wife Roxana.Modern historians have tried to identify the biblical Vashti with that of the Persian queen Stateira, even suggesting that Vashti is a diminutive of Vashtateira.
From the name of Staten Island in New York City, itself after the legislature of the Netherlands, named the Staten-Generaal.
After the legal doctrine of states' rights, which asserts that US states can nullify federal laws that they deem unconstitutional. This was the name of Confederate general States Rights Gist.
Transferred use of the surname Statham.
Feminine form of Statilius. A known bearer of this name was Statilia Messalina, the third wife of the Roman Emperor Nero.
Roman nomen gentile which was derived from Statius. A known bearer of this name was Titus Statilius Taurus, a Roman general and two-time consul from the 1st century BC.

The goddess who gives the baby fitness or "straightness," (i.e. the ability to live) and the father held it up to acknowledge his responsibility to raise it. Unwanted children might be abandoned at the Temple of Pietas or the Columna Lactaria. Newborns with serious birth defects might be drowned or smothered.

An Oscan praenomen mostly used by the Samnites. Statius Gellius was a Samnite General. Later it was a Roman cognomen, and is attested by the Roman poets Publius Papinius Statius and Caecilius Statius.

Roman praenomen (which later also came to be used as a nomen gentile) of Oscan origin. The meaning is uncertain, but it may possibly have been derived from Oscan staít meaning "he stands", which would mean that it is closely related to Latin statuo "to set up, to erect, to cause to stand". Oscan and Latin are both Italic languages, hence the close relation. Also compare the English word statue. A known bearer of this name was the Roman comic poet Caecilius Statius, who lived in the 2nd century BC.
Transferred use of the surname Staton.

Meaning "dust finger". The name of one of the main characters in Cornelia Funke's 'Inkworld' books is dangerously close to the German word Staubfänger "dust collector" colloquially used for books that are standing in a shelf without being used for a long time.
Italian form of Staurakios via its latinized form Stauracius.

Derived from Greek σταυρός (stauros), which originally meant "upright pale, upright stake" but nowadays has the meaning of "cross, crucifix" (see Stavros), combined with the Byzantine suffix -άκιος (-akios). Staurakios was the name of a Byzantine Emperor from the 9th century AD.

Spanish form of Staurophila. The use of this name was probably inspired by Camino real de la cruz (1721), which is one of the earliest Spanish translations of Regia Via Crucis (1635), an important counter-reformation devotional emblem book written by the Dutch-born Flemish Benedictine monk Benedictus van Haeften (1588-1648). The main character of his book is called Staurophila, whose name was hispanicized to Staurofila in the Spanish translations of the book.In original Spanish literature, Staurofila is the name of the eponymous character of the novel Staurofila (1889) written by the Mexican author María Nestora Téllez (1828-1890).

Feminine form of Staurophilos. In literature, this is the name of the main character of Regia Via Crucis (1635), an important counter-reformation devotional emblem book written by the Dutch-born Flemish Benedictine monk Benedictus van Haeften (1588-1648). It was his most important work and was translated thirteen times (among others into French, German and Spanish). The book is known as De heyr-baene des cruys in (archaic) Dutch.

French form of Staurophila. The use of this name was probably inspired by Le chemin royal de la croix (1676), which is one of the earliest French translations of Regia Via Crucis (1635), an important counter-reformation devotional emblem book written by the Dutch-born Flemish Benedictine monk Benedictus van Haeften (1588-1648). The main character of his book is called Staurophila, whose name was gallicized to Staurophile in the French translations of the book. Later translations tend to include her name in the title, such as Staurophile, ou la voie royale de la croix (1859).

Means "friend of the cross" in Greek, derived from the Greek noun σταυρός (stauros) meaning "cross, crucifix" (see Stavros) combined with the Greek noun φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover".This name appears to have been primarily used as a monastic name and pseudonym.
Croatian and Serbian form of Staurakios via its latinized form Stauracius.

Modern Greek diminutive of Stavros, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). Also compare the related name Staurakios.This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.

Possibly a variant of the Greek name Stavros. This is the middle name of James Bond's archenemy, Ernst Stavro Blofeld.

From the English word steadfast, meaning "resolutely or dutifully firm and unwavering." This name is used in reference to God's steadfastness or in reference to one's steadfastness to faith.

From the English surname Stede. This was most notably borne by Stede Bonnet (1688-1718), known as the 'Gentleman Pirate' because he was born into a wealthy English family on the island of Barbados.

Polish diminutive of Stefania and modern German diminutive of Stefanie.
From Old Norse stefnir meaning "coxswain, helmsman, steersman, one who directs".

Short form of names beginning with the Old Norse element steinn "stone", and thus a feminine equivalent of Steinn.

From the mountain pass and town of the same name. The name is of Lombard origin, though the exact etymology is not known. A famous bearer of this name is Italian composer Stelvio Cipriani.

Derived from Greek stamata "to stop", this name was historically given to a girl with older sisters whose parents desperately hoped for a son. They "were literally praying for the curse of daughters to stop".

Combination of the surnames Сталин (Stalin) and Энгельс (Engels), which refer to Joseph Stalin (1878-1953) and Friedrich Engels (1820-1895). This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.

The name of a Divine (god) in the popular video game series 'The Elder Scrolls'.Stendarr 'the Steadfast' is known as the god of mercy, charity, well-earned luck, and justice. He originated as a god of ransom but evolved into one of compassion and righteous rule by might and merciful forbearance, making him a favorite of magistrates and rulers and the patron god of the Imperial Legion. He is most popular amongst Imperials, Altmer (High Elves), Bosmer (Wood Elves), and Bretons. He is also known as the patron god of the Vigilants of Stendarr, a cult devoted to 'justice' and cleansing the world of Daedra and other abominations (werewolves, vampires, witches, etc) in the name of the divine.
Elaborated form of Stena by way of adding the then-fashionable name suffix -etta. This name was recorded in the 18th century.
Combination of Sten and Finn 2. This is the name of a medieval missionary from Hälsingland (Sweden), more known by the name Staffan.
Diminutive of Stefania. Polish singer Stefania Kozłowska went by Stenia Kozłowska.
Portuguese form of Sten. This name is borne by the brazilian actor Stênio Garcia.

Combination of Old Norse steinn "stone" and ketill "kettle, helmet".

Medieval Georgian form of Stephanos (see Stephen). This name was borne by four rulers of Caucasian Iberia (called Kartli in Georgian), the earliest of which reigned from about 590 until his death in 627.
Variant of Stefan. A notable bearer of the name is the american football player Stepfan Lee Taylor.
Dutch form of Stephanus. Also compare Stefaan, which is a little bit more common in Belgium and The Netherlands.

Latin feminine form of the Greek name Stephanos (see Stephen) via its latinized form Stephanus.The blessed Stefana Quinzani (1457-1530) was a Dominican sister from Italy, who is known in English as Stephana de Quinzanis.
Means "crowned,” from Greek στεφανόω, stephanoó, "to crown."

Derived from Greek στεφάνη (stephane) meaning "(brim of a) helmet" as well as "crown, diadem, wreath". In other words: this name is the Late Greek feminine form of Stephanos (see Stephen).In modern times, the name is often masculine: it's usually a variant of Stéphane that is used outside of France. However, it sometimes also appears as an alternate spelling of Stephanie (with the pronunciation intact, at least in the Anglophone world).

Feminine form of Stephan. Stephanetta Johanna Paulina (Nettie) Bredell (1877-1920) was a granddaughter of Paul Kruger (Stephanus Johannes Paulus Kruger), President of the South African Republic (or Transvaal) from 1883 to 1900.

Likely a feminine form of Stephen.

Feminine form of Steponas. In other words, this name is the Lithuanian equivalent of Stephanie.
Likely derived from the Greek stereos (στερεός) meaning "solid".
Derived from Breton sterenn "star" (cf. Steren), this name is occasionally considered the Breton equivalent of Saint Asteria.
Meaning "star-like, stellar", derived from the Kurdish word stêr ("star").
Variant of Sterling, using the popular name suffix lyn.
From Yiddish shtern, "star". It is sometimes used as a Yiddish form of Esther.

Derived from the Greek noun στερόπης (steropes) meaning "lightner", which is ultimately derived from the Greek noun στεροπή (sterope) meaning "flash of lightning" (see Sterope). Also compare the Greek noun στέροψ (sterops) meaning "flashing".In Greek mythology, Steropes is the name of one of the Cyclopes.
From an Italian title of the Virgin Mary, Madonna dello Sterpeto, meaning "Our Lady of Sterpeto". Sterpeto means "scrub, scrubland" in Italian, derived from sterpo "dry twig, bramble".
Derived from Latin stercus, meaning "fertilizer, manure". This was the name of the god of odor and manure in Roman mythology.

Means "establishing the chorus" or "leading the dance", derived from Greek ἵστημι (histemi) meaning "to stand, to set up" and‎ χορός (choros) meaning "dance" or "chorus, choir; band of singers and dancers". This was the name of a Greek lyric poet from the 7th century BC.
Derived from Greek ἵστημι (histemi) meaning "to make to stand, to stand, set" and βροτός (brotós), a poetic term meaning "mortal man, human being".
Feminine form of Steven or variant of Stephanie.

Feminine elaboration of Steven or its short form Steve.

Variant spelling of Stephen. This is the stage name of Stephen Grossman, the creator of the popular kids web-series 'Blippi'.

Variant of Steveland. This is the birth name of American singer-songwriter Stevie Wonder (b. 1950).
Variant of Steven, perhaps influenced by Stefan.Bearers of this name include American former football player Stevon Moore (1967-) and Barbadian former sprinter Stevon Roberts (1971-).
A variant of Stephanie, also the name of the fusion of Steven and Connie from the show Steven Universe.

Diminutive of Stewart. In popular culture, this name is best known for being the name of Stewie Griffin, one of the main characters of the American animated television series Family Guy.
Dutch variant and Afrikaans form of Steijn. In the case of the Afrikaans name, it can also be a transferred use of the Afrikaans surname.
Anglicized version of the French Saint-Georges. It is possibly used in honor of Saint George of Lydda.
Derived from Ancient Greek σθένος (sthenos) meaning "strength, power, vigour" and λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk".
Derived from Ancient Greek σθένος (sthenos) meaning "vigour, strength".
Meaning "strong one" or "forcer", derived from Greek σθένος (sthenos) meaning "strength, might, power"
Derived from the Germanic name elements sær "sea" and þórr "thunder" or a combination of sær "sea" and Þórir.

Maltese form of Stefan (via Sicilian Stefanu).
Variant of Stig. A known bearer was the Swedish writer Stieg Larsson (1954-2004), author of the 'Girl with the Dragon Tattoo' trilogy, born Karl Stig-Erland Larsson.
Form of Stígandr which occurs in Domesday Book.
Possibly means "clear path" or "bright path", from Old Norse stígr "path" and heiðr "bright, clear". Alternatively the second element may be derived from Old Norse heiðr "heath".
Derived from Old Norse stíga "to wander, to step" (see also Stig) combined with Old Norse rún "secret lore".
Meaning unknown, possibly of Frisian origin. Also compare Steije, which is possibly related.A known bearer of this name is the Dutch soccer player Stije Resink (b. 2003).

Derived from Greek στίλβω (stilbô) meaning "to glitter, gleam". This was the name of a nymph who was loved by the god Apollo and bore him Lapithes, the eponymous first king of the tribe, and some say Kentauros (or Centaurus), who mated with mares to produce the tribe of Kentauroi (Centaurs).

Greek variant transcription of Στυλιανός (see Stylianos) as well as an Albanian form.

Simply the English word stingy, meaning "Unwilling to spend, give, or share; ungenerous". In the children's television show LazyTown, Stingy is a selfish and possessive child. He still plays with the gang, but he will always care about his stuff, especially his car and his prized piggy bank. He often says "It's mine!" and has his own song by that name (which names everything in LazyTown as his; he even names "this instrumental break" within the song as his).
Transferred use of the surname Stinson.
From a northern Swedish dialectal word meaning "girl".
Scottish Gaelic variant of the name Stephen.

Stiorra is a name of a character in Bernard Cornwell's book series “The Saxon Chronicles” and its TV adaptation “The Last Kingdom,” the daughter of the main protagonist Uhtred. The character's name is derived from Old Norse stjarna meaning "star", or its Old English cognate steorra.
Croatian male and occasionally female name, derived from Stipan.
Of uncertain origin and meaning, although a direct derivation from Latvian stirna "roe deer" has been suggested. This name was recorded in medieval Latvia.
From the English word "stitch" meaning a "thread or loop of yarn created by movement" or "to mend or make with thread".This an alien from the Disney movie, 'Lilo and Stitch'.
Derived from the Scottish surname Stith, of unknown meaning. This was the name of Stith Thompson (1885-1976), an American folklorist.

Derived from the surname Stock or used as short form of names starting with stock.
Transferred use from the surname Stockard.The stage name of actress Stockard Channing (born Susan Antonia Williams Stockard), most known for playing Rizzo in Grease.

Transferred use of the surname Stockton.A notable bearer of this name is the American businessman Stockton Rush (1962-2023), who was the co-founder of the American submersible company OceanGate. He served as its CEO until his untimely death in the Titan, one of the company's submersibles. It imploded whilst it was on its way to the shipwreck of the RMS Titanic in the North Atlantic Ocean.

Transferred use of the given name Stockwell.As a given name, Stockwell is much less common; in the United States, it is more often used as a middle name than a first name, but even then, a conservative estimate puts it below the top 25,000 names (statistics are conflicting, likely due to the comparatively common surname and the difficulty of categorizing it when used as a middle name).One notable Stockwell is former Canadian politician Stockwell Day, named for his father, Stockwell Day, Sr.

Dutch and German short form of Christoffel, Romansh short form of Cristoffel and Luxembourgish short form of Krëschtaffel. In German-speaking countries, this name fell out off usage as it has developed into an everyday word meaning "boor".
Dutch and German short form of Christoffer.
Derived from Bulgarian стоя (stoya) "to stand, to stay".
Alternate transcription of Bulgarian Стойка (see Stoyka).
Variant transliteration of Стойна (see Stoyna) and Стојна (see Stojna).
Serbian, Croatian, Macedonian and Slovene feminine form of Stojan and Bulgarian variant transcription of Стоянка (see Stoyanka).
Means "the staying of peace", derived from Vlach stoji meaning "stay" and Vlach mir meaning "peace".
Derived from Macedonian стој, the imperative form of стои "to stop, to halt; to stand; to suit, befit" and мир "peace".
Originally a masculine diminutive of Stojan, this name is now also used as a variant of Stojna.
Derived from the Slavic name elements stoj "to stand" and slav "glory, fame".
Transferred use of the surname Stokely. Famously borne by Stokely Carmichael, an American activist.
Transferred usage of the surname Stoker.
Transferred use of the surname Stokes.

Demon from the Ars Goetia, part of The Lesser Key of Solomon book series, those were anonymously written demonology books from the mid-17th century.Stolas (also known as Stolos, Stoppas and Solas) is "a Great Prince of Hell, commands twenty-six legions of demons. He teaches astronomy and is knowledgeable about herbs, plants, and precious stones. He is often depicted as a raven or a crowned owl with long legs."
Transferred use of the surname Stonewall. This name was probably given in honor of the Confederate general Thomas Jonathan "Stonewall" Jackson (1824–1863).
Diminutive for the modern name Stone. One noted bearer is country music artist Stoney Edwards (1929-1997).
Transferred from the surname Stopyra honoring the French football player Yannick Stopyra. It is the name of a Capverdian football player participating in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
Alternate transcription of Pashto ستوری (see Storai).
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Stóri.
Former Swedish dialectal form of Styrger.
Old Norse byname, from Old Norse stórr meaning "large, big".
Greenlandic form of Storm, as well as an English variant.
Transferred use of the surname Stormer.
Derived from the Germanic name elements stórr "large, big" and ulfr "wolf".
From the English word story, ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ῐ̔στορῐ́ᾱ (historia).
Variant transcription of ᛋᛏᛦᚦᛁᚾᚴᚱ and ᛋᛏᚤᚦᛁᚴ (see Styðingʀ).
Old Norse combination of stóð "stud", "flock" (of horses) and ketill "cauldron hat", "helmet".
Transferred usage of the surname Stowe.
Bulgarian form of Strachomir (also compare Strahimir).

The first element of this name is derived from Proto-Slavic strachъ "to fear, to scare" or Proto-Slavic straxъ "fear, fright". Compare Polish strach "fear, fright" and Serbo-Croatian strašiti "to frighten, to scare". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace".

The first element of this name is derived from Proto-Slavic strachъ "to fear, to scare" or Proto-Slavic straxъ "fear, fright". Compare Polish strach "fear, fright" and Serbo-Croatian strašiti "to frighten, to scare". The second element is derived from Slavic slav "glory".
Older form of Strahimir. This name was borne by 12th-century Serbian prince Stracimir Zavidović and 14th-century Serbian noble Stracimir Balšić.
This was the birth name of the Macedonian revolutionary Strašo Pindžur (1915-1943).
Croatian and Serbian variant form of Strahomir. A bearer of this name was Croatian poet Silvije Strahimir Kranjčević (1865-1908).
From the noun strah meaning "fear, dread". Borne by Strahinja Banović, a legendary Serbian nobleman and folk hero.
Croatian and Serbian form of Strachomir.
Based on the Swedish word stråle "ray, beam".
Derived from German strahlen "to shine, to beam" or Strahl "beam; ray (of light)", this name was used as a translation of Feibush and thus Phoebus. It was recorded in 15th-century Frankfurt, Germany.
Transferred use of the surname Stratford. A famous bearer of the name was English author Stratford Caldecott (1953-2014).
Derived from the elements στρατός (stratos) "army" and ἵππος (hippos) "horse" meaning "army horse".
Latinized form of Straton and Italian variant of Stratone.
Latinized form of Stratokles. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 5th century BC.
Derived from Ancient Greek στρατός (stratos) meaning "army" combined with κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Italian form of Straton via Strato.

Masculine form of Stratonike, derived from Ancient Greek στρατός (stratos) meaning "army" and νίκη (nike) meaning "victory". The name Nikostratos is composed of the same elements in reverse order. This was the name of an Eastern Orthodox saint.
Transferred use of the surname Stratton.
From the name of the small, red fruit, from Old English streawberge.
Either transferred from the surname Stream or from the English word stream.
Transferred use of the surname Streeter.

From the name of the flower native to South Africa, also known as bird of paradise flower due to its resemblance to the animal. The genus was named by Joseph Banks in honour of Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, queen consort of George III.

From Russian стрелка (strelka) meaning "little arrow", itself a diminutive of стрела (strela, "arrow"). This is the name of one of the two Soviet dogs (along with Belka) who travelled to space in 1960 and returned safely for the first time.
In ancient Roman religion, Strenua was a goddess of the new year, purification, and wellbeing. According to Johannes Lydos, her name is derived from a Sabinian word strenuae "wellbeing; fortune".
From the English word stretch. This name is almost chiefly used as a nickname.

Stricha (or Dolya) is the ancient Ukrainian pagan goddess of good fate, an incarnation of Rozhanytsa. She tells the fate of married couples and births of children. She determines the destiny of a person, thus determining the virtues, predicting their future. Stricha also appears in Serbian mythology as Sreča (Srecha). The word “стріча (stricha)” also means "meeting" in Modern Ukrainian.

A descriptive name with literal meaning "one who strides". In J.R.R. Tolkien's 'The Lord of the Rings' trilogy, Strider is an alias of Aragorn. Strider Hiryu is the lead protagonist of game studio Capcom's 'Strider' game series.
From the English word strive which comes from Middle English striven—ultimately from Proto-Germanic *strībaną/*stribāną.
Derived from Slavic strogo "severe, harsh, strict" combined with Slavic bor "battle" or borit "to fight".
Derived from Slavic strogo "severe, harsh, strict" combined with Slavic mir "peace".
Name was used by a man who allegedly usurped the Bohemian duchy in circa 883 AD. Name could mean "Build The Peace" or "Build The World" in Czech.

Probably transferred from the originally German surname Strom.A famous bearer of the name is Strom Thurmond, senator of South Carolina for 50 years and the oldest senator in the USA upto now (his term ended when he was 100 years old).

From the name of a Scottish island off Caithness, uninhabited since 1961, which derives from the Norse Straumey meaning "island in the stream" or "current". This was the name of a character in the British children's novel Broken Soup (2008) by Jenny Valentine.
Created from the word maestro by switching syllables.It is the stage name of the Belgian musician Paul Van Haver.
Derived from Greek στρόμβος (strombos) meaning "something round, something spun around; whirlwind, spinning top, spindle, spiral shell".
Stromboli was one of the villains in the 1940 Disney film Pinocchio.
Derived from the Greek adjective στρογγύλος (strongylos) meaning "round, spherical". Associated with the ancient Greek name Strongylion.

Derived from Ancient Greek στρογγύλος (strongylos) meaning "spherical, round". Also compare στρογγύλιον (strongylion) meaning "round pot, flask". Strongylion was the name of an ancient Greek sculptor from the 5th century BC.
Derived from Polish stronić "to avoid, to shun, to eschew" combined with Slavic slav "glory".
From Strother Martin Jr, an American actor (1919-1980).
Transferred use of the surname Struan.
Transferred use of the surname Strummer.

Of uncertain origin. Possibly a transferred use of the surname Stryker. Alternately, from the Norwegian words stryker meaning "stretcher" or from stryke (“use a bow”) +‎ -er or from stryker, indefinite plural strykere, meaning a string player (musician who plays a string instrument).

Derived from Thracian *strūmōn meaning "stream, river", ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *srew- "to flow, stream". This was the name of an Ancient Greek river god and king of Thrace in Greek mythology.
Stryver is a character in the Charles Dickens novel A Tale of Two Cities and in the 10 TV/film adaptations of the story.
A dithematic name from Polish strzec "to guard" and sław "glory". This name is not used as often in the modern day.
Kainai name meaning "reluctant to be woman".
Transferred use of surname Studebaker meaning "white bread baker" from Middle Low German stute "fine white bread" and becker "baker".
Old Norse name and byname, from Old Norse stúfr meaning "stump, stub".
Transferred use of the surname Stukely.
Transferred use of the surname Sturges.
Transferred use of the surname Sturgill.
Transferred use of the surname Sturgis. This was used as a masculine name by J. K. Rowling in her 'Harry Potter' series of books.
A German word meaning "storm". It is used as a name because of St. Sturm (Sturmius).
A new combination of the name elements Sturm "storm" and hard "hard".The name occurred in 'Deutsches Familienstammbuch' in 1940.
A double form created from the names Sturm and Horst.When it became a hot topic on Twitter in June 2015 it was an error, the true given name in this case was Sturmhart.
Italian and Sardinian form of Sturm via it's Latinized form Sturmius.
Latinised version of the German word Sturm "storm".Sturmius was the name of the founder and first abbot of Fulda monastery and abbey.
Russian form of Sturm via it's Latinized form Sturmius.
Transferred use of the surname Sturt.
"Prayer of God," associated with the Goddess Durga
Transferred use of the surname Stuyvesant.

Means "hated, abhorred" as well as "hostile, gloomy, sullen" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology, Stygne was one of the fifty daughters of King Danaus, killing her husband, Polyctor, on their wedding night.
Transferred use of the surname Styles.

Possibly a Greek Cypriot dialectal variant of Styliani. A known bearer of this name was Greek Cypriot convicted murderer Styllou Christofi (1900-1954), who became the penultimate (second to last) woman to be hanged in the United Kingdom for strangling her daughter-in-law to death.

Meaning uncertain. The first element of this name might be derived from στύμα (styma), the Aeolic Greek form of Ancient Greek στόμα (stoma) meaning "mouth", or from στυμνός (stymnos) meaning "solid". The second element might be derived from φάλος (phalos), which can mean "horn" as well as be a term for a certain part of a helmet. However, a derivation from φαλός (phalos) meaning "white" is also a possibility.In Greek mythology, Stymphalos was the son of Elatos, and eponymous king of a town of the same name.
Latinized form of Stymphalos. In Greek mythology, Stymphalus is the name of a son of Elatus, who was treacherously killed by Pelops.
Form of Styrr found in Old Danish and Old Swedish, as well as the modern Icelandic form.
Combination of Old Norse styrr "battle, stir, tumult" and biǫrn "bear".
Modern form of Styrbiǫrn. Combination of Old Norse styrr "noise, battle" and biorn "bear".
Derived from Old Norse styrr "stir, tumult, brawl" combined with Old Norse fastr "firm, fast".
Old Swedish combination of styrr "stir", "noise", "tumult", "battle" and gēr "spear".
From Old Norse styrkr meaning "strength, force, help".
Derived from Old Norse styrr meaning "stir, tumult, brawl".

Meaning uncertain. Maybe Old Norse stuð "support, pole, post" or stóð "herd of horses" combined with the suffix -ingʀ "belonging to, coming from, descending from". The name appears on a few runestones as ᛋᛏᛦᚦᛁᚾᚴᚱ (stʀþinkr) or ᛋᛏᚤᚦᛁᚴ (styþik).
Form of Stephen found in Wycliffe's Bible.

Means "hateful, abhorrent" or "icy cold, shiver, that which gives shivers; horror, monster", derived from Ancient Greek στυγέω (stygeo) meaning "to hate, abhor, detest". In Greek mythology, the Styx is the river that forms the boundary between the underworld and the world of the living, as well as the name of the goddess and personification of that river. To honour her contributions in the war against the Titans, Zeus decreed that the most solemn and binding oaths of the gods would be sworn on the Styx. She is usually called the eldest daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, which would make her an Oceanid nymph, though a later source gives her parents as Nyx and Erebus.
Derived from a Sanskrit prefix meaning "good, pleasant".
From Sino-Vietnamese 事 (sự) meaning "deed, act, affair, happening".
Varient of 世 (see Shi), 字 (see Zi), along with other names pronounced similarly in Hakka.
From Sino-Vietnamese 使 (sử) meaning "to use, to employ" or 史 (sử) meaning "history".
"Suab" means sound, "Nag" means rain. Together, it means "sound of rain".

Related to Latin suadere meaning "to urge, persuade" from Proto-Indo-European *swad- (related to suavis "sweet"). She was the Roman personification of persuasion, seduction and charming speech, equivalent to the Greek goddess or daemon Peitho.
A Gaulish name, composed of swadus "sweet" + rix "king".

column3: 수아(Korean Hangul)|秀雅, 秀娥, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 수아 (see Su-a).

Means "to sink down, to bow down, to humble oneself", some interpretations render the name as: "bowed down, prostation, depression (in the older, physical/spiritual sense)".In The Bible, Shuah (Suah) is listed as a son of Abraham by Keturah, after Sarah's death. Bildad the Shuhite may derive from the same root, indicating he was a descendant of Shuah (Suah).
From the Chinese 夙 (sù) meaning "early in the morning, dawn" or 苏 (sū) meaning "revive, resurrect" or a species of thyme and 霭 (ǎi) meaning "cloudy sky, haze, calm" or 爱 (ài) meaning "love".
From the Arabic سَعِيد (saʕīd) meaning "cheerful, happy, lucky".

column3: 수안(Korean Hangul)|水安, 收安, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 水 (su) meaning “water” or 收 (su) meaning “gather, harvest” combined with 安 (an) meaning “safe, secure, calm, peaceful”. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 素 (sù) meaning "white silk" and 安 (ān) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful"

column3: Су Ана, Су Әни(Tatar)|Су Ана(Kazakh)|سۇ ئان(Uyghur)|Суу Эне(Kyrgyz)
column12: Derived from su meaning "water" and ana meaning "mother", this is the name of a water spirit in many Turkic cultures.
Rare name of Islamic origin, means "flower"

Perhaps derived from Old Irish súanach "sleepy, drowsy, slothful, comfortable, at ease", itself from súan "sleep".This occurs in medieval Irish annals as a masculine name. Súanach is also found as a feminine name in records of medieval Scotland.
From Thai สรวง (suang) meaning "sky, heaven, paradise" and สุดา (suda) meaning "woman, lady, daughter".
Transferred use of the surname Suann.
A combination of Sue and Anne 1.
Possibly from the Turkish şua meaning "ray, gleam, beam".

In "The Face In The Abyss" by A. Merritt, Suarra is a handmaiden to the Snake Mother of Yu-Atlanchi. She leads the main character to an abyss where Nimir, the Lord of Evil is imprisoned in a face of gold.
Means "to count; relating to China" in Hmong.
A prophet that is sent to Midians, Jethro or Arabic Shuhaib.
Older form of Shubael in Bible translations into many languages when the translations are based on the Greek or Latin Old Testament.
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Sundanese bagja meaning "happy" (of Sanskrit origin).
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese bagya meaning "happiness, fortune, wellness".
Means "morning, forenoon, morning sleep" in Arabic.
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" and बल (bala) meaning "strength, might". In the Hindu epic the Mahabharata this is the name of a king of Gandhara and the father of Shakuni and Gandhari.
Means "garuda, eagle" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit सुपर्ण (suparṇa).
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese barkah or Sundanese berkah meaning "blessing, good wishes, prayers" (both from Arabic بركة (baraka)).
Bengali, Odia and Nepali form of Suvarna.

column3: 昴, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|すばる(Japanese Hiragana)|スバル(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 昴 (subaru), the Japanese name for the Pleiades star cluster, as well as other kanji or combinations of kanji pronounced the same way.
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
From the Chinese 夙 (sù) meaning "early in the morning, dawn" or 稣 (sū) meaning "revive, rise again" and 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud".
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese beja meaning "lucky, fortunate".
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese bêkti meaning "devotion, veneration, respect".
From Arabic سُبْحَانَ ٱللهِ (subḥāna llāh) meaning "glory to be God" from سَبَحَ (sabaḥa) meaning "glorified" combined with الله (Allah).
Variant of Subhash. A notable bearer was Indian nationalist and activist Subhas Chandra Bose (1897-1945).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
Alternate transcription of Bengali শুভাশিস (see Subhasish).
From Sanskrit शुभाशिस् (śubhāśis) meaning "good wishes, blessing, benediction".

Derived from the Latin verb subigere meaning "to cause to go under; to conquer, to tame, to subjugate, to subdue" (used of the active role in sexual intercourse, hence "to cause to submit sexually"). According to Augustine, Subigus was the tutelary god of the wedding-night; he caused the bride to give in to her husband.
The wife of King Flualis the Saracen. She received the name of Remissiane in baptism.
Variant transcription of Devanagari सुबिस्ता (see Subista).

From the name of 14th-century Islamic scholar Taqi al-Din al-Subki, whose name was derived from the village of Subk in present-day Egypt. This name may also be given in honour of his son, scholar and historian Taj al-Din al-Subki.
From the English and French word sublime meaning "magnificent, great, wonderful".
From Sanskrit सुबोध (subodha) meaning "right information, good knowledge" or "coherent, comprehensible, easy to understand".

column3: 수봉(Korean Hangul)|秀峰, 守峰, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 秀 (su) meaning "luxuriant, beautiful, elegant, outstanding" or 守 (su) meaning "defend, protect, guard" combined with 峰 (bong) meaning "peak, summit". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Telugu and Kannada variant of Subrahmanya.
Means "a man devoted to doing the right thing" in Odia.
Bengali and Javanese form of Suvrata.
Means "dawn, morning, daybreak" in Indonesian, derived from Arabic صبح (subh).
Form of Shubael used in the Latin Old Testament.

column3: سبل(Balochi, Pashto, Shahmukhi, Sindhi-Arabic, Urdu)|سُبُل(Kashmiri Arabic)|ਸੁਬੁਲ(Gurmukhi)|सुबुल(Hindi, Kashmiri Devanagari)
総, 綜, 統, 覇, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 総 (suburu) meaning "general, overall, total", 綜 (suburu) meaning "arrange threads for weaving", 統 (suburu) meaning "to govern; to command; to control" or 覇 (suburu) meaning "championship; victory" or other kanji which are pronounced the same way.
Derived from Gaulish sucaros "endearing, lovable; well-beloved, much-beloved", ultimately from Gaulish su "good" and cara "dear, lovable; amiable; (female) friend".
From French succès meaning "success". It has got some use in Chad and Côte d'Ivoire.

From the name of a deity that was featured in the Bible (2 Kings 17:30). Her name means "booths of daughters", ultimately derived from Hebrew סכה (sukka) meaning "booth" and בנות (benoth) meaning "daughters". She was described as a hen and her chicks.
This name is chiefly used in Guatemala.
From the devotional title of Mary Nuestra Señora del Buen Suceso meaning "Our Lady of the Good Event", in reference to the presentation of Jesus at the Temple in Jerusalem.
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Thai ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Diminutive of Suligost and other names beginning with the element Suli-.
MEANING - "one who walks or moves excellently ", having beautiful gait, performing well . Here सु means well, excellent + चर means moving, performing
MEANING : "extremely beautiful lady", very delightful or lovely woman, . Here सु means extremely, very + चार्वी means beautiful woman

column3: สุชาติ, สุชาต(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai สุชาติ (see Suchart). Spelled as สุชาต, this is the Thai name for the buddha Sujata.

column3: สุจินต์, สุชิน(Thai)
column12: From Thai สุ (su) meaning "good" and จินต์ (chin) meaning "think, imagine" or ชิน (chin) meaning "used to, accustomed to, familiar with".
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Thai จินดา (chinda) meaning "jewel, gemstone".

The name "Suchira" comes from old Hindhi works and was later classified as a South American name. It is a rare name and means "the beautiful waters" or "tasteful". It is derived from the names Sisira, Suchita, Srisi, and Siri
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" combined with चित्र (citra) meaning "jewel, ornament, picture" or "bright, clear, excellent".
Alternate transcription of Thai สุจิตรา (see Suchitra).
Diminutive of Suligost and other names beginning with the element Suli-.
Means "clean, pure, sacred" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit शुचि (śuci).
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese cipta meaning "creation, idea, hope, desire".
From Indonesian suci meaning "holy, sacred, pure, clean" combined with the feminine suffix -wati.
Transferred use of the surname Suckling.
Sud means Tiger in Thai and tends to be used by Buddhist families in Thailand.

column3: สุดา(Thai)|सुदा(Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi, Nepali)
column12: Means "daughter, woman, lady" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit सुता (sutā).
Meaning uncertain, possibly "having lustrous profit". In the 11th-century Persian epic the Shahnameh this is the name of a queen who seduces and tricks her stepson Prince Siavash.
A Sumerian name for the Akkadian dawn goddess Aya 3, meaning "To be shining" or "precious metal".
From Thai สุดา (suda) meaning "daughter, woman, lady" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "gem, jewel".
Derived from Hungarian sudár "tall; slender; fair".
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" and धर्म (dharma) meaning "that which is established, law, duty, virtue".
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese darma meaning "duty, obligation, contribution, service".
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with the name Darmono.
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese darsana meaning "example, pattern, model", ultimately from Sanskrit दर्शन (darśana).
From Thai สุดา (suda) meaning "woman, lady, daughter" and วรรณ (wan) meaning "colour, tint".
Based on the name of sheikh Abdul Rahmane Ibn Abdul Aziz Al-Sudais, Imam of the great mosque of Mekka. Arab al-sudais means "the sixth".
Alternate transcription of Bengali সুদীপ (see Sudip).
From Hindi देश (desh) meaning "country". Another meaning is सुदर्श (sudarsh), "good-looking".
Name of the wife of King Vitra, of the Hindu epic Mahabharata
Famous bearers include Sudhakar Rao, former Indian cricketer.
From Sanskrit सुधांशु (sudhāṃśu) meaning "moon" or "camphor", derived from सुधा (sudhā) meaning "nectar, honey" and अंशु (aṃśu) meaning "stalk, thread, ray, beam".
This name is derived from Sanskrit and means "lord of knowledge".
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Javanese dibya meaning "splendid, noble, beautiful".
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" and दीक्षा (dīkṣā) meaning "consecration, initiation" (compare Diksha). This is another name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" and दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light".
From Sanskrit सु (su) meaning "good" and दीप्त (dīpta) meaning "luminous, shining, blazing". This is a transcription of both the masculine form সুদীপ্ত and the feminine form সুদীপ্তা.
Alternate transcription of Bengali সুদীপ্ত (see Sudipta).
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with the name Dirman.
From Javanese sudira meaning "brave, courageous, bold".
Older spelling of Sujatmiko influenced by Dutch orthography.
Croatian and Serbian form of Sędomir.
From the Sanskrit prefix सु (su) meaning "good" combined with Sundanese darajat meaning "degree, standing, rank" (of Arabic origin).

Su İyesi translates directly to "The Water Spirit," "The Owner of the Water," or "The Divine Guardian of the Rivers and Lakes" in Turkic mythology. It is a compound name consisting of Su (water) and İye (spirit, master, protector).Linguistically, the word İye descends from the profound Proto-Turkic root īd / iḏ (to send, to master, to possess divine authority). It represents an essential, organic pillar of Tengrist animism. A critical mythological distinction must be made: the Su İyesi is absolutely not a peri (fairy) or a mermaid in the Western or Persian sense. Unlike fairies, which are often depicted as whimsical, separate magical creatures, an İye is the literal, intrinsic spiritual consciousness of the natural element itself. Without the İye, the river is spiritually dead.In Turkic lore, Su İyesi is a revered, ancient matriarchal entity who protects the purity of life-giving waters, heals the weary, and commands the flow of rivers. She is part of the great pantheon of guardians alongside the Yer İyesi (Earth Spirit) and Orman İyesi (Forest Spirit), acting as a strict enforcer of ecological balance.For a child, this name carries an aura of deep spiritual protection, fluid grace, and elemental power. It represents a soul that is adaptable yet unstoppable, possessing the soothing, life-giving properties of a calm stream, alongside the roaring, unyielding power of a great flood.

Armenian and Georgian form of the Jewish name Shambat, which is also found written as Sembat, Shembat and Shmbat.The meaning of the name is not quite certain. According to an English source, Shambat is identical to Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabat) meaning "Sabbath". Meaning uncertain. In the English-speaking world, the name might perhaps be a combination of the English word sun with the French feminine diminutive suffix -ette, which would essentially give the name the meaning of "little sun". Alternatively, the name could also be a combination of two existing given names, namely Susan (or Susanna) with any name ending in -nette, such as Annette and Jeanette.In the Netherlands and South Africa (whose national languages are very closely related), the name might perhaps be a variant form of names like Sünne and Sünneke (which tend to be Frisian and Low German in origin, but such names often manage to find their way in their cousin languages, namely Dutch and Afrikaans), but then with the French feminine diminutive suffix -ette added. And in South Africa, there is also the possibility that (at least in some cases) this name could be a (more or less) gallicized form of an African given name - more precisely, a name that is found in the numerous Bantu languages that are spoken in South Africa.Lastly, it should be noted that this name is quite similar in appearance to the English word sonnet (which is also the same in Dutch and Afrikaans), which is ultimately derived from Old Occitan sonet meaning "little song". Given the difference in pronunciation between sonnet and Sunette, it is probably quite unlikely that Sunette could be derived from sonnet in some cases, but perhaps this possibility shouldn't be entirely discounted, seeing as Sonnet is actually in use as a given name and therefore spelling variations (even non-intuitive ones) of it are very likely to exist.Known bearers of this given name are the South African cricketer and javelin thrower Sunette Viljoen (b. 1983) and the South African former cricketer Sunette Loubser (b. 1982).

The name Suporna (native Bengali: সুপর্ণা; Sanskrit: सुपर्णा) has its roots in Sanskrit and was later adopted into Bengali usage. It is formed from the elements su ("good," "beautiful," "excellent") and parna ("feather," "wing," "leaf"). Thus, the full meaning of the name is "beautiful-winged" or "graceful-feathered."In ancient Sanskrit literature, the related form Suparna is a title for the mythological divine bird Garuda, a revered figure known for his immense strength, speed, and service to the god Vishnu. Over time, the name Suporna evolved to symbolize "grace," "elegance," and "divine beauty" among Bengali speakers, especially in poetic, spiritual, and classical contexts.The use of natural imagery, particularly wings and flight, ties Suporna to ideals of freedom, aspiration, and celestial purity in South Asian cultural and religious traditions.

Susam is derived from the Turkic root sus-, carrying the symbolic weight of "profound silence" or "the quiet power." It represents "the one who listens," conveying a calm, observant temperament.Differentiation: The Turkic name is unrelated to the Persian sûsan/sûsen (lily) or Hebrew shoshanna. The Turkic root is purely onomatopoeic/verbal based on the state of silence (sus-), whereas the others are floral loanwords. Sevan Nişanyan’s suggestion that Susam is a derivative of Susan is etymologically rejected; the morphology of Susam follows native Turkic suffixes, whereas Susan follows the Persian floral etymon.
