Derived from θεμιστος (themistos), meaning "belonging to the law".
Derived from Ancient Greek θεμιστός (themistos) meaning "oracular".
Means "patron of right, one who presides over justice", ultimately derived from Greek θέμις (themis) meaning "law of nature, divine law, custom".
Latinized form of Themistios. This name was borne by a Greek philosopher and rhetorician from the 4th century AD.

From Ancient Greek θεμιστός (themistos) meaning "righteous, lawful" or "oracular, divine", derived from θέμις (themis) "law, divine law, custom". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including the third wife of Athamas, who mistakenly killed her own children in an attempt to murder her step-children, and one of the fifty Nereids.
Name for girls with meaning "a calm breeze"
From Old Norse þengill meaning "prince, king".

Meaning unknown, possibly a shortened form of Parthenia. This name was borne by a daughter of Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings who died in infancy. She was possibly named after one of Sally's sisters, Thenia Hemings (1767-1795).
Diminutive of feminine names that end in -thena and -thenia, such as Athena, Parthena and Parthenia.
A dithematic name formed from the Germanic name elements þeoda "people" and berht "bright".
Variant spelling of Theobald, usually used as a surname.

Latinized form of Greek Θεοβούλη (Theoboule) meaning "divine will", derived from θεός (theos) "god" and βουλή (boule) "will, volition". This is said to be the source of Σίβυλλα (Sibylla) (see Sibyl) via Doric Σιοβόλλα (Siobolla). In mythology this was borne by the mother of Myrtilus by Hermes and the mother of Arcesilaus and Prothoenor by Areilycus.
Means "grace of god", from Greek θεος (theos) "god" and χαρις (charis) "grace, kindness".
Derived from Ancient Greek θεός (theos) meaning "deity, god; divine" and χαρίζω (charizo) meaning "to give graciously, show favour" (see charis "grace, kindness, gratitude").
Latinized form of Theoktiste. This name was borne by a sister of the Eastern Roman emperor Maurice (539-602 AD) as well as by one of his daughters.
French form of Theoktistos via Theoctistus.
Latinized form of Theoktistos. A known bearer of this name was Saint Theoctistus, a 5th-century Byzantine monk from Palestine who was a companion of Saint Euthymius the Great.
Diminutive or variant of Théodrade. Théodrade, wife of Chrodbert II (c. 678), is occasionally referred to as Théoda.
Short form of Theodelinde and Theodelind.
Variant of Theudehad. Theodahad was a 6th-century king of the Ostrogoths.
French form of Theudehard via Latinized form Theodardus.

Variant spelling of Deodata, which was influenced by the Greek word θεός (theos) meaning "god". In some cases, this name can also be a corruption of Theodota.Technically, Theodata can also be the feminine form of the latinized Germanic name Theodatus, but that seems to be the least likely option of all.
Apparently coined as a feminine form of Theodatus.
Old English form of Theobald, derived from the Old English elements þēod "nation, language" (from þeudō) and beald "bold, brave".
Possible Old English cognate of Teutberga or Theudeburg, apparently formed of the Old English elements þeod meaning "nation" and beorg meaning "mountain".
Latinized form of Theodektes. This was the name of a Greek rhetorician and tragic poet from the 4th century BC.

Theodegotha (5th-century – fl. 502) was a Visigoth queen consort by marriage to king Alaric II (494–507). She was the daughter of Theodoric the Great. Her marriage was arranged as an alliance between the Visigoths and the Ostrogoths, though it is disputed when it took place and therefore the exact reasons for the alliance. She was the mother of Amalaric.
Variant of Theudegotho. Theodegotho was a son of Theodoric the Great, a 6th-century king of the Ostrogoths.
Derived from the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek noun δέκτης (dektes) meaning "receiver, beggar".
Variant of Theudemar. Theodemar was the Suebi king of Galicia from 559 to 570 AD.
Variant spelling of Theudemund. Theodemund was a Suebi king of Galicia between 469-550 AD.

Means "king, ruler" in Old English, probably from þeud "people" and þegen "thane, warrior" This name was invented by J. R. R. Tolkien who used Old English to represent the Rohirric language. In his novel 'The Lord of the Rings' (1954) Théoden is the king of Rohan.
Dutch and Swedish form of Theodoric.
Derived from the Old English elements þēod "people, nation" (from þeudō) and gar "spear". Cognate to Dietger.
The first element has been interpreted as a derivative of Old Norse þjóð meaning "people" (which is cognate to Frankish þeoda). The second element is Old Norse dís meaning "goddess".
Derived from Proto-Germanic Þeudōmēraz, using the Old English elements þēod "people, nation" and mære "famous". Cognate to Gothic Theodemir and German Dietmar.

Likely a form or diminutive of Theodore.This name was most notable born by Theodo (Theodo V or Theodo II), Duke of Bavaria circa 670 AD. Bavarian legends include several legendary royals bearing the name as well.
Derived from the Old German elements þeoda "people" and laibu "remnant, legacy". This is the name of a Lombardic duke of Spoleto who reigned in the 7th century.

Variant of Theodelinda. (See also Teodolinda, Dietlinde.) This was borne by Finnish writer Theodolinda Hahnsson (1838-1919), known for being the first woman writing in Finnish. American mystery writer Rex Stout used it in his novel The Hand in the Glove (1937), where it belongs to private detective Theodolinda "Dol" Bonner.

French form of Theodolinde. Théodolinde de Beauharnais, Princess of Leuchtenberg (13 April 1814 – 1 April 1857), Countess of Württemberg by marriage, was a Franco-German princess. She was a granddaughter of Joséphine de Beauharnais, Napoleon's first wife.
Modern Greek diminutive of Theodoros, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.
Anglicized variant of Théodorine, or an elaborated form of Theodora.
Anglicized and germanized form of Theodoretos.Notable bearers of this name include saint Theodoret of Antioch (died in 362 AD) and the theologian Theodoret of Cyrus or Cyrrhus (died around 458 AD).

Derived from the Greek adjective θεοδώρητος (theodoretos) meaning "given by God", which consists of the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" and the Greek adjective δωρητός (doretos) meaning "open to gifts".
Roman cognomen which was derived from Theodorus.

Aeolic and Doric Greek form of Theodorides, because it contains ίδας (idas), which is the Aeolic and Doric Greek form of the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).A notable bearer of this name was the Greek poet Theodoridas of Syracuse (3rd century BC).
Means "son of Theodoros" in Greek, derived from the name Theodoros combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).
Elaboration from Théodore, with "dort" who means sleep in French. A influencer got this names "Theodort" who got creole origins.
Variant of Theodota, which was probably influenced by the similar name Theodosia.
Means "son of Theodotos" in Greek, derived from the name Theodotos combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).
Either a diminutive of Theodotos (see Theodotus) or a patronymic meaning "son of Theodotos" that was turned into a given name; compare Theodotides for this.
Late Greek and modern Greek form of Theodoule.

Derived from Ancient Greek θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with δόξα (doxa) meaning "notion, reputation, honour, glory".This name has regularly been confused with Theodosia, Theodota and Theodotia.
Feminine form of Theodrad. Theodrada was a daughter of Charlemagne and his wife Fastrada.

This is a French form of Theuderada via the Latinized form Theodorada or Theoderada.This name was borne by several royal women of ancient Francia, including the wife of Chrodbert II (c. 678) and the queen consort of Odo of France, King of Western Francia: Théodrate of Troyes (868-903).
Derived from the Old English elements þēod "nation, language" (from þeudō) and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom". From Germanic Theudehard.
A feminine form of Theuderad.Théodrate of Troyes (868–903) was the wife of Odo, Count of Paris and Queen consort of Western Francia.

Derived from the Old English elements þeod "people" and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom". This name was employed by J. R. R. Tolkien who used Old English to represent the Rohirric language. In his novel The Lord of the Rings (1954) Théodred is the deceased son of the king of Rohan.There were also several Catholic bishops named Theodred in 10th-century England.
Derived from Proto-Germanic Þeudōrīks, using the Old English elements þēod "people, nation" and ric "king, ruler". Cognate to Gothic Theodoric, English Derek, and German Dietrich.
Latinized form of Theodoule and its Late Greek form Theodoula.A known bearer of this name was Theodula of Anazarbus, an early Christian saint and martyr from the 4th century AD.
Gothic þiuda 'people, folk' + Old High German wini 'friend'.
Derived from the Old English elements þēod "people, nation" (from þeudō) and wulf "wolf". Cognate to Germanic Theudulf.

Means "joy of the people" in Old English, a combination of the elements thiod meaning "people" and wynn meaning "joy" (compare Éowyn). This name was invented by J. R. R. Tolkien for his novel The Lord of the Rings (1954), where it is borne by a noblewoman of Rohan, who was the sister of Théoden and the mother of Éomer and Éowyn.

Albanian form of Theophanes.A famous bearer was Theofan Stilian Noli, known as Fan Noli (1882–1965), an Albanian writer, scholar, diplomat, politician, historian, orator, Archbishop, Metropolitan and founder of the Orthodox Church of Albania and the Albanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America who served as Prime Minister and regent of Albania in 1924 during the June Revolution.
The name Theofane means "Manifestation of God", combining theos "God" and phanes "to show".
Variant of Theophiel. Known bearers of this name include Dutch cyclist Theofiel "Theo" Middelkamp (1914-2005) and Belgian politician Theofiel Van Peteghem (1879-1960).
Variant of Theudofrid (see Dietfried). With the elements diota "people, tribe" and fridu "peace".
A dithematic name formed from the name elements diota "people" and fridu "piece".
French form of Theogenes. In modern times, this name is found primarily in Rwanda.

Derived from Greek θεός (theos) meaning "god" and γνητός (gnetos) meaning "born". The latter word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb γίγνομαι (gignomai) meaning "to come into being, to be born". Also compare the related names Theogenes and Theognis.
Latinized form of Theognetos. This was the name of a Greek comic poet from the 3rd century BC.
Variant of Theogenes. Bearers of this name include the Greek poet Theognis of Megara (6th century BC) and an Athenian tyrant from the 5th century BC.
From Greek θεογνωσία (theognosia) meaning "the knowledge of God".
French form of Theognostos via Theognostus.
Latinized form of Theognostos. A known bearer of this name was Theognostus of Alexandria, an Alexandrian theologian from the 3rd century AD.
Greek variant transcription of Θεοχάρης (see Theocharis), as well as an Albanian form.
This name was borne by a politically Influential Byzantine Acstetic, born 740.
Feminine form of Theoktistos. This name was borne by saint Theoktiste of Lesbos (9th century AD) and the mother-in-law of the Byzantine Emperor Theophilos (9th century AD).

Means "creation of God", derived from Greek θεος (theos) "god" combined with κτίσμα (ktisma) "creation, edifice, foundation". The latter element is ultimately derived from the Greek verb κτίζω (ktizo) meaning "to people, to build, to create".
Possibly a shortened form of Theolene or Theolinde (compare Theora, Theoda, Theda).
French form of Theoleptos via Theoleptus.

Means "possessed, inspired by divinity; enthusiastic" or "superstitious" in Ancient Greek, derived from θεός (theos) "god, divine" and ληπτός (leptos) "apprehended, taken", itself from λαμβάνω (lambano), which can mean "to take" as well as "to receive". It was also used as a synonym of "blasphemous".
Latinized form of Theoleptos. This name was borne by two Ecumenical Patriarchs of Constantinople.
Old High German short form of Theodolinda.
Contracted form of Théodelinde, folk etymology, however, occasionally considers this name a contraction of Théo and Line.
From the Koine Greek (or Biblical Greek) noun θεολογία (theologia) meaning "theology, science of things divine". Also compare the related Late Greek name Theologos.
Derived from Greek θεός (theos) meaning "god" and βροτός (brotos) meaning "mortal man, human being".

Derived from Greek θεομήστωρ (theomestor) meaning "like the gods in counsel" or "divine counsellor". It consists of the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek noun μήστωρ (mestor) meaning "adviser, counsellor".This was the name of a Greek tyrant of Samos, who lived in the 5th century BC.
Derived from Greek θεός (theos) meaning "god, deity; divine" and μιμνήσκω (mimnesko) meaning "to remind, to remember".

Latinized form of the Greek name Θεωνη (Theone), the feminine form of Theon. In Virgil's 'Aeneid', Theano or Theona was a sister of Queen Hecuba and wife of Amycus. She and her sister gave birth on the same night to their sons Paris and Mimas, respectively.
Possibly a variant of Theon. This belonged to a 3rd-century patriarch of Alexandria who is venerated as a saint as well as others.
Modern Greek transliteration of Θεώνη (see Theone), a feminine form of Theon.
Feminine form of Theon. It was occasionally used as an Anglicization of the name of Saint Teneu.
Derived from Greek θεός (theos) meaning "god" and νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".
Diminutive of Theona. Saint Theonilla of Aegea was a pious Christian woman martyred in the persecutions of proconsul Lysias.
Variant of Dionisius influenced by names starting with Theo-, such as Theonilla or Theodor.
Originally a made up name combining Theophilus and Juanita. This name saw a short wave of popularity in 1957 because 20-year old Theonita Cox was featured on the title of the 'Jet' magazine.

Means "divine wisdom", derived from Ancient Greek θεός (theos) "god, deity; divine" and νόος (noos) "mind, thought". This was the name of multiple characters in Greek mythology. In Greek mythology, Theonoe was a daughter of the prophet Thestor who was kidnapped by pirates, and eventually rescued by her sister Leucippe.
Means "bride of god" from Greek θεος (theos) "god" and νυμφη (nymphe) "bride, young wife". This name belonged to one of 40 holy virgins martyred in Adrianople at the beginning of the 4th century.
Alternate transcription of Greek Θεονύμφη (see Theonymfi).
Variant of Theophilus, from the Greek words theós ("God") and philía ("love or affection").
From Ancient Greek θεός (theos) meaning "deity, god; divine" and πατήρ (pater) meaning "father". This name occurs in the Symposium of Methodius of Olympus, an early Christian theologian.

Derived from the Greek adjective θεοπειθής (theopeithes) meaning "obedient to god", which consists of the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)".This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 1st century BC.

Derived from the Greek adjective θεόπεμπτος (theopemptos) meaning "sent by God", which consists of the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek adjective πεμπτός (pemptos) meaning "sent". Also compare the related name Theopompos.
Latinized form of Theopemptos. A notable bearer of this name is Theopemptus of Nicomedia, a saint from the early 4th century AD.
English form of Theophanes. A known bearer of this name was saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894).
A feminine form of Theophanes. This name was borne by several Byzantine empresses including Saint Theophano, wife of Leo VI.

Variant of Theophania. Theophanu (c. 955 – June 15, 991) was the niece of the Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes. By her marriage with Holy Roman Emperor Otto II, she was Empress consort of the Holy Roman Empire and held regency as Empress dowager upon her husband's death in 983.

Dutch form of Theophilus via its French form Théophile. Known bearers of this name include the Belgian priest Theophiel Verbist (1823-1868) and Theophiel Coopman (1852-1915), a Belgian writer and poet.
Means "pious, god-fearing" in Greek, ultimately derived from θεός (theos) meaning "god, deity; divine" and φόβος (phobos) meaning "fear, terror; awe, reverence".

Latinized form of the Greek given name Θεοφόρος (Theophoros), which was derived from the Greek elements θεος (theos) "god" and φορεω (phero) "to carry, to bear". This is the name that Ignatius of Antioch, who lived in the 1st century AD, often went by.
Derived from Ancient Greek θεός (theos) meaning "god, deity; divine" combined with φράζω (phrazo) meaning "to explain, tell, declare, interpret" as well as "to point out, show".

Derived from Ancient Greek θεόφρων (theophron) meaning "godly-minded, pious", composed of θεός (theos) meaning "god, deity; divine" combined with φρήν (phren) meaning "mind, heart, emotions". In Greek mythology, Theophron is the name of one of the suitors of Penelope, the wife of Odysseus.
Latinized form of Theopistos. This was the name of two saints, one of which was a son of saint Eustace (died in 118 AD).

Means "sent by the gods, godsent" in Greek, ultimately derived from θεός (theos) meaning "god, deity; divine" and πέμπω (pempo) meaning "to send, conduct, escort". Also compare the related name Theopemptos.
Latinized form of Theopompos. This name was borne by a king of Sparta (Greece) from the 7th century BC.
Means "daughter of god" from Greek θεος (theos) "god" combined with the patronymic suffix -πουλος (-poulos).

Derived from the Greek adjective θεοπρεπής (theoprepes) meaning "meet for a god".Also compare the related Greek adjective θεόπρεπτος (theopreptos) meaning "meet for a god" as well as "marvellous". It consists of the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek adjective πρεπτός (preptos) meaning "distinguished, renowned".
Latinized form of Theoprepios. A notable bearer of this name was saint Theoprepius of Illyria (died around 121 AD).
Often a contracted form of Theodora, but there are also instances where it is actually a name on its own, then derived from Greek theorein "to watch, to look at."

Probably derived from Ancient Greek θεωρός (theoros) meaning "spectator, ambassador; envoy sent to consult an oracle" or θεωρία (theoria) meaning "sight, spectacle, viewing; consideration, theory" or "sending of an embassy, mission", both ultimately derived from θέα (thea) "view, sight" and ὁράω (horao) "to see".Theoris of Lemnos was an ancient Greek woman who was tried as a witch.

Derived from Ancient Greek θεοσέβεια (theosebeia) meaning "service or fear of God, reverence for the divine, religiousness", composed of θεός (theos) meaning "god, deity; divine" combined with σέβας (sebas) meaning "respect, reverential awe" (see sebo, sebastos). Also compare the Greek adjective θεοσεβής (theosebes) meaning "god-fearing" and the related name Eusebios.This name was borne by the 4th-century saint Theosebia the Deaconess, who is venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.
Most likely a contracted form of Theodosia.
Latinized form of Theosteriktos. A notable bearer of this name was saint Theosterictus the Confessor (8th century AD).

Derived from the Greek adjective θεοστήρικτος (theosteriktos) meaning "supported by God", which consists of the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" and the Greek adjective στηρικτός (steriktos) meaning "solid, firmly based".A notable bearer of this name was saint Theosteriktos the Confessor (8th century AD).

Derived from the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek noun στίχος (stichos) meaning "row". Also compare the related Greek noun στοῖχος (stoichos) meaning "row in an ascending series". Its similarity to the second element has caused some people to write the name as Theostoichos instead, which is properly latinized to Theostoechus.This was the name of one of the Nine Martyrs of Cyzicus, who died there in the 3rd century AD.
Latinized form of Theostichos. This was the name of one of the Nine Martyrs of Cyzicus, who died there in the 3rd century AD.
Latinized form of Theoteknos. A notable bearer of this name was the 4th-century saint Theotecnus of Antioch.

Means "child of God", derived from the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with the Greek noun τέκνον (teknon) meaning "child".This was the name of an early 4th-century Christian martyr, who was a military commander under either Emperor Galerius or Maximian.
Apparently created as a strictly masculine form of Théotiste.

While apparently originally a unisex name, Théotiste seems to have been used predominantly on females since at least the early 1800s.It is said to be a variant (or, now strictly feminine form) of Théoctiste.According to some scholars, in France itself this name used to be given to foundlings, no doubt due to its meaning.

Theotonius of Coimbra (c. 1082 - 1162) was a Canon Regular and royal advisor. He is noted in Portugal, for being the first prior of the Monastery of the Holy Cross in Coimbra, Portugal. He is celebrated as the reformer of religious life in Portugal, and is the first Portuguese saint.
Théoudehilde was the second wife of Theudebert II, king of Austrasia.
Feminine form of Theoxenos. This name was borne by several Greek noblewomen, one of which was a stepdaughter of Ptolemy I Soter of Egypt.
Derived from the Greek noun θεός (theos) meaning "god" combined with Greek ξένος (xenos) meaning "foreign, strange" as well as "foreigner, guest".
Latinized form of Theoxenos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 2nd century BC.
Referring to Colossians 3:15, "And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful."

Latinized form of Greek Θηραιφόνη (Theraiphone), which probably means "slayer of wild beasts" from Greek θήρ (ther) "a wild beast, beast of prey" or θήρα (thera) meaning "the hunting of wild beasts, the chase", which is ultimately derived from θηράω (therao) "to hunt, to chase", combined with φόνος (phonos) "murder, slaughter". In Greek mythology, Theraephone and Theronice were the twin daughters of Dexamenus, king at Olenus. She married Eurytus and was the mother of Thalpius.

Derived from Greek θηράω (therao) meaning "to hunt, chase" and either μενος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage, force" or μένω (meno) "to stay, wait, remain, last". Theramenes was the name of an Athenian statesman from the 5th century BC.
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek θήρα (thera) meaning "hunt, chase". Theras was a regent of Sparta, who colonised the island Thera and named it after himself.

column3: เทิดศักดิ์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai เทิดศักดิ์ (see Thoetsak).
Medieval Swedish form of Terentius, with recorded use in Finland and Sweden during the 16th century.
Nickname of the given name Teresa, given to me by my Spanish teacher. She is from Hungary, so she spoke Spain Spanish, so the name might not be a Latina name.
Elaboration of Theresa with the suffix -ina.
From Old Norse þjarfr meaning "insipid, flat, unleavened (of bread)".
Latinized form of Therikles. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 6th century BC.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek θήρ (ther) meaning "wild animal, beast of prey" or θήρα (thera) meaning "the hunting (of wild beasts), the chase", both related to θηράω (therao) "to hunt, to chase", combined with κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory". Alternatively, the first element could be θερίζω (therizo) meaning "to reap, to harvest, to mow". As such, the meaning of this name could be either "glorious hunt" or "to reap glory".

Means "beast; wild animal" in Ancient Greek.This is the name of a constellation named by Hipparchus of Bithynia in the 2nd century BC. It was later identified by Ptolemy with a wolf and it is currently known as Lupus.

Aemilia Materna Thermantia was the second Empress consort of Honorius, Western Roman Emperor. She was a daughter of Stilicho, magister militum of the Western Roman Empire, and Serena. Thermantia was a sister of Eucherius and Maria.

Latinized form of Greek Θερμουθις (Thermouthis), which was the Greek name for the Egyptian goddess Renenutet. According to the 1st-century historian Josephus, this was the name of Pharaoh's daughter who adopted the infant Moses. It was used as an English Christian name in the 19th century, apparently (e.g. borne by the mother of Francis Kilvert (1840-1879), British clergyman and diarist).

Derived from Ancient Greek θηράω (therao) meaning "to hunt", ultimately from θήρ (ther) "wild beast". This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including a follower of Artemis, a lover of Apollo, and a nymph who, according to some accounts, was the nurse of the god Ares. As she was a nymph of a town named Therapne, from the same root, it is probable that she was named after the place.

A pseudonym based off of the birth surname of Théroigne de Méricourt (1762-1817), a leading feminist in the first years of the French Revolution, who was born Anne-Josèphe Terwagne in Wallonia (Belgium).

The first element of this name is derived from the Aeolic Greek noun θέρσος (thersos) meaning "courage, confidence, audacity". The second element is derived from either the Greek verb ἀγορεύω (agoreuo) meaning "to orate, to speak publicly" or the Greek noun ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly" as well as "market, marketplace".A known bearer of this name was Thersagoras of Lampsacus, one of the assassins of the Greek tyrant Philiscus of Abydos (4th century BC).
Latinized form of Thersandros. This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of which was one of the Epigoni.
Derived from θέρσος (thersos), the Aolic Greek form of θάρσος (tharsos) meaning "courage, confidence, audacity", combined with ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".

Derived from the Aeolic Greek noun θέρσος (thersos) meaning "courage, confidence, audacity" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".Also compare the Greek name Thersandros, which is closely related and essentially means the same.In Greek mythology, Thersanor is the name of one of the Argonauts.

Derived from Aeolic Greek θέρσος (thersos) meaning "courage, confidence, audacity" combined with λόχος (lochos) meaning "ambush", a word that later came to signify a tactical sub unit of the ancient Greek army. The word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb λοχάω (lochao) meaning "to lie in wait for, to waylay" as well as "to snare".
Latinized form of Thersilochos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 3rd century BC.
Derived from θέρσος (thersos), the Aeolic Greek form of θάρσος (tharsos) meaning "courage, confidence, audacity", combined with ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Latinized form of Thersippos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 10th century BC.
Derived from Aeolic Greek θέρσος (thersos) meaning "courage, confidence, audacity".
Malayalam form of Theresa, borrowed from Portuguese Teresa. Used by Malayalam-speaking Saint Thomas Christians.

In Etruscan mythology, Thesan was the Etruscan goddess of the dawn, divination and childbirth (as well as a love-goddess) and was associated with the generation of life. Her name is derived from Etruscan thesan "divination".
shining star in the middle of the ocean
Abbreviation of Theresa mostly used in Austria

Means "divinely inspired, having words from god" in Ancient Greek, derived from θεός (theos) meaning divine; god, deity" and a form of εἶπον (eipon) meaning "to say, speak". Thespis was a 6th century BC poet and playwright often called the inventor of tragedy. He is credited by some sources as being the first person to appear on stage as an actor, or instead as having introduced the first principle actor in addition to the chorus. The word thespian derives from his name.

Means "divine-sounding, divinely uttered, oracular" or "prodigious, wondrous, mighty; awful, terrible, horrible", a variant form of Ancient Greek θεσπέσιος (thespesios), composed of θεός (theos) meaning "divine; god, deity" and a form of ἐνέπω (enepo) meaning "to tell, tell of, speak". Thespius (also called Thestius) was the king and founder of the ancient city of Thespiae in Greek mythology, who challenged Heracles to kill a lion in exchange for sleeping with his fifty daughters.
The servant of the lady Fenice, so named because she came from Thessaly in Greece.
From the two books of the Bible 1 Thessalonians and 2 Thessalonians, named after the Greek city of Thessaloniki.

Means "victory in Thessaly" from Greek Θεσσαλός (Thessalos) "Thessalian" and νίκη (nike) "victory". This was the name of a 4th-century BC Macedonian princess, the daughter of king Philip II by his Thessalian wife or concubine, Nicesipolis, and as such a half-sister of Alexander the Great. Her name honoured the Macedonian victory at the battle of Crocus Field (353/352 BC), a significant battle in Thessaly which occurred at the time of her birth. Princess Thessalonike married Cassander, who founded the city of Thessaloniki around 315 BC, on or near the ancient settlement of Therma, and named it for his wife.

Thessaly is a traditional geographic and modern administrative region of Greece, comprising most of the ancient region of the same name. This name is borne by Thessaly Lerner, American stage, film and voice actress.

Thödor (Thoedor) is a rare transliteration of the Russian name Ѳёдоръ, which comes from the Church Slavonic Ѳеодоръ, itself from Greek Θεόδωρος (Theódoros). The name is a theophoric compound from θεός (“God”) and δῶρον (“gift”), meaning “gift of God.”In Russian, the Church Slavonic sequence ео developed into the sound "/ɵ/", later represented by the special letter ё (ео → ё). To render the similar sound in Latin letters, the diacritic ö or the digraph oe was used, which parallels Germanic and Scandinavian orthographic traditions (oe → ö). This explains the difference between Theodor (the standard medieval European form) and Theodor / Thoedor, where the position of eo vs. oe reflects distinct orthographic developments in the West and in the East.Modern transliterations of the same Russian name include Fyodor and Fedor, which are more widely known internationally but do not preserve the historical orthographic nuance reflected in Thödor / Thoedor.

As the only known bearer of this name was the only child of two Germanic parents (Cheruscan chieftain Arminius and his wife Thusnelda), this name is probably a latinized form of an obscure Germanic name. It is tempting to say that this name is a latinized form of Greek thymelikos, which is in turn derived from thymele, this was in Greek theatre the altar of Dionysos in the centre of an orchestra circle. But if this were truly so, then the Greek historian Strabo - when writing about Thumelicus - would have given his name as Thymelikos in his works, since he would have written a proper Greek name in its authentic Greek form. He did not so, however, instead writing the name as Thoumelikos, thus indicating that the name does not have authentic Greek origins. Plus, there is also the fact that if Thumelicus was indeed the latinized form of Greek Thymelikos, it would have been spelled as Thymelicus, not Thumelicus. As such, given the ethnicity of the original bearer and his parents, it probably makes the most sense to take this name for a latinized but obscure Germanic name.

Thurid is a Scandinavian female given name, known since medieval times. It is mentioned in the 'Laxdæla saga' and the 'Færeyinga saga'. "The name is composed of the elements Þórr (Thor) and fríðr (beautiful)." A modern bearer is Agnes Thurid Gers (born 1997), a German track and field athlete.The name was also used by author Edgar Rice Burroughs (Tarzan) for a male character in his novels 'The Gods of Mars' and 'The Warlord of Mars'.

The meaning and origin of the first element in this Germanic name is rather uncertain, and so there are various possibilities to the name's meaning. The most likely possibility is that the first element comes from Old High German turs (compare Old Norse Þurs) "giant." An other possibility is that the first element refers to the Thuringii, a Germanic tribe. The etymology of their name is uncertain. The second element in the name comes from Gothic sinths "way, path."

The most likely possibility is that the first element comes from Old High German turs (compare Old Norse Þurs) "giant." An other possibility is that the first element refers to the Thuringii, a Germanic tribe. The etymology of their name is uncertain. The second element in the name comes from Old High German mund "protection" - but it might also be a blend of Gothic môds "mind, spirit" (see Adalmut) with mund.

A known bearer of this name was Thursday October Christian (1790-1831), the first son of the HMS Bounty mutineer Fletcher Christian and his Tahitian wife Mauatua, who was born on a Thursday in October.

From the name Tussinhilda, originally an Old Norse name of which the second element is derived from Old Norse hildr "battle". The etymology of the first element has two possibilities. The first is that it is derived from Old Norse Þurs "giant" (as in, a giant, not an adjective illustrating something big), which would mean that the entire name's meaning is roughly "battle with a giant". The second possibility is that it is derived from Old Norse Þúsund (compare Gothic thûsundi) meaning "thousand", giving the entire name the meaning of "a thousand battles".Thusnelda (c.10 BCE-17 CE) was a Cheruscan princess who eloped with Arminius, the leader of the Germanic tribes who eventually defeated the Romans at the Teutenberg forest. In the year 9 BCE, Thusnelda became the prisoner of Germanicus and was paraded in front of the Romans as a victory prize. In later years she became a symbol for German nationalism.

From Sino-Vietnamese 水 (thủy) meaning "water" and 精 (tinh) meaning "spirit". This is the name of a water god in Vietnamese mythology who was once close friends with the mountain god Sơn Tinh. He is mostly known for fighting with Sơn Tinh over the hand of the princess Ngọc Hoa.

From the name of a city in Asia Minor mentioned in Revelation in the New Testament. According Stephanus of Byzantium, the name of the city meant "daughter" from Greek θυγατήρ (thugatēr), though it may actually be from an older Lydian name. Thyatira was not used as a given name in ancient times.
Means "girl" in Khmer, Lao and Thai.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek θύος (thyos) meaning "burnt sacrifice, offering", or perhaps from θύω (thyo) meaning "to rush in, storm, rage, seethe". In Greek mythology, Thyestes was a king of Olympia, the son of Pelops and Hippodamia. He and his brother Atreus were exiled for the murder of their half-brother Chrysippus and fled to Mycenae, where they eventually took the throne; their ensuing rivalry for sole leadership led to tragedy for their entire family.

Derived from Ancient Greek θύω (thyo) meaning "to offer in sacrifice, burn, slaughter, immolate", "to consult (of oracles)" or "to celebrate". Coincides with θυία (thyia) meaning "stinking juniper, odorous cedar" (species Juniperus foetidissima), which may be related. In Greek mythology, Thyia was a Naiad nymph associated with cults of several major gods in varying accounts, some saying she was the first to sacrifice to Dionysos, or that she was a lover of Apollo or Poseidon. Thyia of Thessaly was the daughter of Deucalion and had two sons with Zeus, Magnes and Makednos
Allegedly derived from Vietnamese Thùy, Thủy or Thy and Lan 1. This name was apparently first used in 2001 by French child model Thylane Léna-Rose Blondeau.

Derived from Ancient Greek θυμαρής (thymares) meaning "suited to the heart; well-pleasing, delightful, beloved", composed of θυμός (thymos) "soul, spirit, heart" and ἀραρίσκω (ararisko) "to join, fit", combined with the patronymic suffix ίδας (idas) (see ides).

Latinized form of the Greek name Θυμβραῖος (Thymbraios) meaning "of Thymbra", from Θύμβρα (Thymbra), the name of an ancient town near Troy, located on a plain of the same name formed by the river Thymbrios. In Greek mythology, Thymbraeus was a son of the Trojan priest Laocoön. He was suffocated by sea serpents, along with his father and his brother Antiphantes. This was also an epithet of Apollo, who had a major temple in Thymbra.
From Old French thym, from Latin thymum, from Ancient Greek θύμον (thúmon).

Derived from German Thymian "thyme". It was used by German author Margarete Böhme (1867-1939) in her novel Tagebuch einer Verlorenen (1905; "The Diary of a Lost Girl"). The book purportedly tells the true story of Thymian, a young woman forced by circumstance into a life of prostitution. When first published in 1905, the book was said to be a genuine diary, though speculation quickly arose as to its authorship; today, Tagebuch einer Verlorenen is accepted as a work of fiction. Due in part to its sensational subject matter, the book proved extremely popular.
Gallicized form of Thymian. This name was coined for the protagonist in the French translation - Journal d'une fille perdue - of Margarete Böhme's 1905 novel Tagebuch einer Verlorenen.

Derived from the Greek noun θυμός (thymos) meaning "soul, spirit" combined with either the Greek noun χαρά (chara) meaning "joy, delight, happiness" or the Greek noun χάρις (charis) meaning "grace, kindness" (see Chares).This was the name of an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 3rd century BC.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek θύω (thyo) meaning "to rush in, rage, storm". This was the new name of Semele after her apotheosis. As the goddess Thyone, she presided over the frenzy inspired by her son Dionysos. A moon of Jupiter is named after her.

Means "at the door, outside the door; absent, abroad" or "belonging to a door" in Ancient Greek, derived from θύρα (thyra) "door, entrance". This was the name of one of the fifty sons of King Lycaon in Greek mythology, the eponymous founder of Thyraeum. It was also an epithet of Apollo.
Younger form of both Þýrví and Þyríðr.
From the name of a mountain in Iceland, which means "whirl" from Old Norse þyrill (referring to wind gusts at the mountain peak). This is also the modern Icelandic word for "kingfisher (bird)".

Means "burnet rose" (literally "thorn-rose") in Icelandic. This is used as the Icelandic name for the fairy tale character Sleeping Beauty, being the Icelandic translation of German Dornröschen, the title character of a Brothers Grimm fairy tale (known as Briar Rose in English).

Derived from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thyrsos), which was the name for a type of staff or wand of giant fennel that was wreathed in ivy and vine-leaves and had a pine-cone at the top. It was often used as an instrument in the cult for Dionysos, the Greek god of wine, revelry, fertility and dance, and θύρσος was also used to refer to his devotees.
Latinized form of Thyrsos. This name was borne by a Christian martyr from the 3rd century AD, who was killed for his faith in Sozopolis (Apollonia), Phrygia during the persecution of Emperor Decius.

Medieval Dutch and Afrikaans short form of Matthys. But in other words, you could also say that this name is the medieval Dutch and Afrikaans equivalent of Thijs.In the Netherlands, the name has survived to modern times, but it is highly rare there currently, especially when compared to its modern counterpart.

From Egyptian tj-ꜥꜣ possibly meaning "the great", derived from a variant of tꜣ "the; she of" combined with‎ ꜥꜣ "big, great, important". Tiaa was an ancient Egyptian queen consort during the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt (1550-1292 BC). She was the Great Royal Wife of Pharaoh Amenhotep II and the mother of Thutmose IV.
Created by Peter Andre as one of the middle names for his daughter Princess. He came up with it by combining his mother's name Thea with the name of his then partner Katie Price's mother's name Amy.

Variant of Thialda. A known bearer of this name is the Dutch singer Tialda van Slogteren (b. 1985), who was a member of the now-defunct German pop group Room2012.

Tialys is a chevalier in Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials book series, first released in 1995.

column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial", 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" or 添 (tiān) meaning "increase, add to" and 梦 (mèng) meaning "dream", 朦 (méng) meaning "condition or appearance of the moon" or 萌 (méng) meaning "bud, sprout".

column3: 恬谧, 恬宓, 甜蜜(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 谧 (mì) meaning "calm, quiet", 宓 (mì) meaning "quiet, in good health" or 蜜 (mì) meaning "honey, nectar".

column3: 恬敏, 甜敏, 天敏, 添敏, 恬民, 甜民, 天民, 添民, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "calm, quiet, tranquil, peaceful", 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven", or 添 (tiān) meaning "add, increase" combined with 敏 (mǐn) meaning "quick, clever, sharp" or 民 (mín) meaning "people, citizens". Other character combinations can form this name as well.A notable bearer of this name is Taiwanese-American actress Constance Wu, whose Chinese name is Wu Tianmin (吴 恬敏, Wú Tiánmǐn).
From Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven" combined with 明 (míng) meaning "bright, light, clear". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 娜 (nà) meaning "elegant, graceful, delicate".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" and 宁 (níng) meaning "peaceful, calm".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet" and 妞 (niū) meaning "girl".
From the Chinese 添 (tiān) meaning "increase, add to" and 女 (nǚ) meaning "woman, girl".
From Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven" combined with 诺 (nuò) meaning "to promise, to approve". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 葩 (pā) meaning "flowers".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 娉 (pīng) meaning "beautiful, charming".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 绮 (qǐ) meaning "fine thin silk" or "beautiful".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 琴 (qín) meaning "Chinese lute".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" or 湉 (tián) meaning "calmness of water" and 晴 (qíng) meaning "fine weather".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 琼 (qióng) meaning "jade, rare, precious".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" and 然 (rán) meaning "yes, certainly" or "pledge, promise".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 娆 (ráo) meaning "graceful, charming, fascinating".

column3: 恬蓉, 天蓉, 甜蓉(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial", or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 蓉 (róng) meaning "hibiscus".

column3: 恬瑞, 天蕊, 甜睿(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial", or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 瑞 (ruì) meaning "felicitous omen, auspicious", 蕊 (ruǐ) meaning "unopened flowers, flower buds" or 睿 (ruì) meaning "shrewd, astute, clever".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 飒 (sà) meaning "sound of the wind, melancholy".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 添 (tiān) meaning "increase, add to" and 珊 (shān) meaning "coral".
Derives from tian (天) "sky," and shi (使) "god." Can be interpreted as meaning “angel” or “immortal.”
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 淑 (shū) meaning "kind and gentle" or 姝 (shū) meaning "beautiful girl".

column3: 恬爽, 天霜, 湉爽(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" or 湉 (tián) meaning "calmness of water" and 爽 (shuǎng) meaning "bright, clear, cheerful, happy, refreshing" or 霜 (shuāng) meaning "frost".

column3: 恬思, 甜思, 甜丝(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 思 (sī) meaning "think, ponder, consider" or 丝 (sī) meaning "silk, fine threads".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 素 (sù) meaning "white silk". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
Reduplication of Chinese 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet" or 湉 (tián) meaning "smoothly flowing, placid". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven" combined with 薇 (wēi) referring to osmunda regalis, a type of fern, as well as other character combinations that can form this name.
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns".

From a combination of the characters 天 (tian, meaning "heaven") and 吴 (wu, referring to the Wu people of southeast China). This is the name of a deity found in the Shanhaijing (山海经 - Classic of Mountains and Seas). Associated with water and hunting, it has the body of a beast with eight heads, eight tails and eight legs.

column3: 恬熙, 甜熙, 甜汐, 甜希, 湉汐, 恬溪(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" or 湉 (tián) meaning "calmness of water" and 熙 (xī) meaning "bright, splendid", 汐 (xī) meaning "night tides", 希 (xī) meaning "hope, hope for, rare" or 溪 (xī) meaning "mountain stream".
From the Chinese 添 (tiān) meaning "increase, add to" and 霞 (xiá) meaning "rosy clouds".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 香 (xiāng) meaning "fragrant, sweet smelling, incense".
From the Chinese 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 笑 (xiào) meaning "smile, laugh".

column3: 湉忻, 恬忻, 恬馨, 天馨, 甜昕, 甜心, 湉心, 湉馨(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 湉 (tián) meaning "calmness of water", 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 忻 (xīn) meaning "delightful, joyful", 馨 (xīn) meaning "fragrant, aromatic, distant fragrance", 昕 (xīn) meaning "dawn, early morning" or 心 (xīn) meaning "heart, mind, soul".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 秀 (xiù) meaning "beautiful, elegant, luxuriant".
From the Chinese 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 煦 (xù) meaning "kind, gentle, gracious".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 璇 (xuán) meaning "beautiful jade" or "star".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" and 雪 (xuě) meaning "snow".
From the Chinese 湉 (tián) meaning "calmness of water" and 洵 (xún) meaning "true, real".

column3: 天雅, 天亚, etc.(Chinese)|天亞, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven" combined with 亚 (yà) meaning "second" or "Asia" or 雅 (yǎ) meaning "elegant, graceful, refined". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 恬嫣, 天妍, 天燕, 甜燕(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 嫣 (yān) meaning "charming, fascinating", 妍 (yán) meaning "beautiful, handsome" or 燕 (yàn) meaning "swallow (bird)".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" and 杨 (yáng) meaning "willow, poplar".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 窈 (yǎo) meaning "obscure, secluded, refined" or 瑶 (yáo) meaning "precious jade".
From the Chinese 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 烨 (yè) meaning "bright, glorious" or "firelight, flame".

column3: 恬懿, 恬谊, 恬亦, 恬艺, 恬益, 恬熠, 甜怡(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 懿 (yì) meaning "virtuous, admirable", 谊 (yì) meaning "friendship" or "appropriate, suitable", 亦 (yì) meaning "also, likewise", 艺 (yì) meaning "art, talent, ability", 益 (yì) meaning "benefit, advantage", 熠 (yì) meaning "bright and sparkling" or 怡 (yí) meaning "happy, joyful".
From the Chinese 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 音 (yīn) meaning "sound, tone".

column3: 天樱, 天英, 天莹, 天滢(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 樱 (yīng) meaning "cherry, cherry blossom", 英 (yīng) meaning "hero, brave" or "flower, petal, leaf", 莹 (yíng) meaning "luster of gems, lustrous" or 滢 (yíng) meaning "clear, pure water, lucid".

column3: 天于, 天宇, 天羽, 天语, 天瑜, 田雨, etc.(Chinese)|天于, 天宇, 天羽, 天語, 天瑜, 田雨, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven" or 田 (tián) meaning "field" combined with 于 (yú) meaning "in, on, at", 宇 (yǔ) meaning "house, eaves, universe", 羽 (yǔ) meaning "feather", 语 (yǔ) meaning "speech, language", 瑜 (yú) meaning "fine jade, lustre of gems" or 雨 (yǔ) meaning "rain". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 恬园, 恬源, 恬媛, 天媛, 天园, 天苑, 天圆, 甜瑗, 甜苑(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful", 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 园 (yuán) meaning "garden, park, orchard", 源 (yuán) meaning "spring, source", 媛 (yuàn) meaning "beauty, beautiful woman", 苑 (yuàn) meaning "pasture, park, garden", 圆 (yuán) meaning "circular, round, complete" or 瑗 (yuàn) meaning "jade ring".

column3: 湉悦, 恬月, 恬悦, 天月(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 湉 (tián) meaning "calmness of water", 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 悦 (yuè) meaning "pleased, contented" or 月 (yuè) meaning "moon".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 珍 (zhēn) meaning "precious, valuable, rare".
From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 智 (zhì) meaning "wisdom, knowledge, intelligence" or 芷 (zhǐ) meaning "angelica, iris".
From the Chinese 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven, celestial" and 珠 (zhū) meaning "bead, pearl, precious stone".

column3: 恬姿, 恬子, 甜子(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 恬 (tián) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful" or 甜 (tián) meaning "sweet, sweetness" and 姿 (zī) meaning "one's manner" or 子 (zi) meaning "child".

column3: 朓, 迢, 窕, 岧, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 朓 (tiāo) meaning "appearance of the moon in the west at the end of a lunar month", in addition to other hanzi that are pronounced similarly.
From the Chinese 窕 (tiǎo) meaning "slender, charming, quiet and modest" and 红 (hóng) meaning "red, vermilion".
From the Chinese 窕 (tiǎo) meaning "slender, charming, quiet and modest" and 瑞 (ruì) meaning "felicitous omen, auspicious".
From the Chinese 窕 (tiǎo) meaning "slender, charming, quiet and modest" and 熙 (xī) meaning "bright, splendid, glorious" or 曦 (xī) meaning "sunlight, sunshine, early dawn".

column3: 天愛宝, 天, 天愛, 千愛星, 星夢, 星子, 星, 王冠, 姫亜来, 美星, 楴愛羅, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 天 (ti) meaning "heaven", 愛 (a) meaning "love, affection" combined with 宝 (ra) meaning "treasure". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Supposedly means "from the body of God" in Yoruba.
Either from Māori tīare meaning "scent" or from Cook Islands Māori and Tahitian name Tiare meaning "flower". Tiāre with a macron on the ā is the Māori form of Charlie or Charles.
From Tahitian tiare meaning "flower, tiare flower" and here meaning "beloved, favourite".
Combination of Tiare and Lei 1. Variant of Tiarehei meaning "garland of Tiare flowers" in Tahitian.
Elaboration of Tiara and Tiare. Also the name of a small woodland flower also known as foamflower.
From the Tahitian tiare meaning "flower, tiare flower" and nui, an archaic term meaning "big".
Means "red flower" in Tahitian, from Tiare meaning "flower" and ura meaning "red".
Meaning unknown, possibly a variant of Tiana.
Meaning uncertain. It may be a variant of Tiarna. It gained some popularity in Australia after rugby player Andrew Ettingshausen gave it to a daughter in the early 1990s.
Tiasa was a Naiad nymph in Greek Mythology. She was a Laconian princess, daughter of King Eurotas.
Variant of Tyasia, It is influenced by the prefix ti-.
Variant form of Sitre. This was the name given to one of the several daughters of pharaoh Ramesses II of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt (1292-1189 BC).
Short form of Theobalda/Theobald and Tabitha. (See also Tibbot).
East Frisian short form of names starting with the Germanic name element þeudō "people" followed by a name element containing the letter b, e.g. burg "protection; protected place".
Languedocian and Provençal form of Theobald.
Meaning unknown. A notable bearer of this name was Saint Tibba of Mercia (7th century), a patron saint of falconers. She was a relative of Saints Kyneburga and Kyneswide of Mercia.
Middle English form of the given name Theobald. According to Wikipedia, it is used in reference to the character of Tybalt or Tibert in the Reynard the Fox folk tale cycle.

Frisian short form of names that have Gothic thiuda or Middle High German diet (both of which mean "people") for a first element, and of which the second element starts with a "b." The names Dietbald and Theudebert are good examples of that.

Alternate spelling of Thibeau. With this particular spelling, this name can also be a medieval French diminutive of Tibère and other given names that start with Tib-, as -eau is a medieval French diminutive suffix.
From Chinese 惕 (tì) meaning "alert, cautious, watchful" combined with 碚 (bèi) from 北碚 (Běibèi), a place in Chongqing. Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the name of the river that runs through Rome.

Roman cognomen which was derived from Tiberius.Notable Roman bearers of this name include the governor Tiberianus (2nd century AD) and the consul Gaius Junius Tiberianus (3rd century AD) and his son Junius Tiberianus, who went on to become a consul as well.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Tiberius.

Means "of the river Tiber" in Latin (also see Tiberius), as -inus is a Latin masculine adjectival suffix.In Roman mythology, Tiberinus is the name of the god of the Tiber as well as of Tiberinus Silvius, a legendary king of Alba Longa who is said to have reigned in the 10th century BC.This name was not restricted to mythology, as the Romans also used it as a cognomen in real life.
Galician, Italian and Spanish form of Tiberius.
Bulgarian and Russian form of Tiberius as well as an alternate transcription of Ukrainian Тиберій (see Tyberiy).
Meaning unknown, possibly a variant of Tiberius. In Roman mythology, Tibertus was the god of the river Anio (present-day Aniene), a tributary of the Tiber.
A character in The Second Nun's Tale. His name was Tiburce before he was christened by Pope Urban I.
Elaboration of Tiba. It saw some usage between the 16th and 19th centuries.
Romanian diminutive for the masculine given name Tiberiu.
From Guanche *tibəyt-abən, meaning "prayer". In Guanche folklore, this was the name of Tamonante's mother.
Tibiriçá means "watchman of the land" in Tupi. He was the leader of the Tupiniquim prior to the Portuguese colonization of Brazil.

According to the Venezuelan historian Tulio Febres Cordero, this was the name of a legendary Chibcha (or Muisca) woman at the time of the Spanish conquest, known as the Enchantress of Mérida (Spanish: La Hechicera de Mérida). This name is most often used in Venezuela.
Meaning, "looking into the sky" or "at one with the sky."
From the Indian language meaning great one, Indian tribe.
Roman cognomen of uncertain origin. The only well-known bearer was Albius Tibullus, a Roman poet and elegist.
French form of Tiburtius (see Tiburcio). A known bearer of this name is the French cartoonist Tiburce Oger (b. 1967).
Feminine form of Tiburcio. Notable bearers include two Argentinian revolutionaries, Tiburcia Haedo (1767-1839) and María Tiburcia Rodríguez (1778-1845).
Italian form of Tiburtius (see Tiburcio).Notable Italian bearers of this name include the composer Tiburzio Massaino (c. 1550-c. 1608) and the sculptor Tiburzio Vergelli (1551-1609).

An Old English personal name, deriving from Old English tiċċen "young goat, kid" in reference to a young person. This name was beared by the founder of Tickton, in East Yorkshire, England which means "Tica's homestead or village".
Meaning, "where the four winds gather their treasures from all parts of the world...the greatest which is knowledge."
From Sino-Vietnamese 錫 (tích) meaning "to bestow, to confer" or 㝜 (tích) meaning "night, darkness".
Derived from either Slovak tichosť "silence" or Slovak tichý "quiet, silent, calm" and the Slavic name element miru "peace, world".
Hungarian short form of Letícia, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Slovak and Hungarian form of Titianus.
Meaning uncertain. The first element may derive from Tizocic combined with nahuac "near" and the suffix -catl, or with the name Nahuacatl.
Of unknown meaning. Possibly of the Lilooet language, from the Salish language tree.

column3: 太陽(Japanese Kanji)|てぃだ(Japanese Hiragana)|ティダ(Japanese Katakana)|ธิดา(Thai)
column12: From 太陽 (tida), the word for "sun" in many Ryukyuan languages, cognate to Japanese 天道 (tendō), referring to the sun or the god of heaven and the earth.
Possibly means "nations" or "peoples". This is the name of a king of the ancient Kingdom of Goyim mentioned in Genesis 14:4.
Derives from Old English elements tid "time" and burg "city".
Meaning unknown. This name is commonly given to cats.
Italian and Spanish form of Tydeus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Tydeus.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Tydeus.
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and friþ "peace".
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and helm "helmet, protection". This was the name of a 10th century Bishop of Hereford.
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and hild "battle".
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and hun "bear cub".
From a French word used to refer to a follower of Tijaniyyah, a Sufi order that originated in Northern Africa.

A dwarf who served Helie, the lady-in-waiting of Queen Esmeree the Blonde of Wales.He accompanied Helie to Arthur’s court to find a champion to remove a curse placed on Esmeree. Helie was furious when Arthur gave her the young, untried Guinglain (Gawain’s son), but Tidogolain encouraged Helie to give him a chance. Tidogolain’s faith was vindicated when Guinglain proved an excellent knight.
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom".
Derived from Shuri Okinawan 天道/太陽 (tiida) (see Tida), given to a character from 'Final Fantasy X'.
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and wine "friend".
Derived from the Old English elements tīd "time" and wulf "wolf".
From Chinese 铁 (tiě) meaning "iron", in addition to other hanzi that are pronounced similarly.
Meaning as of yet unknown. A notable bearer of this name is the Malian politician Tiébilé Dramé (b. 1955).
From Chinese 铁 (tiě) meaning "iron" combined with 城 (chéng) meaning "castle, city" or 成 (chéng) meaning "completed, finished, succeeded". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

Meaning as of yet unknown. Notable bearers of this name include the Malian soccer player Tiécoro Keita (b. 1994) and the Malian soldier Tiécoro Bagayoko (1937-1983), who was once the director of Mali's national security service.
Meaning as of yet unknown; it might possibly be related to Tiécoro.Known bearers of this name include the Ivorian soccer player Tiécoura Coulibaly (b. 1988) and the Malian actor Tiécoura Traoré.

column3: 铁汉, 铁寒, 铁瀚, 铁涵, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 铁 (tiě) meaning "iron" combined with 汉 (hàn) meaning "man, Han, Chinese", 寒 (hán) meaning "cold, wintry", 瀚 (hàn) meaning "vast, wide, extensive" or 涵 (hán) meaning "soak, wet, tolerate, forgive". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
Dutch, West Frisian and Low German form of Till.
West Frisian and medieval Dutch form of Tillmann.
From Sino-Vietnamese 暹 (tiêm) meaning "to rise (of the sun)" or 讖 (tiêm) meaning "prophecy".
Meaning as of yet unknown. A notable bearer of this name is the Malian politician Tiéman Coulibaly (b. 1967).
Meaning as of yet unknown, but likely of Senufo origin.Notable bearers of this name include the Ivorian politician Tiémoko Meyliet Koné (b. 1949) and the Malian politician Tiémoko Sangaré (b. 1957).
Meaning as of yet unknown. A notable bearer of this name is the French soccer player Tiémoué Bakayoko (b. 1994), whose family originates from Ivory Coast.
From Sino-Vietnamese 進 (tiến) meaning "to advance, march forward".
From Sino-Vietnamese 諓 (tiễn) meaning "flattering", 羡 (tiễn) meaning "to envy, to admire, to exceed", or 踐 (tiễn) meaning "to trample, promise".
Meaning as of yet unknown. A notable bearer of this name is the Malian politician Tiéna Coulibaly (b. 1952).
Romani name that has been recorded from the 1800s onwards. Its origin and meaning are uncertain; a current theory, however, links it to the same source as Tiana.
From Sino-Vietnamese 進步 (tiến bộ) meaning "to progress, improve", composed of 進 (tiến) meaning "to advance" and 步 (bộ) meaning "step, pace, walk".
Alternate transcription of Thai เธียรชัย (see Thianchai).
From Sino-Vietnamese 進攻 (tiến công) meaning "to attack, offend, advance".

From Sino-Vietnamese 仙 (tiên) meaning "celestial" and 容 (dung) meaning "beauty". This is the name of a princess in Vietnamese mythology, the older sister of Ngọc Hoa and the wife of Chử Đồng Tử. She is also known as the Holy Lady of Thành Đông province.
Diminutive of Tien, as it contains the Dutch diminutive suffix -ke.In other words, you could also say that this name is an alternate spelling of the very common Tineke.
Possibly a female American form of Taniel, but most likely invented.
From Sino-Vietnamese 進行 (tiến hành) meaning "to carry out, proceed", composed of 進 (tiến) meaning "to advance" and 行 (hành) meaning "to go, carry out".
Frisian diminutive of Christine, Jantine, Martine, and other names ending in tine (compare Tineke).
Variant of Tiana influenced by Sienna.
Means "doctor, doctorate", from Sino-Vietnamese 進士 (tiến sỹ) literally meaning "advanced scholar".
From Sino-Vietnamese 先進 (tiên tiến) meaning "advanced, developed", composed of 先 (tiên) meaning "first, prior" and 進 (tiến) meaning "to advance".
From Sino-Vietnamese 捷 (tiệp) meaning "to win, succeed" or "quick, fast".
The first element of this name is derived from Old High German tiuri "expensive", or tiur "animal." The second element is derived from Old High German mund "protection."
Most likely from Irish tiarna meaning "lord".

Transferred use of the surname Tierney. Known bearers of this fname include the American photographer Tierney Gearon (1963-), American basketball player Tierney Pfirman (1994-), American jazz singer Tierney Sutton (1963-), and American biologist Tierney Thys (1966-).
Possibly deriving from the Fula word cerno, an honorific title meaning "master".
Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Theodoric.
Languedocian and Gascon form of Theodoric.
The first element of this name is derived from Old High German tiuri "expensive", or tiur "animal." The second element is derived from Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Dutch feminine form of Ties and West Frisian variant spelling of Tysje, which is the feminine form of Tys.
Stage name of the Dutch DJ Tijs Michiel Verwest.
From Sino-Vietnamese 節 (tiết) meaning "section, period, verse, melody".

Tifa Lockhart is a character in the massively popular and highly acclaimed 1997 role-playing game game Final Fantasy VII. Contrary to popular belief, Tifa is not a contraction of name Tiffany or the Kabbalah concept Tiferet (beauty). The etymology of Tiffany has no relevence to Final Fantasy VII, and many of the characters in RPGs name's have significant meanings, about their personality or traits (for example, Tifa's surname, Lockhart - Locked Heart). Tifa is simply a beautiful, made-up name, designed to sound pretty, unique and memorable. The "i" and "a" in the name is to preserve a trend where heroines in the Final Fantasy series have similar sounding names e.g Maria and Reina.
Hungarian and Portuguese borrowing of Tiffany, as well as an English variant.
Means "glory, splendour, beauty" in Hebrew (closely related to the word תפארת (tiferet), an important concept in Kabbala).
Means "glory, magnificence" in Hebrew. The term "Tiferet Yisrael" comes from the Israeli Declaration of Independence, sighed on the 14th of May 1948.

Meaning uncertain. It could be derived from Greek τίγρις (tigris) meaning "tiger", but it could also be derived from Tigris, the name of a river in Mesopotamia. Also compare Tigranes.This name was borne by a saint from the early 5th century AD.

Saint Tigris of Britain is traditionally recorded as a sister of Saint Patrick. The origin and meaning of her name are unknown; however, Saint Patrick (and thus his family, too) is thought to be of either Breton or Welsh heritage and so it has been suggested that Saint Tigris's name might be of Celtic origin. One theory tries to connect her name to Celtic *tigir which may or may not be related to Gaelic tigern "lord".Things are further complicated by the existence of 10th-century Spanish saint Tigrida or Tigridia with whom she is sometimes confused. Concerning her name, early 20th-century Irish historian and language scholar Helena Concannon theorized that it suggests a Gallic origin.Tigris is a cousin of president Snow in 'The Hunger Games' by Suzanne Collins.
Latinized form of Tigrios. This was the name of a saint from the 5th century AD.

Tikbalang (also written as Tigbalang, Tigbalan, or Tikbalan) is a bipedal horse creature of Philippine folklore said to lurk in the mountains and forests of the Philippines. It is sometimes believed to be a transformation of an aborted fetus which has been sent to earth from limbo. This name was given to protect the child from evil spirits. Pre-Hispanic Filipinos believed that spirits preyed on beautiful, strong, and desirable children, so the child was given an aversive name.

Tilottama (Sanskrit: तिलोत्तमा, Tilottamā) is an Apsara (celestial nymph) described in Hindu mythology. Tila is the Sanskrit word for sesame "seed" or a "bit" and uttama means "better" or "higher". Tilottama therefore means the being whose smallest particle is the finest or one who is composed of the finest and highest qualities.

Both of the last two names are incorrect to use in relation to the tyrant, for there were no records found in Sinope for either name.

The name of plant of the mint family derives from Latin thymum, from Greek thymon, from Proto Indo European dheu-, a base of words meaning "to rise in a cloud" (related to "fume"); so thyme might be the plant "with a strong odor", or it might be related to thyein meaning "burn as a sacrifice", which would indicate the plant was used as incense.

From Newar तिमिला (timilā), a contraction of तुयु मिला (tuyu milā) meaning "white sky".

The name ‘Timmion’ is an unique African-American name that seem to stem from other older names from different cultures. i.e., Timmy (English), Timothy (Greek), Timon (Greek)

The origins of this name are uncertain. This was the name of a Barbadian slave who was one of the first people accused of witchcraft in the Salem witch trials. In the literary world, said Tituba is featured in Maryse Condé's novel I, Tituba: Black Witch of Salem (1986) as well as in the 1952 play The Crucible by Arthur Miller.Several origins have been suggested. According to Veta Smith Tucker, Tituba is a Yoruba word, a verb meaning "to atone", and titi in Yoruba means "endless". If Tituba hailed from the Caribbean or from South America, she could have surely been given a Spanish name; Spanish titubear means "to stammer". In the 16th century the Spanish identified a tribe of Indians around the Orinoco River that they named Tibetibe, and anthropologists also distinguished a group of Arawaks around the Amacura River called the Tetebetana. In Latin, often a source of slaves' names in Europe and America, tituba means "totter, stagger".

In Greek mythology, Tityos was a giant, the son of Zeus and the mortal woman Elara, carried to term by the earth goddess Gaia. He was killed by Apollo and Artemis when he attempted to assault their mother, Leto, then condemned to Tartarus, where he was stretched over nine acres, and two vultures fed on his regenerating liver for eternity.

From the characters 缇 (tí, meaning “orange red”) and 萦 (yíng, meaning “to entangle” or “to wrap around”). This name was borne by Chunyu Tiying (淳于缇萦), a maiden recorded in the history of the Western Han Dynasty (202 BC–9 CE). According to the Records of the Grand Historian (史记) by Sima Qian, her father was a doctor who had been accused by multiple nobles for refusing to serve them, and was sent to the capital city Chang’an for a mutilating punishment. Tiying accompanied her father there and sent a letter to Emperor Wu of Han. In it she lamented the unjust incrimination of her father and offered to become a palace slave in place of her father’s sentence. The emperor was moved by her filial piety and not only removed her father’s punishment, but also abolished the mutilation punishment altogether.

Meaning uncertain. A known bearer of this given name was Toetela Steinbach (1902-1944), the mother of the Dutch-Sinti Holocaust icon Settela Steinbach (1934-1944). It should be noted that in her case, it is possible that the spelling of her name is "dutchized" and that the original Sinti spelling of her name was actually Tutela. You see, the "oo" sound is written as 'oe' in Dutch, but the sound is usually written as 'u' in foreign languages. Since the letter 'u' is pronounced differently in Dutch, the Dutch tend to "dutchize" foreign names that have the "oo" sound written as 'u', in order to avoid confusion over the proper pronunciation of the names. This is most often seen with Russian given names and surnames (Yulia becomes Joelia in Dutch, and Putin becomes Poetin), but names from other languages and cultures are certainly not exempt from this. For example, the Arabic name Abdul is regularly found written as Abdoel in Dutch, and the Indian name Buddha is always written as Boeddha in Dutch. As for Sinti given names: since the Sinti people speak Sinte Romani, an Indo-Aryan language where the "oo" sound is written as 'u', it is certainly not inconceivable that Sinti names were subjected to this treatment as well.

"Tolgonay" is a deeply melodic Kyrgyz name meaning "Full Moon" (specifically the moon in its most complete, mature state). In Kyrgyz culture, it is synonymous with the wisdom of the earth and the light of the heavens. It represents the fruition of life, maternal wisdom, and a spirit that has reached its full potential.This noble spirit is immortalized in Central Asian culture through the legendary heroine Tolgonay from Chingiz Aitmatov’s world-renowned masterpiece, Mother Earth. As a symbol of ultimate resilience, quiet dignity, and unconditional maternal love, her legacy elevates the name from a poetic description of the cosmos into a powerful testament to the unbreakable human spirit.

column12: This name can be used as 留 (ryuu, ru, todo.maru, todo.meru, to.maru, to.meru, ruuburu) meaning "detail, fasten, halt, stop" or it can be used to combine 登 (shou, chou, to, tou, dou, a.garu, no.boru) meaning "ascend, climb up" with 免 (men, manuka.reru, manuga.reru, me) meaning "dismissal, excuse" or 米 (bei, mai, meitoru, kome, yone, me) meaning "metre, rice, USA."Tome was used in the Edo Period (1603-1868). In German it also the name of an influential band from Hamburg.The name blends well with typical sound patterns of Low German names and is more popular in Northern Germany than in the South.

column3: 十夢, 登夢, 斗夢, 都夢, 富夢, 吐夢(Japanese Kanji)|とむ(Japanese Hiragana)|トム(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name combines 十 (ji', juu, ju', to, too) meaning "ten", 登 (shou, chou, to, tou, dou, a.garu, nobo.ru) meaning "ascend, climb up", (to, tou) meaning "Big Dipper, sake dipper", 都 (tsu, to, miyako) meaning "capital, metropolis", 富 (fu, fuu, tomi, to.mu) meaning "abundant, enrich, wealth" or 吐 (to, tsu.ku, ha.ku) meaning "belch, confess, spit, tell (lies), vomit" with 夢 (bou, mu, kura.i, yume, yume.miru) meaning "dream, illusiom, vision."The first 2 combinations can be used for both genders.Bearers of this name include film director Tomu Uchida (内田 吐夢) (1898-1970) who was born Tsunejirō Uchida (内田 常次郎), actor Tomu Miyazaki (宮崎 吐夢) (1970-) who was born Ichirō Matsuhiro (松代 一郎) and retired Takarazuka actress Tomu Ranju (蘭寿 とむ) (1975-).Usage of this name is most likely due to its phonetic similarity with Tom 1.

Tomura, used by the popular villain Shigaraki Tomura in Boku no Hero Academia, comes from the word “tomurau," which means to mourn and express sorrow over death and farewell.Tomura (木弔) meaning “to mourn (for the dead)”.
Meaning “we give thanks to him”, a longer form of the name is Tomutendaishe, whilst Tom 1 is the shorter form.
Meaning “we give thanks to He who is the Lord”, it is synonymous with the names Tinomutendaishe and Tovatendaishe.
Probably a variant of Tonya, influenced by Tom 1.
Short form of Antoni, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
From Sino-Vietnamese 尊 (tôn) meaning "to respect, honor, revere".
From Sino-Vietnamese 存 (tồn) meaning "to exist, to preserve".
Short form of Antoni, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Diminutive of Antonia. In Scandinavia it is also used as a variant of Tone (the Norwegian form of Þone).Also a short form of Clintona (used by the beauty queen Clintona Jackson).
Derived from Nahuatl tōnac meaning "abundance" and cihuātl "woman, lady". This was the name of an Aztec goddess of fertility.
Older form of Tonalli, meaning "day, sun, solar heat, life force" in Nahuatl.
Means "summer perfume" in Nahuatl, derived from tonalla "dry season, summer" and xochiatl "perfume, rose water".
From the name of a type of red orchid (species Bletia coccinea) commonly known as the brick red bletia in English. Ultimately derived from tonalli "day, warmth of the sun" and xōchitl "flower".

Means "our dear mother" or "our sacred mother" in Nahuatl, from to- "our" combined with nantli "mother" and the diminutive or reverential suffix tzin. This was a title of the Aztec mother goddess, who is popularly linked with the Virgin of Guadalupe.
Means "chief, host of a festival" in Armenian.
Diminutive form of Anton and Antonio via Toni 1.
Originally a diminutive of Antonija, used as a given name in its own right.
The (misspelled) name of an 11 year old girl featured in the 'Jet' magazine in 1955.It comes from Tondelayo, title character in a film from 1942.
The title character of a film in 1942.It is the inspiration of the given name Tondalaya.
Cremish Lombard short form of Antòne.
Meaning uncertain. Possibly means "our useful thing", derived from Nahuatl to- "our" and necoca "usefulness (of something)".
Diminutive of the double names António Manuel or António Leonel.
Diminutive of Tön, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Likely a (slightly corrupted) short form of Antoinette.
Variant of Tùng or from 从 (tòng) meaning "to follow".
From Sino-Vietnamese 宋 (tống) referring to the Song dynasty.

column3: 彤, 童, 樋, 统, 潼, 桐, 瞳, 同, 仝, 通, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red", 童 (tóng) meaning "child", as well as other hanzi that are pronounced similarly.
Means "brave, strong" in Old Turkic. According to Kashgarli Mahmud, “Tonga” is the name of a predatory animal of the leopard species.
From the Malagasy tonga meaning "arrived" and soa meaning "good".
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 贝 (bèi) meaning "seashell".
Alternate transcription of Thai ธงชัย (see Thongchai).
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 蝉 (chán) meaning "cicada".
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 嫦 (cháng), the name of a moon goddess.
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 琛 (chēn) meaning "treasure, valuables".
From 通 (tōng) meaning "to pass, to travel through" and 达 (dá) meaning "smooth".
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 芳 (fāng) meaning "fragrant".
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 荷 (hé) meaning "lotus, water lily".
From the Chinese 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermilion" and 画 (huà) meaning "painting, drawing".
