The literal translation in Hangul (Koreas modern written language) for Ugi (우기) is Monsoon or Rainy season. Ugi (우기) is derived from the Hanja character 雨 (Yǔ meaning rain). Although it is possible that 雨 (Yǔ) was first used/ invented by a Korean during the Gojoseon period (likely established somewhere between 2333bce - 1101bce) as certain regions of modern china were technically considered parts of Ancient Korea (control of these regions switched and evolved over many years many times), it is still most likely the first use of 雨 was in a Chinese dynasty during the use of Old Chinese (Roughly 1766BCE - 256BCE). The Korean word/ name Ugi (우기) translates to Yǔjì and/or Yuqi (雨季) in Mandarin and Yuki and/or Uki (雨季) in Japanese. Since pronunciation and spelling varies depending on the language, Ugi would not retain its meaning in mandarin and Japanese unless Ugi is written in Hangul (우기) then translated directly to the appropriate language. When separated, Ugi could have different meanings for other languages making Ugi a Korean name. For example, in Mandarin, Yù translates to Jade but also Rain. This is not the case in Korean. Regardless, in Korea, China and Japan the name's definition is typically used in reference to its rainy season/ monsoon definition.

Literally means "owl mirror", derived from Icelandic ugla "owl" combined with spegill "mirror, looking glass".This given name is a direct Icelandic translation of Ulenspegel, which is the surname of Dyl Ulenspegel (known in contemporary German as Till Eulenspiegel), a trickster figure from Middle Low German folklore. His surname is a figurative one, in that it not only refers to his ability to trick people, but also to the stupidity of the people that allowed themselves to be tricked by him. You see, in the time and place where the stories of Ulenspegel first surfaced (namely, 14th-century Germany), the owl was a symbol of stupidity, rather than of wisdom (as it is nowadays). In combination with the Middle Low German word spegel "mirror", it is clear that Dyl's surname references to the fact that (by tricking them) he shows people to themselves, to what they really are: as stupid as an owl.

The Japanese deity of food and agriculture is named 宇迦之御魂神 (Ukanomitama), meaning "mighty soul of sustenance."

column12: This name is used as 右近 with 右 (u, yuu, migi) meaning "right" and 近 (kin, kon, chika.i) meaning "akin, early, near, tantamount."One (male) bearer of this name was Ukon Takayama (or Takayama Ukon if surname is used first) (高山 右近) (1552-1615), also known as Dom Justo Takayama, Iustus Takayama Ukon, Hikogorō (彦五郎 - his childhood name) and Shigetomo (重友 - name given after the coming-of-age ceremony), a Sengoku period kirishitan (キリシタン/Christian) samurai and daimyō.One (female) bearer of this name was the Heian period poet Ukon (右近), who was included in the list of Thirty-six Female Poetry Immortals in Japan.

Means "door goddess", from Sami uksa "door" and áhkká "wife, woman, mother". In Sami mythology Uksáhkká lived under the door sill and protected the home against all evil. She watched over children during their first year, especially when they learned to walk.

With regards to 右京, it was only very recently that it started being given to girls, although, right now, it is only a tiny amount compared to the number of boys being given 右京 as their name.Bearers of this name include racing driver Ukyō Katayama (片山 右京) (1963-) and tarento & retired Takarazuka actress Ukyō Takahane (貴羽 右京), born Hitomi Yasuda (安田 ひとみ) (1975-)As a word, Ukyō (右京) means "the right side of the capital," referring to an area west of Suzaku Avenue, which is the central avenue leading to the Imperial Palace from the south in ancient capitals.

Derived from Ūla, which is the name of a river in Dzūkija National Park (located near the villages of Marcinkonys and Merkinė) in southern Lithuania. In turn, the river derives its name from the Baltic root aul-, which comes from Proto-Indo-European *aulo-s or *h₂eulos meaning "tube, pipe". There might also be a relation with Proto-Indo-European *av- meaning "source (of water), spring" as well as "current, flow".

From Mongolian улаан (ulaan) meaning "red" and хүү (khüü) meaning "son, boy" or "dear, beloved".

Means "red iron" in Mongolian, from улаан (ulaan) meaning "red" and төмөр (tömör) meaning "iron".

From the Hebrew אוּלָם (ulam) meaning "porch". This is the name of two people in the Bible, a Benjaminite and a Manassite.
Means "still more happiness" in Mongolian, from улам (ulam) meaning "more, further" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy".
From Kyrgyz улан (ulan) meaning "young man, soldier" and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".

From Kazakh ұл (ūl) meaning "son, boy" and бала (bala) meaning "child". This name was given to girls whose parents hoped their next child would be a boy.
From Ulbertus, possibly a Latinized form of Wulfbert.
From Kazakh ұл (ūl) meaning "son, boy" and бике (bike) meaning "girl, lady".

Means "baby boy" from Kazakh ұл (ul) "son, boy" and бөбек (böbek) "baby, newborn". This name was traditionally given to girls when her family was expecting a boy in hopes that the next child of the family would be male.

Means "let it be a son" from Kazakh ұл (ul) meaning "boy, son" and болсын (bolsyn) "let (it be)". This name was traditionally given to daughters whose families were expecting a boy, in hopes that the next child of the family would be male.
From Kazakh ұл (ūl) meaning "son, boy" combined with Persian دانا (dānā) meaning "wise".

the first ruler of the Huns whose historicity is undisputed.The name is recorded as Ουλδης (Ouldes) by Sozomen, Uldin by Orosius, and Huldin by Marcellinus Comes. On the basis of the Latin variants, Omeljan Pritsak and Otto J. Maenchen-Helfen argue that the name ended on -n, not the Greek suffix -s. Hyun Jin Kim, however, argues that -in is a Greek suffix added to the name.Maenchen-Helfen considers the name to be of Turkic origin. He compares it with the names Ultinzur and Uldach and argues that it is the element *uld or *ult plus a dimuninative suffix *-ïn. He does not give an etymology of the element *uld/*ult.Pritsak derives the root of the etymon from the verb öl-, which survived in Mongolian olje, ol-jei (auspice, happiness, good luck). He argues that the middle suffix jei was originally *di + ge, thus *öl-jige > öl-dige. In place of Mongolian ge, Hunnic would then have the suffix n. He thus reconstructs the form is *öl-di-n (auspicious, happy, lucky, fortunate).Hyun Jin Kim derives the name from the common Turkic word for six, *alti, comparing it to the Chuvash form ultta. He argues that the name was actually a title and may indicate that Uldin was one of the six principle nobles of the Huns rather than a king.

The first ruler of the Huns whose historicity is undisputed.In 400, Uldin ruled in Muntenia, present-day Romania east of the Olt River. The extension of his realm to the north and east is unknown, but to the west probably reached the banks of Danube where Huns had been camped since 378-380.Maenchen-Helfen considers the name to be of Turkic origin. He compares it with the names Ultinzur and Uldach and argues that it is the element *uld or *ult plus a dimuninative suffix *-ïn. He does not give an etymology of the element *uld/*ult.Pritsak derives the root of the etymon from the verb öl-, which survived in Mongolian olje, ol-jei (auspice, happiness, good luck). He argues that the middle suffix jei was originally *di + ge, thus *öl-jige > öl-dige. In place of Mongolian ge, Hunnic would then have the suffix n. He thus reconstructs the form is *öl-di-n (auspicious, happy, lucky, fortunate).Hyun Jin Kim derives the name from the common Turkic word for six, *alti, comparing it to the Chuvash form ultta. He argues that the name was actually a title and may indicate that Uldin was one of the six principle nobles of the Huns rather than a king.
Old Novgorod dialect form of Olaf.
Means "very rich, exceedingly rich" in Mongolian, from үлэмж (ülemj) meaning "very, exceeding, largely" and баян (bayan) meaning "rich, wealthy".
Means "great celebration, much joy" in Mongolian, from үлэмж (ülemj) meaning "very, exceeding, largely" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration".
Means "great virtue, excessive good luck" in Mongolian, from үлэмж (ülemj) meaning "very, exceeding, largely" and буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing".
Means "intimacy, familiarity, harmony, agreement" in Arabic.
Alternate transcription of Arabic ألفة (see Ulfa), as well as an Indonesian variant.
Derived from the Old Norse elements ulfr "wolf" and arinn "fire place, immolation place".
Derived from the Germanic name elements ulfr "wolf" and ǫrn "eagle".
Variant form of Ulfgæirr and a combination of ulfr "wolf" and herr "army".
Derived from Arabic أُلْفَة (ʾulfa) meaning "intimacy, affinity, affection, harmony".
From Arabic ألفة (ulfa) meaning "intimacy, affection" combined with Persian خانم (khanum), the feminine form of khan meaning "king, ruler"
Variant of Wulfcytel. Ulfcytel (died 1016) was an East Anglian military leader who commanded East Anglian forces in an 1004 battle against Danish Viking invaders.
Derived from Old Norse úlfr "wolf" combined with Old Norse dís "goddess, priestess".

Formed from Úlfur and Old Norse ey "island" or ey "good fortune". This is also the Icelandic name for the Hebridean island of Ulva (Ulbha in Gaelic), probably meaning "wolf island" or "Úlfr's island".
Derived from Old Norse úlfr "wolf" combined with Old Norse geirr "spear".
Variant form of Wulfhard and in some cases also of Odalfrid. For the latter, also compare the Frisian cognates Olfert and Ulfert.
Derived from the Germanic name elements ulfr "wolf" and heðinn "jacket of fur or skin".
Swedish and Old Danish form of Úlfhildr.
Derived from the Old Norse elements ulfr meaning "wolf" and hildr meaning "battle". An 11th-century Norwegian princess bore this name.
An ancient British name which means "little wolf". Most well known in the Arthurian legends of Geoffrey Monmouth, where Sir Ulfin plays a role in Merlin's plot for King Arthur to be born.

The noble knight Sir Ulfius became Uther Pendragon’s confidant (councillor) in the matter of Uther’s love for Igraine. It was Ulfius who conceived the idea of fetching Merlin to help the king consummate his desire. When Merlin gave Uther the likeness of Igraine’s husband and himself the likeness of Gorloïs’ knight Jordanus, he gave Ulfius the likeness of Sir Brastias, another of the Duke’s men. After Duke Gorloïs death became commonly known, Ulfius arranged the treaty and forwarded the marriage between Uther and Igraine.Ulfius may well have been a companion of the Round Table when Uther had it. The service Malory records Ulfius as doing for Arthur comes before the young king received his father’s Table from Leodegrance; Ulfius may have retired or died before Arthur’s marriage, but if the old knight did remain long enough in Arthur’s court, he would surely have been reinstated or elected to the Round Table.
Old Norse short form of Ulfkætill.
Derived from the Germanic name elements ulfr "wolf" and ketill "cauldron hat, helmet".
Old Norse and Icelandic variant of Ulfkæll.
Derived from Old Norse úlfr "wolf" combined with Old Norse kettil "kettle, cauldron" (see also Kettil).
Derived from the Germanic name elements ulfr "wolf" and -ljótr "shining, bright".
Short form of names beginning in Ulf- like Ulfhard.Ulfo Peters was a Afro-German boxer.
Derived from the Germanic elements wulf "wolf" and rik "power; ruler".This is the name of a major character in 'The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim', Ulfric Stormcloak.
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Ulfríkr.
Old Norse combination of ulfr "wolf" and ríkr "mighty, distinguished, rich".
Derived from Old Norse ulfr meaning "wolf" and týr meaning "god" (or the name of the Norse god Týr, which is identical).
Derived from Old Norse úlfr "wolf" combined with Old Norse viðr "tree".
Ülgen is son of Kayra and Yer Tanrı and brother of Umay, Erlik, Koyash, and Ay Ata. He has 7 sons: Karşıt, Pura, Burça, Yaşıl, Karakuş, Er Kanım, and Baktı. Ülgen is creator deity.

Derived from "Ülker", the Pleiades; and "Ülgen", a Turkic creator-deity from Tengrism, an ethnic Turkic, Yeniseian, Mongolic religion.Ülgen symbolizes goodness, welfare, and abundance; furthermore, he is the creator of earth, heaven and all living beings. He controls the atmospheric events and movements of stars. He was regarded as the patron god of shamans and the source of their knowledge.It is believed that Ülgen has been created from Kayra (Tengere Kayra Khan). He is the highest deity after Tengri in the pantheon. Often, Ülgen is compared with Tengri and at times they are thought to be on par, or even the same. In some sayings, the name/function of Ülgen may be (partially) interchangeable with that of Tengri.His symbol is the Pleiades, "Ülker" in Turkish, a name most likely derived from Ülgen itself.This modern spelling is a mix of Ülgen and Ülker, and the name itself bears both meanings; the Pleiades and the name of the deity.
Derived from the Uzbek ulgi meaning "example, model" and boy meaning "rich, wealthy".
Masculine form and feminine short form of Uliuli.
A wicked giant who, with his brothers Margan and Durkion, served Lord Karedoz of Malmontan. All of the giants were slain by Arthur’s Sir Tandareis.
Croatian and Serbian form of Ulysses.
Deriving in part from the Hittite element ulili ("field"). Name borne by a goddess of vegetation and fertility, known from Hittite ritual and oracle texts.
The name Ulinka is probably derived from Ulrike via the short form Uli.
Corsican form of Oliver via Oliviero.

Classical Latin form of Odysseus.'Some insist that only Ulixēs is correct for Classical Latin and that the spelling Ulyssēs is incorrect; but the form Ulysses is not uncommon, especially in later periods.'
Derived from Finnish uljas "proud, noble, valiant". This is also a Finnish translation of Greek Ptolemaios.

The first element of this name is as of yet uncertain. The second element should be derived from the Uzbek noun жон (jon) meaning "soul". It ultimately comes from the Persian noun جان (jān) meaning "soul, being, spirit" as well as "life". The latter word can also be an affectionate suffix, which roughly means "dear, darling" when attached to given names and titles.
Derived from the Uzbek ulkan meaning "great, grand" and nazar meaning "look, glance".
West Frisian variant form of Oelke and North Frisian cognate of Oelke, although it should be noted that it is strictly masculine in North Frisia.
Means "bad, evil", deriving from the Proto-Celtic element *ulkos ("bad, evil). This is a Lepontic name known from a coin found on the Italian side of the Gran San Bernardo pass.
Variant of Ülkü used outside of Turkey.

An Asherite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:39 in the Bible.The etymology of this name is disputed. It may derive from the Hebrew word עָלֶה (aleh), meaning "leaf", the Hebrew word עֲלִיָה (aliyah) meaning "ascension", or the Hebrew word יֶלֶד (yeled) meaning "young child". In the book of 1 Chronicles, Ulla is a descendant of Asher.
Rare combination of Ulla and Elisabeth.
Rare Swedish combination of Ulla and Karin.
Variant of Üllo. The name coincides with Estonian üllas "noble".
Swedish combination of Ulla and vé 'home, temple, sanctuary'.
Taraškievica Belarusian variant form of Ulyana.

Name of a Magyar chieftain. Meaning unknown.
Means "sweet little star", derived from Greenlandic ulloriaq "star" (cf. Ulloriaq) combined with the diminutive suffix nnguaq meaning "sweet, dear, little".
Derived from Old Germanic wulþuz "glory". This was the name of a Norse god associated with skiing, bows, and hunting. In the Edda, he's a son of Sif and a stepson of Thor.
Probably a short form of Ursula
Derived from Kazakh ұл (ul) meaning "son, boy" and мекен (meken) meaning "home, abode".
Ulmo was the King of the Sea in J.R.R. Tolkien's, The Silmarillion.

Uloopi is a Naga Princess mentioned in the Mahabharata — she is the daughter of King Kauravya and the second wife of the Pandava, Arjuna . She played a large role in raising Arjuna’s son with Chitrangada, Babruvahana and brought Arjuna back to life after a battle with Babruvahana.
Derived from the Uzbek uloq meaning "baby goat" or "knot" and boy meaning "rich, wealthy".
Means "blade of a harpoon or lance" in Greenlandic.
Derived from Kazakh ұлпа (ulpa) meaning "fluffy, soft, tender".

Derived from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz "wolf". Saint Ulphia of Amiens was said to be a young girl living on the banks of the Noye who became a hermit at what would become Saint-Acheul, near Amiens in the Kingdom of the Franks, under the spiritual direction of Saint Domitius. At the end of her life, she formed and directed a community of religious women at Amiens.
Feminine form of the Roman nomen gentilicium Ulpius, ultimately derived from either an Umbrian cognate of the Latin word lupus meaning "wolf", or vulpus meaning "fox".

Perhaps derived from Latin lupus meaning "wolf". A famous bearer was Ulpio Minucci, father of smooth jazz guitarist Chieli Minucci.

From Finnish ulpukka meaning "spatterdock, yellow water-lily, cow lily, yellow pond-lily (flower)".
Derived from the Uzbek ul meaning "son" and qo'zi meaning "lamb".

Queen Ultrogotha (510 - after 566/67) was a Frankish Merovingian queen and the wife of Childebert I.

From Latin ultimūs meaning "final". This is the name of a Tarzan inspired character who appears in about 14 novels written by film industry veteran Julián Amich and drawn by Enrique Pertegás. A famous real bearer is Cuban baseball player Ultus Álvarez.

Greenlandic combination of Ulo and -lik (suffix that denotes that the the root word is a form of amulet or helper spirit).

Feminine form of Sanskrit उलूप (ulūpa) meaning "spreading creeper, grass, reed". This is the name of a naga princess mentioned in the epic the Mahabharata. She is a wife of the hero Arjuna and the mother of Iravan.
From an obsolete Uzbek word meaning "nation, state".
Greenlandic variant form of Orûsît or from Greenlandic uluusiit meaning "cloudberry".
Means "he is love" in Ndebele and Zulu.
From the Hawaiian uluwehi, "a lush and beautiful verdure; a place where beautiful plants live".
Swedish and Norwegian form of Ulfva, an Old Swedish byname meaning "she-wolf".This is a cognate of Ylva. Also compare the masculine equivalent Ulv.
Old Swedish and Norwegian younger form of Ulfarr.

Derived from the place name Ulvi in Ida-Viru County, Estonia.
Derived from the Arabic word "ulviyye", meaning "noble," "high," or "elevated."

Means "little mother" in Arabic, being a diminutive of the word أُمّ (ʾumm) "mother; origin, source". Umama bint Abi al-As, also called Umama bint Zaynab (died c. 685 AD), was a granddaughter of the Prophet Muhammad. She married twice (once to her sister Fatima's widower, Ali bin Abi Talib) and had one son, also named Muhammad.

Means "blessing of Uma" from Thai อุมา (uma) referring to the Hindu goddess Parvati and พร (phon) meaning "blessing".

Combination of the given name Umar and Persian جان (jân) meaning "soul, life".

Derived from Japanese 馬 (uma) "horse", 太 (ta) "thick, big, great", and 郎 (ro) "son". A notable fictional bearer of the name is Dr. Umataro Tenma, a character in the manga Astro Boy and its subsequent anime adaptations. He is a scientist who builds Astro Boy in the likeness of his late son, but eventually rejects and disowns the robot when he noticed that he fails to grow.

Unferth's name can be understood in a number of ways. A common reading, by Morton W. Bloomfield is to see it as un + frith, "mar peace": similarly, J. R. R. Tolkien considered the name to mean Unpeace/Quarrel, or perhaps 'Unfriend'. However, Searle's Onomasticon Anglo-Saxonicum lists several mentions of medieval historic personages, such as bishops and archbishops, named Hunfrith. Another reading, by Fred C. Robinson, is to see it as un + ferth, "no wit".Other scholars, such as R. D. Fulk, have suggested that Unferth's name should not be associated with frið (peace) but with ferhð, which translates as “soul, spirit, mind, and life.” Fulk writes that it is difficult to assign significance to names in Beowulf because some of the characters involved are historical figures. However, Fulk argues that this can be done in the case of Unferth because the name Un-ferth is not known to appear in history, or in any manuscript other than the Nowell Codex. But the Chronicon Ex Chronicis, a 12th-century history of England, variously attributed to Florence of Worcester ("Florentii Wigorniensis") or to John of Worcester, mentions an 8th-century bishop of Winton whose name in Latin is given as Hunfridus and Hunfertho.The first element of the name, un, appears exclusively as hun in the sole manuscript of Beowulf. Fred C. Robinson suggests that this h is a Celtic scribal habit which indicates that u has a vocal function by adding an unpronounced graphic. Fulk argues, however, that this use of the letter h does not appear anywhere else in the Beowulf manuscript.In Old English, un usually functions as a negative prefix. However, in certain contexts the meaning must be interpreted as 'abnormally', rather than 'not' (cf. German Untiefe, un-depth, which may mean either an excessive or an insufficient depth, or Old English unhar, "very old"). This use of un could add new possibilities to the meaning of the name Unferth. Despite the vast amount of research that has gone into the etymology of Unferth's name, there can be no easy consensus about its meaning.

Presumably a masculine form of Urbinia, the name of an Ancient Roman Vestal Virgin. It appears to be the nomen of Ancient Roman moneyer Quintus Urbinius, who served from 111-110 BC as one of the 'tresviri monetales' responsible for striking the year's denarii. Little is known about Quintus Urbinius beyond the survival of his name on his coinage; he is not attested in any other known historical records. It is also the praenomen of one of the many figures from 'Memorable Sayings and Doings Volume II, Book 6' by Valerius Maximus. In Chapter VIII ('Of the Loyalty of Slaves to their Masters'), Maximus tells the story of Urbinius Panapio, a slave who demonstrated his loyalty to his master, Panapio, by swapping clothes with him and staying in his bedroom when he, Urbinius, learned of a plot by a group of soldiers to kill Panapio.

King of Gore and Rheged.The husband of Morgan le Fay and the father of two sons named Ywaine (Owain). In Welsh tradition Urien of Rheged fathered the twins Morfudd and Owain.Uriens was among the allied kings - probably one of the ringleaders - in the first rebellion against the young Arthur. He fought in the battle of Bedegraine and afterward hosted his fellow rebels in his city of Sorhaute. He did not join the second rebellion, however, and was reconciled with Arthur, either between the two rebellions or when he came with his wife Morgan to the rich funeral Arthur gave Lot and the other kings who died in battle before Castle Terrabil.On the advice of King Pellinore, Uriens was made a companion of the Round Table after the decisive battle on the Humber against the invading kings of Denmark, Ireland, the Vale, Soleise, and Longtains.Uriens went hunting with Arthur and Sir Accolon of Gaul on the expedition that led into Morgan's engineered attempt on Arthur's life, but, after the three hunters had fallen asleep aboard the mysterious boat, Uriens woke up next morning in his wife's arms, abed in Camelot. After the failure of her attempt on Arthur's life, Morgan attempted to salvage something by killing her husband, at least, with his sword as he slept, but their son, Ywaine le Blanchemains, prevented her. Although Ywaine promised to keep the secret, on condition his mother try no such thing again, the incident seems to have marked a permanent separation between Uriens and his wife; Morgan shortly thereafter left court and it appears likely that the royal couple never met again. Uriens remained faithfully with Arthur, being listed among those who attempted to heal Sir Urre of Hungary.In Chrétien's works, Gore is the land of King Bademagu - here, a monarch of quasimystial propotions - but Uriens is clearly identified as Ywaine's father. Like his son, Uriens appears originally to have been a real person who lived in the kingdom of Rheged, in southern Scotland and northern England, in the sixth century.

Southeast Asia, particularly within the Mon-Khmer language family, it is an autonym for the Wa people of Myanmar and China, where the word historically means "cave" or denotes an ethnonym rooted in local creation mythology. In Vietnamese, "Vá" can serve as a vocabulary-derived name meaning "to patch" or "mend," though it is rare as a standalone given name. Alternatively, in West African languages like Ewe, Va is a short, imperative verb meaning "come," sometimes integrated into longer, meaningful names. Across these distinct regions, the name carries varied etymological roots ranging from indigenous ethnic identity to action-oriented vocabulary.

The name of the mountain comes from the Samoan myth of the giant Vaea who, in grieving for the loss of his son, petrified and became the mountain.

Linguistically, the name Vaelen is a modern American blending that draws from diverse historical roots, primarily operating as a creative variation of the Latin name Valen or Valens meaning "strong," "vigorous," or "healthy." It incorporates the "ae" digraph, a stylistic element traditionally found in Latin and Greek ligatures (like æ) and Welsh or Gaelic naming traditions (resembling the Celtic Faelan), which is frequently utilized in modern English to evoke an ancient, mythic, or fantasy-inspired aesthetic. Ultimately, while its structural components connect to classical Indo-European roots signifying strength and nature, its specific synthesis is distinctly contemporary—combining the trendy "V" initial and "-len" suffix popular in 21st-century Anglophone naming conventions.

The meaning of this name as a whole is uncertain, as both of its two elements are uncertain, due to there being several possibilities for their etymology.The first element is either vai-, vaid- or vait-. In the case of the first one, that means that the element is either derived from the old Lithuanian verb vajoti meaning "to chase, to pursue" or from the old Lithuanian noun vajys meaning "messenger, courier". But if the element is actually vaid-, then it is derived from the old Lithuanian verb vaidyti meaning "to visit, to appear", which is related to the modern Lithuanian verb vaidentis meaning "to haunt" as well as "to appear, to see". Combination of the Old Norse name elements valr "the dead, the slain (in Valhalla)" and ey "island; flat land along a coast" or ey "good fortune".
Swedish and Finnish form of Walafrid and Waldfrid, much more common as a male name. Valfrid Palmgren (1877-1967), a Swedish politician and teacher, was a famous female bearer of the name.
Feminine form of Valfrid, though Valfrid has also occasionally been used as a feminine name.
Latvian form of Walafrid and Waldfrid.
MEANING - a bridle, rein, Goddess Durga
Old Norse masculine form of Valgerðr.
Derived from Old Norse valr "the slain" and gautr "goth".

Derived from the Old Norse elements valr meaning "the dead on a battlefield, the battle-slain" (as found in the word valkyrja) and garðr meaning "fence, defense". Alternatively the first element may be derived from Primitive Germanic *walha- meaning "Celtic, Welsh, foreign".
Derived from Erzya валдо (valdo) meaning "light" and кужо (kuzho) meaning "glade".
In Norse mythology this is the name of Odin's enormous hall where half of all warriors go after they die.

Derived from the Old Norse elements valr meaning "the dead on a battlefield, the slain" (as found in the word valkyrja) and hildr meaning "battle". Alternatively the first element may come from Primitive Germanic *walha- meaning "Celtic, Welsh, foreign".

Possibly derived from Old Germanic walhaz meaning "foreigner". In Norse mythology, Váli is the son of Odin and Rindr, born to avenge Baldr's death. Icelandic historian and author Snorri Sturluson (1179-1241) calls Váli a son of Loki in chapter 50 of the Prose Edda, though it is argued that Sturluson misinterpreted one of his sources and accidentally invented a second Váli.
Derived from Arabic وَلِيّ‏ (waliyy) meaning "helper, protector, benefactor".

In Bulgaria and Russia, this name is a variant transcription of the unisex name Valya.In Georgia, this name is a diminutive of Valentina and Valerian, though there can certainly be cases where it is the georgianized form of the aforementioned Valya. In this day and age, Valia is primarily used on women in Georgia.In Greece, this name is strictly feminine and is a pet form of Vasilia and Vasiliki.Known bearers of this name include the Georgian revolutionary Valerian "Valia" Bakhtadze (1896-1930) and the Greek model Valia Kakouti (b. 1981).
From Arabic وَلِيّ (waliyy) meaning “neighbor, friend” and the name Abdullah.
Means "heir to the throne" in Uzbek.
Derived from the names Vali and Akbar.
Main character in Jennifer Bell's book series "The Uncommoners".

From the English word valiant, which denotes a person who has and shows courage. The word is derived from Anglo-French vaillant "brave, strong, worthy", which itself is ultimately derived from Latin valens meaning "strong, vigorous, powerful". In literature, this is the name of the main character in the comic strip "Prince Valiant in the Days of King Arthur", created by Hal Foster (1892-1982). It was later adapted into an animated television series called "The Legend of Prince Valiant", which ran from 1991 to 1993. The comic and the animated series have inspired people in some countries to name their son Valiant. The Netherlands is one of those countries, as in 2010, there was a total of 26 bearers (of all ages) in the entire country. Also, in popular culture, Valiant is the name of a wood pigeon in the 2005 computer-animated film of the same name.

Presumably from the Spanish word valiente meaning "brave, valiant", ultimately from Latin valere "to be strong" (compare Valerius; or perhaps from the Spanish surname Valiente which was originally a nickname based on the Spanish word). It is uncertain whether or not this is used as a given name in Spain itself, although it seems to have been used in Mexico at least once (if so, its usage may be influenced by the name Valencia).
From the name of a traditional Malagasy bamboo lute.
Diminutive of Valéria, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Derived from the names Vali and Karam.
Diminutive of Valeri, Valerian and their short form Valo.
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word murod meaning "aim, wish, desire".
Meaning and origin unknown.May be based off of the Sanskrit name Valin meaning "tailed."
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word nafas meaning "breath".
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word nazar meaning "look, glance".
Possibly a combination of Val and the name suffix inda (also compare Valena 1).
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word niyoz meaning "entreaty, alms".
Picard and Walloon form of Valentin.
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word nur meaning "ray, beam, light".
From Finnish valio meaning "an outstanding individual, a pick, choice, elite".
Derived from the given names Vali and Rahim.
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word rasul meaning "prophet".
Combination of Vali meaning "friend / close ally to God" and the suffix -ş.
Possibly a combination of the phonetic prefix va (from a name such as Valerie, Vanessa or Valinda) and Lisa.Also compare Jaleesa/Jalisa, Malisa, Talisa, Alisa.
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word sher meaning "lion".
Means "reward", or from the Malagasy name for the Scaevola plumieri shrub.
Derived from Uzbek valiy meaning "saint" or "messenger".
Derived from the given name Vali and the Uzbek word yor meaning "friend".
Derived from Albanian valë "wave" and jetë "life".

Of uncertain origin and meaning. Some modern-day academics suggest a derivation from Latvian valks "brook, brooklet", while others see a connection to the Latvian placename Valka, and a third group theorizes a connection to Finnish and Estonian valkoinen "white". It might also be a Baltic adoption of Low German Walke.
From Old Norse valkyrja meaning "chooser of the slain" (see Valkyrie).
Means "guide, mentor", "ruler, leader", or "generous" in Uzbek.

Means "valley" in Spanish, taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de la Valle and Nuestra Señora de la Valle, meaning "The Virgin of the Valley" and "Our Lady of the Valley" respectively.She is the patroness of a number of municipalities in Spain as well as in Venezuela and Argentina.
Medieval German and archaic French form of Valentine 1.
Variant of Valerie. It appears in the 1968 song Valleri by the Monkees.
Valletta, the name of a city in Malta, it is a transferred use of the surname of Jean Parisot de la Vallette, Grand Master of the Order of Malta.
Transferred use of the surname Valley, as well as a diminutive of Valerie, or Valentine 1. Could also come from the English word.
Both a transferred use of the surname Vallie and a diminutive of Valerie and Valentina.

From the Valencian title of the Virgin Mary, Mare de Déu de Vallivana, meaning "Mother of God of Vallivana."She is venerated at the sanctuary in the city of Morella in the Valencian province of Castelló.
From Northern Sámi vallji meaning "plentiful, abundance".
Means "poppy" in Swedish, thus making it a Swedish cognate of Poppy.
Originally a diminutive of Voldemar and Valentin, now used as a given name in its own right.
Spanish form of Violet reflecting the English pronunciation.
In Roman mythology, Vallonia was the goddess of valleys (cf. Latin vallis "valley").
Alternate transcription of Thai วัลลภ (see Wanlop).
Variation of Valerie, most popular in the mid 20th century.
Variant of Valerie, the spelling is influenced by that of Mallory.
Pet form of names beginning with Val-, Wal-.
19th-century coinage derived from Finnish valmu meaning "poppy".
Variant of Valmai influenced by Marie as well as a combination of Valerie and Marie.
Possibly a borrowing of Finnish Valma.
From Sanskrit वल्मीक (valmīka) meaning "anthill". This is the name of a legendary poet believed to have authored the Hindu epic the Ramayana.

This name came into usage after the Battle of Valmy, which was the first major victory by the army of France during the Revolutionary Wars that followed the French Revolution. The battle took place on 20 September 1792 as Prussian troops commanded by the Duke of Brunswick attempted to march on Paris. The victory emboldened the newly assembled National Convention to formally declare the end of monarchy in France and to establish the French Republic. Valmy permitted the development of the Revolution and all its resultant ripple effects, and for that it is regarded by historians as one of the most significant battles in history. The name is borne by Belgian politician Valmy Féaux (* 1933).
Swedish and Norwegian form of Valný.
From Old Norse valr "those slain in battle" combined with nýr "new".
Georgian form of Valodya, which is the Armenian form of Volodya.

Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a derivation from Valona, the former name of the city of Vlorë (compare Vlora), a derivation from Albanian valë "wave" and a derivation from Albanian valon "to seethe; to simmer; to boil".
Possibly from Valônia, the Portuguese name for the Belgian region of Wallonia.
From the English word valor meaning "bravery, courage". From the Latin valor "value".
Possibly an elaboration of Valora influenced by Valeria.

Valour is a variant spelling of the virtue name Valor, both derived from the Latin valorem, meaning “strength, worth, courage.” In English, “valour” (with a u) is the traditional British spelling, while “valor” is used in American English. Both forms denote great bravery in the face of danger, especially in battle.As a given name, Valor has grown in popularity in the United States as part of the broader trend of virtue and word names. Valour, while less common, appears as an alternative spelling among speakers of British, Canadian, South African, and Australian English, where the -our ending is standard.
Italian and Czech form of Walburga.

Derived from Old Norse valr meaning "the dead on a battlefield, the battle-slain" (as found in the word valkyrja) and rún meaning "secret lore, rune". Alternatively the first element may be derived from Primitive Germanic *walha- meaning "Celtic, Welsh, foreign".
Perhaps derived from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (balsamon) meaning "balsam tree" (of Semitic origin).
Created from Serval by inverting the order of syllables.It is the stage name of the Kamerunian rapper and political activist Gaston Serval Abe.
Possibly from the English word vault. Valt Aoi is the protagonist of the television series 'Beyblade Burst Evolution'.
Pre-Christian Finnish name deriving from the word "valta" meaning power or might.
Bulgarian and variant Russian and Ukrainian forms of Balthazar.
Valtazar is a Serbian form of Balthazar.A famous bearer of the name is the jurist and pioneer of sociology Valtazar Bogišić.
Silesian German contracted form of Valentin.
Swedish and Danish variant of Walter.
From Old Norse valr "those slain in battle" (also found in the place name Valhalla and the word valkyrja) combined with the name of the Norse god Þórr (see Thor).
Short form of Valters, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Diminutive of Valtteri or other names with the element valt.
A diminutive of Valentin and names ending with -vald such as Evald and Osvald. Valtti is also a Finnish word, meaning "trump" (both figuratively and in card games).
Finnish pet form of names containing the name element vald "ruler, mighty one, powerful one".
Combination of Old Norse valr "the slain (in Valhalla)" and tívar "gods" (see Tyr).
Old Slovene name, possibly meaning "wolf" from slovene "volk" or perhaps older "vәlәkә". Was worn by the first ruler of Carantania.
Icelandic younger form of Valr. Valur is also a modern Icelandic word for gyrfalcon.

From Latin Vallis Venaria meaning "valley of water veins". This is the name of a title of the Virgin Mary, Nuestra Señora de Valvanera, venerated in the monastery of Valvanera as the patron saint of La Rioja, Spain.

From the Spanish titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de Valvanuz and Nuestra Señora de Valvanuz, meaning "The Virgin of Valvanuz" and "Our Lady of Valvanuz," venerated at the sanctuary in Selaya in Cantabria, northern Spain. For this reason, usage of this name is particularly concentrated in that autonomous community.
Derived from Estonian valve "to guard; watch over".

A variant form of Gawaine. The eldest son of King Lot of Orkney and Queen Morgawse (or Anna), Arthur’s sister or half-sister. Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.
Most likely a variant of Valvo.
Modern Greek spelling of Balbinos, which is the ancient Greek form of Balbinus.
Russian diminutive or pet form of Valentina.
Means "rely on, trust" in Hmong Daw.

Means "dwarfish, small, short-statured" in Sanskrit. This is the name of one of the avatars of the Hindu god Vishnu, who appears as a dwarf man to recover the three worlds (earth, heaven and the netherworld) from the demon king Bali.
From a character in a novel with the same name by Estonian writer Andres Saal (1861-1931). Possibly derived from the name of Varbola castle or from the old Estonian word vambas, which means "mace".
In the case of the daughter of Indian actress Anushka Sharma, it is likely derived from the name of her father Virat and her mother Anushka, or from a name for the goddess Durga.

This name (not to be confused with Bamini, Padmini, Yamini, Jamini, or Kamini) was a very much in use in India before 1700’s. It was a name only taken by female babies in royal families or women of highest status and caste.The name was known to be another name of Goddess Parvathy in the earlier time. The women with the name were believed to have a avatar of Goddess Parvathy reside in them. Hence why only royal families, families of highest caste status name their daughters this name because it they were believed to be divine beings or demi-gods, that live in human bodies.The name Vamini was used in almost every Indian Language, but since of its exclusivity in only royal families, high caste use in a country very caste oriented the name became only used by less women. But as Divine as the name is, it is also known to be careful in naming the daughters Vamini because it is still believed in many parts in India that women with that name are another avatar of Goddess Parvathy.Why many fear the name Vamini?There were many royal women in many parts of India with that name but we have a story in Kerala that has been passed down many centuries. In the years 1529-1550’s there was a Princess of the Chandradevan Thampuran Royal Family. She was beautiful, smart, kind, caring, with sharp eyes always wearing beautiful kajal. She was also very brave she learned all war strategy and fighting strategy. No commoner could see her, she comes to Amme Bhagavathy temple and everyone saw her as Goddess Durga herself.Thampuran had 3 wives and (വാമിനിദേവി) was the daughter of first Sree Akhilandeshwari Thampurati. In the stories it’s told as the other 2 wives also had daughters and nobody respected them like the did for Vamini Devi. On one of the Full Moon rituals there is a tradition for people to do Firewalking on fire pits. The other wives of Thampuran had planned and on a (പൂർണ ചന്ദ്രൻ) Special full moon as usual when Vamini Devi is going to do the Firepit walking ceremony, they paid some men who work in the forest to use bamboo blowpipe with snake venom on the darts, on Vamini Devi when she is going to walk on the pit. They had used oil on the bottom of the Mundu of Vamini Devi was going to wear.They said on that day, it was raining. The moon was covered as a sign of inauspicious, but for the welfare of the family, and village Vamini Devi prayed Goddess Parvathy and was getting ready for the firepit ceremony. Since it was raining a little that day they added so much coal for burning, so the fire doesn’t stop with the rain. As Vaminidevi stepped in the firepit after her third step her clothes quickly caught on fire. As the fire started the men with the poisonous blowpipe blew the Venom dart on her throat and the poison spread fast. Which is why she couldn’t get out of the fire. She was paralyzed and fell into the fire screaming burning alive.Many say her scream can still be heard in the older villages around Kodungallur. The curse of death wiped out the entire empire and not one person in the whole family died naturally. All were horrific deaths. The names of the entire Chandradevan Thampuran clan were completely wiped out from history. They only live through passed down stories. Many have claimed to have seen a beautiful women wearing lots of gold and wearing very luxurious mundum neriyatum smile, and walk around the forests. Some worship her as even a goddess, and pray to her to bring rain to their soil. Because they think she is angry that’s why it doesn’t rain.
Combination of Old Norse vá "accident, damage" and móðr "wrath". The name can be found on the Rök runestone in Sweden. According to the runes, Vámóðr was the son of Varinn.
From Sanskrit वंशी (vaṃśī) meaning "flute", referring to the divine flute played by Lord Krishna in Hinduism, often made of bamboo but sometimes jewels.
From Sino-Vietnamese 萬 (vạn) meaning "ten thousand, myriad".
From Sino-Vietnamese 問 (vấn) meaning "to ask, inquire".
From Sino-Vietnamese 運 (vận) meaning "luck, fortune, ship, transport".
Means "heaven, sky, firmament" or "fortune, luck, fate, destiny" in Hakha Chin.

Possibly derived from Vanaheimr, home of the Vanir (a type of Old Norse gods). Vana was the wife of Sveigðir and mother of Vanlandi. She appears in the epic works 'Heimskringla' and 'Ynglinga saga' written in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson.
Possibly a combination of the phonetic elements va and nay.
Means "forest-born" from Sanskrit वन (vana) meaning "forest" and ज (ja) meaning "born".

From Sanskrit वनमालिन् (vanamālin) meaning "adorned with a garland of forest flowers", derived from वन (vana) meaning "forest, wood" and मालिन् (mālin) meaning "garlanded, crowned, encircled by". This is an epithet of the Hindu god Krishna.
An invented name, possibly based on the sounds found in names such as Vanessa, Venetia, Janasia and Danasia. This name is borne by Vanasia Bradley, an American artistic gymnast.
Transferred use of the surname Vanburen. See also Van Buren.
Alternate transcription of Thai วันชัย (see Wanchai).
Latinized form of Vandalar. Vandalarius was the name of the father of Valamir, a 5th-century king of the Ostrogoths.
A Saxon warrior slain by Gawain in a skirmish at Roestoc.
From Sanskrit वन्दना (vandanā) meaning "praise, commendation, reverence, worship".

Derived from the Lithuanian noun vandenė meaning "mermaid", which is derived from the Lithuanian adjective vandens meaning "aqueous, aquatic", itself ultimately derived from the Lithuanian noun vanduo meaning "water". Also compare Undinė, which is etymologically related.
Probably a contraction of the two words van der "from the" occurring as part of Dutch surnames like Van Der Waal promoted to a given name.
Transferred use of the surname Vanderbilt. Used in honor of the American business family, the Vanderbilts.

From a Brazilian surname, itself derived from the Dutch surname Van Der Leij. One bearer of this name is Brazilian professional footballer or soccer player Vanderley Dias Marinho (1987-), also known as Derley.This name and its variants Wanderley, Wanderlei and Vanderlei are not uncommon in Brazil. Other bearers of the name include former mixed martial artist Wanderlei Silva (1976-) and former soccer players Wanderley Paiva (1946-) and Vanderlei Luxemburgo (1952-).
Masculine form of Vanda. Also compare Wando.
From Lao ວັນ (van) meaning "day" and ດີ (dy) meaning "good, fine, nice".
Meaning uncertain. A famous bearer is Vaneeza Ahmad (1971-), a Pakistani model and actress.

Coined in the Disney animated film 'Wreck-It Ralph' (2013), telling the story of the eponymous arcade game villain who rebels against his role and dreams of becoming a hero. He travels between games in the arcade and eventually meets Vanellope von Schweetz (the second protagonist), a glitchy character from the in-universe video game 'Sugar Rush', a candy themed kart-racing game. Her name is a combination of Vanilla and Penelope.
Nickname for "Vanessa" Not commonly used. The name 'Vanessa' was invented by the Anglo-Irish Jonathan Swift in 1708.
Possibly a variant of Vanessa influenced by Valeska.
My name also resembles butterfly in Greek and star in the book of Hebrew
Derived from the Spanish name Juanita or from the Italian name Giovannetta.
Diminutive of Evangeliya and Vangeliya. Vangeliya Pandeva Gushterova (1911 – 1996), commonly known as Baba Vanga, was a Bulgarian attributed mystic and healer who claimed to have foreseen the future.
Variant of Hoàng Oanh, from a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 黃鶯 (vàng anh).
Diminutive of Evangelina or Evangeline. A famous bearer was Brazilian singer Vange Leonel (May 4th 1963 - July 14th, 2014), her real first name was Maria Evangelina.
Short form of Evangeliya. Vangeliya Pandeva Gushterova (1911 – 1996), commonly known as Baba Vanga, was a Bulgarian attributed mystic and healer who claimed to have foreseen the future.
Combination of Swedish vän "fair, beautiful" and the Old Norse name element hildr "battle, fight".
Means "white-eye (bird)", from Vietnamese vành meaning "outer ring" and Sino-Vietnamese 圈 (khuyên) meaning "ring", referring to the white ring of feathers around the birds' eyes.
Means "voice, speech, language" in Sanskrit. This is an epithet of the Hindu goddess Saraswati.
Italian and Romanian form of Vanya as well as Italian variant of Vanna 1 and Bulgarian diminutive of Ivana.
One of many sons of Bani named in Ezra 10:36.
Russian diminutive of Ivan. It has also seen some use in Armenia and Georgia, due to historical Russian influence in these countries.
Alternate transcription of Thai วนิดา (see Wanida).
Combination of ва (va) and нихер (niher) meaning "lover, beautiful".
MEANING : little wood, groveUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Diminutive of Ivane via its short form Vano.
Perhaps from Greek βανίλια (vanilia) meaning "vanilla" or Italian vaniglia meaning "vanilla".
From the Finnish word vanilja, meaning "vanilla".

From the English word vanilla referring to "the fruit or bean of the vanilla plant, or the extract made from it, or the distinctive fragrant flavour/flavor characteristic of vanilla extract". The word is derived from Spanish vainilla, literally "little pod", a diminutive form of vaina "pod, scabbard, sheath", from Latin vagina "sheath (of an ear of grain), husk, hull of a plant".
Means "vanilla" in French. A famous bearer is the character Vanille in the Final Fantasy video games.
Possibly a truncated form of Ivanilson or Evanilson.
Means "expanse of sky, firmament" in Samoan.

Corsican short form of Ghjuvannina. The name was borne by 16th-century Corsican noblewoman Giovannina "Vannina" d'Ornano (also known as "Vanina").This was used by the French writer Stendhal in his novella Vanina Vanini (1829), where it belongs to a Roman princess. It is borne by Italian fashion photographer Vanina Sorrenti (1973-). The name received a boost in popularity in France due to the song Vanina (1974) by Dutch Francophone singer Dave.

Meaning as of yet unknown. It might perhaps be related to the Russian name Vanya, which is typically rendered Vania in Georgian.A notable bearer of this name was the Georgian author and playwright Vanion Daraseli (1909-1954).
Means "queen of the universe" or "pure" in Hindi and Nepali.
From the English word vanity. This name surged in 1983 coinciding with the revival of the magazine 'Vanity Fair'.
Means "Vanilla" in Creole, His name has given many first names like Aniy.
Variant of Vangie, which is a diminutive of Evangeline. Miss Vanjie is the stage name of José Cancel, an American drag performer known for competing on the reality show RuPaul's Drag Race.
Diminutive of Ivana (Bulgarian, Macedonian) or Ivan (Russian).
Means "gift from the God who created us" in Mizo.

Means "man from Vanaheimr" in Old Norse. Vanaheimr was the home of the Vanir, a group of gods. Njǫrðr, Freyr and Freyja were members of the Vanir.Vanlandi was a legendary Swedish king, son of Sveigðir and father of Visbur. He appears in the epic works 'Heimskringla' and 'Ynglinga saga' written in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson. Vanlandi also appears in the 9th century poem 'Ynglingatal', possibly written by the Norwegian skald Þjóðólfr ór Hvini.
Alternate transcription of Thai วัลลภ (see Wanlop).
Transferred use of the surname Vanlow.
Variant of Van, or transferred from the English surname Vann.
Either a variant of Vanna 1 or a short form of Savannah
Transferred use of the surname Van Nevar.
Means "fairy", from Sino-Vietnamese 雲 (vân) meaning "cloud" and 娥 (nga) meaning "beautiful woman".
Probably either a feminine form of Van or a diminutive of Savannah, Evangeline, and other names containing van.
Adaption of the Dutch surname van Niel.
Derived from the Manx name for the Isle of Man, Ellan Vannin.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Giovanna. The most notable bearer of this name was Vannozza dei Cattanei, the mistress of Pope Alexander VI and the mother of Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia.
Diminutive of Giovanni via the form Giovannozzo.

Medieval Italian diminutive of Vanni, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.In addition to that, this name was also often used as a short form of Giovannuccio.A known bearer of this name was the Italian journalist and politician Vannuccio Faralli (1891-1969).
Probably a Romani and Ossetian form of Ivan.Vano Bamberger is a German gypsy guitarist.

Variant of Wannour or Wannore, an old Scottish form of Guenore (see Guinevere). Vanora’s Grave in Meigle, Scotland is a grass-covered mound in front of which two Pictish carved stones of Christian date are known to have once stood, though as a given name Vanora isn't found before the 19th century.
From Sino-Vietnamese 萬國 (vạn quốc) meaning "international", composed of 萬 (vạn) meaning "ten thousand, myriad" and 國 (quốc) meaning "nation, country".
MEANING - lineage, race, dynasty. It was the name of an Apsara.

column3: វណ្ណសូដានី(Khmer)

column12: From Sino-Vietnamese 萬事 (vạn sự) meaning "everything", as in the phrase 萬事如意 (vạn sự như ý) meaning "may you have everything you wish".
Possibly an invented name combining the element van with the name T'angelo.
Etymology uncertain, perhaps from the Lao ວັນທາ (wán tʰá́) meaning "bow, salute".
Means "Mexican marigold (Tagetes erecta)", from Sino-Vietnamese 萬 (vạn) meaning "ten thousand, myriad" and 壽 (thọ) meaning "long life, longevity, lifespan".
Transferred use of surname Vancetti in honour of Bartolomeo Vancetti.
Combination of Вань (Van'), possibly from the Russian nickname for Ivan, Vanya, and the suffix -тюк (tyuk).
Meaning uncertain, it could be derived from the Latin word vannus, which refers to a winnowing basket. Alternatively it may be a diminutive of Vânia.
From Lao ວັນ (van) meaning "day" and ໄຊ (xay) meaning "victory".
Combination of Ванюр (Vanyur) which is from the Russian name Vanya (Ivan) and the suffix -ка (ka).
Old Norse byname, from Old Norse vápn meaning "weapon".

Probably derived from the Germanic element wēraz "true, reliable, friendly. This was the name of a Norse goddess associated with oaths and contracts, including those of marriage. The name coincides with the Old Norse word vár meaning "spring".
Means "granting wishes," "bestower of boons" (blessings), or a "benefactor" in Hindi and Sanskrit.
Name of an Indian river situated in Karnataka, a state in the south western region of India. It is with believed that this river has religious ties with gods Durga and Lakshmi.
Means "twenty-ninth day of the month" in Armenian.

Feminine form of Varaha. This is the name of the shakti (female counterpart) of the Hindu god Vishnu and the sixth of the eight Matrikas (mother goddesses). She is usually depicted as a woman with the head of a boar.
Varaidzo means "One who keeps company". This is given to acknowledge your child as one with whom you keep company. It is common to give this name to a child born in your later years.
Derived from Arabic وَرَق (waraq) meaning "foliage, leaves".
From Sanskrit वर (vara) meaning "blessing, boon" combined with the name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi. This is the name of a manifestation of Lakshmi who bestows boons.
Variant of Gvaram. A known bearer of this name was the influential Georgian feudal lord Varam Gageli (died in 1249 or 1251 AD).
Alternate transcription of Thai วราภรณ์ (see Waraphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai วราภรณ์ (see Waraphon).
Derived from Old Armenian վարազ (varaz) meaning "wild boar", which itself is ultimately derived from Middle Persian varāz or warāz "boar".

Derived from Middle Persian warāz meaning "boar" combined with Middle Persian dādan "to give". For the latter element, also compare Old Persian dāta, which can mean "law" but also "gift" as well as "gave, given" (as past tenses of the verb dadātuv "to give, to put"). As such, the name roughly means "to give boars" or "giver of boars". This name was borne by a 4th-century Roman client king of Arsacid Armenia.
A character in JRR Tolkien's works, a quasi-divine figure who created the stars. The name is derived from an honorific title in the fictional Quenya language, and means "sublime, exalted, lofty".
Means "jewel of Varda". In Tolkien's Legendarium this is the name of the second King of Númenor. He was the son of Elros, nephew of Elrond, and grandson of Eärendil.
From Armenian վարդ (vard) meaning "rose" and անոյշ (anush) meaning "sweet".

From the name of the river Vardar, itself from Thracian Vardários, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European (PIE) *(s)wordo-wori- meaning "black water". Folk etymology, however, links the name to вардя (vardya) meaning "to shield, protect".
Historically common name for first born Melungeon males.

Probably the Georgian form of the Armenian name Vardan. Vardan is also in use in Georgia, but Varden is more common. A known bearer of this name was Varden Tsulukidze (1865–1923), a Georgian military commander.
Means "prosperous, thriving, growing, increasing" in Sanskrit. This was the birth name of Mahavira, the 24th and final tirthankara in Jain tradition.
Pet form of Varden (masculine) and Vardo (feminine).

A character mentioned in the works of JRR Tolkien. The name is derived from the fictional Quenya language. Although it is of uncertain etymology, it is possibly a contraction of Vardandilme, a compound of the name Varda and a feminine form of the name element ndil meaning "friend of, lover, devoted to".
Combination of the Old Norse name elements vár "spring (the season); woman (in a poetic context); truth" and dís "goddess; woman, lady; sister" or dis "wise woman, seeress; woman, virgin".
Diminutive of Varda, Vardina, or Vardiya.
Alternate transcription of Thai วารี (see Wari).
Possibly derived from Latvian varens "mighty, powerful, forceful, strong; famous, great".
Affectionate-diminutive form of Varvara. It is the name a heroine in Fyodor Dostoevsky's 'Poor Folk' and a minor character in Leo Tolstoy's 'Anna Karenina'.
It’s a name contained with all india gods

Comes from the name of the Zulu mythological goddess Mbaba Mwana Waresa, also known as Nomkhubulwane. Nomkhubulwane is the Zulu goddess of rainbows, rain, agriculture, and beer. The name could also be a variant of Vanesa.
Combination of the Old Norse name elements vár "spring (the season); woman (in a poetic context); truth" and auðr "prosperity, fortune, riches; fate, destiny".
Derived from Old Norse elements vǫr "vigilant, cautious" and feitr "fat" from Fæitr.

Relatively modern name (early 20th century), perhaps created by combining the Swedish words vår "spring" (the season) and frid "peace, peacefulness". Alternatively, created by combining the Old Norse elements vǫr "vigilant, cautious" (from names like Eivor, Hervor and Gunvor) and fríðr "beautiful, beloved" (from names like Frida 2 and Majfrid).
A heathen duke who, under King Oriel, fought Kings Urien and Angusel at the battle of Coranges.
Made up of vár "spring" and hild "battle".

Either from Sanskrit वारिद (vārid) meaning "incidence, occurence," a combination of Sanskrit वारि (vāri) meaning "water" and Sanskrit दा (dā) meaning "giving", or the Indian vernacular name for the plant Pavonia odorata.
Variens of Sasiaborg is one of Arthur’s kings in the Norse Erex Saga. He was present at the wedding of Erec and Enide.

Primordial mother goddess in Cook Islands mythology. Her name has been attested as meaning "goddess of the beginning" or "the mud at the bottom". It may be derived from vari meaning "mud" and takere meaning "bottom of a canoe".
Elaboration of Vör, perhaps influenced by Karin. It is also associated with the Norwegian word vår meaning "spring (the season)".
Possibly a variant of Varinia. This name was most notably borne by Varina Davis (1826-1906), the second wife of Jefferson Davis and the First Lady of the Confederate States of America.
From Sanskrit वर (vára) "environing, enclosing, space" or "boon, gift, reward, benefit" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra.
Formed from Varinder and Sanskrit जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Bulgarian and Russian form of Varinius.

From the name of a Germanic tribe, the Varini, whose name means either "defenders" or "living by the river". The name could also be derived from the Swedish historical land Värend. Varinn was the runemaster of the 9th-century Rök runestone, the first known piece of Swedish literature. According to the stone, Varinn carved the runes in memory of his fallen son Vámóðr.
Italian and Spanish form of Varius.
Derived from Latvian varēt "to be able to". This name was used by Latvian playwright Anna Brigadere in her play Maija un Paija.
MEANING - year, rain. It has different meaning from VaarishUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Means "rainy season, the rains", from Sanskrit वर्ष (varṣa) meaning "rain".
MEANING : ( excellent, widest, largest, chief, most preferable )Usage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist Hindi : वरिष्ठा
Asturian truncated form of Evaristo and Venetian regular form of this name.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Vara.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Varius.
Estonian variant of Varje and Slovene short form of Barbara via Varvara.
Name of the main protagonist in SF Said's novel, Varjak Paw.
Folk form of Varvara. Spelt as Варька it is also diminutive of Varvara in Russian.
Short form of Varghese (itself from Geevarghese), used as an independent name.
Form of Varlam with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Means "great army of Lenin", from великая армия Ленина (velikaya armiya Lenina). This name was used by communists in the Soviet Union who wanted to use non-traditional names for their children.
Swedish feminine form of Verner. It may also be derived from Swedish värna "to protect, to defend".
Swedish variant of Verner. It may also be associated with Swedish värn "defense". It's a relatively modern name, first used in 1913.
Swedish variant of Verner. It may also be associated with Swedish värn "defense".
Transferred use of the surname Varney. It is mainly used in Liberia.
Combination of Swedish vår "spring" (from Old Norse vár) and the common name element ny "new" (from Old Norse nýr; compare names like Majny, Helny, etc.).
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Varus.
Alternate transcription of Armenian Վարուժան (see Varuzhan).
Chuvash feminine name derived from varlă meaning "kind, friendly" and pikke meaning "lady".
Finnish dialectal variant form (East Finland) of Valborg.
The name conferred upon an early martyr of the Baha'i religion (Mirza 'Ali-Muhammad Varqa) by the founder of that religion, Baha'u'llah. Means "dove" in Persian.

In the Dragon Age video game series, Varric Tethras is a "surfacer" dwarf (who traditionally live underground), merchant, and best-selling novelist. His most notable traits are his loyalty, sense of humor, gravelly voice, chest hair, and a one-of-a-kind semi-automatic crossbow named Bianca. As of his latest appearance in the series, he has ascended to Viscount of his beloved home city-state of Kirkwall.He first appears as the narrator of Dragon Age II, recounting his adventures with the main character, Hawke. He appears again as a supporting character in the sequel, Dragon Age: Inquisition.

Roman cognomen of which the etymology is obscure, though there is a possibility that it might be of Etruscan origin. Known bearers of this name are Roman consul Gaius Terentius Varro (3rd century BC), Roman scholar Marcus Terentius Varro (1st century BC) and Roman poet Varro Atacinus (1st century BC).
German and Russian form of Varronianus.
Italian and Spanish form of Varronianus.
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Roman nomen gentile Varronius. A bearer of this name was the son of Roman Emperor Jovian (4th century AD).
Feminine diminutive of Varronius. This was the name of a Vestal Virgin.
Roman nomen gentile which was derived from Varro.
MEANING : to rain, to be powerful, to effuseUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Endearing form of Varsha using the element ka (see also Nitika, Radhika, Devika).
Name : Varshita वर्षिताMEANING : to rain, state of raining, , to cause to rain, be powerful
MEANING : to rain, be powerfulUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Means "of a star" in Georgian. It is derived from Georgian ვარსკვლავის (varskvlavis), which is the genitive of the Georgian noun ვარსკვლავი (varskvlavi) meaning "star".
Russian and Ukrainian form of Barsanuphius.
Means "rose, flower" in Armenian, ultimately from Persian.
From Armenian վարդենի (vardeni) meaning "rosebush, rose shrub".
Etymology uncertain, with the first element from the Armenian վարդ (vart) meaning "rose".
Alternate transcription of Greek Βαρθολομαίος (see Vartholomeos).
Modern Greek form of Bartholomaios (see Bartholomew).
Combination of Chuvash варлă (varlă) meaning "kind, friendly" and тилет (tilet) with an unknown meaning.
Combination of Варт (Vart), which is of Arabic origin meaning "roses" and the suffix -ук (uk) also meaning "rose".
A Syrian knight present at the tournament of Sorgarda, which Gawain won.
Alternate transcription of Malayalam വർഗീസ് or വർഗ്ഗീസ് (see Varghese).
Alternate transcription of Armenian Վարուժան (see Varuzhan).
Russian and Ukrainian form of Baruch.
Means "liquor, wine" in Sanskrit. This is the name of a Hindu goddess of wine and the consort of Varuna.
Alternate transcription of Thai วรัญญา (see Waranya).
This name is a Roman family name meaning "bow-legged, knock-kneed, bent, crooked."One bearer of this family name was Roman general and politician Publius Quinctilius Varus (46 BC-9 AD).
Skolt Sami female name, a cognate of Barbara, perhaps taken from the Russian Varvara.

Varys is the name of an eunuch character from the Song of Ice and Fire books by GRR Martin and the TV show Game of Thrones based upon the former. Being a recent invention for a fictious world resembling Medieval Europe, no actual or alleged etymology is known, but it may be intended to resemble Roman Varius or Varus.

From the Ancient Greek adjective βαρύτιμος (barytimos) meaning "very costly, of great value", a word used in the New Testament (itself composed of βαρύς (barys) "heavy, deep" and τιμή (time) "value, esteem").
Dialectal speech variant of Vasya and Komi form of Vasiliy.
Alternate transcription of Thai วสันต์ (see Wasan).
Alternate transcription of Thai วาสนา (see Watsana).
Means "spring jasmine" in Sanskrit (species Jasminum sambac), from a combination of Vasanta and Mallika.
Derived from the Lithuanian noun vasara meaning "summer".
Variant form of Vasara as well as the feminine form of Vasaris.
Derived from the Lithuanian noun vasaris meaning "February" (as in, the month). There are also several cases where this name is the masculine form of Vasara.
Variant Anglicized form of Waseem or Wasim commonly used by Pakistanis.
Derived from Uzbek vasf meaning "praise" and jahon meaning "the world".
Derived from Uzbek vasf meaning "praise" and jamol meaning "beauty".
Either a diminutive of Vasily, Varvara, Valeriy, Valeriya or Ivan.
Combination of the prefix va- with Shawn.
Khanty and Mansi variant and diminutive of Vashchkigi.
Khanty and Mansi variant of Vasiliy.

Variant of Vashisht, which is a varaint of Vashistha. In Hinduism, Vashistha is one of the Saptarishis (seven great Rishis) in the seventh, i.e. the present Manvantara, or age of Manu. Vashista is a manasputra (mind-son) of Brahma.

Meaning, "and second" given to a second born.Read in 1 Chronicles 6:28 the King James Version (Hebrew 13) as the name of the firstborn son of Samuel. According to 1 Chronicles 6:33 (Hebrew 18) and 1 Samuel 8:2, Samuel's oldest son was Joel, and the second Abijah. The explanation of this is that in 1 Chronicles 6:28 the word taken then as a proper name is really "and second"; so following Septuagint, Lucian, and Syriac we read (as the Revised Version (British and American)), "And the sons of Samuel: the first-born, Joel, and the second Abijah."A noted bearer is Vashni (Vash) Young, an American author of motivational and self-improvement books with a popular following during the Great Depression.

Diminutive of Vasil and perhaps in some cases also of Gervasi.
Derived from Arabic وَسِيلَة (wasīla) meaning "means, medium, method".
Romanian form of Vasilakis. This name has fallen out of use and now only survives as a patronymic surname.

Modern Greek diminutive of Vasilios and Vasilis, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.
Form of Vasil with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Alternate transcription of Greek Βασιλεία (see Vasileia). Also compare the masculine equivalent Vasilios.
Albanian feminine form of Vasil and Greek variant of Vasiliki.

Russian form of Basiliscus. This is also the Russian word for "basilisk" (a type of mythological creature). This was borne by Russian avant-garde poet Vasilisk Gnedov (1890-1978), real name Vasiliy Ivanovich Gnedov.
Modern Greek form of Basiliskos, used to refer to the 4th-century Greek saint Basiliscus of Comana.
Diminutive of Vasiliki, as -ίτσα (-itsa) is a Greek feminine diminutive suffix.

Albanian form of Vasilakis. Unlike the original Greek name, the Albanian form is used as an official name on birth certificates.A notable bearer of this name was the Albanian actor Vasillaq Vangjeli (1948-2011).
Feminine form and male variant of Vaskrsije.
A literal translation of the Greek name Anastasios, meaning "resurrection". A suitable name for an Easter child.
Variant of Václav. Vaslav Nijinsky (1890 - 1950) was a Polish-born ballet dancer and choreographer cited as the greatest male dancer of the early 20th century.
Diminutive of Vasiliki (formed of Vaso 2 and the Greek feminine diminutive suffix -ούλα (-oula)).
Son of the famous knight named Guiron the Courteous. Vaspariano guarded the castle of Crudele, at which he was slain in combat by Sir Lamorat, who had to assume his post.
Derived from Arabic وَصْفِيّ (waṣfiyy) meaning "attributive, descriptive" or perhaps "praising".
Variant of Vasya.Vassa Zheleznova is the protagonist of a play by Maxim Gorky.
The name for "Greasy Mouth" an eccentric and erratic culture hero and might be derived from the Algonquin Wesucechak.

Meaning unknown. This is the name of a demon who appears in several works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown) and the Liber Officiorum Spirituum (author and date of publication unknown).
Alternate transcription of Thai วาสนา (see Watsana).

Transferred use of the surname Vassar. Notable namesakes are Vassar Carlton Clements (1928 - 2005) American folk musician known as the Father of Hillbilly Jazz and female poet Vassar Miller (1924 - 1998).
Transferred use of the surname Vassie.
Estonian and French transcription of Russian Василий (see Vasiliy).
Estonian and Italian transcription of Russian Василиса (see Vasilisa).
Short form of Old Swedish names ending in -vast (see Fasti).

Vastolla was the princess and principal love interest of "Peruonto' an Italian literary fairy tale written by Giambattista Basile in his 1634 work, the Pentamerone.
Malagasy form and Romani variant of Vashti.
Malayalam and Tamil form of Vasudeva.

Derivative of Sanskrit वसुक (vasuka) meaning "jewel on the head" — a name of Kashyapa — derived from वसु (vasu) meaning "jewel, gem" combined with क (ka) meaning "head". In Hindu and Buddhist mythology Vasuki is the king of the nagas and the son of Kashyapa and Kadru. He is associated with the Hindu god Shiva and is often seen coiled around Shiva's neck in Hindu iconography. In Buddhist tradition he and the other naga kings are regarded as protectors of the Buddha and other enlightened beings.It is also used as a given name in parts of South India, where it is more commonly feminine. The name was borne by an ancient Tamil woman who lived between the 1st century BC and 5th century AD, the virtuous wife of the poet-philosopher Valluvar.
Means "earth" in Sanskrit. This is another name for the Hindu goddess Bhumi.
Variant of Vasylyna influenced by Vasilisa.
Old Persian name possibly meaning "bestowed by Vata", from Old Persian *vātah "wind, Vata" and *fradātah "bestowed".
Vatanchu refers to the "Straight God," a mountain god from the Postclassic Manche Chʼol Maya civilization.
Alternate transcription of Thai วัชระ (see Watchara).
Alternate transcription of Thai วัชรี (see Watchari).
Alternate transcription of Thai วัชรินทร์ (see Watcharin).
Means "brave" or "heroic" in English. It is often given to boys born on or around Easter Sunday.
From the Arabic واضحة (wâḍıḥa(t)) meaning “sunrise, sunshine”.
From the Khmer word វឌ្ឍន (vŏətthĕəʼnĕəʼ) meaning "progress, growth, prosperity".

"Vathsalya" means "Eternal Love". It is a form of expressing feelings. It is one of the five forms expressing feelings of devotion - Shantha (Serenity), Sakhya (friendliness), Vathsalya (eternal love), Anuraga (affection) and Madhura (sweetness).
Variant of Vagitanus, with the spelling possibly altered due to the Vatican Hill in Rome.
Derived from the Germanic name elements vatn "water, waters, river, brook, tears" and herr "army". Vatnarr was the name of a legendary Norwegian king.
Means "pearl" or "gems" in Malagasy. From vato (meaning stone) and soa (meaning good). Vato soa literally means "good stones".
From Serbian ватра (vatra) meaning "fire" and мир (mir) meaning "peace" or "glory". Thus the name means "vigorous or passionate for glory/peace".
Alternate transcription of Thai วาสนา (see Watsana).
Feminine form of Vatslau (Belarusian) or Vatslav (Ukrainian).
Means "provisions for a voyage" in Malagasy.
Possibly a feminization of the French surname Vaudin.
Variant of Waldrade via the form Waldrée. This name was borne by a 7th-century saint, the first abbess of Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnais in Metz, France.
Vaula is both a flower/flowering plant genus ("Asarina" in Latin) and in old Finnish language a little wooden ring that kept a bunch of silver birch branches together in a sauna.
Means "longing for the good", from Old Persian 𐎺𐎢 (vahu) "good" and isa "desirous, wishing, seeking".
From vaa, variant of vaka, meaning "canoe" and ura meaning "red, bright", or a variant of vai ura meaning "bright water" in Tahitian.
Transferred use of the surname Vaux.

Romanian, Russian and Serbian form of Babylas.

"He appeared." The God of Abraham, Issac, and Jacob appeared.

Vayira (வயிரா) is a Tamil baby name associated with the word Vairam (வைரம்), meaning "diamond." The name symbolizes strength, brilliance, resilience, and precious value. It is also connected to the Sanskrit word Vajra (वज्र), meaning "diamond" or "thunderbolt," a symbol of divine power and protection. For families connected to Navaratri, Vayira can represent the strength, courage, and divine energy of Goddess Durga.
Combination of the phonetic elements vay and la.
Combination of the phonetic elements vay and lee.
The masculine name Vaylen is used in American. Other countries in which name Vaylen being used are. Vaylen is not a very common name for a boy. It Is not ranked with in the top 1,000 names.
Perhaps an invented name, using the same sounds found in names such as Vale, Taylor, Baylor, Saylor and Naylor. The American musician Butch Trucks (1947-2017) used this name for his son.
Chuvash form of Baitullah meaning "Kaaba" or "House of God", which is a Muslim shrine in Mecca.
From Mari važ meaning "root" and cora meaning "boy".
Variant of Vászoly via the Old Hungarian form Wazul. Vazul, (before 997–1031 or 1032) was a member of the House of Árpád, a grandson of Taksony, Grand Prince of the Hungarians.

Derived from vé, a Germanic shrine or sacred enclosure. In Norse Mythology, Vé is the brother of Odin and Vili. According to the Prose Edda, the three of them created the world and the first humans. However, in Völuspá, the names Vili and Vé are replaced by Hœnir and Lóðurr.
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 畫 (vẽ) meaning "to draw, to paint".

Vëannë (named Melinir by Eriol) was a child who resided at the Cottage of Lost Play in Tol Eressëa.The Tale of Tinúviel, the earliest version of the story of Beren and Lúthien, was once narrated by Vëannë at the cottage, on the same night that Littleheart afterwards told the tale of the Fall of Gondolin.
Skolt Sami female name, possibly a cognate of Vera 1 and influenced by the Russian.

Meaning uncertain.The lack of inferrable etymology or similarities to other names point towards it being an invented name.A notable bearer of the name is Vecepia Towery, winner of Survivor: Marquesas.
Ancient Russian form of Vyacheslav or Vatslav.
Means "evening", used in Russian fairy tale “Zorka, Vechorka, and Polunochka” by Aleksandr Afanasyev.
Means "carrier" in Latin. This is the name of two fictional characters; Vector the Crocodile from the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, and a villain from Despicable Me.
A character appearing in the 4th series of 'The Tribe', a British TV series.
Stage name of silent film actress Vedah Bertram (1891-1912)
Means "From the Vedas". The Vedas are a large body of religious texts originating in ancient India.

From Sanskrit वेदान्त (vedānta) referring to a Hindu philosophical tradition based on ideas described in the Upanishads. The word itself means "conclusion of the Vedas", from वेद (veda) meaning "knowledge, Veda" and अन्त (anta) meaning "end, conclusion".
French form of Vedastus. This given name is no longer in use in France today, but it still survives in francophone countries in Africa, such as Rwanda.
Feminine form of Védaste, which is the French form of Vedastus.

Italian and Spanish form of Vedastus. The name is also in use in the Philippines, which is a remnant of the influence that Spain has had over the country, what with the country having been part of the Spanish Empire for several centuries.
Possibly a combination of Veda and the French feminine diminutive suffix -ette.
Derived from Old Norse vé meaning "temple, sanctuary" and dís meaning "goddess".
Short form of names beginning with V.
An Indian name that is said to mean “vision” or “knowledge”.

From Sanskrit वीणापाणि (vīṇāpāṇi) meaning "lute-hand, with a lute in hand", composed of वीणा (vīṇā) referring to an ancient Indian musical instrument (also compare Veena) and पाणि (pāṇi) meaning "hands". This is another name of the Hindu goddess Saraswati, who is often depicted holding or playing a veena on the back of a swan.

Meaning unknown; most likely of Cornish origin. This was the name of a 6th-century Cornish saint. Almost nothing is known about the saint - there is debate over whether Veep was male or female. S/he is the namesake of the village St. Veep.
Alternate transcription of Hindi वीर or Punjabi Gurmukhi ਵੀਰ (see Vir).
Alternate transcription of Vira. It is sometimes used as a feminine name in India while it is only masculine in Thailand.
