Derived from Old Norse vé "holy place, temple, sanctuary" (which is related to Gothic weihs "holy") combined with Old Norse garðr "enclosure".

Clipping of the English word vegetable. Vegeta is a fictional character in the Dragon Ball manga series created by Akira Toriyama. All the names of members of the Saiyan race, such as Vegeta, are puns on vegetables.
From the Armenian վեհ (veh) meaning "majestic, sublime" and անուշ (anush) meaning "sweet".
Turkish and Albanian form of Wahab.

Possibly means "and he is God", derived from Hebrew וְ (ve) meaning "and", הוּא (hu) meaning "he" and אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God". This is the name of an angel belonging to the order of the Principalities. He is one of the 72 angels bearing the explicit name of God (the Shem HaMephorash), as interpreted by some Christian Kabbalists.
From the Armenian վեհ (veh) meaning "majestic, sublime" and the feminine suffix ուհի (uhi).

Possibly means "and he is Yahweh", derived from Hebrew וְ (ve) meaning "and" combined with הוּא (hu) meaning "he" and יָהּ (yah) referring to the Hebrew God. This is the name of an angel belonging to the order of the Seraphim. He is the first of the 72 angels bearing the explicit name of God (the Shem HaMephorash), as interpreted by some Christian Kabbalists.
Short form of Old Norse names containing the name element veig "power, strength".
Derived from Old Norse veig "strength" combined with herr "army, warrior". It can also be viewed as a masculine form of Veiga.
Derived from Latvian veikls "dexterous, skillful, able; agile".
Derived from Latvian veiksme "luck; good fortune; success".
Irish form of Venus. It does not appear to be in use as an Irish given name.
The Etruscan god of revenge. He is portrayed as a young man wearing a laurel wreath and holding arrows in his hand. A goat stands next to him.
From the Lithuanian word vėjas meaning, "wind."
Derived from the Lithuanian noun vėjas meaning "wind".

Derived from Latin vē-, a prefix meaning "not, anti" and Jovis, referring to Jupiter, literally meaning "anti-Jupiter". This was the name of a Roman god of Etruscan origins, said to be a god of healing. He was associated with Asclepius, and occasionally with Apollo and young Jupiter.
Bosnian form of the Turkish name Veysil
Means "Heap of Birds, Many Birds" in Cheyenne.
Revolutionary name created in the early period of the Soviet Union. Contraction of великий коммунизм торжествует (velikiy kommunizm torzhestvuyet) meaning "great communism triumphs".
Feminine diminutive of Velasco. Velasquita Ramírez was an 11th-century queen consort of León as the first wife of King Bermudo II.
Derived from the Old Norse elements vé meaning "temple, sanctuary" and laug possibly meaning "vowed, promised, bound in oath".

Recorded in Latvia in the late Middle Ages, this name is of unknown origin and meaning. Theories include a direct derivation from vēlava, itself a Latvian dialectal word describing an accessory mark at the end of the mast of a fishing boat, a derivation from Lithuanian vėliava "flag, banner" and a derivation from Latvian vēls "late".

Flavia Veldicca is a name found on a Roman-period tombstone in Caerleon, Wales. Veldicca would have been her cognomen, probably her original given name. (Flavia is the feminine form of her husband's nomen, or family name.) The reading is difficult; the name has also been interpreted as Vledicca or Ledicca.
Velebit is the largest mountain range in Croatia.

Veleda was a priestess and prophet of the Germanic tribe of the Bructeri who achieved some prominence during the Batavian rebellion of AD 69–70, headed by the Romanized Batavian chieftain Gaius Julius Civilis, when she correctly predicted the initial successes of the rebels against Roman legions.Her name is of uncertain origin and meaning. A current theory believes that it might be Celtic in origin and in fact be a generic title for a prophetess, in which case it would likely be derived from Proto-Celtic *welet- "seer" (ultimately from *wel- "to see").
Could be a variant of Valeria
Of uncertain origin and meaning, although a derivation from Latvian veldze "refreshment" has been suggested.
Derived from the adjective velik, meaning "big, large in size".
Old Russian name meaning "multiscious, much-knowing", derived from Old Church Slavonic велии (velii) "great" combined with мѫдръ (mǫdrŭ) meaning "wise".
Derived from Slovene and Serbo-Croatian velik "great". In Slovenia this name is also considered a derivative of Velimira.
Contraction of Великая Октябрьская революция (Velikaya Oktyabrskaya revolyutsiya) "Great October revolution".

Contraction of Russian великий рабочий (velikiy rabochiy) meaning "great worker" as well as of Владимир Ленин и революция (Vladimir Lenin i revolyutsiya) meaning "Vladimir Lenin and the revolution". This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.
Feminine form of Velir. This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.
Derived from the adjective velik, meaning "big, large in size".
Modern Greek transcription of Belisarios (see Belisarius).
Latinized form of Velislav. Velislaus was the name of a canon who commissioned the Velislaus Bible, an illuminated manuscript of the Bible.
Derived from Estonian veli or velje “brother”.
Derived from the Erzya verb вельмемс (veľmems) meaning "to come to life, to be resurrected".
Bulgarian feminine form of Velmir as well as a Hungarian borrowing of this name.
From the Proto-Balto-Slavic root weliā, meaning "dead". This was the name of the Baltic god of the underworld, whose name became associated with the Devil after Christianization.

Basically means "I had expected you", derived from Georgian ველოდი (velodi) meaning "I expected", which ultimately comes from the verb ლოდინი (lodini) meaning "to expect, to await".This name literally refers to the fact that the child in question was expected and desired by its parents.

From vello (meaning undetermined, but also found in the name Vellocatus) + riga, a feminine form of Old Celtic rīxs, "king." Veloriga is a feminine personal name found on a Roman-era curse-tablet in Bath, Somerset.
Possibly derived from English velour, which refers to a fabric that is similar to velvet. This is also the name of a 1990 song by the American alternative rock band Pixies.
Alternate name of Voltumna, an etruscan god.
Diminutive of Velvet but has been used as a name in its own right for decades.
Combination of Velvet with the feminine suffix -etta.
Combination of Velvet with the feminine suffix -ette.
Transfered use of the surname Velzy. It is possibly given after the surfboard shaper Dale Velzy (1927-2005), credited with being the world's first commercial shaper.
Contraction of Великая мировая революция (Velikaya mirovaya revolyutsiya) "Great world revolution".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 完 (vẹn) meaning "to keep one's promise, to be complete, intact". Compare Hoàn, also from 完.
Short form of Vena, Venice, Venicia, Venetia, Vanessa, Veronica, Veronique, Venus, Venustus, Venustian, and other names beginning with or otherwise containing ven-.
Short form of Alvena or Lavena; variant of Vina 3.
Variant form of Venancijus, which is the Lithuanian form of Venantius.
Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of Venantia.
Feminine form of the Roman name Venantius.Nowadays, this name is probably best known as the name of the Namibian model Venantia Otto.
Derived from venessa. Venasha is a very unique name. Nicknames are Venasha or Nash pronounced N-AYsh
Means "huntress" in Latin. This was an epithet of the goddess Diana.
Means "one sent to conquer over evil" in Latin.
Banatswabian and Romansh form of Wendelin.
Transferred use of the surname Vendetta or from the word vendetta, from Italian vendetta "a feud, blood feud," from Latin vindicta "vengeance, revenge."
Variant of Venetia. As a Spanish name it could be a variant of Benecia or taken from the Spanish place name (see Venecia).
Georgian form of Venediktos, which is the modern Greek form of Benedictus (see Benedict).The traditional Georgian form of Benedict is Benedikte, which is even rarer.
Variant Greek feminine form of Venediktos.

Derived from Венелин (Venelin), the surname of the Russian slavist and philologist Yuriy Venelin (1802-1839), who is best known for his research on the language, history and culture of Bulgaria and the Bulgarian people. One of his published works has been credited with popularizing the Bulgarian culture and history in the Russian Empire as well as with influencing the national feelings of many Bulgarian expatriates.His surname is said to be derived from the Russian noun венец (venets) meaning "crown, wreath, garland", which ultimately comes from Old Church Slavonic вѣньць (věnĭcĭ) meaning "crown".This name was first used in Bulgaria towards the end of Ottoman rule in the 1870s. Known bearers include the Bulgarian politician Venelin Ganev (1880-1966) and the Bulgarian soccer player Venelin Filipov (b. 1990).
Feminine form of Venelin. A known bearer of this name is the Bulgarian high jumper Venelina Veneva-Mateeva (b. 1974).
French form of Venera 2 as well as a feminine form of Vénère.
Derived from Bulgarian венец "wreath, garland; crown; halo, nimbus, aureole".
From the name of the country Venezuela.
From Venjamin which comes from Benjamin

Perhaps originally a Christianized variant of Venus, now either an English vernacular form of Venetia, or else directly from the English name of the city in Italy. The name was revived in the 19th century significantly when the name Florence was beginning to become fashionable.
Either a variant of Venetia apparently influenced by Venice and Felicia (American English) or else a variant of Benicia (Hispanic American).

From the Latin noun venīlia meaning "water of a wave that washes the beach", which comes from the verb veniō "to arrive, to come (to a place), to reach". In Roman mythology this was the name of several sea nymphs. In The City of God, Augustine writes: 'Venilia is the wave which comes to the shore, Salacia the wave which returns into the sea.' In Virgil's Aeneid, Venilia was the mother of King Turnus. According to Ovid's Metamorphoses, this name belonged to the wife of Janus.

Venissa, according to Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th century Historia Regum Britanniae, was a daughter of the Roman Emperor Claudius, whom he gave in marriage to the British king Arvirargus once he had submitted to Rome.According to Geoffrey's account she was very beautiful, and so enchanted Arvirargus that he preferred her company to anyone else's. He founded Gloucester, supposedly named after Claudius, in her honour. When Arvirargus fell out with Rome and Vespasian was sent to enforce a reconciliation, Venissa acted as mediator between them.Venissa cannot be considered historical. She is not mentioned in authentic Roman history; her supposed husband Arvirargus is known only from a cryptic reference in a 2nd-century satirical poem by Juvenal; and it is in any case inconceivable that a daughter, even an illegitimate daughter, of a Roman emperor could be given in marriage to a barbarian without attracting comment. Nonetheless, she and her husband, identified with the historical Caratacus, appear in many uncritical genealogies originating in the Tudor period.
Estonian transcription of Russian Вениамин (see Veniamin).
Věnka is short form of Slavic feminine name Věnceslava. The diminutive can mean "wreath".
From the name of the sacred hill of Venkata in Andhra Pradesh combined with the name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
Alternate transcription of Telugu వెంకటలక్ష్మి (see Venkatalakshmi).
From the name of the sacred hill of Venkata in Andhra Pradesh combined with Sanskrit रमण (ramaṇa) meaning "pleasing, delightful".
Alternate transcription of Telugu వేంకటేశ్వరుడు (see Venkateswara).

Means "lord of Venkata" from Sanskrit वेङ्कट (veṅkaṭa) referring to a sacred hill in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh combined with ईश्वर (īśvara) meaning "lord, god". This is an avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu particularly revered in southern India. The Venkateswara Temple in Tirumala is dedicated to him.

Short form of Veniamin and Venelin as well as a variant of Wenceslas. This name is borne by Macedonian writer and poet Venko Andonovski (b. 1964) and Veniamin "Venko" Markovski (1915-1988), a Bulgarian writer of Macedonian descent.
Possibly a nickname for names like Venice, Vanessa, Veronica and other names that begin with the letter V.
Finnish form of Svenne and diminutive of Werner.
Transferred use of the surname Venner.
A diminutive of Verner and Vendela.
Not sure, it was given to 6 girls in Alabama in 1913, looks like a diminutive of a longer name that became independent, perhaps Venetia or Venicia.
Means "white moon" from Tamil வெண் (veṇ) meaning "white, pure" and நிலா (nilā) meaning "moon".
Middle name of Captain Ross Poldark, the main character in the historical television series Poldark. Ross Vennor Poldark is his full name on the BBC show.
Contracted or alternative form of the name Venčeslav (or Venceslav; see Václav).
Transferred use of the name of the river Venta which flows through north-western Lithuania and western Latvia.

From the Latin word venti, meaning "winds" or "of the wind". This is the name of a playable character in the 2020 video game Genshin Impact.This name was also used by the Romans to refer to a group of Hellenic wind deities (known as the Anemoi in Greek), which were associated with the cardinal directions.
Derived from Italian ventura "fortune'. It was occasionally used a diminutive of Bonaventure.
Italian name derived from the name Bonaventura. This name was borne by Italian preacher Venturino of Bergamo.
Means "wind" in Latin. A main character from Square Enix and Disney's video game "Kingdom Hearts: Birth by Sleep" bore this name.
Means "flute" in Sanskrit and usually refers to the Lord Krishna.
This name may be an elaboration of Venere, via its Latin form Venus.
Spanish form of Venustianus. A notable bearer was Venustiano Carranza (1859-1920), one of the leaders of the Mexican Revolution.
Roman cognomen that was a derivative of of Venustus, a personal name meaning devoted to Venus. Used by a saint who was a companion with Sabinus of spoleto.
Roman cognomen derived from the name of the Roman god Venus or meaning beautiful. Used by a couple of saints.
Venutius was a 1st-century king of the Brigantes in northern Britain at the time of the Roman conquest.
Taken from Italian venuto "arrived; newcomer" and sometimes used as a diminutive of Benvenuto.
Old Norse name derived from the elements vé "temple, sanctuary" (related to Gothic weihs "holy") and nýr "new".
From Lao ແວວ (veo) meaning "bright, brilliant, shining" and ມະນີ (many) meaning "gem, jewel".
Possibly a female version of DeAndre or Deondre, or Ondre combines with the prefix Ve. Used my TikToker Ve’Ondre Mitchell
Short form or variant of Vepkhia.
Derived from Albanian veprim "to act; action".
Bosnian, Catalan and Croatian form of Verus.
Derived from Old Norse verr "man" and valdr "ruler, mighty one, powerful one".
Possibly a contraction of Vera 1 and Alicia. It is mainly used in El Salvador.
The first name of the protagnist in The Immortals quartet by Tamora Pierce. A diminutive of the name is Daine.
Variant of Veralynn. Combination of Vera and Lyn.
Masculine form of Vera 1, meaning "faith". Also associated with the adjective veran, pronounced with a stress on the first syllable, meaning "loyal, faithful".

Variant of Verdandi used by John Thelwall in his play The Fairy of the Lake (written 1801; based on Arthurian legend), where it belongs to one of the three Fatal Sisters - the others being Urd and Schulda - who preside over the past, present and future. In Thelwall's play, Rowenna, wife of Vortigern, seeks their foresight during her quest to seduce Arthur.
Of unknown origin. This name was borne by members of the Egnatia gens, an obscure Plebeian family.
From the name Vera 1 combined with the feminine suffix -wati.
Exact origin unknown, however it does mean "willow" in Ukranian.It has historically been most common within Amish communities

The Celtic goddess of the river Wharfe (North Yorkshire, England) known from a single inscription found in Ilkley, England and therefore interpreted as a local deity.There have been attempts to link her name to Proto-Celtic *wera- "rain" and either *beja- "to strike" or bei-e/o "to live".

Verbt is a weather and storm god in Albanian mythology and folklore, who causes hailstorms and controls fire, water, and the northern wind which fans the flames of fire. The name itself is of uncertain origin and meaning; theories include a derivation from Albanian vorbëtinë "whirlwind, vortex, swirl".
Name of horka Bulcsú from the Chronicles.

Vercana was a goddess who was venerated by the Gauls in Roman times, it is, however, uncertain whether she was a Germanic or a Celtic goddess. Since inscriptions dedicated to her were found near healing springs, it has been proposed that she may have been a goddess of healing and waters and attempts have been made to link her name to Germanic *Werkanô "she who does deeds" and to *Berkanô "goddess of birch trees".

Variant of Uercassiuellaunos. Uer could mean "on, over, supreme." The meaning of cassi is disputed, but one possible meaning is "tin" or "bronze." The meaning of the final element, uellauno, is also disputed and could mean "chief, commander" or "good." The whole name might therefore mean "supreme chief of bronze."
Italian form of Vercingetorix mainly used for the historical person. It is rarely used as a given name in Italy.
Derived from the Spanish verde, meaning "green," combined with the suffix -ell. A notable bearer is Native American singer Verdell Primeaux (1966-).

While its precise origin is uncertain, it may be related to names like Verdell, which derives from the French "vert" or Latin "viridis," meaning "green." The "-ella" suffix suggests a feminine elaboration, following a pattern common in African American naming traditions of the early 20th century.See also the diminutive Verdie.
From Latin viridis "green" (via Vulgar Latin virdis) and rosa "rose".

Transferred use of the surname Verdi. A famous person with the surname is Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi. A famous namesake is Australian Olympic weightlifter Verdi "Vern" Barberis, who is in the AWF Hall of Fame.
Contracted form of Veridiana. This was the name of an Italian saint from the 13th century AD.
Possibly from Arabic ورد (ward) meaning "roses" and جنان (jinan) meaning "gardens, paradises".

Meaning uncertain, possibly a variant or diminutive of the feminine Verity, Verdella, Vera 1 or the masculine Verdell. This name was most well used in the Southeastern United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It was used for a character, Verdie Foster, on the American television series The Waltons (1972-1981).

The lady of the castle Aspetta Ventura in La Tavola Ritonda. She suffered from leprosy and could only be cured by the blood of a royal virgin. In the quest to heal her, her knights bled hundreds of virgins, most of whom perished. She was finally cured by the blood of Agresizia, Perceval’s sister, who subsequently died. She appears in the Vulgate Queste del Saint Graal but is unnamed.
Transferred use of the surname Verdon.

From the name of the city in France which derives from the Latin 'Verodunum', meaning "strong fort". This name was first used during the First World War when the city became well-known due to the Battle of Verdun (1916). In the years thereafter the name was not uncommon in the United Kingdom, and was especially popular in Wales. Its use was unisex, though it leaned male.

Means "paths, lanes" in Spanish, taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de las Veredas and Nuestra Señora de las Veredas, meaning "The Virgin of the Paths" and "Our Lady of the Paths" respectively.She is venerated at the sanctuary in Torrecampo in the Andalusian province of Córdoba.
Medieval Slavic form of Jeremiah, likely influenced from Slavic вѣра (věra) "faith".
Italian feminine form of Wermund and Warimund.
Latinized form of Waramunt and variant of Veremund.
Verenia was one of the first Vestal Virgins, selected by Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome.
Apparently a Spanish variant of Berenice.
Alternate transcription of Malayalam വർഗീസ് or വർഗ്ഗീസ് (see Varghese).
Used by Zora Neale Hurston in her 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. The main character, Janie, marries and finds love with a man called Tea Cake whose real name is Vergible Woods.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Virgil.
From the Armenian վեհանձն (verhantsn) meaning "generous" and the feminine suffix ուհի (uhi).
Anglicized form of Verianus. This was the name of a saint from the 3rd century AD.
Roman cognomen that was derived from Verus.This was the original name of saint Verian (3rd century).
Russian diminutive of Veronika, which in Armenia and Georgia is primarily used as a diminutive for Vera 1.

This name either came into being as a variant form of Viridia, or as a shortened form of Veridiana (see Viridiana). Both names ultimately come from the same root (Latin viridis "green"), so etymology-wise it does not really matter which of the two possibilities is the correct one.

Portuguese, Venetian and Spanish form of Viridiana as well as an Italian variant of this name. Blessed Veridiana was a Benedictine virgin and recluse. Originally from a noble family of Castelfiorentino, Tuscany, Italy, she went on a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela and, after returning, had herself walled up in a hermitage near the Elba River.
Latinate form of Veerle, recorded in the early 13th century.
Roman cognomen which is ultimately derived from the Latin adjective verus "true".
Comes from latin Veritas which means Truth
Italian form of Verissimus and masculine Verissima.
Diminutive of Verónica, via its short form Vero 2.
Verkina Flower is a retired actress.
An English language form of a French name meaning "truthful" and a variant of Verle.
Likely given in honour of French poet Paul Verlaine (1844-1896). Usage in France is feminine.
An English language form of a French name meaning "truthful".
From Latin origin meaning "virile" or "manly".Notable bearer is American football player Verlin Adams (1918-1985) who played for the New York Giants from 1943-1945.
Possibly a combination of Verla and Linda.
Likely a corruption of Verlinda by using the diminutive suffix ine
Transferred use of the surname Verlon.
a combined name of verly and lynne. verly is derived from the old english name beverly, meaning “dweller at the beaver meadow”. lynne is a name of welsh origin meaning “lake”.
Meaning unknown. It could be a rhyming variant of names like Irma, or a variant of Varma.
Vermettya Royster was a member of the R&B ensemble 'The Sisters Love'.
The wife of King Amoroldo of Ireland, a friend of Tristan.
Derived from Old French vermeillon "vermilion", ultimately from Latin vermiculus "little worm", in reference to Kermes vermilio, from which crimson dye was made.
From the Old French word vermeillon, meaning "little worm" or "small worm".
Meaning unknown. Verminus was the god who protected cattle from disease in Roman mythology.

From the name of the state in the United States of America (see Vermont). The place name originated from French Verd Mont meaning "green mountain", the name that French explorer Samuel de Champlain gave to Vermont's Green Mountains on his 1647 map.
Visigothic name from the Ancient Germanic name Wermund, possibly composed of the elements wer "true", and mund, "protector".
Combination of either Old Norse verr "man" or verja "to defend", with mundr "protector". The name appears on an 11th century copper box that was engraved with runes.
Swedish feminine form of Verner. It may also be associated with Swedish värna (Old Norse verna) "to protect, to defend".
Transferred use of the surname Vernal.
Combination of Verna and Lisa, perhaps inspired by the name of Italian actress Virna Lisi (1936-2014).
The name Verna with the suffix -lyn.
Possibly a combination of Vernon and Bernard.
Variant of Vern, or transferred use of the surname Verne.
Variant of Vernel, or possibly an elaborated form of Verna and Vernon.
Combination of the name Vern with the feminine suffix -elle.
Possibly an attempt at creating a feminine form of Verne influenced by Vanessa.
Diminutive of Veronica and names containing vern, such as Vernon, Verna or Laverne.
Allegedly a Gallicization of Werner, this name was recorded up until the 1700s. Today, it survives as a surname.
From the genus of flowering plants also known as ironweed.

Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Verus.
Medieval Flemish form of Veronus. Also see Veroon.
Derived from the elements vera "faith" and "ljub" "love", literally meaning "lover of faith".
French form of Veronus. It is no longer in use, so now it only survives in the surname Véron.

Feminine form of Veronus.The most notable bearer of this name is the 9th-century folk saint Verona of Leefdaal. At the time, the village was located in Frankish territory, but today it is situated in the region of Flanders in Belgium. Saint Verona was the twin sister of saint Veronus of Lembeek and a great-granddaughter of Charlemagne (748-814). There is some doubt as to whether she ever existed, but if she did, then she might possibly be the same person as the blessed Verona of Leuven/Mainz (9th century), with whom she is often confused.

Presumably directly taken from the Italian word, and medieval byname, veronese meaning "from Verona".A known bearer of this name was Veronese della Scala, daughter of Mastino II della Scala, a 14th-century lord of Verona, sister of Viridis and Altaluna, who eventually married Giacomo Trissino.
Variant of Véronique using the French diminutive suffix ette.
Elaboration of Verona, a a city on the Adige River in Veneto, Italy. Rarely used as a given name.
Greek form of Veronika and possible Dutch variant of Veronique.

The best known bearer of this name is the 9th-century folk saint Veronus of Lembeek. At the time, the village was located in Frankish territory, but today it is situated in the region of Flanders in Belgium.Saint Veronus was probably Frankish himself, as he is said to have been a cousin of the Frankish king Charles the Bald (823-877) and a great-grandson of Charlemagne (748-814). As such, his name is probably a latinized Germanic name, though a fully Latin origin cannot be ruled out completely. In that case, the name is most likely derived from (or related to) Latin verus meaning "true, genuine" as well as "right, just" (see Verus).In the case of a Germanic origin, the original name was probably something like Wero (also compare Wiro). Such a name was typically a short form. Often the linguistic root of these names is relatively easy to pinpoint, but not in this case, as there are several possibilities for Wero. The most notable of those are Old High German wer meaning "man", weri meaning "defence, resistance", war meaning "aware, cautious" and war meaning "true" (which is etymologically related to the aforementioned Latin verus).
Transcription of Veronika from Russian Cyrillic spelling in Ukrainian transcription.

Dutch short form of Verona, Veronica and its variant Veronika. In that capacity, the name is extremely rare as an official name on birth certificates; it is almost always used informally.As a masculine name, Veroon is the Flemish form of Veronus. It is completely archaic: these days, the name is almost exclusively used to refer to the 9th-century saint Veronus of Lembeek (Flanders), in whose honour the annual Sint-Veroonmars ("Saint Veroon's march") is organized.
Possibly a madeup name inspired by Veronica and Jessika or other names ending in -ika.

From a French occupational surname that meant "glassmaker" or "glassblower", ultimately from French verre meaning "glass" (see Verrier). A notable bearer was Verrier Elwin (1902-1964), full name Harry Verrier Holman Elwin, a British-born Indian anthropologist, ethnologist and tribal activist.

A high-born damsel, of Guenevere’s court was mute until the arrival of Sir Percival, when at last she spoke. Greeting him, she led him to his seat at the left of the Siege Perilous and predicted his future greatness. She also predicted her own death, which took place four days later; she was buried in the cathedral at Cardiff. From the circumstances of the miracle, one can assume she had led a holy life.

This name sporadically appears outside the U.S. top 1000 in the American South in the early 20th-century. It is most likely inspired by the Latin word "versus" (verse; line) probably used by Southern Baptists in reference to the verses of the Bible. Versie also sporadically appears. It is also the name of a tributary of the Po river in Italy.
Transferred use of the Italian surname Versace as a given name, possibly used in reference to the Italian luxury fashion company Versace.
From the city of Versailles in France.
Recently coined word name, used in 2024 by Kailyn Lowry. Verse has a twin named Valley.
Means "turner of hearts" from Latin vertere "to turn, turn about" and cor "heart" (genitive cordis). This was an epithet of the Roman goddess Venus.

A variant of Vortigern, a British king who ruled several generations before Arthur, famed for bringing misery to Britain by welcoming the Saxons. Bede is the first to mention him by name, but the figure first appears in Gilda’s De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae as the superbus tyrannus (generally translated as “proud tyrant,” but likely indicating the less pejorative “supreme soveregin”) who employed the Saxons against the barbarian Picts and nearly lost the island as a result.

From the name of a Cornish town, which is taken from Sen Veryan meaning "Saint Veryan", a Cornish corruption of Severian, itself a corrupted form of Symphorian (the saint to whom the village church is dedicated). Today this name is more commonly found on women than on men.

Illyrian name probably derived from Proto-Indoeuropean *h₁wesu-ḱléw- "of good fame". With this derivation, the name is cognate to the Greek name Euclid.

Bosnian and Croatian form of Vespasian.

Meaning uncertain, it could be related to the Latin vesperum meaning "evening" or the Latin and Italian vespa meaning "wasp". From the Italian surname Vespucci, except Latinized. Given in honor of Amerigo Vespucci, most likely to be paired alongside Americus.

Given name derived from the Latin vetus > veturius, meaning "senior, veteran, expert, with long experience". The gens Veturia, anciently called Vetusia, was a patrician family at Rome, which also had plebeian branches. The patrician branch was of great antiquity. According to legendary history, Mamurius Veturius lived in the time of Numa Pompilius, and made the sacred Ancilia. Veturia was a Roman matron, the mother of the possibly legendary Roman general Gaius Marcius Coriolanus. Veturia came from a patrician family and encouraged her son's involvement in Roman politics. Gawain’s foster-father, a poor but nobly-born fisherman living near the city of Narbonne in Gaul.Gawain’s mother had given Gawain, as a baby, to some merchants, who docked their ship and left it unattended near Viamundus’s home. Viamundus came across the ship, found the infant and a pile of unguarded wealth within, and helped himself to both. Finding no way to spend his ill-gotten gains without arousing suspicion, Viamundus eventually journeyed to Rome with the spoils, representing himself as a noble Roman warlord from Gaul.The ruse worked, and the Roman Emperor awarded Viamundus a manor with in the city, where he lived out his days in relative luxury, raising Gawain to be an honorable and skillful knight. On his deathbed, he repented to the Emperor and to Pope Sulpicius, confessing his crime and deception. The Emperor, who had been his friend, forgave him and buried him in a tomb among the other Roman nobles.

This name was borne by Pierre Victurnien Vergniaud (31 May 1753 – 31 October 1793), a lawyer and statesman, and a significant figure of the French Revolution.10th-century records mention a certain Saint Victurnien, a 5th-century anchorite, who left his name in the name of the village Saint-Victurnien in southern France.The origin and meaning of his name are uncertain; one theory however links his name to Victorinus, which becomes Vartunio in the patois of the langue d'Oc and Vertunian in Occitan. This leads some scholars to theorize that the three forms might have "blended" into one and, with Standard French added to the mix, formed the name Victurnien.

Vidigoia was a Thervingian Gothic warrior. His name means either "the man from the forest zone" or "the forest-barker/wolf". Vidigoia figured during the campaigns of Roman Emperor Constantine the Great across the Danube around 330 AD. Having been driven from the Danube by the Romans, the Thervingi began infiltrating the Tisza Sarmatians. Vidigoia was probably the leader of this infiltration. Herwig Wolfram designates Vidigoia, along with Geberic, as one of the first reiks, who were military kings emerging among the Goths at this time.

Derived from the Germanic name elements víg "fight, battle" and maðr "man".
Old Swedish and Norwegian form of Vígmundr.
Derived from Old Norse víg "fight, battle" and mund "protection".

Possibly a combination of Vignesh and Tamil வர்ணம் (varṇam) or Malayalam വര്‍ണ്ണം (varṇṇaṁ) both meaning "colour", likely derived from Sanskrit वर्ण (varna) which has the same meaning. Alternatively, Vigneshwaran could derive from विघ्नेश्वर (vighneśvara) meaning "lord of obstacles" in Sanskrit, referring to Ganesh's primary function in Hinduism as the master and remover of obstacles.
Derived from the Old Norse element víg "war".
Derived from Old Norse víg "fight", "battle" and njóta "to use".
Croatian and Galician form and Swedish and Danish variant of Viggo as well as a Dutch borrowing of the Scandinavian name.
A modern form of Wigalois.Borne as a second given name by the German writer Albert Vigoleis Thelen.
Derived from Latin vigor "vigor, strength, liveliness".
Derived from the Latin vigor meaning ''liveliness, activity, power, strength''. A 13th century Italian Painter, Vigoroso da Siena, bore this name.This now means "vigorous" in Italian.
From Old Norse vígr meaning "in fighting condition, able to fight".
Derived from Old Norse víg "fight", "battle" and ráð "advise", "counsel", "decision".
Derived from Old Norse víg "fight, battle" and starkr "strong, healthy".
Combination of Old Norse víg "war, battle" and the name of the Norse god Þórr (see Þór).
Derived from Old Norse víg "battle, fight" and þorn "thorn".
Derived from Old Norse víg "fight, battle" and ulfr "wolf".
Derived from the Germanic name elements vé "home, temple, sanctuary" and gunnr "battle, fight".
The name Vigya is derived from Sanskrit word Vigy...Vigya means a versatile genius
Feminine equivalent of Vihanga.Derivative of विहग in sanskrit, which literally means "bird". This name expresses freedom and individualism.
Dena'ina Athabaskan meaning "Luminous inside". English equivalent is "Crystal".
Originally an old Estonian vernacular form of Sofia, now used as a given name in its own right.
Finnish short form of names containing the name element VIG "battle, fight" or a Finnish spelling of Viki.
From a Finnish word meaning "strong wind".
Either the Estonian form of Vivika or a diminutive of Viivi.
Means "lightning" or "sparkling" in various Indian languages.
From Sanskrit विजय (vijaya) meaning "victory" combined with the name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi. This is a form of Lakshmi who bestows victory.
Malayalam and Tamil variant of Vijaya.
Combination of Sanskrit विजय (vijaya) meaning "victory" and Tamil ரத்தினம் (rattiṉam) (see Ratna).
Alternate transcription of Hindi विजेन्द्र or विजेंद्र (see Vijendra).
From Sanskrit विजय (vijaya) meaning "victory" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra.
Ijekavian form of Vesna. Borne by Vijessna Ferkic (b. 1987), a German actress of Croatian descent.
Alternate transcription of Thai วิจิตร (see Wichit).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิจิตรา (see Wichitra).

This name can be the Lithuanian form of Viola as well as be an independent, authentic Lithuanian name. In the case of the latter, the name is derived from Vijolė, the name of a river in the Lithuanian county of Šiauliai. In turn, the river derives its name from the old Lithuanian verb vijotis meaning "to curl, to coil, to twist", which is related to the modern Lithuanian noun vija meaning "strand" as well as "coil, winding, spire, loop". Also compare the Latvian noun vija meaning "garland, wreath", which is probably etymologically related.
Both a variant of Violeta and a direct derivation from Latvian vijolīte "violet".
Dutch and German short form of Viktor or Viktoria.
Short form of Viktoriya. Also short for Veranika in Belarusian.
Old Norse short form of Víkætill.
Derived from the Germanic name elements vé "home", "temple", "sanctuary" and ketill "cauldron".
Etruscan version of the Greek Icarus
From Sanskrit विकास (vikāsa) meaning "development, progress, growth, expansion".
Alternate transcription of Hindi विकास (see Vikas).

Means: Radiant, cheerful. hearty or ungrudging, promoting or inducing cheer , pleasant, bright, bright with joy, hope, etc emitting rays of light, shining, bright, Physics emitted or propagated by radiation, a point or object from which rays proceed, full of cheer , in good spirits, characterized by or expressive of good spirits or cheerfulness
Diminutive of both Viktaryna and Viktoryja.
Variant transcription of Vikentiy. A bearer of this name was the Russian writer and medical doctor Vikenty Veresaev (1867-1945).

Vikramaditya (102 BC) one of the greatest kings in Indian history. (𝘷𝘪𝘬𝘳𝘢𝘮𝘢) means "valour" and (𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘵𝘺𝘢) means "sun"
Tamil and Malayalam variant of Vikrama.
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਵਿਕਰਮਜੀਤ (see Vikramjit).
From Sanskrit विक्रम (vikrama) meaning "stride, pace, valour" and जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Alternate transcription of Thai วิกรม (see Wikrom).
Directly taken from Latvian vīksna "elm tree". This name was recorded in medieval Latvia.
Variant of Viktoria. This is also the Estoninan name of a genus of water-lilies (known as Victoria in English).
Esperanto form of Victorina or Victoria.

Derived from Swedish viktualier meaning "victuals". This is one of the middle names of Pippi Långstrump (English: Pippi Longstocking), full name Pippilotta Viktualia Rullgardina Krusmynta Efraimsdotter Långstrump, a character invented by Swedish author Astrid Lindgren.
Czech and Slovak form of Vikusha. Also compare Vikuška.
Russian diminutive of Viktoriya. Also compare Vikushka and Vikusya.

Czech and Slovak form of Vikushka. Also compare Vikuša.
Russian diminutive of Viktoriya. Also compare Vikusha and Vikushka.

Derived from the initials of the Russian politician and communist revolutionary Vladimir Ilyich Lenin (1870-1924), who founded the former Soviet state. This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.Known bearers of this name include the Russian journalist Vil Lipatov (1927-1979) and Vil Mirzayanov (b. 1935), a Russian chemist of ethnic Tatar origin.
Etruscan version of the Greek Iolaos
Alternate transcription of Thai วิไล (see Wilai) or Lao ວິໄລ (see Vilay), both of the same origin.

Alternate transcription of Thai วิลาวัณย์ (see Wilawan).
Means "beautiful, handsome, fine" in Lao, a borrowing from Tamil விலை (vilai) meaning "price, value".
Means "governorate, province" in Azerbaijani, ultimately deriving from Arabic وِلَايَة (wilāya).
From Lao ວິໄລ (vilay) meaning "beautiful, handsome, fine" and ຄຳ (kham) meaning "gold".
From Lao ວິໄລ (vilay) meaning "beautiful, handsome, fine" and ພອນ (phone) meaning "blessing".
From Lao ວິໄລ (vilay) meaning "beautiful, handsome, fine" and ສຸກ (souk) meaning "health, ease, happiness".
From Lao ວິໄລ (vilay) meaning "splendid, beautiful" and ວັນ (vanh) meaning "sun, day".
Derived from the Old Norse elements vili meaning "will, desire" and bogi meaning "bow".
Derived from Arabic وِلْدَان‏ (wildān) meaning "children". It is also a Bashkir variant transcription of Uyildan, of the same origin.

Basically means "hoping to work", derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas) combined with Lithuanian daryti meaning "to do, to act" as well as "to work". In other words: this given name is basically the same as Darvilas, but with the name elements in different places.
Means "much hope", derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas) combined with Lithuanian daug meaning "much" (see Daumantas).
Derived from the Old Norse elements vili "will, desire" and dís "goddess; woman, lady".
Modern coinage taken from Vilhelm and the feminine ending -(f)rid.
Short form of feminine names that start with Vil- (such as Vilgailė and Vilmantė) or end in -vilė, such as Akvilė and Norvilė.
Czech and Slovak diminutive of Vilém or Viliam.
Very rare name in Croatia, exclusively for women and most commonly used in the coastal region. Meaning uncertain, possibly coming from the mythological creature ''Vila'' (Slavic fae).
Contraction of В. И. Ленин — отец революции (V. I. Lenin — otets revolyutsii), meaning "V. I. Lenin is father of revolution".

Either from abbriviation of В. И. Ленин, Октябрьская революция (V. I. Lenin, Oktyabr'skaya revolyutsiya) "V. I. Lenin, October Revolution" or contraction of В. И. Ленин — организатор революции (V. I. Lenin — organizator revolyutsii) "V. I. Lenin is organiser of revolution".
Alternate spelling of Villette, a French word for a small town or village.

Means "strong hope", derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas) combined with old Lithuanian gailas, which usually means "strong, potent" but has also been found to mean "sharp, jagged" as well as "angry, fierce, violent" and "miserable, sorrowful, remorseful". Also compare the modern Lithuanian noun galia meaning "power, might, force".

The first element of this name is derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas). The second element is either derived from the Lithuanian verb gaudyti meaning "to take" as well as "to catch, to hunt" or from the Lithuanian adjective gaudus meaning "sonorous, resonant, ringing, loud, echoing".
Old Norse combination of vil 'will, desire' and garðr 'enclosure', 'protection'.
Basically means "to defend hopefully", derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas) combined with Lithuanian ginti meaning "to defend, to protect".

Basically has the (more or less) figurative meaning of "to hear hopefully", derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas) combined with the Lithuanian noun girdas meaning "rumour", which is ultimately derived from the Lithuanian verb girdėti meaning "to hear". Also compare the related Lithuanian noun gandas meaning "rumour, hearsay".
Hungarian, Lithuanian, Swedish, Finnish and Norwegian form of Wilhelma.
Icelandic and Slovak form of Wilhelmina.
Danish and Norwegian form of Wilhelmine.

Means "will" in Old Norse. Vili is the brother of Odin and Vé in Norse mythology. According to the Prose Edda, the three of them created the world and the first humans. However, in Völuspá, the names Vili and Vé are replaced by Hœnir and Lóðurr.
Abbreviation of В. И. Ленин и Академия наук (V. I. Lenin i akademiya nauk), meaning "V. I. Lenin and academy of science".
Archaic spelling of Viilissi, the Greenlandic form of Felix.
A feminine form of Vili or a short form of Akviliina.

From the name of the river which flows in Lithuania through it's capital city Vilnius. Official river name is Neris, but it has a second name - Vilija. The reasons for the dual naming of the river as Neris by the Lithuanians and Viliya (formerly Velja, meaning "big, great" in Slavic) by the Slavs are complex. Even in Vilnius, there are toponyms including both names, e. g. Neris remains in the riverside names of Paneriai and Paneriškės while Velja is a part of the name Valakampiai, which means "an angle of Velja" in Lithuanian.
Derived from the Slavic element vila meaning "fairy".
Contraction of Владимир Ильич Ленин и Октябрьская Революция (Vladimir Ilyich Lenin i Oktyabr'skaya Revolyutsiya), meaning "Vladimir Ilyich Lenin and October Revolution".
Short form of names beginning with Vil- (of either Baltic or Germanic origin), like Viltautas or Vilhelmas.
From initals of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin and Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin.
From initials of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin.

Vilkas is part of the Lithuanian language which means "wolf". This name is most famously used in the video game "The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim" where one of the characters is named Vilkas.Vilkas also, in the Finnish language, means "lively" or "brisk".
Transferred use of the surname Villamor.

Derived from Latin villana "villein, feudal tenant" (compare Villanus). Villana de' Botti (1332 - 1361) was an Italian Roman Catholic professed member of the Third Order of Saint Dominic. She turned to the Dominicans after a sudden conversion from a dissolute life and was noted for her simplistic life born out of her conversion. De' Botti had fierce detractors due to her stating she had religious ecstasies at Mass - which was true - and these opponents had even acknowledged her as a true living saint. She was beatified on 27 March 1824.
This was used by English writer Jeanette Winterson in her novel 'The Passion' (1987). She may have taken it from the English word for a form of poetry, which is ultimately cognate with Villana.
Medieval Latin name meaning "farmhand", a derivative of villa "country house, farm". It was borne by an Italian Catholic saint of the 13th century.
Means "hamlet" in Spanish. It is taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Villar meaning "Our Lady of the Hamlet".
Variant of Willard or transferred use of the surname Villard.

From the titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de Villaviciosa and Nuestra Señora de Villaviciosa, meaning "The Virgin of Villaviciosa" and "Our Lady of Villaviciosa" respectively.She is venerated at the church of San Lorenzo in the Andalusian city of Córdoba.

This name was first used by the Swedish writer August Strindberg (1849-1912) for one of his poems. He may have based it on the names Vellamo or Wilhelma, or perhaps he combined the Old Norse name element vil, vili "will, desire" with Scandinavian mor "mother" (compare Lillemor, Moa).
Means "wild" in Finnish. It could also be used as a shortening of Villiam.

Recently created name intended to mean "wild maiden" from Old Norse villr "wild" (compare Icelandic villiblóm "wildflower") combined with mey "maiden, girl" (an alternative form of mær). This was invented by Norwegian-Swedish author Margit Sandemo (1924-2018) for Villimey Kalebsdóttir, a character in her Ísfólkið series of books. It was approved as an Icelandic given name in 2012.

Recent Hungarian name based on the title of Zoltán Kodály's children's choir formed in 1925. The word villő occurs in poems and songs sung during the old Hungarian winter cemetery ceremony and seeing as the girls walked the village with twigs during the shooting, villő is probably derived from the Latin villus "tuft of hair" (referring to the fine soft hairs on fruits, flowers, and other parts of plants). Another theory, however, links this word to Czech and Slovak víla "fairy (mythical being)".
Abbreviation of Владимир Ильич Ленин — Лидер Октябрьской Революции (Vladimir Ilyich Lenin — Lider Oktyabr'skoy Revolyutsii), meaning "Vladimir Ilyich Lenin is leader of October Revolution".
Originally a short form of Villem, now used as a given name in its own right (compare Ville).
Scandinavian form of Willy, predominantly used by men.
Low German and Frisian diminutive of Wilma.

The name may either come directly from the Lithuanian word vilna meaning "wool" or vilnis "to surge." The name may also be used in reference to the Vilnia river as well as the name of the city, Vilnius which both share the same etymological root with vilnis.
From the name of the Lithuanian capital, named after the Vilnia River, ultimately from vilnis meaning "wave".
Means "light of Lenin", from the initials of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin (VIL) and Tatar нур (nur), meaning "light".
From Old Norse vili "will, desire" combined with nýr "new".
Contraction of Владимир Ильич Ленин — Организатор Революции (Vladimir Il'ich Lenin – Organizator Revolyutsii) "Vladimir Ilyich Lenin is Organiser of Revolution".
Abbreviation of Владимир Ильич Ленин — организатор рабочего движения (Vladimir Ilyich Lenin — organizator rabochego dvizheniya), meaning "Vladimir Ilyich Lenin is organiser of worker's movement".
Contraction of Владимир Ильич Ленин — организатор (Vladimir Ilyich Lenin — organizator), meaning "Vladimir Ilyich Lenin is organiser", referring to October Revolution.
Abbreviation of В. И. Ленин — освободитель рабочих и крестьян (V. I. Lenin — osvoboditel' rabochikh i krest'yan), meaning "V. I. Lenin is liberator of workers and peasants".
Finnish dialectal variant form of Filpus.
Transferred use of the surname Vilsaint.
Transferred use of surname Wilson, probably influenced by VIL, initials of Vladimir Lenin.
Abbreviation of Владимир Ильич Ленин — создатель Октябрьской революции (Vladimir Ilyich Lenin — sozdatel' Oktyabr'skoy revolyutsii), meaning "Vladimir Ilyich Lenin is creator of October Revolution".

Derived from the Lithuanian noun viltis meaning "hope", which is ultimately derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope".This name is also encountered as a short form of masculine compound names that start with Vilt- (such as Viltaras and Viltautas) or end in -viltas, such as Doviltas and Eiviltas.
Latvian form of Wilhelm and William.
Contraction of Владимира Ильича Ленина-Ульянова заветы (Vladimira Ilyicha Lenina-Ulyanova zavety), meaning "testament of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin-Ulyanov".
Transferred use of surname Williams, likely influenced by VIL, initials of Vladimir Lenin.

Abbreviation of Владимир Ильич любит рабочих/Россию/Родину (Vladimir Ilyich lyubit rabochikh/Rossiyu/Rodinu), meaning "Vladimir Ilyich (Lenin) loves workers/Russia/motherland". Last word varies by interpertation of parents or bearer.
Means "have faith in God" in Shona.
Means "carry in the arms, carry in the hands" in Malagasy.
Alternate transcription of Thai วิมล (see Wimon).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิมลรัตน์ (see Wimonrat).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิมลวรรณ (see Wimonwan).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิมล (see Wimon).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิมลรัตน์ (see Wimonrat).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิมลวรรณ (see Wimonwan).
Derived from Sanskrit विमुक्ति (vimukti) meaning "release, liberation".
Derived from the Germanic name elements vé "home, temple, sanctuary" and mund "hand, protection".
From the name of Vimy in the Pas-de-Calais department of France, where the Battle of Vimy Ridge took place from 9 to 12 April 1917 during the First World War.
The name Vin is a generally a boy's name, Latin, meaning conquering. It is also the name of a character from Mistborn
Alternate transcription of Hindi विनय or Telugu వినయ్ (see Vinay) or Thai วินัย (see Winai), both of the same origin.
Meaning uncertain. This name might possibly be an Old Norse cognate of Winand.

Derived from Georgian ვინ არის (vin aris) meaning "who is", which in turn is derived from the Georgian pronoun ვინ (vin) meaning "who" and the Georgian verb არის (aris) meaning "to be".This is an independent name that is likely intended to mean something along the lines of "Who could ever be like you?" (as in: no one can ever compare to the bearer of the name). However, it is possible that in some cases, Vinari is a short form of Mzevinar.

Means "vineyards" in Spanish, derived from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de las Viñas meaning "Our Lady of the Vineyards". She is the patron saint of various Spanish towns, especially of the city of Aranda de Duero in the province of Burgos (where the usage of the name is most concentrated), in which a sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin is located.According to folk legend, some locals from the town of Quintanilla de las Viñas were faced with the 8th-century Muslim invasion of Spain and fled with an image of the Virgin, taking refuge near the Douro river. Years later, the Virgin appeared to a farmer from Aranda de Duero to tell him where the image was hidden and where she wanted the sanctuary to be built. As the people of the city did not believe what the farmer said, the Virgin gave him a bunch of grapes as proof.

According to Hindu legends, Vinata is the mother of birds. She is one of the thirteen daughters of Prajapati Daksha. Married to Kashyapa along with her 12 sisters. She bore him two sons, named Aruṇá, and Garuda (Suparna).
Means "taking away, removing" in Sanskrit. This is an epithet of the Hindu god Ganesha.
MEANING - remover of obstacles, female leader, female preceptor, a term for wife of lord Ganesha
Derived from Old Norse vinr "friend" and bjǫrg "help, save, rescue".
Derived from vinca, the Latin name for the "periwinkle", ultimately from Latin vincio "to bind". This name has been in use since the 20th century.
Short form of Vincentė. In other words, you could say that this name is the feminine equivalent of Vincas.
Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Vincent.
Hungarian and Slovak feminine form of Vincent.
Croatian, Serbian, and Slovene feminine form of Vincent.
Banat Swabian variant of Vinzenz and Piedmontese and Romansh form of Vincent.
Lithuanian and Croatian feminine form of Vincent.
Feminine form of Vincentas. Also compare Vincė.
Name of a 7th century French Saint. He lived as a hermit in the forest near Corrèze, in the diocese of Tulle, France, praying, preaching and helping the poor.
Rare French feminine form of Vincent.
Archaic Italian form of Vincentius. This was used in Shakespeare's comedy 'Taming of the Shrew' (1593).
Romanian form of Vincentius (see Vincent). A notable bearer of this name was the Romanian lawyer, journalist and politician Vincențiu Babeș (1821-1907).
Romansh variant of Vincens and Milanese Lombard form of Vincent.
The name Vincia is used in the modern Italian language. It's a feminine form of Vincent.
A feminine form to Vincent.It was the name of the storm that flooded Hamburg in 1962.
Picard and Walloon form of Vincent.
Means "Come on a Cone" in Spanish
Taken from Mitravinda, one of the eight principal queen-consorts of the Hindu god Krishna.
Means "finding glory", from Old Persian vind meaning "to find" or "to provide" and farnah meaning "glory, splendour".

Means "belonging to the grape harvest", "of the vintage" or "born during the grape harvest". From vīndemia (“grape harvest”) +‎ -ālis (adjective-forming suffix), the latter from vinum (“wine”) +‎ demō (“take away”) +‎ -ia (“noun-forming suffix”).

Means "(female) grape harvester" in Latin. This is the name of the third brightest star in the constellation Virgo, and is so named because it rises in early autumn, the beginning of the wine harvesting season.
Means "wind-frozen". Svipdagr uses this as an alias when he goes to woo Menglǫð.
Perhaps from the surname Vine. This was borne by the Native American activist, writer and theologian Vine Deloria, Jr. (1933-2005).

Derived from Georgian ვინც ელის (vints elis) meaning "who is waiting" or "who is expecting", which in turn is derived from the Georgian pronoun ვინ (vin) meaning "who" and the Georgian verb ლოდინი (lodini) meaning "to expect, to await". Also compare names like Vinari and Velodi.
Means "deceased" in Chukchi. This name was given to children as a reference the spirits or souls of deceased ancestors or family members.
Italian form of Winfred and variant of Vinfrido.
Italian and Portuguese form of Winfred and Italian variant of Vinfredo.
Means "gulf, bay" in Vietnamese. It can also be from Sino-Vietnamese 詠 (vịnh) meaning "to describe in poetic language".
From Sino-Vietnamese 榮譽 (vinh dự) meaning "honor".
Means "honor, privilege", from Sino-Vietnamese 榮 (vinh) meaning "glory, honor" and 幸 (hạnh) meaning "luck, favor".
Means "everlasting, permanent", from Sino-Vietnamese 永 (vĩnh) meaning "perpetual, eternal" and 遠 (viễn) meaning "distant, remote, far".
MEANING - instruct, guide, educate, chastise, elicit, restore, avert, exel, accomplish, train, remove, induce, pay off, drive away
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Vinicianus.
This Roman cognomen is an extended form of Vinicius. A bearer of this name was Annius Vinicianus, a Roman senator from the 1st century AD.
From Sanskrit विनीतरुचि (vinītaruci) meaning "modesty, humility". Vinītaruci (?-594) was an Indian Buddhist monk who preached in China and Vietnam.

Derived from Gothic ''Winid-haria'' meaning "pasture-armyman" or "Winidas-armyman". In Tolkien's legendarium, this is the birth name of Eldacar, who is given a name from his mother's people due to his birth in Rhovanion.
Means "one who works on the vineyard, wine-grower". From the Latin vinitor.
Either derived from of Old Norse vinr "friend" and herr "army" or based on place names that contains the Old Norse element vin "meadow, pasture".
Transferred use of the surname Bin Laden. This is the middle name of Peruvian footballer Osama Vinladen Jiménez López, whose name was inspired by Islamic fundamentalist Osama bin Laden.

Combination of Vinnie with the French feminine diminutive suffix -ette (or with a name that contains it, such as Annette). Also compare the similar name Vinette, which can also be a surname.A notable bearer of this name is the American playwright and stage director Vinnette Justine Carroll (1922-2002).

Diminutive of Lavinia. A notable bearer was the American sculptor Lavinia Ellen "Vinnie" Ream Hoxie (1847-1914), known professionally as Vinnie Ream, who is most well known for her statue of President Abraham Lincoln on display in the United States Capitol rotunda. Vinnie Ream sculpted statues of other well known figures of the late 19th century.
Icelandic and Faroese variant of Winnie.
Breton diminutive masculine name derived from the name Gwenneg.

Means "good luck" in Malagasy. From vintana (meaning luck) and soa (meaning good).
Old Swedish form of Vetr meaning "winter" as well as the modern Scandinavian word for "winter" (see Winter).
Combination of Swedish vinter "winter" and ny "new".

Romanian name of unclear origin, used as both a masculine personal name and a family name. Vintilă Florescu was a Wallachian boyar who is said to have married Alexandra, daughter of Vlad II Dracul.
Transferred use of the surname Vinton.

Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Dzintra and a feminine form of Lithuanian Vintaras.
Belarusian form of the name Vincent.

Possibly from the Russian phrase Владимир Ильич не умрет никогда (Vladimir Ilinich nye umret nikogda) meaning "Vladmir Ilyich (Lenin) will never die". The ending нур (nur) is most likely influenced by the Bashkir word нур (nur) meaning "ray, beam (of light)", ultimately of Arabic origin. This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.
Variant of Venusha or feminine form of Vinushi.
Alternate spelling of the word vignette.
Variant of Feyel, recorded in medieval Frankfurt, Germany.
Icelandic and Faroese form of Viola.

Likely an elaboration of Violanda (a form of Violante) using the suffix andra (from names such as Alexandra and Cassandra). This was the name of a princess in the comedy Absurda Comica oder Herr Peter Squentz (1658) by Andreas Gryphius.
Italian variant and Romansh form of Violante.

Spanish word for "violence", which has been occasionally used as a given name.
Cognate of Violante. The name of a ghost character in Shakespeare's play 'All's Well That Ends Well' (first published 1623).

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai วีรยุทธ or วีระยุทธ (see Wirayut).

Possibly derived from Latin vir, meaning "man", and bis, meaning "twice", with the intended meaning of "twice a man". In Roman mythology, Virbius is the name given to the resurrected Hippolytus of Athens after he fell from his chariot to his death.
Possibly a diminutive of Alverda or other similar names.
Serbian, Macedonian and Lithuanian form of Virginia.
Alternate transcription of Khmer វីរៈ (see Virak).
From Sanskrit वीर (vīra) meaning "hero, man, brave" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra.
From Latin vireo, a word Pliny uses for some kind of bird, perhaps the greenfinch, from virere "be green" (see Viridius), which in modern times is applied to an American bird.

The first element of this name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vyrauti meaning "to prevail, to (pre)dominate", which is etymologically related to the Lithuanian noun vyras meaning "man". The second element is derived from old Lithuanian gailas, which usually means "strong, potent" but has also been found to mean "sharp, jagged" as well as "angry, fierce, violent" and "miserable, sorrowful, remorseful". Also compare the modern Lithuanian noun galia meaning "power, might, force".
Short form of masculine names that start with Virg-, such as Virgailas, Virgaudas and Virgilijus.

The first element of this name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vyrauti meaning "to prevail, to (pre)dominate", which is etymologically related to the Lithuanian noun vyras meaning "man". The second element is either derived from the Lithuanian verb gaudyti meaning "to take" as well as "to catch, to hunt" or from the Lithuanian adjective gaudus meaning "sonorous, resonant, ringing, loud, echoing".
Perhaps a blend of Virgie and Georgene.
Medieval form of Brígida. The respelling with V may be influenced by the word virgen "virgin".

German cognate of Fergal and Feirgil. This name used to Germanize Fergal and Feirgil in Austria and the southern part of Germany thanks to the Irish-born bishop and astronomer Virgilius von Salzburg (known in English as Vergilius of Salzburg).
Catalan. Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Virgil.
Portuguese, Catalan and Hungarian form Virgilia.
Feminine form of Vergilius (see Virgil). This is the name of Coriolanus' wife in Shakespeare's play of the same name.
Simply from the English word virgin, meaning "pure".
A known bearer of this name is the Romanian politician Virginel Iordache (b. 1959).

Derivative of Latin virgo meaning "maiden, virgin". According to Augustine, Virginiensis was a Roman goddess that presided over the loosing of the bridal zone, the zone being a belt or girdle worn by adult women which was meant to be knotted prior to a bride's wedding and untied by her husband on their wedding night; see also Cinxia.

The first element of this name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vyrauti meaning "to prevail, to (pre)dominate", which is etymologically related to the Lithuanian noun vyras meaning "man". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian verb ginti meaning "to defend, to protect".

The first element of this name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vyrauti meaning "to prevail, to (pre)dominate", which is etymologically related to the Lithuanian noun vyras meaning "man". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian noun girdas meaning "rumour", which is ultimately derived from the Lithuanian verb girdėti meaning "to hear". Also compare the related Lithuanian noun gandas meaning "rumour, hearsay".
Variant of Virgie, which itself is a diminutive of Virginia.
Alternate spelling of Vira or Virha
Possibly a female form of Viriato.

Viriathus was the most important leader of the Lusitanian people that resisted Roman expansion into the regions of western Hispania (as the Romans called it) or western Iberia (as the Greeks called it), where the Roman province of Lusitania would be finally established after the conquest.

From a Swedish fairy tale by Anna Maria Roos 'Prins Florestan eller sagan om jätten Bam-Bam och feen Viribunda' "Prince Florestan or the saga of he giant Bam Bam and the fairy Viribunda" that inspired Astrid Lindgren's novel 'Mio, my son'.The name contains the Latin word viridis "green; young, fresh, youthful" and the Latin suffix -bundus, together meaning "greening, florishing".
Viridi is the Goddess of Nature who debuted in the game Kid Icarus: Uprising, displaying the physical appearance of a sarcastic 8-year-old little girl who commands the Forces of Nature.
From the name of the blue-green pigment, which is derived from Latin viridis, meaning "green".
Ultimately from the Latin viridis meaning "green", it is cognate of Viridiana.
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Roman nomen gentile Viridius.

Derived from the Latin color word viridis "green".As a given name, Viridis was intended to refer to the colour of growing foliage and thus acquired the transferred meaning of "young; youthful; fresh; lively; blooming".A known bearer is Viridis della Scala (died 1394), daughter of Mastino II della Scala, lord of Verona, and wife of Niccolò II d'Este, lord of Ferrara, Modena and Parma.Her niece Viridis Visconti later went on to marry Duke Leopold III of Austria.

Latinized form of Viridios, which is of Celtic origin but the meaning is not known for certain. There are theories that it is derived from Proto-Celtic wird "green", or from Proto-Celtic wīrjā "truth" combined with dī- "from, has" (thus meaning "he who has the truth"). This was the name of a god who was venerated in Roman Gaul.-------------------------------------From a Roman nomen gentile, which was derived from Latin viridis "green".

Claimed to be a Mordvin name meaning "seeing in the forest". This was used for the title character of 'Virineya' (1969), a Soviet film which was ultimately based on a 1924 novel by Lidiya Seyfullina (1889-1954).
Mainly a diminutive of Virginia. This can also be a diminutive of Veronica and other names containing vir or ver.
Attia Viriola was a client of the ancient Roman lawyer and statesman Pliny the Younger (61-113), whose legal case he described in his Epistles.

Russian and Ukrainian form of Bathsheba via its modern Greek form Virsavee.

Virtrika (वीरत्रिका) is a unique, modern Indian name created from two powerful roots: "Vir" (meaning bravery or strength) and "Tri" (representing the divine trinity or Trishul). The name signifies One who carries strength, divine protection of the trinity, and uniqueness.In Marathi: “वीरत्रिका — धाडस, त्रिशक्तीचे संरक्षण आणि दिव्यता यांचे प्रतीक
This name was very occasionally used by Puritan parents in 17th century England. It ltimately derived from Latin virtus "manliness; valor; worth".
Means "virility, courage, virtue" in Latin. In Roman mythology, Virtus was the name of the god of bravery and military strength, with his Greek counterpart being Arete.
Means "growth, increase, sprout" in Sanskrit. This is the name of a deity in Buddhist tradition, one of the Four Heavenly Kings who rules over the south.
Derived from the Germanic name elements vé "home, temple, sanctuary" and rún "secret".

The first element of this name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vyrauti meaning "to prevail, to (pre)dominate", which is etymologically related to the Lithuanian noun vyras meaning "man". The second element is derived from Baltic vald meaning "rule" (see Visvaldas).
Directly taken from the Swedish word virvla "to swirl; to whirl".
Vīrya (Sanskrit; Pāli: Viriya) is a Buddhist term commonly translated as "energy", "persistence", "persevering", "vigour", "effort", "exertion", or "diligence". (Wikipedia)
From the Mordvin word вирь (vir') meaning "forest".
Means "large, vast, broad" or "good, excellent, fine" in Khmer, ultimately from Sanskrit विशाल (viśāla).
Basically means "a full salary" or "full of wages", derived from Baltic vis meaning "all" (see Visvaldas) combined with Lithuanian alga meaning "salary, wage, pay" as well as "reward".

Form of Bessarion (via Vissarion) in several languages.Notable bearers of this name include the 17th-century Bulgarian saint Visarion of Smolensk (also Smolyan) and the Serbian saint Visarion Saraj (1714-1744).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิศาล (see Wisan).

Means "undoubted son" in Old Norse. Visbur was a legendary Swedish king, son of Vanlandi and father of Dómaldi. He appears in the epic works 'Heimskringla' and 'Ynglinga saga' written in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson. Visbur also appears in the 9th century poem 'Ynglingatal', possibly written by the Norwegian skald Þjóðólfr ór Hvini.
Transferred use of the surname Vischer.
Visel is a name of German origin and the meaning is unknown

Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series of fantasy novels A Song of Ice and Fire and the television adaptation House of the Dragon (2022-). In the series, Visenya Targaryen is the older sister of Aegon the Conqueror, and one of the first two queens of Westeros. Visenya is also a name given to other Targaryen princesses.
The name Viserys is a name created by George R. R. Martin for his A Song Of Ice and Fire books.

Basically means "entirely strong", derived from Baltic vis meaning "all" (see Visvaldas) combined with old Lithuanian gailas, which usually means "strong, potent" but has also been found to mean "sharp, jagged" as well as "angry, fierce, violent" and "miserable, sorrowful, remorseful". Also compare the modern Lithuanian noun galia meaning "power, might, force".

The second element is either derived from the old Lithuanian verb gedauti meaning "to ask" or from the (more) modern Lithuanian verb gedėti meaning "to mourn, to grieve" as well as "to miss" and "to long, to yearn, to pine (for)".
Means "to defend all", derived from Baltic vis meaning "all" (see Visvaldas) combined with Lithuanian ginti meaning "to defend, to protect".

Basically has the (more or less) figurative meaning of "he who hears all", derived from Baltic vis meaning "all" (see Visvaldas) combined with the Lithuanian noun girdas meaning "rumour", which is ultimately derived from the Lithuanian verb girdėti meaning "to hear". Also compare the related Lithuanian noun gandas meaning "rumour, hearsay".

From Sanskrit विशाखा (viśākhā) meaning "branchless", derived from वि (vi) meaning "without" and शाखा (śākhā) meaning "branch". This is the name of the 16th nakshatra (lunar mansion) in Hindu astrology, as well as the name of a daughter of king Daksha in Hindu mythology.

Means "superior practice" from Sanskrit विशिष्ट (viśiṣṭa) meaning "distinguished, excellent, superior" and चारित्र (cāritra) meaning "conduct, behaviour, observance, practice". This is the name of a bodhisattva mentioned in the Buddhist text the Lotus Sutra, believed to represent the selflesness of Buddhahood.
Form of Vishnu chiefly used in Mauritius as well as an Indian variant.
This name comes from विष्णुव्रत (Viṣṇuchandra) meaning "moon of Vishnu" in Sanskrit

From viś "settlement, village" and bala "strong", "protecting the settlement" or "strong settlement". It's the name of a famous warrior queen in the Rigveda according to Griffith, a famous indologist. Another interpretation due to Karl Friedrich Geldner say that Viśpálā is a horse. In both cases, she lost her leg during the Khela battle (or race) and receive a iron one from the Ashvins. It's considered as one of the earliest mention of a prothesis and a female warrior.

Means "virtuous practice" from Sanskrit विशुद्ध (viśuddha) meaning "clean, pure, virtuous" and चारित्र (cāritra) meaning "conduct, behaviour, observance, practice". This is the name of a bodhisattva mentioned in the Buddhist text the Lotus Sutra, believed to represent the purity of Buddhahood.
Means "all, whole, world, universe" in Sanskrit. This is another name for the Hindu god Vishnu.

Means "being in everything" or "being everywhere" from Sanskrit विश्व (viśva) meaning "all, every" and भू (bhū) meaning "to be, place of being". In Buddhist tradition this is the name of the 24th of the 27 buddhas preceding Siddhartha Gautama, known in Pali as Vessabhū.
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi विश्वजीत (see Vishwajit).

From Sanskrit विश्वकर्मन् (viśvakarman) meaning "all-doing, all-making", derived from विश्व (viśva) meaning "all, every" and कर्मन् (karman) meaning "action, work". In Hindu mythology this is the name of the divine architect and craftsman of the gods. Originally the term was used as an epithet for any supreme deity, such as Indra and Surya.

Means "friend of the world" from Sanskrit विश्व (víśvā) meaning "world, universe" and मित्र (mitra) meaning "friend". This is the name of a renowned ancient Indian sage (rishi). The Gayatri Mantra in the Rigveda is traditionally attributed to him.
Means "lord of the universe" from Sanskrit विश्व (víśva) meaning "world, universe" and नाथ (nātha) meaning "master, lord". This is an epithet of the Hindu god Shiva.

Means "taking all forms, universal, omnipresent" from Sanskrit विश्व (viśva) meaning "all, every, whole, universe" and रूप (rūpa) meaning "shape, form". This is the name of the supreme form of the Hindu god Vishnu, depicted with thousands of heads and arms in Hindu iconography.
Alternate transcription of Hindi विश्व (see Vishva), as well as the Sinhala form.
Means "conquerer of the universe", from Sanskrit विश्व (viśva) meaning "all, whole, entire, every" or "world, universe" and जित् (jit) meaning "conquerer, conquering, defeating".
Alternate transcription of Hindi and Marathi विश्वनाथ (see Vishvanath), as well as the Konkani form.

Middle English (denoting a supernatural apparition) via Old French from Latin visio(n- ), from videre ‘to see.'

Old Norse name of unknown origin and meaning. Visna is the name of a warrior-like queen mentioned in the Gesta Danorum.

Vithimiris was a king of the Greuthungi, ruling for some unspecified time in the area of present-day southern Ukraine. He succeeded to Ermanaric, meaning that he probably reigned in 376. Ammianus Marcellinus, the only known source on him, states that after Ermanaric´s death he tried to resist the Alani, who were allied with the Huns, with the help of other Huns hired as mercenaries. He did so "for some time" (aliquantisper), but eventually, "after many defeats" (post multas clades), he died in battle. It is then assumed that he most probably ruled in 376, possibly also in 375.According to Herwig Wolfram, Vithimiris was "certainly not" the son of Ermanaric.

From the name विट्ठल (Viṭṭhala) of uncertain etymology. Another theory suggests the meaning of "one who receives the ignorant" from Sanskrit विद् (vid) meaning "knowledge, understanding", ठ (ṭha) meaning "cypher, privation, destitution" and ला (lā) meaning "to receive".This is the name of a regional Hindu god primarily worshipped in the Indian states of Maharashtra and Karnataka (and to a lesser extent Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Goa and Tamil Nadu). He is considered a form of Vishnu, specifically his avatar Krishna.

God whom endows the fetus with vita, "life" or the vital principle or power of life (see also quickening). These two gods, he suggests, should merit inclusion among the di selecti, "select" or principal gods, instead of those who preside over physical functions such as Janus, Saturn, Liber and Libera. Both Vitumnus and Sentinus were most likely names that focalized the functions of Jove.

In Nennius’s Historia Brittonum, Vortigern’s eldest son, brother of Catigern, Faustas, and Pascentius.When the lesser kings of Britain became disgusted with Vortigern’s open-door policy towards the Saxons, they placed Vortimer on the throne in his father’s place. Vortimer proved a much nobler king than his father. He led Briton armies against Hengist and the Saxons, and fought four battles against them.When he writes of Vortimer, Nennius employs the Welsh spelling Guorthemir. This has variants of its own, but the fifth-century original from which it derives as a British form Vortamorix, which, like Vortigern, would probably have been a title or designation. The syllable vor meant “over”; tamo- was a superlative suffix; rix meant “king”. As Vortigern is the “over-king”, so Vortimer is the “over-most” or “highest” king. Its etymological closeness to “Riothamus” or Rigotamos, the designation of a king who was certainly real, may be thought to favor Vortimer’s own reality.

In other words, this name is the Croatian and Serbian cognate of Wilkomir. A bearer of this name is retired Serbian football player Vukomir Mijanovic (b. 1978).

The first element of this name is derived from Serbo-Croatian vuk "wolf", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic vьlkъ "wolf". The second element is derived from Slavic slav "glory". The meaning of this name is thus roughly "glorious wolf". Bearers of this name include 14th-century Croatian duke Vukoslav Hrvatinić and 14th-century Serbian duke Vukoslav (head of the Vukoslavić noble family).

Also compare the modern Lithuanian noun galia meaning "power, might, force".

The first element of this name is derived from Baltic vyd meaning "to see" (see Vytautas). The second element is derived from the Lithuanian verb minėti meaning "to celebrate" as well as "to remember, to commemorate".

Also compare Vydutė.

The second element is derived from old Lithuanian gailas, which usually means "strong, potent" but has also been found to mean "sharp, jagged" as well as "angry, fierce, violent" and "miserable, sorrowful, remorseful". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian noun girdas meaning "rumour", which is ultimately derived from the Lithuanian verb girdėti meaning "to hear". Derived from Sanskrit वैजयन्ती (vaijayantī) meaning "banner, flag" combined with माला (mālā) meaning "garland, wreath". A known bearer is Vyjayanthimala Bali (1936-), a Tamil Indian actress and dancer.

A historical Lithuanian masculine name of Baltic origin, borne by a 13th-century duke of Samogitia who played a key role in early Lithuanian statehood and fought in the Battle of Saule against the Livonian Order. The name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vykti, meaning "to go", "to proceed", or "to happen". Its etymology can be broken down into the element vyk meaning "go" or "proceed", and the suffix -intas, a masculine participial form. The name can be interpreted to mean "he who proceeds" or "the one who goes forth".

Feminine form of Vykintas, a name of Baltic origin borne by a 13th-century Lithuanian duke who played a key role in the formation of the early Lithuanian state. The name is derived from the Lithuanian verb vykti, meaning "to go", "to proceed", or "to happen". Its etymology can be broken down into the element vyk meaning "go" or "proceed", and the suffix -intė, a feminine name-forming suffix. Thus, the name can be interpreted to mean "the one who proceeds" or "she who goes forth".
Probably an invented name based on the sound of names such as Isla, Lyla, Myla, Nyla, Kyla, etc, though it is possibly also viewed as a contracted variant of Viola.
An invented name combining the phonetic sound vy with the popular suffix lee, likely inspired by popular names such as Miley, Riley/Rylee, and Kylie/Kylee.

The first element of this name is either derived from Baltic vyd meaning "to see" or from Baltic vyti meaning "to chase, to drive away" (see Vytautas). The second element is derived from the Lithuanian noun liaudis meaning "people, folk", which is etymologically related to the Germanic element leud meaning "people" (see Leopold and Leutwin).

The first element of this name is either derived from Baltic vyd meaning "to see" or from Baltic vyti meaning "to chase, to drive away" (see Vytautas). The second element is derived from the Lithuanian verb liautis meaning "to stop, to cease".With that said, it should be noted that this name is sometimes encountered as a variant form or spelling of Vyliaudas.
