Means "white cloud", from Ojibwe waabaanakwad 'white cloud'.A noted bearer is Chief Wabanquot (c.1830 - 1898), born at Gull Lake, Minnesota. He succeeded to the office of chief of the Ojibwa at the death of his father, Wabojeeg, one of the principal chiefs for the Gull Lake Band of Mississippi Chippewa. After the Dakota War of 1862, the Gull Lake Band was removed to the Leech Lake area. There, Wabanquot was considered by many to be the principal chief of the removed Mississippi bands of Chippewa. He was a signatory to the Treaty of Washington (1867) (16 Stat. 719).

Means "green one; papyrus-colored one". From the Ancient Egyptian wadj, which was the word for the color green, in reference to the color of papyrus, and et, which indicated the name of a woman.In Egyptian mythology she was originally the ancient local goddess of the city of Dep, which eventually came to be known as Per-Wadjet ("house of Wadjet"). She was said the be the patron and protector of Egypt, formerly just of Lower Egypt. As a patron goddess she was associated with the land and thus frequently depicted as a woman with a snake's head, typically an Egyptian cobra, or a woman with two snakes' heads, or a snake with a woman's head. Because of her association with Lower Egypt she is sometimes also depicted as the sun disk, uraeus, which was the emblem on the crown of Lower Egypt.

Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.the variant 'Walwain" belongs to the Anglo-Norman "Insular" tradition of late 12th-century England and Northern France. It represents the phonetic stage where traveling Breton or Norman storytellers were actively speaking the name in England, retaining the Germanic and Celtic initial "W" instead of adopting the Central French "G" (Gauvain)The most famous literary showcase for this variant is found in the work of Marie de France, the earliest known French woman poet, who wrote her courtly "Breton Lays" for the Anglo-Norman court of King Henry II and Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine.The spelling is rooted to some of the earliest historical records written in Latin within England. Around 1125, English historian William of Malmesbury wrote his Gesta Regum Anglorum (Deeds of the English Kings).In it, he records that the 14-foot-long tomb of Arthur’s noble nephew had recently been discovered on the coast of Wales. William records his name in Latinized script as Walwen or Walwin, which were the descendants of the the vernacular Anglo-Norman spelling Walwain.

A variant form of Gawaine. The eldest son of King Lot of Orkney and Queen Morgawse (or Anna), Arthur’s sister or half-sister. Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.While standard translations of Geoffrey's text use Walgainus or Gualguanus, a prominent family of surviving 12th- and 13th-century Latin manuscripts explicitly utilizes Walwainus, such as "Arthur and Gorlagon", an anonymous Latin romance.Because of the heavy influence of the Norman conquest and Anglo-Latin literacy, latin names like Walwainus increasingly retreated to the realm of formalized Latin documentation.While William of Malmesbury originally wrote 'Walwen' in 1125, late 12th-century scribes copying or translating his work into standardized clerical Latin frequently updated it to Walwainus. In 12th-century Brittany and Western England, Norman and Breton knights who were named after the famous hero had their names recorded in formal Latin legal documents and property charters as Walwainus.

The meaning and origin of the first element of this Germanic name is very uncertain - at least five possible meanings exist. We know that it comes from varin, but we don't know where varin itself comes from. Latinized form of Warin. This was the name of a 7th-century Franco-Burgundian martyr, the son of Saint Sigrada and brother of Saint Leodegarius.
Means "heir, inheritor" in Arabic, from the root ورث (waritha) meaning "to inherit". In Islamic tradition الوارث (al-Warith) is one of the 99 names of Allah.
Of uncertain etymology, possibly deriving from the Dharug word warrawal ("milky way"). Name borne by an Eora woman who was the sister of prominent leader Bennelong.
Perhaps based on the English word war, as this name was most popular during WWII.

This name is derived from the word of the same name, which is another name for a wizard. The word used to mean "traitor" or "oath-breaker" since the word is derived from a combination of Old English wærloga "traitor, liar, enemy, devil", which comes from wær meaning "faith, fidelity, a compact, agreement, covenant" (from Proto-Germanic *wera-, which then comes from Proto-Indo-European *were-o- meaning "true, trustworthy"), and an agent noun related to leogan meaning "to lie."It was first used as a name in England in the 18th century. Since then, it maintained its very rare usage.Warlock is the name of a child believed to be the anti-Christ in 'Good Omens,' by Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett. It is also the title of a character in 'The Magic Went Away,' by Larry Niven.
Name of a Bishop of Konstanz (11th century).
Contraction of Warembold and Warimbold, which are both medieval variants of Warinbald.
Means "colour" in Indonesian and Sinhala, ultimately from Sanskrit वर्ण (varṇa). It is a unisex (more commonly feminine) name in Indonesia, while it is masculine in Sri Lanka.
Variant of Warinhar, probably influenced in its spelling by Old High German wachar "vigilant" (see Wacharulf).
Dutch variant form of Warner (see Werner).
Dutch and German form of Warinfrid.
From Javanese warna meaning "form, appearance, colour", ultimately from Sanskrit वर्ण (varṇa).
Place name; a town in the West Gipppsland region of rural Victoria in Australia. Its name is derived from warrigal, from a local language meaning "wild, wild dog (dingo)".
Of uncertain origin and meaning; theories include a short form of Walraven.
Means "winter, season of wet and cold" in one of the Indigenous languages from around the Sydney area.

From the English word meaning "soldier, person engaged in warfare" (and by extension "anyone fighting for a particular cause"), which comes from Anglo-Norman warrier, itself from Old French guerreier or guerroieor, from the same source as Medieval Latin guerra "war". It has been in occasional use as a personal name since the 19th century, and is also a surname (see Warrior).

Wars and Sawa are legendary characters from the origin myth of the founding and etymology of the city of Warsaw, capital of Poland. There are several versions of the legend with their appearance.According to one version of the legend, Sawa was a mermaid living in the Vistula river with whom a fisherman named Wars fell in love.
Means "good news", derived from Somali war meaning "information, news" and same "good, positive".

Means "good news", derived from Somali war meaning "news" combined with the Somali feminine name suffix -san, itself a derivative of Somali wanaagsan meaning "good". A notable bearer of this name is Warsan Shire (1988-), a British writer, poet, editor and teacher of Somali descent.
Derived from Sinhalese වැස්ස (væssa) meaning "rain", of Sanskrit origin (see Varsha).
From Javanese warsita meaning "teaching, advice, instruction, guidance", ultimately from Sanskrit भाषित (bhāṣita).
Alternate transcription of Burmese ဝါဆို (see Waso).
From Javanese warsa meaning "rain" or "year" combined with either the masculine suffix -na or ana meaning "being, having, holding".

Wart is the main antagonist of Super Mario Bros. 2, released for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1988. His name comes from the non-cancerous viral growths, usually occurring on the hands and the feet, but can also affect other locations, such as the genitals or the face.
Pomeranian form of Vratislav. Name of many dukes of Pomerania.
From Javanese warta meaning "news", ultimately from Sanskrit वार्त्ता (vārttā).
Means "the one from the west" in Kikuyu.
Means "rain" in Thai, derived from the name of the Hindu god Varuna.
Thai form of Varuni as well as a Sinhalese alternate transcription of the same name.
From Thai วรุณ (warun) meaning "water, ocean", derived from the name of the Hindu god Varuna, and ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour".
Means "one who possesses blessings", from the Thai element พร (pon) ("blessing, benediction, favour").
Alternate transcription of Thai วรัญญา (see Waranya).
Form of Barbara influenced by Russian Varvara.

column12: From Japanese 和 (wa) meaning "peace, harmony, Japan" combined with 沙 (sa) meaning "sand". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Alternate transcription of Arabic وسن (see Wassan).
Alternate transcription of Thai วาสนา (see Watsana).
Alternate transcription of Thai วสันต์ (see Wasan).
Alternate transcription of Sinhala වසන්ත (see Wasantha).
Means "spring (the season)" in Sinhalese, ultimately from Sanskrit वसन्त (vasanta).
Alternate transcription of Arabic وسيلة (see Wasila).
Alternate transcription of Arabic وسيمة (see Wasima).

column3: وسیم الدین(Shahmukhi, Urdu)|ਵਸੀਮੁੱਦੀਨ(Gurmukhi)|وسيم الدين(Sindhi-Arabic)|وسیم‌دین(Balochi)|वसीमुद्दीन(Hindi, Kashmiri Devanagari)|وَسیٖمُ الدیٖن(Kashmiri Arabic)
column12: Arabic-origin compound name consisting of elements Waseem and dīn.
Alternate transcription of Arabic واصل (see Wasil).

Alternate transcription of Arabic واثق (see Wathiq).
Combination of the name prefix Wa and Shawn, or from Quashawn.
From the surname English surname Washburn.

column3: 鷲夫, 鷲男, 鷲雄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 鷲 (washi) meaning "eagle" combined with 夫 (o) meaning "husband", 男 (o) meaning "male" or 雄 (o) meaning "manly". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Nickname of Cordell Walker in the TV series: 'Walker, Texas Ranger'. In the show, the name is claimed to be Cherokee for "lone eagle", although this is unlikely. The name is more likely inspired by the Washoe people.
Means "to be good; pretty; handsome; attractive" in Lakota. From the Lakota wašté (wash" tay).
Alternate transcription of Arabic وسيلة (see Wasila), as well as the Indonesian form.
Means "self-cultivator, self-judge, one who conquers their own desires" in Thai.
Alternate transcription of Arabic واثق (see Wathiq), as well as the Urdu form.
From the name of the fourth month of the traditional Burmese calendar, which roughly corresponds with the months of June and July.
German transcription of Vassa.The name is known from the play Wassa Shelesnowa by Maxim Gorki.
Alternate transcription of Thai วาสนา (see Watsana).
German transcription of Vasilisa.It is mainly connected to the Russian fairy tale Die schöne Wassilissa or Wassilissa, die wunderschöne "Vasilisa the beautiful".
Dutch form and Romani variant of Vashti.

Possibly a Germanic name in which the second element is rad meaning "counsel, advice". This was the name of the mother of Saint Gregory of Utrecht, a widow and model Christian matron of the 8th century who became a Catholic saint. In her later years she joined a religious community in Susteren, although it is uncertain whether she actually became a nun.
Means "wealth, riches" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वसु (vasu).

column3: わたこ(Japanese Hiragana)|綿子, 渡子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 綿 (wata) meaning "cotton" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible as well.
Alternate transcription of Thai วัฒนา (see Wattana).

column3: 渉, 渡, 渉理, 和多里, 和多利(Japanese Kanji)|わたり(Japanese Hiragana)|ワタリ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This is, essentially, a variant of Wataru (compare Hikari to Hikaru and Nozomi to Nozomu).This name can be used as 渉 (shou, wata.ru) meaning "ferry, ford, port" or 渡 (to, wata.su, wata.ru, watari) meaning "cross, ferry, ford, import, migrate."Examples of this name with 3 kanji include 和多里 and 和多利 with 和 (wa, o, ka, yawa.ragu/eru, nago.mu, nago.yaka, a.eru) meaning "harmony, peace," 多 (ta, oo.i, masa.ni/ru) meaning "many," 里 (ri, sato), referring to a unit of distance called ri, or otherwise meaning "village," and 利 (ri, ki.ku) meaning "profit, benefit, advantage."This name is rarely given.

column3: ワタルコ(Japanese Katakana)|わたるこ(Japanese Hiragana)|亘子, 渉子, 弥子, 渡流子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渡 (wataru) meaning "transit" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other combinations of kanji characters can form this name.
Means "vajra, lightning bolt, diamond" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वज्र (vajra).
From Thai วัชร (watchara) meaning "diamond" or "lightning bolt" and พล (phon) meaning "force, strength, power".
Alternate transcription of Thai วัชรี (see Watchari).
Means "lord of vajra" or "vajra of Indra" from Thai วัชระ (watchara) meaning "vajra, lightning bolt" and อินทร์ (in) referring to the Hindu god Indra (also meaning "lord, master").
Meaning, "watching or observing someone or something closely; alert and vigilant." Referring to watching and waiting for the end-times.
Welsh form of Watkyn or Watkin, a medieval English diminutive of Walter.
Alternate transcription of Arabic وتين (see Watin).
Alternate transcription of Thai วัฒนา (see Wattana).
Alternate transcription of Arabic واثق (see Wathiq).
Means "certain, sure, confident" in Arabic, from the root واثق (wāthaqa) meaning "to agree".

Means "bright path" in the Meskwaki-Sauk language, possibly in part from the Meskwaki-Sauk word wâpâthowa ("light, be bright"). This was the Meskwaki-Sauk name of Jim Thorpe, an American athlete and Olympic gold medalist.
Burmese form of Phra Mae Thorani.
Means "the Lord has loved us" in Shona.
Means "he (God) has given us again" in Tumbuka.
Perhaps a blend of Juanita and Latisha.
Means "let's go" in Balanta, spoken in Guinea Bissau.
Derived from Maori wātō rea meaning "sunset". This name was used for a tropical cyclone in 1976 near Australia.
Means "luck, fortune (brought about by merit or virtue)" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वासना (vāsanā).
Means "pretty girl" in Potawatomi, from the Potawatomi winsakeekyahgo "pretty girl".

Meaning uncertain. Possibly related to Old English hwatu "omen, divination", itself derived from Old Germanic *hwatō "incitement, motivation", or to wadan "to go, advance, travel". Watt or Wattus was a king in present-day Sussex in southern England, who ruled possibly around 692 to 700 CE.Unrelated, this was also a variant of Wat, used as a medieval short form of Walter.
Alternate transcription of Thai วัฒนา (see Wattana).
From Thai วัฒนะ (watthana) meaning "development, progress" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".

column3: วัฒนศักดิ์(Thai)
column12: From Thai วัฒนะ (watthana) meaning "development, progress" and ศักดิ์ (sak) meaning "power, honour".
Transferred use of the surname Watts.
Meaning "white crane", from Ojibwe waab- meaning "white" and ajijaak or ojijaak meaning "crane, sandhill crane".

Wauchier de Denain was a French writer and translator in the langue d'oïl, active at the start of the 13th century. He is most notable for writing the first and second continuations of Chrétien de Troyes' "Perceval".
From Old English wafian (verb), from the Germanic base of waver; the noun by alteration (influenced by the verb) of Middle English wawe ‘(sea) wave’.
Transferred usage of the surname Waveland.

From the place name Waveney, in occasional use as a given name since the 19th century.One bearer of this name was English (female) playwright Waveney Bicker-Caarten (1902-1990) who wrote under the name Waveney Carten.
Possibly from the Chinese 瓦 (wǎ) meaning "earthenware, pottery, tile" combined with itself.

A variant form of Gawaine. The eldest son of King Lot of Orkney and Queen Morgawse (or Anna), Arthur’s sister or half-sister. Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.

column3: 和々佳, 和々花, 和々香, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 和 (wa) meaning "peace, harmony" duplicated and combined with 佳 (ka) meaning "beautiful, good", 花 (ka) meaning "flower, blossom" or 香 (ka) meaning "fragrance". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 和 (wa) meaning "peace, harmony", 輪 (wa) meaning "wheel, flower" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other kanji combinations are also possible.
Sundanese diminutive of masculine containing the sound wan (or other similar sounds), such as Gunawan, Setiawan or Hermawan.
From Japanese 和 (wa) meaning "peace, harmony", 輪 (wa) meaning "wheel, flower" combined with 奈 (na) meaning "apple tree". Other kanji combinations are possible.
This is borne by Wawiriya Burton, an Australian Aboriginal artist from Pipalyatjara, who is also a ngangkaṟi (traditional healer).
Alternate transcription of Pashto واورينه (see Wowreena).
Means "one who is satisfied" in Taita.
From the Chinese 娃 (wá) meaning "doll, pretty girl" and 雪 (xuě) meaning "snow".
Transferred use of the surname Way.
From Balinese wayah meaning "old, mature", ultimately from Sanskrit वयस् (vayas) meaning "energy, strength, age" + balik "back". A name given to a 5th child.
Probably an invented names with the -ayden trend in names such as Jayden, Brayden, and Hayden
Variant of Waylon or Wayland using the phonetic element lyn.
Transferred use of the surname Wayman. A famous bearer is the late NBA basketball player and smooth jazz bassist Wayman Tisdale.
Probably a variant of Weimar.Waymar Royce is a character in the prolog of the first volume of 'The song of fire and ice' by GRR Martin.
Found academic translation is "French woman". This Ojibwe woman was married (young) to a French fur trader...
Allegedly intended as a feminine form of Wayne.
Rhyming variant of names such as Dayshawn and Kayshawn
Derived from Quechua wayta "flower" and mayu "river".
Thai form of Vayu, also used as a Thai word meaning "wind, air, breath, storm".
Derives from Old English weald "powerful, mighty" or "leader, ruler" and burg "fortress". Anglo-Saxon hypothetical form of Walburga. This was theorized to be the original name of Saint Walburga.
From Old English weald "powerful, mighty" or "leader, ruler" and helm "helmet, protection". Cognate to Germanic Waldhelm.
From Old English weald "powerful, mighty" or "leader, ruler" and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom".
Derived from the Old English elements weald "powerful, mighty" and ric "ruler, king". Old English cognate of Walderic.
Hypothetical Old English name, composed of weald "powerful, mighty" and wine "friend". This may be the source of the English surnames Walwyn or Woolwine.
Means "interpreter, translator" in Old English, derived from wealh "foreigner, Celt" and the unknown element stod.
Composed of Old English wealh "foreigner, Celt, slave" and þeow "servant". Wealhþeow is a queen of the Danes as the wife of king Hroðgar in the anonymous 8th-century epic poem 'Beowulf'.

From Middle English welth, welthe, weolthe (“happiness, prosperity”), from Old English *welþ, *weleþu, from Proto-Germanic *waliþō (“wealth”).Alternatively, possibly an alteration (due to similar words in -th: compare helth (“health”), derth (“dearth”)) of wele (“wealth, well-being, weal”), from Old English wela (“wealth, prosperity”), from Proto-Germanic *walô (“well-being, prosperity”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“good, best”); equivalent to weal +‎ -th.
Meaning, "having a great deal of money, resources, or assets; rich." In this case, spiritual blessings from God. From Middle English welthy, welþi, equivalent to wealth +‎ -y.
Alternate transcription of Arabic وئام (see Wiam).
Transferred use of the surname Weatherford.
Transferred use of the surname Weatherly.
Transferred use of the surname Weathers.
Transferred use of the surname Weaver 1 or Weaver 2.
Derived from the Dakota word wiiyaye meaning "sunset".
Transferred use of the surname Webb.
A knight in Arthur’s service who participated in the Roman War.
Diminutive of names formed with the secondary name element waz. The name element waz can be derived from warjaną (cf. Werner) or from wadją, probably from Gothic vadi "pledge, pact".
Feminine short form of names containing the Germanic name element WID "wood".
From the Scottish Surname Wedderburn. It has also been used as a given name.
Transferred use of the surname Wedge.

Transferred use of the surname Weedon. This was borne by the English actor and writer Weedon Grossmith (1854-1919), full name Walter Weedon Grossmith. It was also borne by Weedon Osborne (1892-1918), a U.S. Navy Dental Surgeon who was killed in World War I while carrying a wounded officer to safety on June 6, 1918, at age 25 years; he was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor, America's highest military decoration.
Many sites list is as meaning "pretty" in Sioux, when in fact it's a slang form of wikoska meaning "venereal disease". It's likely an invented name.
Short for Josephina taken from George Orwell's "The Time Machine," where the Weena is the name of the main love interest.

Means "Touching Leaves Woman" in the Unami (now extinct but being revitalized) language of the Lenape people. A notable bearer was Nora Thompson Dean (1907-1984), a traditionalist and one of the last fluent speakers of the southern Unami dialect of the Lenape language.
In reference to Luke 7:13, "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not."
Alternate transcription of Thai วีระ (see Wira).

Allegedly means "sweet heart" in the Native American Wampanoag language.A noted bearer is Weetamoo (c. 1635-1676), a Pocasset Wampanoag leader. She was born in the Mattapoiset village of the Pokanoket and died at Taunton River. Her father was Corbitant, sachem (chief) of the Pocasset tribe in present day North Tiverton, Rhode Island She had five husbands, the most famous of whom was Wamsutta, the eldest son of Massasoit, grand sachem of the Wampanoag and participant in the first Thanksgiving with the Pilgrims.
The orphaned heroine of Lost on the Trail by Isabella Macdonald Alden, well-known 19th century American, Christian author.
Possibly a diminutive form of Old English names beginning with weoh "idol, image" or "sacred, holy", such as Weohstan. This was the name of one of the first kings of East Anglia.
From the Chinese 薇 (wēi), a type of fern, and 安 (ān) meaning "quiet, calm, peaceful, safe".

column3: 伟光, etc.(Chinese)|偉光, etc.(Traditional Chinese)

From the Chinese 玮 (wěi) meaning "rare, valuable", or the name of a type of jade, and 娜 (nà) meaning "graceful, elegant, delicate".

The name is made up from the German word Welle "wave" and the name element gunda "battle".A Rhinemaiden, one of the three water-nymphs (Rheintöchter or "Rhine daughters") who appear in Richard Wagner's opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen, the others being Woglinde and Flosshilde. Of the 34 characters in the Ring cycle, they are the only ones who did not originate in the Old Norse Eddas. Wagner created his Rhinemaidens from other legends and myths, most notably the Nibelungenlied which contains stories involving water sprites (nixies) or mermaids of the Danube. The Rhinemaidens are the first and the last characters seen in the four-opera cycle, appearing both in the opening scene of Das Rheingold, and in the final climactic spectacle of Götterdämmerung, when they rise from the Rhine waters to reclaim the ring from Brünnhilde's ashes.

From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 欣 (xīn) meaning "happy, joyous, delighted" or 新 (xīn) meaning "fresh, new". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 文兴, etc.(Chinese)|文興, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 兴 (xīng) meaning "rise, start, flourish, prosper". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 雄 (xióng) meaning "hero, male, manly" or 熊 (xióng) meaning "bear (animal)". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 玟 (wén) meaning "streaks in jade, gem" and 绣 (xiù) meaning "embroidery, ornament".
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 栩 (xǔ) meaning "be glad, pleased", also a species of oak, or 煦 (xù) meaning "kind, gentle, gracious".

column3: 文轩, 文宣, 文瑄, 文萱, etc.(Chinese)|文軒, 文宣, 文瑄, 文萱, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 轩 (xuān) meaning "high, lofty, tall" and also referring to a type of high-fronted curtained carriage, 宣 (xuān) meaning "declare, announce", 瑄 (xuān) referring to a type of large ornamental piece of jade or 萱 (xuān) meaning "orange daylily" (scientific name Hemerocallis flava). Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" or 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" and 雪 (xuě) meaning "snow".
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 勋 (xūn) meaning "meritorious deeds".
From Chinese 文雅 (wényǎ) meaning "elegant, refined". Other combinations of Wen and Ya are possible.

From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "language, writing" or 汶 (wèn) referring to a river in China combined with 雁 (yàn) "wild goose" or 岩 (yán) "cliff, mountain", as well as other character combinations that can form this name.
From 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 瑤 (yáo) and meaning "jade, mother of pearl". Other Hanzi combinations can be used.
From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" and 岩 (yán) meaning "cliff, rocks" Other character combinations are possible.

column3: 文怡, 文意, 文一, 文漪, 文仪, 温义, etc.(Chinese)|文儀, 溫義, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
文怡, 文意, 文一, 文仪, 文漪, 温义, etc.(Chinese)|文怡, 文意, 文一, 文儀, 文漪, 溫義, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" or 温 (wēn) meaning "warm" combined with 怡 (yí) meaning "joy, harmony", 意 (yì) meaning "thought, mind, idea, sense", 一 (yī) meaning "one", 仪 (yí) meaning "ceremony, rites", 漪 (yī) meaning "ripple, wave" or 义 (yì) meaning "justice, righteousness". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 殷 (yīn) meaning "many, great, abundant, flourishing".

column3: 文英, 文颖, etc.(Chinese)|文英, 文穎, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 英 (yīng) meaning "flower, petal, brave, hero" or 颖 (yǐng) meaning "clever, skillful, ear of grain, tip". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 友 (yǒu) meaning "friend, companion, friendly".

column3: 文宇, 文玉, 文雨, 文钰, 文裕, etc.(Chinese)|文宇, 文玉, 文雨, 文鈺, 文裕, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 宇 (yǔ) meaning "house, eaves, universe", 玉 (yù) meaning "jade, precious stone, gem", 雨 (yǔ) meaning "rain", 钰 (yù) meaning "metal, treasure" or 裕 (yù) meaning "abundant, rich, plentiful". This name can be formed from other combinations of characters as well.

column3: 文元, 文媛, 文渊, 文远, etc.(Chinese)|文元, 文媛, 文淵, 文遠, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" combined with 元 (yuán) meaning "first, origin", 媛 (yuàn) meaning "beautiful woman", 渊 (yuān) meaning "deep, profound, abyss" or 远 (yuǎn) meaning "distant, remote, far". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 文岳, 文樾, 雯越, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 越 (yuè) meaning "exceed, go beyond". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 昭 (zhāo) meaning "bright, luminous".
From the Chinese 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns" and 祯 (zhēn) meaning "lucky, auspicious, good omen".
From the Chinese 玟 (wén) meaning "streaks in jade, gem" and 珠 (zhū) meaning "bead, pearl, precious stone, gem".

Derived from the Old English elements weoh "idol, image" or "sacred, holy" and stan "stone". Cognate to Old Norse Vésteinn. This name was borne by an ealdorman of Wiltshire at the beginning of the ninth century.
Diminutive of Old English names beginning with he element weoh- "idol, image" or "holy, sacred".

Composed of the Old English elements weorc meaning "work" and guð meaning "battle". This unattested/reconstructed name might have given rise to the name of Worsley, a village in the historic county of Lancashire, England; according to the Dictionary of British Place Names, the place name could mean "woodland clearing of a woman named Weorcgyth or a man named Weorchaeth" (the second element in either case being Old English leah).
Possibly derived from Old English weorþ "worth, deserving, honoured, esteemed" and giefu "present, gift".
A name of unknown meaning used in Ancient Egyptian times.A notable Wepay was a wife of Djefai-Hapi I, nomarch of Asyut and high priest of the nome's temples during the 1800s BCE.
Means “he open the ways” in Egyptian. In Egyptian mythology he was the God of war and funerary rites.
Latinized form of Wærburg (see Werburg). This was the name of a 7th-century English saint and the patroness of Chester. She was the daughter of King Wulfhere of Mercia and Saint Ermenilda.

Variant of Warinfrid via the Latinized form Werinfridus or Werenfridus. This was the name of an 8th-century saint and Benedictine missionary, also known as Werenfridus, who was allegedly born in England and assisted Saint Willibrord in his labors to convert the Frisians to Christianity.
Dutch and German form of Warnfried.
From Egyptian wr-n-r, the first element derived from wr "big, great, important; chief".
Means "great one of magic", "great enchantress" in Ancient Egyptian. This was the name of an Ancient Egyptian goddess, the personification of supernatural power.
Possibly composed of the elements wer "true" and mund "protector".
Dutch form and German variant of Wernhard.
A Finnish variant form of Werner.
From the Germanic name element warin "guard" and fridu "peace".
Diminutive of names that contain the Germanic element warin (related to war meaning "aware, cautious"), such as Werner and Wernfried.
Middle English Latinised form of Anglo-Saxon name Weorðgifu.
Meaning "of beauty; a girl or woman of beauty".
Derived from Old High German wara "protection, watch" and Old High German walt "power, authority".
Alternate transcription of Arabic وصال (see Wisal).
Variant of Wesley, more commonly used for girls.
Combination of Wesley and a variant of the popular name suffix -lynn in an attempt to create a feminine form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic وسام (see Wisam).
German transcription of the Bulgarian name Veselin.
German transcription of the Bulgarian name Veselina.
Possibly a unisex diminutive of Wesley.
From the English word, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *wes-pero- "evening, night". It may also be considered transferred use of the surname West or a short form of Weston.
Of uncertain origin and meaning; a derivation from Wetser has been suggested.
From the English word "western" meaning "from the west" or from the surname Western.
Combination of 'West' and the popular name suffix -lyn.
Possibly a Geʽez form of Eutychius. This was the name of a Coptic Christian saint, listed in the Ethiopian Coptic Church calendar, who was a follower and disciple of the apostles.
A Zuni name of unknown etymology. We'wha was a Zuni Native American lhamana from New Mexico, and a notable weaver and potter.
Variant of Waylon sometimes used for girls.
Probably a feminine form to Weimar.The name is borne by the German philosopher Weyma Lübbe.
Variant of Weimar.Weymar Rois is the name of Waymar Royce in the German translation of 'The song of ice and fire'.
Variant of Wyntje. This name was found among Dutch colonists in America in the 1600s and 1700s.

column3: Уэз, Оз(Western Circassian, Eastern Circassian, Circassian)

column12: Derived from Arabic al-wazn, meaning "weight". This is the traditional name of the star Delta Canis Majoris in the constellation Canis Major.
From Arabic وزير (wazir), meaning "assisant" and geldi meaning "came, arrived".

column3: Уэзтемыр, Уэздемыр, Оздемыр, Озтемыр(Western Circassian, Eastern Circassian, Circassian)

column12: The first name of the 1992 Miss World contestant from Columbia.
Means "thunder" in Maori. Whaitiri is the female personification of thunder in Maori mythology. She is a blind, cannibalistic goddess.
Means "crashing thunder" in Maori. This is one of the names of Whaitiri.
Means "dramatic" in Māori. Whakaari/White Island (Te Puia Whakaari, lit. "the dramatic volcano") is an active stratovolcano situated in the Bay of Plenty in New Zealand's North Island.
Transferred use of the surname Whalen.
Transferred use of the surname Whaley.

Means "house of Kauri" in Māori. Māori name for the Chatham Islands since 1835. This came from a settlement on Chatham Island named Wharekauri. Moriori, the inhabitants of the Chatham Islands called the islands, Rēkohu.

This name means "school of learning". Its also the name of a building where tohunga (priest) taught esoteric lore to students of his. This was the name of a Ngati Tama chief named Te Wharekura of the Ngati Wai Ngati Tama clan who along with his clan killed and cooked 50 Moriori in the mid-1800s at Te Raki in what is now Chatham Islands.
Transferred use of the surname Wharton.
English translation of Latin quod vult Deus meaning "whatever God wants", referring to the will of God. Also see Quodvultdeus.
Transferred use of the surname Wheat. Famously borne by Wheat Carr.
Wheatley is a fictional artificial intelligence from the Portal franchise first introduced in the 2011 video game Portal 2.
Transferred use of the surname Wheaton.

This is a name of Korean origin. It means, "shining person".Jung Whee-in (1995-) is a South Korean singer who goes under the mononym, 'Wheein'. She is one of four members of South Korean girl group 'MAMAMOO'.
Transferred use of the surname Wheeler.
Transferred use of the surname Wheelock.
Transferred use of the surname Whelan.
Means "land, nation" in Maori. Cognate of Fenua.

This particular spelling of the given name Wilhelmina originated in older times, when people had varying degrees of literacy and when the Dutch and German languages were not yet standardized to the degree that they are today. Because of this, it could be considered a misspelling or a corruption of the name. However, the spelling could also simply have been influenced by the related name Gulielmus, which was sometimes written as Ghulielmus in older times, just like many other words and names starting with g- or G-.However it came about, one thing is for certain: this particular spelling of the name has always been very rare and little known. The dominant and most widespread form and spelling has always been Wilhelmina.
Variant of Wim, coinciding with an English word meaning "a whimsical idea".
Māori form of Josephine, and short for Āwhina. Dame Whina Cooper (born Hōhepine Te Wake; 1895-1994) was a Māori activist from New Zealand, her activism helped to improve the rights for Māori people.
From the English word whisper, meaning "speaking softly without vibration of the vocal cords", itself from Proto-Germanic *hwisprōną (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”).
Possibly from the English word "white" or a diminutive of Whitney or other names beginning with Whit.
Transferred use of the surname Whitcomb.
Transferred use of the surname White.
Transferred use of the surname Whitefield.
Probably inspired by the White House, the house of the American President
Transferred use of the surname Whitelaw.
A nickname given to people often in reference to white skin or hair color.

Transferred use of the surname Whitfield. A known bearer of this surname as a first name is the American cryptographer Whitfield Diffie (b. 1944), son of American historian, professor and author Bailey Wallys Diffie (1902-1983).
Transferred use of the surname Whitford.
Transferred use of the surname Whitman.
Transferred use of the surname Whitmore.
Transferred use of the surname Whitson.
Name given in relation to Whitsuntide, referring to the time around Pentecost.
Diminutive of Whitney, Whitaker, or other names starting with Whit-.
Transferred use of the surname Whittaker, a variant of Whitaker.
Variant of Whitney influenced by Brittany.
Transferred use of the surname Whitton or a variant of Whitten.
Short form of names beginning with Whitt-.
Meaning, "conducive to or promoting moral well-being."
Whoopi Goldberg is the stage name of Caryn Elaine Johnson.The name Whoopi derives from the word whoopee cushion "farting bag".
Alternative spelling of whin, an evergreen bush.
West Frisian pet form of feminine Germanic names containing the element wig meaning "war, battle".
Alternate transcription of Arabic وئام (see Wiam).
From Thai เวียง (wiang) meaning "walled city, town" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Directly taken from Polish wiara "belief, faith", reinforced by the Slavic names Vera 1 and Vjera.

Derived from Polish wiara "faith, belief, trust" (which is probably ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic věra "faith, belief") combined with Slavic slav "glory". The meaning of this name is thus roughly "glorious faith".

This name is often encountered as a variant form of Wigbald and Witbald. However, it can also be a name in its own right, in which case its first element is derived from either Old High German wîh meaning "holy, sacred" or from Old High German wîp meaning "woman". As with the aforementioned names, the second element of the name is derived from Old High German bald meaning "bold, brave".

Frisian short form of names whose first element is derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" or Gothic vilja "will, desire." Also, the second element of those names starts with a "b", e.g. Wibrand and Wilbert.

This name is often encountered as a variant form of Wigbert and Witbert. However, it can also be a name in its own right, in which case its first element is derived from either Old High German wîh meaning "holy, sacred" or from Old High German wîp meaning "woman". As with the aforementioned names, the second element of the name is derived from Old High German beraht meaning "bright".
Polish form of Vibiana, used in reference to the saint.
A diminutive of Wibo.It is the name of the founder of the German town Wiebelskirchen (now part of Neunkirchen (Saar)).

Javanese and Sundanese form of Vibhishana. In Javanese wayang (shadow puppetry) he is a younger brother of the demon king Rahwana. He ultimately sides with the hero Rama and becomes king of Alengka after his elder brother's defeat.
Saint Wiborada is a famous bearer.

This name is often encountered as a variant form of Wigbrand and Witbrand. However, it can also be a name in its own right, in which case its first element is derived from either Old High German wîh meaning "holy, sacred" or from Old High German wîp meaning "woman". As with the aforementioned names, the second element of the name is derived from Old Norse brand meaning "sword".
Feminine form of Wibrand.It is the name of one of the lengendary companions of St. Ursula

Frisian form of Wibern, an ancient Germanic given name which was often encountered as a variant form of Wigbern and Witubern. However, it can also be a name in its own right, in which case its first element is derived from either Old High German wîh meaning "holy, sacred" or from Old High German wîp meaning "woman". As with the aforementioned names, the second element of the name is derived from Proto-Germanic beran or bernu meaning "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German).With that said, it should be noted that in Frisia, the name Wibren has also been used as a variant form of Wibrân.
From Javanese wicaksana meaning "wise, experienced", ultimately from Sanskrit विचक्षण (vicakṣaṇa).
From Lakota wičháȟpi "star" and wakȟáŋ "sacred, holy".
Old English personal name derived from wicga "insect, earwig". This byname gave rise to the surname Wignall.
Means "knowledge, subject" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit विद्या (vidyā).
Dutch, Frisian and German form of Wighard.
Alternate transcription of Thai วิเชียร (see Wichian).
Means "exquisite, beautiful, fine" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit विचित्र (vicitra).
The name of a character from the 2009 movie "Zombieland". Wichita is also a city in Kansas, United States.
From Thai วิจิตร (wichit) meaning "exquisite, beautiful, fine".
Alternate transcription of Thai วิชชุดา (see Witchuda).
Bishop and Catholic saint, also called Wicho.
From Sanskrit विध (vidha) meaning "form, manner, act".
Sundanese form of Widodo, as well as a Javanese variant.
From Javanese widagda meaning "clever, knowledgeable, adept, skilled", ultimately from Sanskrit विदग्ध (vidagdha).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิชชุดา (see Witchuda).
Alternate transcription of Arabic وداد (see Widad) chiefly used in North Africa.

Derived from the Old Prussian adjective videvis meaning "aware, informed" as well as "known" combined with an Old Prussian diminutive suffix that is the equivalent of the modern Lithuanian masculine diminutive suffix -utis. Also see Vaidevutis and Videvutis.This name is best known for being the name of a legendary king of the Old Prussians, who is said to have lived in the 6th century AD.
Derived from the Old English elements wīd "wide" (from wīdaz) and here "army". Cognate to Old Norse Víðarr.
Derived from Sanskrit विधि (vidhi) meaning "rule, law, fate, destiny".
Older spelling of Wiji influenced by Dutch orthography.
German name composed of the elements witu "wood" and mari "famous".
From Javanese widada meaning "safe, healthy, successful, prosperous".
From Javanese widayaka meaning "wise man, poet", ultimately from Sanskrit विधायक (vidhāyaka).
Benedictine abbot of Flavigny, France, also called Ware.
Alternate transcription of Thai วิษณุ (see Witsanu).
meaning- learned or clever, skilled, intelligent
From the name of a type of shrub that produces white or lavender-coloured flowers (scientific name Calotropis gigantea).
Means "blessings, good wishes, worship, praise" in Javanese.
Combination of the name Widya and the feminine suffix -wati.
From Javanese widya meaning "knowledge", ultimately from Sanskrit विद्या (vidyā).
Old Polish name for men, composed of members Więce "more" and Mil "nice" . Means "one who is nicer than the others".
Variant of Wiebe or from Low German and Old Frisian wîf meaning "wife, woman".
Variant of Wiebke or diminutive of Wiefe.
Wieger is a derivative from Wigger, composed of the elements wig "war, battle" and heri "army".
Limburgish short form of Wilhelmus and Willibrordus.Known Limburgian bearers of this name include the soccer player Wiel Coerver (1924-2011) and the politician Wiel Nolens (1860-1931).
From Polish wielki "great, large" and sława "glory".
Alternate transcription of Arabic وئام (see Wiam) chiefly used in North Africa.
18th-century coinage of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Więcesław, influenced by Russian Vyacheslav.
Variant form of Wiard.Known Dutch bearers of this name include the long distance ice skater Wierd Wijnia (1925-1998) and the long track speed skater Wierd Osinga (b. 1987).
Polish masculine name, possibly meaning a person who comes from Wierzchosław in Goleniów County.

Means "to believe in peace", derived from Polish wierzyć "to believe, to trust, to rely" (which is probably ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic věra "faith, belief") combined with Slavic mir "peace".

This name is unisex in Dutch and Flemish, but strictly feminine in Limburgish.For male bearers, Wies is a short form of Aloïs, Aloysius and Louis.For female bearers, the name is a short form of Aloysia, Louisa and Louise.This name is far more commonly seen on women than on men in the Netherlands, especially as an official given name on birth certificates. The exact opposite applies to Flanders (the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium).

The name Wiet is mostly used in West Frisian, but can be found in every part of the Netherlands. The name is derived from Wietse. The meaning of the name is "voluntarily" and "warned". The name is also the dutch translation of "weed".
Variant spelling of Wytse.Known bearers of this name include the Dutch archer Wietse van Alten (b. 1978) and the Dutch programmer and physicist Wietse Venema (b. 1951).
Frisian and Low German variant of Wiefe.
Frisian and Low German variant of Wiefke.
Possibly a Romani form of William or a transferred use of the surname Wiflin.
Derived from the Old English elements wif "woman, wife" and run "whisper, secret, runic letter".
The title hero of an Arthurian novel by Wirnt von Grafenberg.
A rare personal name from the town so-named in Lancashire, itself apparently derived from a Celtic personal name.It could also be a variant of Wigand.
Means "bold warrior", derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Derived from Old High German wîg meaning "warrior" combined with Proto-Germanic beran or bernu meaning "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German).
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Gothic biutan "to offer" or Old High German boto "bid, offer."
Derived from the Old English elements wig "war, battle" and flæd possibly meaning "beauty".
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Derived from the Old English elements wig "war"and friþ "peace". Old English cognate of Wigfrid.
A dithematic name formed from the name elements wig "battle" and ger "spear".
Derived from the Old English elements wig "war, battle" and heah "high". This was the name of an 8th century Bishop of London.
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Old High German helm "helmet, protection."
Possibly a German form of Vigilius.

From Old English wig "battle, war" and laf "remains, remainder" (see laibō).In the epic poem Beowulf, Wiglaf son of Weohstan (weoh, with guttural H, is a variant pronunciation of wig) is a loyal thane and distant relative who succeeds Beowulf as king of the Geats.Wiglaf was also the name of a king of Mercia in the early 9th Century. His son was Wigmund, and his grandson Wigstan.A modern bearer of the name is the German satirist Wiglaf Droste.
Old English cognate of Wigmar. Derived from the elements wig "war, battle" and mære "famous, illustrious, known" meaning "famous war".
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with man "man."
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Gothic nand "bravery" (or Gothic nanthjan "to venture, to risk, to dare").
From Javanese wignya meaning "clever, wise, capable, skilled", ultimately from Sanskrit विज्ञा (vijñā).
English form of Vigarr, Wīggār, or Wiggēr.
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with hraban or hramn "raven."
Derived from the Old English elements wig "war, battle" and ric "ruler, king". The surnames Guerry and Weigrich are derived from this name.
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with þruþ "strength."
Derived from Old High German wîg "warrior" combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Means "sweetgrass" in Cree. This was the name of a 19th-century Crow man who became one of the leading Plains Cree chiefs in the Battleford region of Saskatchewan, Canada.

From the Old English elements wiht meaning "living being, creature, person" and gar "spear". This was the name of an 11th-century East Anglian thegn (whose paternal grandfather was also named Wihtgar). It was used by Bernard Cornwell for one of the primary antagonists in his series of historical novels The Saxon Stories (2004-2020) as well as the television adaptation The Last Kingdom (2015-2022).
Derived from the Old English elements wiht "thing, creature" and lāc "play, sport" or "gift, offering" (from laikaz).
Derived from the Old English elements wiht "thing, creature" and mund "protection".
Derived from the Old English elements wiht "creature, being" and ræd "counsel, advice".
Derived from Sanskrit विजय (vijaya) meaning "victory". It is sometimes used as a feminine name in Indonesia.

Derived from Sanskrit विजयतुङ्गदेवी (vijayatuṅgadevi) meaning "victory of the high goddess". This name was borne by Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi (also known as Tribhuwannottunggadewi Jayawishnuwardhani (from Sanskrit त्रिभुवनतुङ्गदेवी जयविष्णुवर्धनी (tribhuvanatuṅgadewi jayavishnuvardhani) meaning "high goddess of the three worlds, victory of Vishnu's prosperity"), a Javanese queen regnant and the third Majapahit monarch, who reigned from 1328 to 1350.
Means "emotion, affection, compassion, conscience" in Arabic.
Means "seed, grain, point, mark" in Javanese, ultimately from Sanskrit बीज (bīja).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิจิตร (see Wichit).
Alternate transcription of Thai วิจิตรา (see Wichitra).

Dutch form of Winand. Known bearers of this name include the Dutch painter Wijnand Nuijen (1813-1839), the Dutch self-taught artist Wijnand Otto Jan Nieuwenkamp (1874-1950) and the Dutch general Johan Wijnand van Goor (1650-1704).
Variant form of Winanda. In other words, you could say that this name is the feminine form of Wijnand.
Dutch diminutive of names that contain the element wijn or win, both of which ultimately come from Old High German wini "friend".
Older spelling of Wiyono influenced by Dutch orthography.
Likely derived from Old Dutch wit, meaning "white" and man, meaning "man".
Wikash (derived from the Hindi name Vikas) means expanding, progress or development in Sanskrit. It is often used as a male name in (Greater) India.
Means “week” in Maori. Also Maori form of Vicky.
Frisian short form of names that contain the Old High Germanic element wîg, such as Wigbert and Wigmar.

Derived from Sanskrit विक्रम (vikrama) meaning "stride, pace, valour" and वर्धन (vardhana) meaning "increasing, growing, thriving". This was the name of the fifth king of the Majapahit Empire who reigned from 1389 to 1429.
Means "courage, bravery" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit विक्रम (vikrama).
Hopi name meaning "one who brings", derived from Hopi wíkva "bring, fetch" (plural wíkvaya).

"Sister goddess" of Embeth and Borbeth and one of "The Three Bethen" or "Three Virgins", a group of allegedly pre-Christian goddesses who later became "unofficial" saints.Their cult is somewhat of a mystery: having been known since the Middle Ages, it is only regionally distributed, mainly in Bavaria, Baden, South Tyrol, Alsace (above all Strasbourg) and the Rhineland. If there had ever been antique records of this Triple Goddess cult, those have been lost. The oldest authentic records of Wilbeth date back to the 14th century, when she was quickly linked to Embeth whose veneration had been attested since the 12th century.Either way, their cult became fairly popular when the "girls" got appointed companions of Saint Ursula in the 15th century.The origins and meanings of their names have been lost to time. Since the Romantic period, there have been speculations that their names might be corruptions of some not yet identified Ancient Germanic names - a theory which in recent times is being taken more and more seriously. Research on it is being done.
Transferred use of the surname Wilbraham.

Medieval Spanish name of Visigothic origin. Most notable bearer was Wilesindo, bishop of Pamplona between the years of 845 and 860.
Diminutive of names beginning with Wilf-, like Wilfred.
Derived from Old English willa meaning "will, desire" and Old English flæd, possibly meaning "beauty".

Variant or corrupted form of Vulfedrudis, which was a Latinized form of Wulfetrude or Wulftrude, itself derived from the Germanic elements wolf meaning "wolf" and drud "strength" (alternatively, the second element could be *trut "maiden"). Compare the Old English cognate Wulfthryth, which has been Latinized as Wilfrida.This was the name of a 7th-century Frankish saint; also known as Wulfetrude and Vulfetrude, she was a niece of Saint Gertrude who co-founded the Benedictine abbey of Nivelles in Brabant, Belgium. Wilfretrudis succeeded her aunt as abbess of Nivelles in 659.
Latin form of the Old English name Wulfþryð meaning "wolf strength". This was the name of the mother of Saint Eadgyð (Edith) by King Edgar the Peaceful.
Transferred use of the ancient surname Wilgar having Olde English and Scottish origins.

The first element of this name is derived from Gothic vilja "will, desire." The second element is derived from gardan "to hedge in, to enclose, to fence in" or from Gothic gards "house, garden, (court)yard."

This name is best known for being the name of a late medieval saint, who was discovered to be fictional in the late 16th century but continued to be venerated in some places until 1969, when the Church finally removed her from the liturgical calendar and supressed her cult. Her feast day used to be on July 20th. In addition to her own name, the saint is also known under an epithet in several countries, such as Uncumber in England, Kümmernis in Germany and Livrade in France.Saint Wilgefortis was a young girl who had taken a vow of chastity. When later her father arranged for her to be married, she prayed to God and asked him to make her so unsightly that her prospective husband would refuse to marry her, thus enabling her to stay true to her vow. God heard her prayer and answered it by giving her a beard and a moustache, which ended up successfully repelling her betrothed. However, this turn of events angered her father so much that he subsequently had his daughter crucified.The etymology of her name is uncertain. It is often said to be derived from Latin virgo fortis meaning "strong maiden", which in turn is derived from the Latin words virgo meaning "maiden, virgin, young woman" (see Virgo) and fortis meaning "strong" as well as "brave, courageous". However, an equally plausible possibility is that the name is actually a corruption of medieval German hilge vartz (also fratz) meaning "holy (deformed) face". Compare the modern German adjective heilig meaning "holy, sacred" and the noun Fratze meaning "deformed face" as well as "grimace".

From Old English willa "will, desire" and gisl "pledge, hostage" (from gīslaz). A famous bearer includes Wilgils of Ripon, was a seventh century saint and hermit of Anglo-Saxon England, who was the father of St Willibrord.

Low German diminutive of names containing the name element vil meaning "wish", "desire".

Diminutive of William.A notable bearer is the German politician and expert on apportionment and voting systems Wilko Zicht.

The first element of this name is derived from Polish wilk "wolf", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic vьlkъ "wolf". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, this name roughly means "peaceful wolf".
Variant of Willodean. A notable bearer is Willadeene Parton, the oldest sibling of country singer Dolly Parton.
English variant of William and medieval Dutch variant of Willem.
A feminine form of William or a contraction of Wilhelmina.
Possibly an elaborated feminine form of Will.

Willanie is a female compound name. The "Will" is derived from "Willem" (German variant of William) which means determination and will. The "anie" is derived from the name Stephanie which means crown, victorious. It is an Afrikaans first name for females.
Spanish form of Willard, or transferred from surname Willardo.
Transferred use of the surname Willbanks. Commonly diminutized to Banks.
Derived from Old High German willo "will" and bero "bear".
Formed from the Germanic name element willo "will" and burg "castle, protection".
Dutch variant of Willibrord. A notable bearer of this name was the Dutch astronomer and mathematician Willebrord Snellius (1580-1626).
Latinized form of the Old German or Old English name Willehad.

Variant of Willehelm.In medieval German literature, this is the name of the eponymous character of the epic poem Willehalm (13th century) written by the German poet Wolfram von Eschenbach (died around 1220).
Possibly formed from elements which correspond to the Old High German words willo "will" and heri "host, army". Willehari was an Alemannic duke in the Ortenau in the early 8th century.
Benedictine monk, a disciple of St. Swithbert.
Old English form of William, derived from the Old English elements willa "will, desire" and helm "helmet, protection".
Diminutive of Willemijn. This name was borne by Dutch swimmer Willemijntje "Willy" den Ouden (1918-1997).
Feminine elaboration of Willie using the common name suffix lene, or perhaps a contraction of names such as Wilhelmina, Wilmadeene, and Willodean.
An enchanted parrot from Rigomer castle, owned by Queen Dionise. Dionise sent the bird to help Gawain find his way to the castle, which he was destined to conquer.

Archaic form of Willbert and Wilbert.

Derived from the Old English elements willa meaning "will, desire" and brord meaning "prick, point" as well as "spearhead" and "blade, lance, javelin".This name was most notably borne by the Anglo-Saxon saint Willibrord (c. 658-739). He is ultimately the reason behind the introduction of the name to the Low Countries.A notable Dutch bearer of the name was the journalist and television presenter Willibrord Frequin (1941-2022).
Latinized form of Willibrord. A known bearer of this name was the Indonesian dramatist and poet Willibrordus S. Rendra (1935-2009).

From Willigisus, the Latinized form of a Germanic name derived from the elements willo "will, desire" and gisal "pledge, hostage". This was the name of a 10th- and 11th-century German saint and archbishop of Mainz.
The name of a Benedictine abbot who is now a Catholic saint.

Transferred use of the surname Willman.
Variant of Wilmot, which in Cornwall survived the Middle Ages as a strictly feminine name.
Variant of Wilona. Willona Woods is a character from the 1970s TV show 'Good Times'.

The name Willowdeen is a girl's name with American origins, derived from the name William. It is a combination of the word "willow" referring to the tree, and the suffix "-deen," which can indicate a feminine form or a place. The name gained popularity in the 1920s.
Combination of Willow and Mae. According to the SSA, Willowmae was given to 5 girls in 2018.

A combination of Wilma and Dean. Wilma Dean "Deanie" Loomis is a main character of the 1961 movie Splendor in the Grass. Wilmadeene "Deenie" Fenner is the protagonist of the 1973 young adult novel Deenie by Judy Blume.

Either a combination of names beginning with Wil-, such as Wilma, Willem or Wilfredo, and Marie or a feminine form of Wilmar. Regarding usage in the Spanish Caribbean, it is mainly used in Puerto Rico.

However, it can also be a name in its own right, in which case its first element is derived from Old High German wîh meaning "holy, sacred" and its second element from Gothic nand meaning "bravery" (or from Gothic nanthjan meaning "to venture, to risk, to dare").Known bearers of this name include the Dutch geologist Winand Staring (1808-1877), the German composer Winand Nick (1831-1910) and the Polish long-distance runner Winand Osiński (1913-2006).

He is rumoured to have gained the the name as he was born durring a bushfire.

The first element of this Germanic name comes from Old High German wini "friend." The meaning and origin of the second element is rather uncertain: we know that it comes from gis (the original form was possibly gîs), but we don't exactly know where gis itself comes from. But there are a few possibilities. It might come from Gallo-Celtic gaiso "spear" (see Gaiseric) or it might be a short form of gisel, which means "hostage" or "pledge" (see Giselle).
Derived from Old High German wini "friend" combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy."

From the Maori name of Christmas orchids (Dendrobium cunninghamii), a type of orchid that is endemic to the New Zealand. This name could also be written as Te Winika, which means "the Christmas orchid".
Derived from Old High German wini "friend" combined with man "man."

Means "protective friend", derived from Old High German wini "friend" combined with Old High German mund "protection."
Derived from Old High German wini "friend" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."

Derived from Old High German wini "friend" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler."
Means "train, scourge" or "govern, administer" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit विनीत (vinīta).
Means "strong friend", derived from Old High German wini "friend" combined with þruþ "strength."
A diminutive for names starting with Wi-, such as William, Winifred or Winston.

On the Modena Archivolt, the name of a lady apparently held in a tower by a lord named Mardoc and his knight, Caradoc. Arthur and his knights, including Yder and Gawain, are embroiled in an attempt to rescue her.Her name is a variation of Guinloie or Guinevere, Arthur’s wife. “Guinloie” also belongs to Yder’s lover in the French romance of Yder.
Name of one of the characters in Tamora Pierce's books Trickster's Choice and Trickster's Queen.

In connection with the bird, the name "Winnard," possibly derived from the Cornish word for "redwing," can positively represent attributes associated with this bird. The redwing is a migratory bird known for its resilience, adaptability, and the beauty of its song. Thus, the name "Winnard" could symbolize qualities such as strength, flexibility, and a sense of aesthetic appreciation.
Perhaps intended to be a Latinate form of Winifred. It was borne by Winnaretta Singer (1865-1943), an American heiress.

The name of a dog in the children's novel Because of Winn-Dixie (2000) by Kate DiCamillo, as well as the 2005 movie adaptation. In the story, which is set in Florida, the dog is named after the Winn-Dixie chain of supermarkets.
The name is believed to originate from the Potawatomi language, meaning 'beautiful place"
Means "giver of spiritual gifts" from maka meaning "give" and namaka meaning "give food to him/her/it" in Paiute.
Diminutive of Winifred used in 18th- and 19th-century America.
Possibly a combination of Winnie and the suffix -ette, or transferred use of the surname Winnette.
Possibly a combination of Winifred and Jennifer, or a variant of Gwenhwyfar.

Old English form of Winwaloe, Gunwalloe or Guenole. A Breton name which means “he who is fair”.Saint Winnold was a 6th century Cornish saint. He was the son of a prince and a holy woman called Gwen who is supposed to have had three breasts as a sign of God’s favour (almost certainly a confusion with some local pagan deity).His family fled to Brittany to avoid the Saxons, and this is where he grew up. He founded an abbey, and his Rule was the standard one for monks until Saint Benedict.His feast day is the 3rd of March. According to English weather folklore, this day of the year is supposed to be especially windy, as seen in this piece of verse:“First comes DavidNext comes ChadThen comes Winnold, roaring like mad”.(St David’s Day is the first day of March and St Chad’s Day is the second day).
Variant of Winnoc or Winwaloe. Breton saint. Honored by several churches in Cornwall, England, probably the area of his missionary labors as part of the great evangelizing efforts of the era.
From wini meaning "friend" or wig meaning "battle, fight".
Probably after Lake Winola in Pennsylvania.
From Javanese winata meaning "virtuous", ultimately from Sanskrit विनत (vinata).
Possibly a diminutive of Winifred. Winry Rockbell is a character in the Full Metal Alchemist anime and manga, though in that case, the etymology is unknown.

From an English surname that was derived from places meaning "Wine's clearing" in Old English. (See the surname Winsley.)Known bearers of this name include Winsley Cedras, a Seychellois singer, and Georgie Winsley Cupidon (1981-), a Seychellois badminton player.
A variant of Winsley, itself likely derived from the surname Winsley meaning "one who lives on Wine's hill."

This name is best known for being the name of the Franco-Flemish abbess and saint Wivina of Groot-Bijgaarden (c. 1103-1170). She is known in modern French as Wivine de Grand-Bigard. After her lifetime, the usage of this name has mainly been in her honour.The meaning of her name is uncertain, but it is generally agreed that the name is at least partially of Germanic origin. According to French sources, the name is a compound name that consists of the Germanic elements witu meaning "forest" and wini meaning "friend". Meanwhile, Dutch sources derive the first element from Old Dutch wîf meaning "woman, wife", though in my opinion the obscure Germanic element found in Alavivus could also be a viable candidate. As for the second element: the Dutch sources neglect to explain it. However, in the case of the saint at least, it seems plausible that -ina is a latinization or variant of the Old French feminine diminutive suffix -ine. The saint's name would then be a diminutive of the original Germanic compound name.Finally, a Spanish source claims that the name is a Germanic adaptation of the Latin name Viviana. This option seems to be the least likely of all, for it appears to be based on nothing but the visual resemblance between the two names.

The name is made up from the poetic German word Woge "wave" and the name element lind "linden tree, lime; soft, flexible; shield (made of lime wood)".A Rhinemaiden, one of the three water-nymphs (Rheintöchter or "Rhine daughters") who appear in Richard Wagner's opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen, the others being Wellgunde and Flosshilde. Of the 34 characters in the Ring cycle, they are the only ones who did not originate in the Old Norse Eddas. Wagner created his Rhinemaidens from other legends and myths, most notably the Nibelungenlied which contains stories involving water sprites (nixies) or mermaids of the Danube. The Rhinemaidens are the first and the last characters seen in the four-opera cycle, appearing both in the opening scene of Das Rheingold, and in the final climactic spectacle of Götterdämmerung, when they rise from the Rhine waters to reclaim the ring from Brünnhilde's ashes.
