column12: From the name of a species of jasmine that produces small fragrant white flowers (scientific name Jasminum auriculatum), itself borrowed from Hindi जूही (juhi).
Means "to be sweet" in Bangi, the main lexical source of Lingala.
Alternate transcription of Bengali জুনায়েদ (see Junaid).
Malay and Indonesian variant of Junayda.
Means "moonlight, shine of the moon" in Urdu.

Feminine form of Zunair. Zunairah al-Rumiya ('the Roman') was a disciple (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad. She and her sister Umm Ubays converted to Islam while they were slaves in Mecca, and were persecuted for becoming Muslims, but were freed by Abu Bakr. Zunairah lost her eyesight due to being severely beaten by Abu Jahl; however, Muslim sources assert that she recovered fully by way of divine intervention after being emancipated.
Urdu alternate transcription of Zunaira as well as the Malay and Indonesian form.
Likely related to Aisha which means "living, alive" in Arabic.
Alternate transcription of Bengali জুনায়েদ (see Junaid).
Derived from beltz meaning "black" in Basque.
Possibly from zun, the Yiddish word for "son", with the diminutive suffix -el (ל).
Alternate transcription of Burmese ဇွန် (see Zun).
Alternate transcription of Urdu زنیرہ (see Zunaira).
Variation of the word 'Zoon' which means moon in Kashmiri
Of unknown meaning, possibly a form of the Arabic name ذو النون (Dhūl Nūn) through the Turkish forms, Zünnûn or Zun-Nûn.
From the Chinese 佐 (zuǒ) meaning "assist, aid" and 花 (huā) meaning "flower".
From Chinese 左 (zuǒ) "left, below, east" and 己 (jǐ) "self, oneself". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 佐 (zuǒ) meaning "assist, aid" and 兰 (lán) meaning "orchid".
From the Chinese 佐 (zuǒ) meaning "assist, aid" and 玲 (líng) meaning "tinkling of jade".
From the Chinese 佐 (zuǒ) meaning "assist, aid" and 琴 (qín) meaning "Chinese lute".
From the Chinese 佐 (zuǒ) meaning "assist, aid" and 琼 (qióng) meaning "jade, rare, precious".
From Chinese 作为 (zuòwéi) meaning "accomplishment, achievement". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From Chinese 祚 (zuò) meaning "blessing" or "throne" combined with 庥 (xiū) meaning "to protect, to shelter". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From Chinese 作 (zuò) meaning "to begin to grow, to start" and 义 (yì) meaning "justice".
Either from Persian زور (zur) meaning "force, strength, power" or a form of the Arabic name Zahra.
Form of Zurab with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Indonesian and Malay form of Zoraida.
Malay and Indonesian form of Zoraida.
Means "six" in Kalmyk, traditionally referring to a family's sixth-born child.
Short form of Zurab and its diminutives Zurikela and Zuriko.

Medieval Basque calque of Blanca and Blanche, derived from Basque zuri meaning "white". During the Middle Ages, this name was popular in all regions of the Basque Country. Although the form Zuriñe (created by Sabino Arana) is more common nowadays, Zuria has also been revived in modern times.

Diminutive of Zuriko, which in turn is a diminutive of Zurab. In other words: this name is a double diminutive of Zurab.In Georgian literature, Zurikela is the nickname of Zuriko, the central character of the book Granny, Iliko, Illarion, and I (1960) written by Nodar Dumbadze (1928-1984). A film based on the book was released in 1962.

Diminutive of Zurab. In Georgian literature, Zuriko is the name of the central character of the book Granny, Iliko, Illarion, and I (1960) written by Nodar Dumbadze (1928-1984). A film based on the book was released in 1962.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Zurishaddai. In Latin America it is unisex, though predominantly feminine.

Means "my rock is Shaddai" or "rock of Shaddai" in Hebrew, from the noun צוּר (tsur) meaning "rock" combined with the suffix י (i) (which together gives a meaning of either "my rock" or "rock of") and Shaddai being another name of God. In the Old Testament Zurishaddai was the father of Shelumiel, the prince of the Tribe of Simeon.
The primordial god in Persian religion, and the god of infinite time and space. Zurvan is the father of the good god Ahura Mazda and the evil god Angra Mainyu.
Variant of Zuri used predominately in Latin America.
Transferred use of the surname Zuse, borne by engineer Konrad Zuse, inventor of the first programmable computer, though it may also be a variant of Zeus. It was used in the 2010 film 'Tron: Legacy'.
Derived from the (slightly antiquated) Dutch noun zuster meaning "sister", which makes this name the modern form of the medieval name Suster.Also compare Sister and Syster.
Derived from Basque zutabe "pillar". This name is considered a direct translation of Spanish Pilar.
It is a Dalmatian dialectical form of the Venetian Zuana or a Croatian form of Junia.
Means "day; daylight; sun; sunlight" in Shona.
Meaning “sun”, it is also synonymous with Zuva.

column12: From Chinese 祖 (zǔ) meaning "grandfather; earliest ancestor, originator" combined with 贤 (xián) meaning "virtuous, worthy, wise". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 祖雁, 祖炎, 祖彦, 祖艳, 祖燕, 祖岩, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From 祖 (zǔ) meaning "ancestor, forebearer" and 雁 (yàn) meaning "wild goose", 炎 (yán) meaning "blaze, red, power", 彦 (yàn) meaning "elegant, handsome, learned", 艳 (yàn) meaning "beautiful, gorgeous", 燕 (yàn) meaning "swallow (bird)", or 岩 (yán) meaning "cliff, rocks". Other character combinations are also possible.

column12: From 祖 (zǔ) meaning "ancestor, forebearer" or 珠 (zū) meaning "pearl" combined with 颖 (yǐng) meaning "clever" or 英 (yīng) meaning "flower, petal, brave, hero" or 樱 (yīng) meaning "cherry blossom". Other character can form this name as well.
Derived from Basque zuzen "just; fair; righteous", this name is considered the Basque equivalent to French Justine and Spanish Justa.
Slovak diminutive of Zuzana, not used as a given name in its own right.
Diminutive of Zuzana and Zuzanna, or variant of Susie.
Diminutive of Susan, used in Frank Capra's film 'It's a Wonderful Life' (1946).
From the name elements звонъ (zvonŭ), meaning "sound, chime" and слава (slava), meaning "glory".
Derived from звезда (zvezda) meaning "star". In Russia, this name was used mostly during the Soviet era as a communist name referencing the red star.

The first element of this name is derived from Bulgarian zvezda "star", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic gvězda "star". Also compare Czech hvězda and Slovak hviezda, both of which mean "star". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". In other words, this name is the Bulgarian cognate of Hvězdomír.
Means "despise, look down upon" in Shona.
Alternate transcription of Hebrew צביקה (see Tzvika).
Croatian and Serbian form of Svinimir.

It is the plural of Chiyo. It means "grains". This is a name that symbolizes the smallness of grains which when planted and in their own season and time, grow and are harvested for multitudes and nations. It is a name of abundance.
Derived from dialectal Croatian zvizda meaning "star". The standard form is zvijezda or Serbian zvezda.

This was the name of the Lithuanian goddess of the hunt and the forest as well as the protector of wild animals who was first recorded in Russian chronicles of the 13th century. These documents mention that Žvoruna had the shape of a female dog, which is why her name was early on understood as being derived from žvėris "wild animal; game". However, her name has also been linked to Žvėrinė "evening star".There have been speculations that Žvoruna was in fact an epithet (or "euphemism") for the goddess of the hunt whose real name might be lost. For this reason some scholars argue that she might be identical with Medeinė, another goddess who was ascribed the exact same functions as Žvoruna.
Derived from the Germanic element swan "swan".
An Old German rendering of Svatopluk. Zwentibold was the name of a 9th-century Carolingian king of Lotharingia. It may also be interpreted as a variant of Swindebald.
Transferred use of the surname Zwingli as a given name, used in honor of the pastor Ulrich Zwingli (1484-1531), a leader of the Protestant Reformation in Switzerland.
Probably a variant of the name Zxavian influenced by the names Xavier, Xzavier and other names ending -avier (eɪ.vjəɹ) etc.
Alternate transcription of Arabic زياد (see Ziyad).
Combination of the popular phonetic elements zy (found in names such as Zion, Zyaire and Xylon), ya and na, perhaps modelled on Ayanna.
From Turkmen zyba meaning "beautiful" and Turkmen gözel meaning "beautiful, pretty, lovely".

The first element of this name is derived from Polish życie "life, existence, lifetime", which is derived from Polish żyć "to live, to be alive, to exist". Also compare Croatian živjeti and Czech žít, both of which mean "to live, to exist". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic slav "glory". As such, this name roughly means "to live gloriously".

The first element of this name is derived from Polish życie "life, existence, lifetime", which is derived from Polish żyć "to live, to be alive, to exist". Also compare Croatian živjeti and Czech žít, both of which mean "to live, to exist". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, this name roughly means "to live peacefully".
Possibly a combination of the phonetic element zy (cf. Zyaire, Zyana) and Elle.
Possibly used in reference to Zyeth Atham, or the eighth day of the bright half of Jyeshtha (May–June), a Brahmin festival. For example, the usage Bodhi.

The first element of this name is derived from the Lithuanian noun žygis meaning "march" as well as "hike, trip", which is ultimately derived from the Lithuanian verb žygiuoti meaning "to march, to parade" as well as "to hike". The second element is either derived from Lithuanian mantus meaning "intelligent" (see Daumantas) or from Lithuanian manta meaning "property, estate" as well as "wealth, riches, fortune".With that said, this Lithuanian name has sometimes been anglicized and/or germanized as Sigismund. Vice versa, that Germanic name (as well as its Polish form Zygmunt) has sometimes been lithuanized as Žygimantas, even though Sigismundas is the main Lithuanian form of Sigismund. In addition to all of this, Sigmund (which is a younger version of Sigismund) has almost always been lithuanized to Zigmantas, thus making Zigmantas the main Lithuanian form of Sigmund. As a result, the Lithuanian name Žygimantas is often confused with Zigmantas (and all other similar-looking Lithuanian forms of Sigmund and Sigismund).

Lithuanian form of Zygmunt, which is the Polish form of Sigmund. Also compare Zigmantas and Žygimantas.This name is very rarely used in Lithuania, which has most likely always been the case, because it is purely a lithuanized form of a foreign (in this case Polish) name, as in Lithuania foreign names tend to be lithuanized in order to make them easier to understand and pronounce to Lithuanian speakers.
Variant of Xyla, or simply a combination of the popular phonetic elements zy and la.
Possibly an invented name based on Silas.
Combination of the popular sounds zy and lee, probably influenced by names such as Kylie and Riley. Also compare Zyla.
Modern invention based on similar-sounding names such as Tyler, Skyler and Kyler.
Variant of Zilpah; also see Zilpha.
In the case of the Barbary corsair Zymen Danseker (c.1579-c.1611), it is an anglicized form of the Dutch name Siemen.
Variant of Zamir 1 resembling names like Tymir and Kymir.
Most likely a variant of Zamira.
Variant of Simon 1 primarily used in the Philippines.

Late medieval German form of Symphorian, possibly via its rare variant spelling Zymphorian.This name is not to be confused with the name Zyprian, which looks very similar but has an entirely different etymology.
Variant of Zinayida, overwhelmingly found in city Ismail with over 1/4 of bearers living there.
Variant of Zinoviy in Western Ukraine. 1/3 of bearers of this name live in Lviv.
Germanised spelling of Cynthia.As a given name mostly used in the Americas.
Contracted form of Sigwald or Sigbald.

Medieval German form of Cyprianus (see Cyprian), which is still in use today, albeit barely so. The name is more common as a patronymic surname.A known bearer of this name was Zyprian von Serntein (born around 1457, died in 1524), a chancellor for the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I.
Elaboration of Quan with the popular prefix Zy-.
Derived from żyr, an obsolete word meaning "prey", and the Slavic name element bor meaning "fight".
An invented name, blending the phonetic prefix zy and the name Tyrell.
Likely a combination of the phonetic elements zy and ren or a variant of Zyron.
Name of an Austrian monk. Germanised version of Cyril.
This can be a variant of Cyrine or transferred from the (originally Russian) surname Zyrina (feminine form of Zyrin).
A king once defeated in combat by Perceval in "Parzival" by Wolfram von Eschenbach, 1200–1210.
Possibly an invented name formed using the same sounds found in names such as Zion, Byron and Tyron.
Derived from the Slavic elements żyro meaning "endorsement" and slava meaning "fame, glory".
Combination of the prefix zy with Shawn.

Variant of Zyshawn. Some usage was generated in the late 1990s and early 2000s due to the fact that several media outlets wrongly identified this as the real name of American rapper Silkk the Shocker (1975-), for example he was called Zyshonne Miller by Jet magazine in May 1998 and by the Washington Post in September 2000. His real name is Vyshonne or Vyshonn Miller.
Polish Yiddish name, presumably related to Zysla. Found in documents from the early 1800s regarding contemporary Yiddish-speakers in Poland.
Russified form of Zöhrä. Zyugra (1946) is a ballet by Nazib Gayazovitch Zhiganov.

Coined by Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz for the titular character of one of his early works. It is uncertain where he found the inspiration for this name. One theory derives this name from Lithuanian žygiuoti "to move; to march" and viltis "hope", while other scholars believe this name to be a much-mangled form of Zizili, the name of an obscure fertility goddess of whom nothing else is known; should the name indeed be derived from Zizili, then its meaning would be lost. Yet another theory considers this name to be based on Żywie or Żywia.

The first element of this name is derived from Polish żywy "alive, living, lively" or żywot "life", both of which are ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic živъ "alive". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mil "gracious, dear".

The first element of this name is derived from Polish żywy "alive, living, lively" or żywot "life", both of which are ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic živъ "alive". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace". Also compare Życiomierz.
Derived from the Polish element żywy "alive, living, lively" or żywot "life" and the Slavic element slav "glory". Compare Życiesław.
Possibly a variant of the surname Zick, meaning "descendant of Sigo", or a diminutive of Isaac. It may also simply from the last three letters of the English alphabet (compare Abcde).
From the place name Zzyzx. According to the United States Social Security Administration's public name dataset, this name was given to 5 boys in both 2010 and 2018.
